Minnesota Cannabis & Hemp Research — Combined Parts 0–12

Run 1 (Parts 0–6) + Run 2 (Parts 7–12) · Original facts accessed 28 October 2026 · Last audited: 30 October 2026 · Single self-contained HTML file

Regulator: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management (OCM). Governing law: Minnesota Statutes Chapter 342; Minnesota Rules Chapter 9810. Run 1 standalone file: minnesota-cannabis-hemp-run1/minnesota-cannabis-hemp-run1-parts-0-6.html (untouched). Source reports: research_notes/minnesota-cannabis-hemp-run1-20261028/report.md (419,714 bytes) and research_notes/minnesota-cannabis-hemp-run2-20261028/report.md (681,815 bytes).

Read this first — Run 2 corrections to Run 1 (do not cite Run 1 alone on these points)

  • Dual cannabis + hemp holding — AUDIT RESOLVED (30 Oct 2026): “may hold.” Consolidated §342.43, subd. 2(d) reads: a person/cooperative/business holding an LPHE licence “may hold a cannabis business license,” and House Research, Laws 2026 ch. 123, §90, summarises it the same way (“Allows a person … that holds a hemp business license to also hold a cannabis license”), effective by default 1 Aug 2026. The “may not hold” text is the pre-ch. 123 2025 Supplement §342.43(d) and the as-introduced draft, not the enacted ch. 123 text; consolidated §342.44, subd. 2 likewise contains no “must not hold a cannabis licence” eligibility bar. The former highest-priority [VERIFY] is removed. Sources: §342.43, House Research ch. 123 Act Summary §90.
  • Seed-to-sale vendor RESOLVED: Metrc. Run 1 marked it [UNAVAILABLE]; Part 11 resolves it from OCM’s Inventory Management page.
  • Licence transfers: §342.12, not §§342.18/342.21. Social-equity licences: social-equity buyers only for 3 years, then any entity, with Division of Social Equity review + prior written OCM approval.
  • On-site consumption provision corrected: §342.245 is the 2026 general endorsements framework; the endorsements themselves are §342.28, subd. 10 (microbusiness), §342.46, subd. 8 (LPHE retailer), and §342.40, subd. 8 (events).
  • No per se THC driving limit — RESOLVED. §169A.20, subd. 1(7) “any amount” expressly excludes cannabis; cannabis is charged under the impairment clause, subd. 1(8).
  • DATWA exempt positions: §181.951, subd. 9 (7 categories). Delivery amount resolved: $5,000 per delivery route (Minn. R. 9810.2600).
  • Tribal instruments: 8 compacts + 1 cooperative agreement (Red Lake, 12 Dec 2025), not “9 compacts.” Dates are unchanged.
  • §342.57, subd. 5a notice CORRECTED: written notice “at the time” of action, not “14 days.”
  • Multifamily medical smoking QUALIFIED: §342.56, subd. 1(b) excepts medical use from the $250 fine on its text, but Court of Appeals OPa251279 (4 May 2026) holds it does not create a statutory right to smoke medical cannabis in multifamily housing.
  • LPHE cap — AUDIT CORRECTION (30 Oct 2026): the 50 mg/package cap SURVIVES. Laws 2026, ch. 123, §4 amended only the definition in §342.01, subd. 50 (adding serving-level CBD/CBG/CBN/CBC figures of 100 mg each / 400 mg combined, and the 20:1 artificially-derived-cannabinoid ratio in subd. 50(b)(1)(iii), alongside the unchanged 5 mg delta-9/serving non-beverage and 10 mg delta-9/container beverage figures). It did not repeal the packaging cap in §342.62, subd. 2(f)(1): a multi-serving non-beverage LPHE package is still capped at 50 mg delta-9 THC. The Part 1 §1.5.2 packaging table (5 mg/50 mg; single beverage 10 mg; multi-serving beverage ≥750 mL, ≤5 mg/serving, ≤17 servings; CBD etc. 1,000 mg each per non-beverage package, 200 mg each per single beverage, 400 mg per multi-serving beverage) is therefore correct and stands. The earlier Run 2 claim that ch. 123 removed the 50 mg cap is deleted wherever it appears. Sources: §342.01, §342.62, OCM LPHE consumer page (still states 5 mg/serving / 50 mg/package).
  • Expungement counts must never be summed across tracks. Automatic track: 57,780 records sealed in May 2024. Board (felony) track, through Aug 2026: 13,062 preliminarily reviewed, 731 Board-voted, 676 court expungement orders.
  • Still unresolved / unavailable: no single open-store count; supply-chain merger date (1 Aug 2026 vs 1 Jan 2027); testing-facility roster as an official roster (count 5 corroborated, names/scopes secondary only); OCM holder-download link/file name and MDA holders canonical URL (not verified, do not guess); tribal medical as “state-licensed” for Schedule III/280E; federal combination-business cost allocation; tribal tax-sharing percentages; aggregate tribal sales (the $250m+ first-year and $45.6m tax figures are state-licensed only).
  • Federal baseline (fixed, not re-researched): medical marijuana Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; 280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical only; hemp PL 119-37 §781 eff. 12 Nov 2026, limited by PL 119-103 §2019 until 11 Dec 202626, after which the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-lab enforcement delayed to 31 Dec 2026; federal medical appropriations rider through 11 Dec 2026; no federal cannabis banking law.

AUDIT — Independent fact-check, 30 October 2026 (read before citing the report below)

Last audited: 30 October 2026. This audit was done by a separate pass from the original writers, against primary sources only: Minnesota Statutes (including Chapter 342), session laws and bill pages on revisor.mn.gov and leg.mn.gov, Minnesota Rules and the State Register, the Office of Cannabis Management (OCM), the Department of Health (historic medical programme), the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Revenue, the Office of Administrative Hearings, the BCA and the Cannabis Expungement Board, court records, official tribal government sources and compact texts, and official county/city codes. News, law-firm blogs, trade press and AI summaries were not used to confirm anything; where only a secondary source exists the claim is marked Unverified below.

Federal baseline — applied as given, not re-audited. Scheduling is split: under a final rule at 91 FR 22714 (effective 28 April 2026), FDA-approved cannabis products and state-licensed medical marijuana are Schedule III; all other marijuana, including all adult-use, remains Schedule I; the broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is NOT final. IRS 280E relief follows that split (Treasury: rescheduling generally removes 280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances, guidance forthcoming); adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: Public Law 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but Public Law 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesised; the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA has delayed enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement until 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted. Any statement in the original report contradicting this baseline has been corrected to match it in the rewrite below. In particular: Schedule III and 280E relief are applied to medical activity only (combination/macrobusinesses must split medical and adult-use activity; no shared-cost allocation method was located — [VERIFY]); all adult-use activity is treated as Schedule I; tribal medical is not presented as “state-licensed” for Schedule III/280E without federal guidance — that question stays [VERIFY] (see audit row, Part 10); and Minnesota's lower-potency hemp market is explained on the correct federal timeline (12 Nov interim window, full definition/cap only after 11 Dec, DEA-lab delay is testing relief only).

How to read the counts in this file (do not mix units). “Licensed businesses” (369, September 2026 OCM one-year snapshot) ≠ “licences issued” (392, Market Monitor extraction, data through 25 September 2026, extracted 1 October 2026) ≠ “retail sites” (223 adult-use sites in that extraction, including micro/mezzo/other retail-authorised types; only 18 licences classified specifically as retail) ≠ “open stores” (no OCM open-store count was located). The most authoritative holder-level source is the OCM Summary Application Data workbook dated 26 October 2026 (file MN_OCM_licensed_businesses_10262026_tcm1202-714418.xlsx via OCM Summary Application Data); its spreadsheet contents could not be text-extracted in this audit, so no workbook total is asserted in this file — open the .xlsx directly before republication. The Cannabis Market Monitor is an interactive Power BI dashboard, not a download file. Expungement tracks must never be summed (see Part 12 row).

Verdict counts (this table only): 67 rows — 42 Confirmed, 19 Corrected, 1 Removed, 5 Unverified. “Corrected” means the rewrite below uses the corrected wording everywhere that claim appears (including in Research Notes, where superseded Run 1/Run 2 claims are now annotated as superseded rather than left standing). “Removed” means the claim is deleted as a current rule, not merely reworded. Every other section and detail of the original is preserved unchanged except where a row below changes it.

RUN 1 — PARTS 0–6

PART 0 — HEADLINES: MINNESOTA CANNABIS & HEMP

As of 28 October 2026. Regulator: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management (OCM). Governing law: Minnesota Statutes chapter 342; rules: Minnesota Rules chapter 9810. All Minnesota references are to Minnesota, not to same-named places in other states.

At a glance

Measure Figure Date / basis
State-licensed adult-use sales began 16 September 2025 First state-licensed stores, not tribal-only sales
Combined adult-use + medical sales, first year More than $250 million — about $150 million adult-use, about $100 million medical OCM one-year update, 15 September 2026
Cannabis + lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) tax revenue $45.6 million September 2025–July 2026, latest Department of Revenue figures available to OCM at that date
Licensed cannabis businesses 369 at 15 September 2026; 392 licences in the next Market Monitor extraction (data through 25 September, extracted 1 October 2026) Licences issued, not open stores
Licensed adult-use retail sites 223; medical retail sites 48 Market Monitor extraction through 25 September 2026
Registered medical patients More than 59,000 at launch (September 2025); more than 90,000 by September 2026 OCM launch release and one-year reporting
Tribal agreements 9 of Minnesota’s 11 federally recognised Tribal Nations Compacts / cooperative agreements completed

1. Adult-use rollout: a year in, still converting licences into open stores

  • Tribal sales came first. Several Tribal Nations began opening adult-use and medical dispensaries on Tribally owned land beginning in August 2023, after the original cannabis bill passed. The first Tribal-state compact, with White Earth Nation, was finalised in May 2025 and established a framework for dispensaries in Moorhead and St. Cloud, Minnesota. — OCM launch release (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • State-licensed adult-use sales began 16 September 2025. The launch ran through the two existing medical providers under new medical cannabis combination business licences: all eight Green Goods dispensaries (Minneapolis, Blaine, Bloomington, Burnsville, Duluth, Moorhead, Rochester, and Woodbury, Minnesota) opened adult-use sales that morning, with RISE dispensaries in Brooklyn Park, Eagan, Mankato, New Hope and Willmar, Minnesota, following, plus a first Tribally grown sale through licensed Duluth microbusiness Legacy Cannabis in partnership with White Earth Nation. — OCM launch release (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • First-year sales passed $250 million. OCM’s 15 September 2026 one-year update attributes about $150 million to adult-use and about $100 million to medical cannabis since state-licensed sales began 16 September 2025. The $45.6 million tax figure for September 2025–July 2026 is not the tax on that $250 million alone: it combines cannabis and LPHE sales, and LPHE sales are not required to pass through the state’s seed-to-sale tracking system, so no LPHE sales total is published on that basis. — OCM one-year reporting (Accessed 2026-10-28); OCM newsletter summary (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Monthly sales were still rising into summer 2026, on dashboard data. OCM Market Monitor figures reported secondarily show combined adult-use + medical sales of $27.55 million in July 2026 ($17.53 million adult-use, $10.01 million medical) and $27.88 million in August 2026 ($18.42 million adult-use, $9.46 million medical). September 2026 monthly sales were not yet published in the extracts reviewed. — Market Monitor extracts, September 2026 report (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Licences ≠ open stores — the key reading warning for Part 0. In the extraction with data through 25 September 2026, OCM reported 392 business licences issued, of which 172 (44%) were held by social-equity-classified applicants, but only 18 licences were classified specifically as retail; the 223 adult-use retail sites figure is higher because microbusinesses, mezzobusinesses and other licence types can also be authorised for retail. The same extraction lists 168 cultivation sites, 57 manufacturing sites, 9 transporting sites and 5 testing sites. — Market Monitor reporting, 5 October 2026 (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Supply expanded sharply in summer 2026, but plants are not yet product. OCM’s one-year summary reports 95 newly licensed cultivators in June–August 2026 and tracked plant inventory rising from 72,083 plants in 2025 to 486,720 plants, with nearly three-quarters of cultivation-authorised holders being microbusinesses. Harvest, testing and manufacturing capacity — not plant counts — will determine shelf availability. — OCM one-year reporting (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Testing was the 2026 bottleneck. OCM paused Legend Technical Services’ cannabis testing authorisation in May 2026 after launch-era variances expired and outstanding security/testing requirements remained; the lab returned hundreds of samples (reported as more than 400) and then exited cannabis and hemp testing in June 2026. Secondary reporting puts OCM’s licensed testing-facility count at five by autumn 2026, with only two authorised for a full compliance panel — a capacity split that should be confirmed against the live OCM list in Parts 1–6 [VERIFY]. — Legend closure reporting (Accessed 2026-10-28); Testing-capacity analysis, September 2026 (Accessed 2026-10-28)

2. Licences and lotteries: no new capped lottery in 2026

  • The lotteries that matter were in 2025, not 2026. Capped cultivator, manufacturer, mezzobusiness and social-equity retailer selections were drawn 5 June 2025; the general retailer lottery followed 22 July 2025, selecting 75 applicants from a pool of 569 (288 general, 281 social-equity applicants not selected on 5 June). There was no 5 June 2026 lottery — that date in 2026 was an OCM community listening session in Duluth, Minnesota. — Q3 2026 market report (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Capped categories remain closed, with a hard pipeline deadline. No application window was open for the capped types at the time of reporting, and no next window had been scheduled; qualified-applicant status earned before 1 June 2026 lapses 1 January 2027. The capped pools to 1 July 2027 are, per pool (social-equity and general each): cultivation 25, manufacturing 12, retail 75, mezzobusiness 50. At 15 September 2026, verified social-equity owners held 43% of Minnesota’s 369 licensed cannabis businesses. — Social-equity guide, citing OCM one-year update and Minn. Stat. § 342.14 (Accessed 2026-10-28); Q3 2026 market report (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Pipeline still large. An OCM application table dated 12 October 2026, reported secondarily, showed 402 licences issued, 1,214 preliminary approvals and 3,541 applicants across all cannabis licence types. These are preliminary figures that change as preliminary approvals convert — or lapse. — OCM application-table reporting, 12 October 2026 (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Municipal retail is real but tiny. Anoka, Minnesota, opened the state’s first city-owned dispensary with a ribbon-cutting 5 February 2026 and sales from 6 February 2026 (AUDIT CORRECTION — do not collapse to a single “opened 5 February” date); Osseo, Minnesota, had broken ground but was not open at the time of reporting. Municipal applicants numbered 13, with 8 preliminarily approved and 1 issued in OCM tables dated 14 September 2026. — Municipal-retail reporting (Accessed 2026-10-28)

3. Litigation: historic lottery litigation resolved; no new 2026 OCM lottery case found

  • Preapproval lottery stay and abandonment (2024). A Ramsey County District Court judge stayed the cannabis licence preapproval lottery originally scheduled for 26 November 2024; OCM then ended the preapproval process and moved to a standard licensing cycle for both social-equity and general applicants beginning early the following year. — OCM news release on next steps after the stay (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • April–June 2025 court outcomes. A Minnesota district court found in April 2025 that OCM had unlawfully broken a statutory duty by cancelling the preapproval lottery; on 2 June 2025 the Minnesota Court of Appeals dissolved the stay and denied a prohibition petition by qualified applicants, holding they had not shown the district court exceeded its authority in enjoining the lottery. OCM then proceeded with the standard June/July 2025 lotteries above. — Court of Appeals decision, A24-1936 (Accessed 2026-10-28); Q3 2026 legal summary (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • No new 2026 lottery injunction was located. A 2026 federal case found in searching (Perry, D. Minn., order 23 June 2026) concerns a city’s home-occupation ordinance and a cannabis applicant’s zoning dispute, not an OCM lottery. An industry-coalition report of a court order barring OCM from enforcing a direct-to-consumer hemp sales ban without rulemaking could not be verified against a court record in this Part 0 window [VERIFY] — do not cite it as settled law. — Federal order, Case No. 0:25-cv-03352 (Accessed 2026-10-28)

4. OCM rules and the 2026 omnibus: the biggest structural change since 2023

  • Base rules are in effect. Minnesota’s adult-use cannabis rules were approved by an administrative law judge on 2 April 2025 and published in the Minnesota State Register on 14 April 2025, as Minnesota Rules chapter 9810. — OCM rules page (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • 2026 omnibus (SF 4401, Laws 2026, chapter 123), signed 26 May 2026; most provisions effective 1 August 2026. It creates a new macrobusiness licence effective 1 January 2027, capped at eight through 2030, replacing the medical cannabis combination business licence; it merges the previously separate medical and adult-use supply chains into a single seed-to-sale system; it allows a business to hold a hemp licence and a cannabis licence simultaneously (previously prohibited); and it allows a single investor to hold up to 33% controlling ownership in up to four social-equity businesses. The exact effective date of the supply-chain merger itself is stated differently across secondary summaries (1 August 2026 vs 1 January 2027) [VERIFY against the chapter 123 text in Parts 1–6]. — Q3 2026 market report (Accessed 2026-10-28); 2026 omnibus operator summary (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • What the omnibus does not do: it does not create a new capped-licence round before 1 July 2027, and it does not change adult possession limits (21+: 2 oz flower in public, 2 lb at home, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg THC in edibles in public) or home-grow limits (up to 8 plants per residence, no more than 4 mature/flowering, enclosed locked space) as reported in secondary summaries [VERIFY against chapter 342 in Parts 1–6]. — 2026 omnibus consumer guide (Accessed 2026-10-28)

5. Tax: 15% + sales tax for adult-use; medical exempt; no new 2026 rate change found

  • Adult-use rate (unchanged in 2026): 15% cannabis gross receipts tax on retail sales of taxable cannabis products, raised from 10% for sales after 30 June 2025, plus 6.875% state general sales tax and any applicable local sales tax where the transaction takes place — a minimum combined state rate of 21.875% before local tax. No cannabis-only local tax is permitted, and the former local cannabis aid programme was eliminated from 2026. — OCM tribal-compacts page, taxation section (Accessed 2026-10-28); Q3 2026 market report (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Medical cannabis is exempt from both the 15% gross receipts tax and state sales tax when sold to a patient enrolled in the state medical registry by a business with a medical retail endorsement; sales to tribal-programme patients and visiting patients are reported as not exempt [VERIFY the visiting/tribal-patient boundary in Parts 1–6]. LPHE products pay the same 15% cannabis tax plus sales tax as adult-use. — Minnesota tax guide, citing Department of Revenue sales guide updated 11 June 2026 (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Off-reservation tribal sales are taxed like state sales. OCM states that sales of cannabis products off Tribal lands are subject to all state and local taxes (15% + 6.875% + local), with each Tribal Nation able to enter a separate cannabis tax agreement with the Department of Revenue for payments related to production/supply and taxes paid by Tribal members at that location. — OCM tribal-compacts page (Accessed 2026-10-28)

6. Tribal compacts: 9 of 11 Nations; up to 8 off-reservation stores each

  • First compact: White Earth Nation, 20 May 2025. OCM’s compacts page confirms the state has completed negotiations with nine of the 11 federally recognised Tribal Nations sharing territory with Minnesota, and that each accord is unique, with Tribal regulatory agencies licensing Tribal enterprises to standards meeting or exceeding OCM’s. Tribal Nations with negotiated off-reservation activities may open up to eight off-reservation retail locations each, following non-cannabis-specific local ordinances (zoning, land use, setbacks) and chapter 342 operating-hours limits. — OCM compacts page (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Other completed accords reported on the OCM list include Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe (10 September 2025), Prairie Island Indian Community and Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa (20 October 2025), Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe (30 October 2025), Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians cooperative agreement (12 December 2025), Bois Forte Band (18 December 2025), Lower Sioux Indian Community (9 March 2026) and Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community (10 March 2026) — dates taken from the OCM compacts list as returned in search; the live OCM page text opened for this part did not reproduce the dated list, so re-confirm each date against the signed compact PDF in Parts 1–6 [VERIFY]. — OCM compacts list (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Tribal product must still be tested and tracked into the state market: testing at state-licensed labs for potency, stability, homogeneity and contaminants, plus seed-to-sale entry when product moves off Tribal lands, and state packaging/labelling including the universal cannabis symbol. — OCM compacts page (Accessed 2026-10-28)

7. Federal Schedule III / 280E — medical only, and the combination-business trap

Per the fixed federal baseline for this project (not re-researched here): state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS § 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use.

  • Medical sales get the federal relief; adult-use sales do not. A Minnesota medical sale to a registered patient through OCM’s Division of Medical Cannabis is Schedule III activity for 280E purposes; the same product sold to a 21+ adult-use customer at the same counter is Schedule I activity and remains subject to full 280E disallowance. Schedule III does not legalise cannabis federally, does not authorise interstate commerce, and does not cover the adult-use market. — Federal-baseline application, Minnesota summary (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Medical cannabis combination businesses (and, from 1 January 2027, macrobusinesses) therefore run two federal tax regimes in one business. Green Goods and RISE — the two original medical providers that opened adult-use sales in September 2025 — must split revenue and, critically, shared costs (rent, payroll, marketing, overhead) between the medical (deductible) and adult-use (280E-disallowed) sides. No OCM or IRS default allocation method for Minnesota combination businesses was located in this Part 0 window [UNAVAILABLE]; operators should not assume a pro-rata-by-sales split is safe without tax advice. — OCM launch release, combination licences (Accessed 2026-10-28); Minnesota cannabis accounting analysis (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Minnesota state-level 280E conformity is CONFLICTED — do not publish a single answer yet [VERIFY]. One secondary tax analysis states Minnesota decoupled from federal § 280E for medical manufacturers from tax year 2019 and for all licensed cannabis and hemp businesses under HF 100 from tax year 2023; another Q3 2026 summary states both that Minnesota “lets licensed cannabis and hemp businesses subtract 280E-disallowed expenses on the state return (tax years 2023 and later)” and that Minnesota “has not enacted its own state-level 280E decoupling statute.” The Department of Revenue position must be confirmed from an official source in Parts 1–6 before any state-tax claim is made. — Minnesota cannabis accounting analysis (Accessed 2026-10-28); Q3 2026 legal summary (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Medical demand did not collapse after adult-use launch — it grew. The registry rose from just over 41,000 patients before the 2023 fee elimination and 2024 eligibility expansion, to more than 59,000 at adult-use launch (September 2025), to more than 90,000 by September 2026, with about $100 million in first-year medical sales. The tax exemption (gross receipts — see tax section; sales-tax exemption remains [VERIFY]), 18+ access (vs 21+ adult-use) and pharmacist consultation are the retained medical advantages. AUDIT CORRECTION: there is no 90-day (or 30-day/monthly) purchase cap in current §342.51; the operative patient rule is §342.09, subd. 1(d) (adult-use possession limits do not apply to a registry patient possessing patient-labelled product). Any “90-day supply” limit elsewhere in this file is deleted. — OCM launch release (Accessed 2026-10-28); Medical-program growth reporting, September 2026 (Accessed 2026-10-28)

8. Lower-potency hemp: Minnesota’s flagship market, facing the federal cliff — but state law has not changed

  • Minnesota built the country’s most open low-dose hemp market. LPHE products — hemp-derived THC edibles, beverages and tinctures — are sold in liquor stores, bars, restaurants, co-ops and general retail, not only in dispensaries. The historic state limits are 5 mg of any THC per serving and 50 mg total THC per package for edibles, and AUDIT CORRECTION — the 2-serving/container rule is NOT the LPHE rule. LPHE beverages: single-serving container ≤10 mg delta-9 (§342.62, subd. 2(g)(1)); multi-serving resealable beverage ≥750 mL, ≤5 mg/serving, ≤17 servings (§342.62, subd. 2(i)). The 2-serving/container (20 mg) rule is the adult-use beverage rule (§342.27, subd. 2(e)) and the ratio-product rule (§342.01, subd. 63a(d)); the 2026 omnibus raised some food/beverage caps and created a new “ratio hemp-infused cannabis product” category, but the precise post-omnibus beverage/container limits must be confirmed against chapter 342 as amended [VERIFY]. — Q3 2026 legal summary (Accessed 2026-10-28); 2026 omnibus operator summary (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Registration → licensure cutover completed 31 March / 1 April 2026. LPHE regulation moved from Minnesota Department of Health registration under former Minn. Stat. § 151.72 to full OCM licensing under chapter 342; the MDH paradigm sunset 31 March 2026, with OCM LPHE applications taken in October 2025. By 31 August 2026, OCM licensing data reported secondarily showed 2,005 LPHE licences: 1,887 retailer, 68 manufacturer, 50 wholesaler. Hemp-derived consumer products (vapes, flower) are not LPHE products and are available only under cannabis licences. — Minnesota hemp roundup, April 2026 (Accessed 2026-10-28); August 2026 market report, OCM licensing data (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Scale at risk: an estimated $180–210 million market (secondary estimate, May 2026, not an OCM figure). That range is the only published size estimate located; OCM itself states LPHE sales figures are not available because LPHE sales are not tracked in seed-to-sale. Do not present $180–210 million as an official total. — OCM legislative-proposal analysis, 5 May 2026 (Accessed 2026-10-28); OCM newsletter, LPHE sales not tracked (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Federal dates (per project baseline, confirmed by OCM): PL 119-37 § 781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 § 2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. OCM’s updated guidance (originally 31 August, updated for the new date) states the federal change “effectively bans hemp products containing more than 0.4 milligrams (mg) of THC per package” and will take effect 11 December 2026 unless other federal action occurs. — OCM federal hemp changes page, opened directly (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • Minnesota’s state response — guidance, not a change in state law. OCM states explicitly: “This federal definition change does not change how Minnesota law defines lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) products and LPHE retailers, manufacturers and wholesalers or the legality of those products in the state.” LPHEs are defined in Minn. Stat. § 342.01, subd. 50, and Minnesota’s LPHE definitions “will not change after the federal definition changes on Dec. 11, 2026.” But many Minnesota-compliant products (e.g. any package over 0.4 mg THC — i.e. essentially every current LPHE edible and beverage) “will become federally noncompliant,” with particular risk for import/export endorsement holders, who must ensure imported product complies with both Minnesota and federal law. OCM also notes federal bills to watch (Lawful Hemp Protection Act; Beverage Regulatory Parity Act) — neither had received a vote in either chamber at the time of the guidance — and convened a hemp industry forum in late September 2026. — OCM federal hemp changes page, opened directly (Accessed 2026-10-28)
  • No Minnesota legislative fix to the LPHE definition was found as of 28 October 2026 [UNAVAILABLE]. The only state-law bridge located is the 2026 omnibus removal of the ban on holding hemp and cannabis licences simultaneously, plus OCM’s stated options for LPHE holders ahead of renewal: renew, surrender (including conditional surrender to a new entity), let the licence expire, or enter the adult-use market — while noting there is no currently open cannabis licence application window. Whether Minnesota will defend, amend or let LPHE products go federally noncompliant after 11 December 2026, and what federal enforcement posture will actually follow, are open questions. — OCM federal hemp changes page, opened directly (Accessed 2026-10-28)

PART 1: LAWS

Scope note. Part 1 only. Statutes/regulations in force as read on official Minnesota sources. Every fact carries official source link and “Accessed 2026-10-28”. Where page could not be opened in full, or last-amended date / final bill status could not be confirmed on official page, fact flagged [VERIFY] or [UNAVAILABLE] and not presented as settled law. No secondary summary, news, law-firm blog or AI summary used as authority for law; secondary sources used only where expressly labelled, for non-law facts.

Federal baseline applied, not re-researched: Split scheduling — state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; 2024 rescheduling proposal not final. IRS §280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 Nov 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 Dec 2026; after 11 Dec 2026 full total-THC hemp definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp delayed to 31 Dec 2026. Federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 Dec 2026. No federal cannabis banking law. Any Minnesota text appearing to contradict baseline flagged, not silently harmonised.

1.1 Legal status — what is legal, for whom, and where

1.1.1 Both medical and adult-use legal under Minnesota state law

  • Medical cannabis existed since 2014, originally under Minn. Stat. §§ 152.22–152.37, now administered under Minn. Stat. Chapter 342, §§ 342.51–342.60. Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.02, subd. 3 (transfer of §§ 152.22–152.37 powers from Department of Health to Office of Cannabis Management) — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.02 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Adult-use cannabis became legal for possession, use and home grow on 1 August 2023 under 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 63 (HF 100). Source: Minnesota House, “New Laws” summary — “Beginning Aug. 1, 2023, personal possession of up to 2 pounds of marijuana is no longer a crime” and “HF100*/SF73/CH63” — https://house.mn.gov/NewLaws/story/2023/5516 — Accessed 2026-10-28; Governor’s signing release — “Chapter 63, House File 100 legalizes adult-use cannabis” — https://mn.gov/governor/newsroom/press-releases/?id=1055-579413 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • OCM states same effective date: “Effective Aug. 1, 2023, full decriminalization allows the possession, use, and home grow of cannabis in Minnesota for people 21 and older.” Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/consumers/adult-use/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Licensed adult-use retail sales are separate step from legal possession. Possession/use/home grow legal from 1 Aug 2023; state-licensed non-tribal retail sales did not open until 2025. Tribal dispensaries opened earlier on tribal land under tribal regulation and later state-tribal compacts. Do not conflate “legal to possess since 2023” with “legal to buy at state-licensed store since 2023.”

1.1.2 Exactly what is legal for adult 21+ — verbatim operative text

Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(a) provides, verbatim:

“An individual 21 years of age or older may: (1) use, possess, or transport cannabis paraphernalia; (2) possess or transport two ounces or less of adult-use cannabis flower in a public place; (3) possess two pounds or less of adult-use cannabis flower in the individual’s private residence; (4) possess or transport eight grams or less of adult-use cannabis concentrate; (5) possess or transport edible cannabis products or lower-potency hemp edibles infused with a combined total of 800 milligrams or less of tetrahydrocannabinol; (6) give for no remuneration to an individual who is at least 21 years of age: (i) two ounces or less of adult-use cannabis flower; (ii) eight grams or less of adult-use cannabis concentrate; or (iii) an edible cannabis product or lower-potency hemp edible infused with 800 milligrams or less of tetrahydrocannabinol; and (7) use adult-use cannabis flower and adult-use cannabis products in the following locations: (i) a private residence, including the individual’s curtilage or yard; (ii) on private property, not generally accessible by the public, unless the individual is explicitly prohibited from consuming cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products on the property by the owner of the property; or (iii) on the premises of an establishment or event licensed to permit on-site consumption.”

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Activity (adult 21+) Legal? Limit / condition
Possess/transport paraphernalia Yes §342.09, subd. 1(a)(1)
Possess/transport flower in public Yes ≤2 ounces
Possess flower at private residence Yes ≤2 pounds
Possess/transport concentrate Yes ≤8 grams
Possess/transport edibles (cannabis + lower-potency hemp combined) Yes ≤800 mg total THC combined
Gift, no payment, to another adult 21+ Yes Same public limits: ≤2 oz flower / ≤8 g concentrate / ≤800 mg THC edibles
Use at private residence incl. curtilage/yard Yes §342.09, subd. 1(a)(7)(i)
Use on private property not generally accessible to public Yes, unless owner explicitly prohibits §342.09, subd. 1(a)(7)(ii)

1.1.3 What is NOT legal — prohibitions in same section

Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(b) provides, verbatim in substance (clauses (1)–(9)):

“Except as provided in paragraph (c), an individual may not: (1) use, possess, or transport cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products if the individual is under 21 years of age; (2) use [them] in a motor vehicle as defined in section 169A.03, subdivision 15; (3) use [them] in a manner that involves the inhalation of smoke, aerosol, or vapor at any location where smoking is prohibited under section 144.414; (4) use or possess [them] in a public school, as defined in section 120A.05, subdivisions 9, 11, and 13, or in a charter school governed by chapter 124E, including all facilities, whether owned, rented, or leased, and all vehicles that a school district owns, leases, rents, contracts for, or controls; (5) use or possess [them] in a state correctional facility; (6) operate a motor vehicle while under the influence of [them]; (7) give for no remuneration [them] to an individual under 21 years of age; (8) give for no remuneration cannabis flower or cannabis products as a sample or promotional gift if the giver is in the business of selling goods or services; or (9) vaporize or smoke [them] in any location where the smoke, aerosol, or vapor would be inhaled by a minor.”

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Medical carve-out — §342.09, subd. 1(c): “The prohibitions under paragraph (b), clauses (1) to (4), do not apply to use other than by smoking or by a vaporized delivery method, possession, or transportation of medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products by a patient; a registered designated caregiver; or a parent, legal guardian, or spouse of a patient.” Source: same link — Accessed 2026-10-28. Carve-out expressly limited to non-smoked/non-vaporized use for clauses (1)–(4); does not authorise smoking/vaping in vehicle, school or correctional facility, and does not lift driving-under-influence ban in clause (6).

Possession limits do not apply to registry patients with patient-specific labelling — §342.09, subd. 1(d): “The possession limits in paragraph (a), clauses (2) to (5), do not apply to a person enrolled in the medical cannabis patient registry program under section 342.52 if the person possesses cannabis flower or cannabinoid products that include patient-specific labeling according to sections 342.51, subdivision 2, and 342.63, subdivision 4.” Source: same link — Accessed 2026-10-28. Adult-use 2 oz / 2 lb / 8 g / 800 mg ceilings therefore do not cap registry patient holding properly patient-labelled medical product. Whether separate medical purchase/possession ceiling exists in rule is [VERIFY] — no numeric medical possession cap located in §§342.51–342.52 as opened.

Public use — general rule: No general right to use cannabis in public place. Use authorised only in three locations in §342.09, subd. 1(a)(7). OCM consumer page restates: cannabis “can be used by people 21 and older on private property (unless owner prohibits use…), private residences and at places with approved licenses or an event permit” and “cannot be used when operating a motor vehicle or operating heavy machinery and where smoking and vaping are prohibited under the Minnesota Clean Indoor Air Act,” and cannot be used or possessed in public/charter schools and school buses, state correctional facilities, where smoke/aerosol/vapor could be inhaled by minor, on federal property, in federally subsidised housing, or on employer’s premises / operating employer’s vehicle, machinery or equipment. Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/consumers/adult-use/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Local ordinances may further prohibit smoking/vaping in public places — OCM note on same page. Local public-use petty-misdemeanour ordinance power was in original 2023 act (Art. 4, §19, Minn. Stat. §152.0263, subd. 5, as cited in county ordinance summary) — exact current text of §152.0263 [VERIFY]; not opened directly in this window.

[VERIFY] whether Revisor’s online Chapter 342 already reflects 1 Jan 2027 language ahead of effective date; chapter page as read lists §342.295 as “CANNABIS MACROBUSINESSES” and §342.515 as “[Renumbered 342.295]” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.2.3 Key cross-cutting Chapter 342 provisions (verbatim)

OCM creation and mandate — §342.02, subd. 1: “The Office of Cannabis Management is created with the powers and duties established by law. In making rules, establishing policy, and exercising its regulatory authority over the cannabis industry and hemp consumer industry, the office must: (1) promote the public health and welfare; (2) protect public safety; (3) eliminate the illicit market for cannabis flower and cannabis products; (4) meet the market demand for cannabis flower and cannabis products; (5) promote a craft industry for cannabis flower and cannabis products; and (6) prioritize growth and recovery in communities that have experienced a disproportionate, negative impact from cannabis prohibition.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.02 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

OCM potency authority — §342.02, subd. 2(a)(17) and subd. 2(b): OCM may “establish limits on the potency of cannabis flower and cannabis products that can be sold to customers by licensed cannabis retailers, licensed cannabis microbusinesses, and licensed cannabis mezzobusinesses with an endorsement to sell cannabis flower and cannabis products to customers” and, “until January 1, 2027,” has additional powers in subd. 2(b) including establishing adult-use potency limits. Source: same link — Accessed 2026-10-28. 1 Jan 2027 sunset in subd. 2(b) is further reason not to treat any OCM potency limit as permanent without checking authority after that date [VERIFY].

Lawful activities — §342.80(a): “Notwithstanding any law to the contrary, the cultivation, manufacturing, possessing, and selling of cannabis flower, cannabis products, artificially derived cannabinoids, lower-potency hemp edibles, and hemp-derived consumer products by a licensed cannabis business or hemp business in conformity with the rights granted by a cannabis business license or hemp business license is lawful and may not be the grounds for the seizure or forfeiture of property, arrest or prosecution, or search or inspections except as provided by this chapter.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.80 — Accessed 2026-10-28. §342.80(b) adds good-faith age-verification defence for retail agent who sells to person under 21 after complying with §342.27, subd. 4 — same link.

No licence in Indian country without tribal consent — §342.13(j): “Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions, the state shall not issue a license to any cannabis business to operate in Indian country, as defined in United States Code, title 18, section 1151, of a Minnesota Tribal government without the consent of the Tribal government.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.13 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.3.2 Home grow — verbatim and conditions

§342.09, subd. 2(a), verbatim:

“Up to eight cannabis plants, with no more than four being mature, flowering plants may be grown at a single residence, including the curtilage or yard, without a license to cultivate cannabis issued under this chapter provided that cultivation takes place at the primary residence of an individual 21 years of age or older and in an enclosed, locked space that is not open to public view.”

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Conditions: Per residence, not per adult — text says “at a single residence” — two adults in one home do not each get 8 plants. Mature/flowering cap: ≤4 of 8 may be mature, flowering at any time. Location: primary residence of individual 21+, including curtilage/yard — outdoor grow not banned per se, but must still be in enclosed, locked space not open to public view. Penalty for excess: §342.09, subd. 6(e): “The office may assess a civil penalty of up to $500 for each plant grown in excess of the limit on a person who grows more than eight cannabis plants or more than four mature, flowering plants, without a license to cultivate cannabis issued under this chapter.” Source: same link. Landlord/lease: §342.09 itself does not state landlord veto over home grow; OCM consumer guidance warns renters to check leases, and §342.57, subd. 3(b) (medical) bars landlord from refusing to lease / penalising registry or tribal patient solely for enrolment, subject to federal-law / federal-benefit exceptions. Whether landlord may prohibit adult-use home grow by lease term is [VERIFY] — no statute text on that point located in §§342.09/342.57 as opened. Caregiver home grow: see §1.4.4 (up to 8 for one patient household, plus up to 8 for personal adult use, max 16 total, max 8 mature/flowering — §342.09, subd. 2(b)).

1.3.3 Home extraction

§342.09, subd. 3, verbatim: “No person may use a volatile solvent to separate or extract cannabis concentrate or hemp concentrate without a cannabis microbusiness, cannabis mezzobusiness, cannabis macrobusiness, cannabis manufacturer, or lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer license issued under this chapter.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Implication: solventless home methods (e.g. rosin pressing, ice-water extraction) not prohibited by this subdivision; volatile-solvent (butane, CO₂, ethanol-type) home extraction prohibited without listed licence. Whether specific solvent counts as “volatile” [VERIFY] in rule/guidance — statute does not list solvents.

1.3.4 Public consumption, vehicles, driving

  • Use locations: only private residence/curtilage, private property not generally accessible to public (unless owner prohibits), and licensed on-site consumption premises/events — §342.09, subd. 1(a)(7). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Smoking/vaping bans: §342.09, subd. 1(b)(3) (Clean Indoor Air Act locations) and §342.56, subd. 1(b) (multifamily housing — below).
  • Multifamily housing — §342.56, subd. 1(b), verbatim: “Except for the use of medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products, the vaporizing or smoking of cannabis flower, cannabis products, artificially derived cannabinoids, or hemp-derived consumer products is prohibited in a multifamily housing building, including balconies and patios appurtenant thereto. A violation of this paragraph is punishable through a civil administrative fine in an amount of $250.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.56 — Accessed 2026-10-28. OCM restates $250 fine authority — https://mn.gov/ocm/consumers/adult-use/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note medical exception: medical smoking/vaping excepted from multifamily ban as written; whether building’s lease or federal housing rules separately bar it is different question.
  • Vehicles — use: §342.09, subd. 1(b)(2) bans use in motor vehicle (§169A.03, subd. 15). Vehicles — driving: §342.09, subd. 1(b)(6) bans operating motor vehicle while under influence. DWI charges under §169A.20. Vehicles — open package: §169A.36 makes possession of open/non-compliant package in motor vehicle misdemeanour — exact packaging-compliance conditions [VERIFY].
  • No per se THC blood limit for driving located in Chapter 342 or §169A.20 as searched. Minnesota DWI for cannabis as charged is impairment / under-the-influence based in charging language seen. Do not state Minnesota ng/mL per se driving limit — [UNAVAILABLE] / [VERIFY] in §169A text.
  • Medical driving limits — §342.56, subd. 1(a)(4): nothing in §§342.51–342.60 permits “operating, navigating, or being in actual physical control of a motor vehicle, aircraft, train, or motorboat or working on transportation property, equipment, or facilities while under the influence of medical cannabis flower or a medical cannabinoid product.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.56 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.3.5 Gifting

  • Gift, no remuneration, to adult 21+: ≤2 oz flower, ≤8 g concentrate, or ≤800 mg THC edibles — §342.09, subd. 1(a)(6). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Gift to person under 21: prohibited — §342.09, subd. 1(b)(7). Gift as sample/promotional gift by person in business of selling goods/services: prohibited — §342.09, subd. 1(b)(8). Retailers separately “shall not… give away immature cannabis plants or seedlings, cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products” — §342.27, subd. 12(3). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.27 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Unlicensed sale ban — §342.09, subd. 4, verbatim: “No person may sell cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products without a license issued under this chapter that authorizes the sale.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Import for sale ban — §342.09, subd. 5: no import of LPHEs / hemp-derived consumer products manufactured outside Minnesota with intent to sell in Minnesota (or to person/business intending to sell in Minnesota) without Chapter 342 licence authorising importation; “This subdivision does not apply to edibles or products lawfully purchased for personal use.” Source: same link.

1.3.6 Allowed product types — adult-use

Definitions (Chapter 342, §342.01, as opened in part): - “Adult-use cannabis flower” means cannabis flower approved for sale by OCM or substantially similar to approved product; “does not include medical cannabis flower, hemp plant parts, or hemp-derived consumer products” (§342.01, subd. 3). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.01 — Accessed 2026-10-28. - “Adult-use cannabis product” means cannabis product approved for sale by OCM or substantially similar; “includes edible cannabis products but does not include medical cannabinoid products or lower-potency hemp edibles” (§342.01, subd. 4). Same source. - “Adult-use cannabis concentrate” means cannabis concentrate approved for sale by OCM or substantially similar; “does not include any artificially derived cannabinoid” (§342.01, subd. 2). Same source. - “Edible cannabis product” means product intended to be eaten or consumed as beverage by humans; containing cannabinoid other than artificially derived cannabinoid in combination with food ingredients; not drug; and OCM-approved type or substantially similar type, “including but not limited to products that resemble nonalcoholic beverages, candy, and baked goods”; “does not include lower-potency hemp edibles” (§342.01, subd. 31). Same source. - “Cannabis flower” means “the harvested flower, bud, leaves, and stems of a cannabis plant” and includes adult-use and medical flower, but “does not include cannabis seed, hemp plant parts, or hemp-derived consumer products” (§342.01, subd. 16). Same source.

What licensed retailer may sell (adult-use): immature cannabis plants and seedlings, adult-use flower, adult-use products, LPHEs, and hemp-derived consumer products — but only to individuals at least 21 — §342.27, subd. 2(a)–(b). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.27 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Retailers may also sell paraphernalia (including childproof storage), hemp-derived topicals, and non-cannabis items listed in §342.27, subd. 3 (sealed non-alcoholic drinks, books/videos, magazines, multiple-use bags, branded clothing, hemp fibre/grain products, fentanyl-detection products) — same link.

Edible caps — adult-use (statute, not rule): - Eaten edibles: “Edible cannabis products and hemp-derived consumer products intended to be eaten may not include more than ten milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol per serving and a single package may not include more than a total of 200 milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol. A package may contain multiple servings of ten milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol provided that each serving is indicated by scoring, wrapping, or other indicators designating the individual serving size.” — §342.27, subd. 2(d). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.27 — Accessed 2026-10-28. - Beverages: “Edible adult-use cannabis products and hemp-derived consumer products intended to be consumed as beverages may not include more than ten milligrams of tetrahydrocannabinol per serving. A single beverage container may not contain more than two servings.” — §342.27, subd. 2(e). Source: same link. Therefore adult-use beverage container max = 20 mg THC (2 × 10 mg). Distinct from LPHE beverage max of 10 mg per single container — see §1.5.2. Do not conflate them. - 2026 omnibus edible-cap change claim: secondary summary states 2026 omnibus “raised edible package limits to 200 mg per package while keeping 10 mg serving cap.” 200 mg package figure confirmed in current §342.27, subd. 2(d) as opened; whether 200 mg is raise from prior lower figure, and effective date, is [VERIFY] in pre-2026 text / 2026 c. 123 — do not assert prior figure without that check.

Vapes / concentrates / potency caps: - Vapes and concentrates within “cannabis product” / “cannabis concentrate” as defined above; no separate vape ban located in Chapter 342 as opened. Commonly repeated “80% THC vape cap / 50% concentrate-combination cap” found only in secondary sources and NOT confirmed in §342.06 or §342.27 text as opened — [VERIFY] in Chapter 9810 / OCM product-approval lists before publishing any vape/concentrate potency cap. OCM statutory authority to set potency limits is §342.02, subd. 2(a)(17) / (b) and §342.06, subd. 1(c) (OCM “may establish” / in pending bills “must enforce” limits — see §1.9 for pending-bill version; current enacted wording of §342.06, subd. 1(c) not opened in full [VERIFY]). - Product-approval bars in §342.06 (as described in pending-bill text quoting current law): OCM “shall not approve any cannabis product, lower-potency hemp edible, or hemp-derived consumer product that: (1) is or appears to be a lollipop or, ice cream, a pastry, candy, or a chocolate confection; (2) bears the likeness or contains characteristics of a real or fictional person, animal, or fruit; (3) is modeled after a type or brand of products primarily consumed by or marketed to children; (4) is substantively similar to a meat food product; poultry food product… or a dairy product…” — quoted from SF 3591 bill text reproducing §342.06, subd. 1(e) (as introduced 2026). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/94/2026/0/SF/3591/versions/0/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Treat as [VERIFY] against current §342.06 text — bill text is legislature source for bill, not official current statute publication, and “candy” bar sits in tension with §342.01, subd. 31 definition (“including… candy”) and gummy sales in practice; reconciliation (approved product categories vs. appearance bars) is [VERIFY] in OCM approvals / Rule 9810. - Flower potency: No enacted adult-use flower THC % cap confirmed in statute text opened. Pending bill (SF 3591, §1.9) would impose 15% flower / 30% concentrate caps — proposal, not current law.

Effective dates for product rules: Adult-use possession/use/home-grow rules: 1 Aug 2023. Retail per-transaction and edible-cap rules in §342.27 apply to licensed retail sales, which could only occur once licensing/rules in place (Chapter 9810 effective 14 Apr 2025; retail opening 2025). Statute does not state separate later effective date for §342.27, subd. 2(d)–(e) as opened [VERIFY].

1.4 Medical programme

1.4.1 History and current code

  • Medical cannabis existed since 2014, originally under Minn. Stat. §§ 152.22–152.37, now administered under Minn. Stat. Chapter 342, §§ 342.51–342.60. Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.02, subd. 3 — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.02 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Transfer from the Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) to the Office of Cannabis Management (OCM) was effective 1 July 2024 under 2024 Minn. Laws ch. 121, originally scheduled for 1 March 2025 under 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 63. Statutory basis: § 342.02, subd. 3 — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.02 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Do not date the transfer to March 2025: the 2024 session law moved it forward to 1 July 2024.

1.4.2 Qualifying conditions

  • The 2024 § 152.22, subd. 14 list names 19 diagnoses. The practitioner-discretion lead-in is equally operative and must not be dropped: a patient qualifies on either a condition for which the patient’s own health care practitioner has recommended/approved/authorized cannabis or one of the 19 named diagnoses. Source: Minn. Stat. § 152.22 (2024 text) — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/152.22 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Renumbering of the qualifying-condition definition into § 342.01, subd. 63 is [VERIFY] — the subd. 63 text was not opened in full (see Part 1 Gap 2: the § 342.01 continuation lines 331–770 could not be opened due to a single 429 rate-limit error on that one request, not evidence the page does not exist).
  • Patient counts (context, from Part 6/Part 0, secondary/OCM reporting): more than 90,000 registered medical patients by September 2026 (OCM), up from just over 41,000 before the 2023 fee elimination and 2024 eligibility expansion, and more than 59,000 at adult-use launch (September 2025). A secondary 20 August 2026 figure of 91,360 active patients and 2,893 doctors authorised to certify is [VERIFY — registry page not opened directly]. No official patient-count series by year for 2015–2024 was located [UNAVAILABLE for a full series].

1.4.3 Practitioner certification

  • “Practitioner” is defined at § 342.01, subd. 32. Certification must be dated within 90 days before application — § 342.52, subd. 2(b). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.52 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Practitioner duties are at § 342.55 and the penalty provision at § 342.58 — full texts [VERIFY] in the final check (see Gap 6). Do not summarise duties or penalties beyond the section citations until those texts are opened in full.

1.4.4 Patient registration

  • OCM administers registration. The application contents are prescribed by § 342.52; OCM must approve or deny within 30 days, and denial is available on only five grounds stated in the statute. Registration is registry verification, not a statutory “card” — do not describe a Minnesota medical cannabis card as a statutory instrument.
  • Continued enrolment: 3-year enrolment period. Failure to notify OCM of a name or address change within 30 days carries a $100 fine. Revocation grounds are stated in § 342.52; re-application is permitted 12 months after a subd. 6 revocation.
  • Source for this section: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.52 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Fees: no fee is stated in § 342.52 as opened. Any “$0” claim is [VERIFY] against the OCM patient fee schedule — do not cite § 342.52 for $0. The 2023 fee elimination is the reason patient numbers rose from just over 41,000, but the current fee schedule itself must be checked on OCM before publishing a fee figure.

1.4.5 Veterans alternative certification

  • Veterans have an alternative certification route under § 342.52, subd. 3. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.52 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Detail of the alternative route beyond the subdivision citation is [VERIFY] in the full text.

1.4.6 Caregivers, parents, guardians, spouses

  • Caregivers — § 342.52, subd. 9: a caregiver must be at least 18; may serve a maximum of 6 registered patients at one time, with patients at the same residence counting as one; a caregiver may cultivate up to 8 plants for one patient household only if the patient assigns the cultivation right and notifies OCM, and the patient is then prohibited from personal cultivation. In addition, a caregiver retains their own § 342.09, subd. 2 grow, so the maximum at the caregiver’s residence is 16 plants total / 8 mature. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.52 and https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Parents, guardians and spouses — § 342.52, subd. 10. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.52 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.4.7 Patient home grow

  • A patient may home-grow 8 plants / 4 mature unless the cultivation right has been assigned to a caregiver (see § 1.4.6 above), in which case the patient is prohibited from personal cultivation. Source: §§ 342.09, 342.52 — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.09 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.4.8 Allowable delivery methods, distribution, and product types for medical use

  • Allowable delivery methods are at § 342.52, subd. 7a. Distribution procedure and consultation/final approval are at § 342.51, subd. 2(a) and subd. 3(a). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.51 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Vaporized products to under-21 patients are barred — § 342.51, subd. 2(c). Source: same link — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Medical retail endorsement duties and high-medical-need product types include: pill; water-soluble multiparticulate; orally dissolvable lozenge/gum/mint/buccal/sublingual; tincture. Source: § 342.51 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Medical purchase limits: no numeric limit was located in §§ 342.51–342.52 as opened. Any 30-day or monthly supply cap is [UNAVAILABLE] in the statute text opened — check Rule 9810 / OCM medical guidance before publishing a cap. Registry patients with patient-specific labelling are exempt from the § 342.09, subd. 1(a)(2)–(5) possession limits (§ 342.09, subd. 1(d); see § 1.3 above).

1.4.9 Out-of-state / visiting patients

  • Visiting-patient distribution is allowed under § 342.51, subd. 2a: distribution with out-of-state verification plus photo ID, patient-specific labelling, and weekly reporting to OCM including the tracking number, plus 7 conditions for motor-vehicle distribution. No duration, similarity, quantity cap, or registry enrolment for visitors is stated in subd. 2a as opened. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.51 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Adult-use tribal compacts listed in the medical section of the research notes are secondary summaries; compact texts are [VERIFY].

1.5 Lower-potency hemp (LPHE) and industrial hemp

1.5.1 History

  • LPHE law began as § 151.72 in 2022. OCM took over regulation on 1 July 2024. Chapter 342 LPHE licensing opened 1 October 2025; the first window closed at noon CDT 31 October 2025, with rolling issuance thereafter. A second rolling window reopening 1 April 2026 is reported in a secondary summary and is [VERIFY on OCM].
  • Registration-to-licensure cutover completed 31 March / 1 April 2026 (MDH registration under former § 151.72 sunset 31 March 2026; OCM LPHE applications October 2025). By 31 August 2026, secondarily, 2,005 LPHE licences: 1,887 retailer, 68 manufacturer, 50 wholesaler.
  • Source for OCM LPHE regulation: https://mn.gov/ocm/ — Accessed 2026-10-28; former § 151.72: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/151.72 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.5.2 LPHE THC caps — statute table (do not conflate with adult-use caps)

Product Cap — § 342.62
Non-beverage LPHE 5 mg delta-9 THC per serving / 50 mg per package — § 342.62, subd. 2(f)(1)
Single-serving beverage 10 mg per container — § 342.62, subd. 2(g)(1)
Multi-serving resealable beverage, ≥750 mL ≤5 mg per serving, ≤17 servings — § 342.62, subd. 2(i). The implied 85 mg arithmetic maximum is not to be stated as a statutory package cap without checking subd. 2(i) in full
Other cannabinoids (CBD/CBG/CBN/CBC) — non-beverage package 1,000 mg each — § 342.62, subd. 2(f)(2)
Other cannabinoids — single beverage 200 mg each — § 342.62, subd. 2(g)(2)
Other cannabinoids — multi-serving beverage 400 mg each — § 342.62, subd. 2(i)(4)

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.62 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

  • § 342.01, subd. 50 serving-level figures and the 2026 c. 123 “100 mg / 400 mg” combination language (House Act Summary § 4) — unit (per-serving vs per-package vs per-container) and effective date [VERIFY]. There is a presentation conflict between the § 342.62 package figures above (1,000/200/400 mg) and subd. 50 serving-level extracts (100 mg): subd. 50 full text [VERIFY] before publishing any serving-level CBD cap.
  • Adult-use comparison (different caps — do not conflate): adult-use eaten edibles 10 mg/serving, 200 mg/package; adult-use beverages 10 mg/serving, maximum 2 servings/container = 20 mg/container. LPHE beverage is 10 mg/container. The LPHE and adult-use beverage caps differ by design.

1.5.3 Allowed LPHE categories — and what is NOT LPHE

  • Allowed LPHE categories per Minnesota Rules 9810.2100: edible products, beverage products, and hemp-derived tinctures only. Source: Minnesota Rules chapter 9810 — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/9810/ — Accessed 2026-10-28 (part-by-part check [VERIFY], see Gap 9).
  • NOT LPHE — hemp-derived consumer product (cannabis-business-only). Rule 9810.2100/9810.2101 approved categories are only dried hemp flower and hemp-derived oils for combustion/vaporization, at ≤0.3% total THC. Hemp flower, vapes and concentrate are no longer allowed as LPHE.
  • Smokable hemp / THCA flower: there is no separate smokable-hemp retail category for LPHE retailers. The THCA calculation for the 0.3% hemp-derived consumer product figure (delta-9 only vs total THC) is [VERIFY].
  • Delta-8: OCM guidance says delta-8 is no longer allowed for sale in Minnesota by any businesses, with possible export exceptions, but current status against § 342.01, subd. 50 / § 342.06 approval lists is [VERIFY] — do not publish delta-8 as currently allowed.
  • Artificially derived cannabinoid is defined at § 342.01, subd. 6. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.01 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.5.4 Minimum age, licence types, fees, transferability

  • Minimum age for LPHE purchase: 21+ — § 342.46, subd. 1(a). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.46 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • LPHE licence fees (§ 342.11 extract): manufacturer application $250 / initial $1,000 / renewal $1,000; wholesaler $250 / $10,000 / $10,000; retailer $250 per location / $250 per location / $250 per location. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.11 — Accessed 2026-10-28. (Full fee table: Part 4.)
  • LPHE licences are non-transferable — § 342.44, subd. 2 — with a conditional-surrender route described on the OCM federal-hemp page. Dual cannabis + hemp holding, previously prohibited, was removed by 2026 c. 123 (see § 1.9).
  • Retailer display/storage — § 342.46, subd. 4: non-beverage LPHE behind the checkout counter or in a locked case; beverages excepted. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.46 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Liquor stores/bars: no Chapter 342 section as opened prohibits an LPHE retailer also holding a liquor licence or operating in a liquor store/bar — but that is not permission to consume on site. On-site consumption needs a licence/endorsement — § 342.09, subd. 1(a)(7)(iii); § 342.245. An off-site event claim for LPHE retailers with an on-site consumption endorsement is [VERIFY] in 2026 c. 123 / § 342.245.
  • Hours: § 342.27, subd. 7 cannabis retail hours expressly do not apply to LPHE retailers (§ 342.27, subd. 14). LPHE hours are [VERIFY] in § 342.46 / Rule 9810.

  • Testing — § 342.61, subd. 1(a): testing before sale/transfer. Subd. 1(b): ISO/IEC 17025 lab window for non-intoxicating LPHE/hemp consumer products until 31 May 2027. Subds. 2–4: contaminants, potency, homogeneity, failed batches. Results retained at least 5 years, public on request in plain language — subd. 5(b)–(c). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.61 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.63 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.62 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.5.7 Minnesota response to the federal hemp definition — OCM position (verbatim core)

  • OCM Federal Hemp Changes page, opened directly: https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/resources/hemp/federal-hemp-changes.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28 (originally 31 August, updated for the new date).
  • Federal change “effectively bans hemp products containing more than 0.4 milligrams (mg) of THC per package” effective 11 December 2026 unless other federal action occurs.
  • OCM states verbatim in substance: “This federal definition change does not change how Minnesota law defines lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) products and LPHE retailers, manufacturers and wholesalers or the legality of those products in the state.” Minnesota LPHE definitions “will not change after the federal definition changes on Dec. 11, 2026.”
  • But OCM does NOT say Minnesota LPHEs remain federally legal after 11 December 2026: many Minnesota-compliant products (any package over 0.4 mg THC — essentially every current LPHE edible/beverage) “will become federally noncompliant,” with particular risk for import/export endorsement holders who must ensure imported product complies with both Minnesota and federal law.
  • Federal bills to watch on the OCM page: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act of 2027 (moving the ban 12 November → 11 December); Lawful Hemp Protection Act; Beverage Regulatory Parity Act — none enacted as described; the signing date “2 vs 3 September” detail is [VERIFY].
  • OCM convened a hemp industry forum in late September 2026.
  • Separate Minnesota guidance on the 12 November 2026 narrow federal category is [UNAVAILABLE].
  • No Minnesota statute/session law was located amending § 342.01, subd. 50 to conform to the federal 0.4 mg cap [UNAVAILABLE]. No Minnesota legislative fix to the LPHE definition was found as of 28 October 2026.
  • OCM options for LPHE holders ahead of renewal: renew, surrender (including conditional surrender to a new entity), let the licence expire, or enter the adult-use market — while noting no currently open cannabis licence application window.
  • The only state-law bridge located is the 2026 omnibus removal of the ban on holding hemp + cannabis licences simultaneously.
  • Whether Minnesota will defend, amend, or let LPHE products go federally noncompliant after 11 December 2026, and what federal enforcement posture will follow, are open questions.
  • Contradiction flagged, baseline retained: OCM September 2026 release text as crawled dates the federal signing to “November 2025,” which does not match the commission baseline (PL 119-37 § 781 effective 12 November 2026, limited by PL 119-103 § 2019 until 11 December 2026). The baseline is taken as given; the OCM dating is [VERIFY], and it is not used to date the federal change.

1.8 Employment and drug testing — three separate regimes, do not collapse them

1.8(A) Lawful consumable products — § 181.951 as amended by 2023 c. 63

  • Off-premises, non-working-hours use is protected from hire/discipline/discharge decisions. On-premises/working-hours/employer vehicle/machinery/equipment use, possession, impairment, sale or transfer is NOT protected. Cannabis is a lawful consumable product for Minnesota law regardless of federal or other-state law. Current subdivision numbering is [VERIFY]. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.951 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.8(B) DATWA cannabis testing limits

  • Pre-employment cannabis testing as a condition of employment is broadly prohibited — § 181.951, subd. 8, verbatim in substance: (a) an employer must not request/require a cannabis test unless otherwise required by state/federal law; (b) must not refuse to hire solely because a test indicates cannabis; (c) must not test on an arbitrary/capricious basis; (d) must comply with §§ 181.953/181.954 safeguards. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.951 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • The exempt-positions list is NOT in § 181.951, subd. 8 as extracted. Secondary lists (safety-sensitive positions, peace officers, CDL/DOT drivers, childcare, federally funded/mandated positions) are [VERIFY] mandate-by-mandate — do not publish a definitive list from secondary summaries.
  • Employee testing is permitted on reasonable suspicion (§ 181.951, subd. 5: under the influence, violation of written work rules, personal injury, work-related accident/machinery/vehicle) and for treatment-programme testing (subd. 6, during evaluation/treatment and up to 2 years after completion).
  • Random-testing circumstances and the DATWA circumstance list are [VERIFY] in §§ 181.951, subds. 2–4.
  • Discipline after a positive test (§ 181.953, subd. 10a, secondary summary) is [VERIFY] against the current text (clearness-of-intellect/control test, confirmatory test, written work rules/policy, state/federal authorisation or federal-benefit loss).
  • Safeguards — § 181.953: written policy (§ 181.952), licensed/accredited/certified lab, chain of custody, confirmatory test, written result notice within 3 working days, employee explanation right, confirmatory retest request, oral-fluid testing (subd. 5a, 2024 amendment). § 181.951, subd. 7: no legal duty to test. Whether the first-positive rehabilitation rule applies identically to cannabis is [VERIFY] in §§ 181.953–181.954.
  • Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.951 and https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/181.953 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.8(C) Medical-registry-patient protections — § 342.57

  • § 342.57, subd. 5, verbatim in substance: no discrimination in hiring, termination, terms, or penalty based on registry status, Tribal medical programme patient status, or a positive cannabis test, unless the patient used/possessed/sold/transported/was impaired on work premises, during working hours, or while operating employer machinery/vehicle/equipment; federal-law/federal-benefit exception applies; an employee may present registry/Tribal verification as part of a § 181.953, subd. 6 explanation. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.57 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Related § 342.57 protections: 14-day notice (subd. 5a); school/landlord (subd. 3); medical care including organ transplants (subd. 4); custody/visitation (subd. 6); retaliation (subd. 6a); damages of the greater of actual damages or $1,000 plus attorney fees, and injunctive relief (subd. 7); parole/supervised/conditional release (subd. 8); professional licensing (subd. 2(h)). Source: same link — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • What employment law does NOT do: it creates no general adult-use right to be impaired at work, to use on premises, or to refuse lawful reasonable-suspicion/post-accident/treatment testing; and it does not override federal DOT/contractor mandates.
  • Licence-holder employee provisions (§ 342.151) and licensee criminal-history provisions (§ 342.15) are licensing provisions whose text was not opened [VERIFY] — they are not summarised here as employment rights.

1.10 Schedule III / § 280E analysis (analysis, not Minnesota statute)

S.1 Medical only

  • State-licensed medical activity = a Chapter 342 licensee with a medical endorsement (§ 342.51) selling medical flower/products to a registry patient (or visiting/tribal patient as in § 342.51, subds. 2, 2a, 5) with patient-specific labelling (§ 342.63, subd. 4), plus the underlying cultivation/manufacture for that channel.
  • Adult-use and LPHE activity remains Schedule I / § 280E under the federal baseline even if the same business holds a medical endorsement.
  • No Minnesota statute located in this Part implements, decouples, or allocates federal § 280E. Minnesota state-tax § 280E conformity and Department of Revenue Schedule III guidance are [VERIFY] — see the Part 2 reconciliation in the combined notes: Part 2 concludes from statute text that Minnesota DOES decouple for state tax purposes (§ 290.0132, subd. 29), which supersedes Part 4’s “unavailable in Part 4 sources” on the state question, but federal allocation guidance remains open.

S.2 Combination / macrobusiness

  • The pre-1 January 2027 former combination business (renumbered § 342.515 → § 342.295) and any business holding both a medical endorsement and adult-use authorisations serves two federal channels from one entity. The baseline grants relief to Schedule III medical activity, not to the entity as a whole. Segregation of inventory, sales, and expenses is required (analysis; [VERIFY] with federal tax guidance/counsel).
  • The 2026 c. 123 merger effective 1 January 2027 increases the segregation burden; it does not convert adult-use sales to Schedule III. An OCM rule on segregation after the merger is [VERIFY].
  • Medical-endorsement canopy/retail benefits are state licensing benefits, not tax benefits (micro +1,000 sq ft indoor / ¼ acre outdoor; mezz +3,000 sq ft / ½ acre; cultivator +6,000 sq ft / 1 acre; additional retail locations in high-medical-need areas, § 342.51). State tax-exempt medical sales are distinct from federal § 280E relief. Visiting/tribal-patient sales tax treatment is [VERIFY].

S.3 Hemp / LPHE and § 280E

  • LPHE/hemp-derived products are hemp-derived, not “marijuana” medical activity. The Schedule III move does not move them. After 11 December 2026, products over 0.4 mg/container become federally noncompliant hemp — a hemp-definition consequence, not a § 280E consequence. Whether § 280E ever applied to hemp businesses is [VERIFY] with federal guidance.

S.4 Tribal medical — short answer: [VERIFY], not established

  • Chapter 342 recognises Tribal medical programme patients/boards for state-law distribution/protection, and § 342.51, subd. 2a(b)(1) recognises visiting-patient verification issued under Tribal Nation law for distribution — but that is not a statement that the tribal programme is “state-licensed.”
  • The federal baseline says “state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana” (91 FR 22714 as given). A tribally licensed programme is on its face tribally licensed, not state-licensed, unless (a) a compact expressly provides state licensing, (b) federal DEA/IRS guidance treats a compact/tribal medical programme as state-licensed for Schedule III/§ 280E, or (c) the tribal patient is concurrently enrolled in the Minnesota registry (the HF 3162 model, not confirmed enacted).
  • Do NOT present tribal medical sales as Schedule III / § 280E-relieved without federal guidance or compact text. The same caution applies to tribal adult-use (Schedule I / § 280E regardless of § 295.81, subd. 4(d) compact tax treatment).

S.5 Other federal interactions

  • Banking: no federal law; § 342.67 legal assistance is not banking law [VERIFY] § 342.67 text.
  • The appropriations rider through 11 December 2026 is a federal spending limitation; post-11 December 2026 status is [VERIFY] in federal appropriations law.
  • Firearms/housing/immigration: § 342.57 protections are state-law protections subject to federal-law/federal-benefit exceptions as written; they do not override federal firearms consequences (18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) as amended by the Schedule III baseline — analysis required), federal housing, or immigration consequences.
