Stat. § 290.0134 — returned 429 rate-limit error and was not re-attempted; current subdivision numbering therefore flagged [VERIFY].

2.1 Headline answer

Minnesota has no wholesale, weight, or cultivation excise tax in Minn. Stat. § 295.81. Cannabis tax is retail gross receipts tax, plus ordinary state and local sales taxes. Medical sales to qualifying registry patient exempt from gross receipts tax by statute; sales-tax position for qualifying medical sales stated in Department of Revenue guidance as exempt, but precise sales-tax subdivision was not located in full current text of Minn. Stat. § 297A.67 opened for this Part — see § 2.4 and gaps list. No separate lower-potency hemp tax: lower-potency hemp edibles (LPHE) pay same gross receipts tax as adult-use cannabis.

On $100 adult-use product price, before any local sales tax, two state taxes are $15.00 + $6.88 = $21.88, i.e. 21.875% of price. Both taxes calculated on product price, not tax-inclusive subtotal, per Department of Revenue guidance summarised below.

Tax / charge Current rate Base Who bears it in practice
Cannabis gross receipts tax, Minn. Stat. § 295.81, subd. 2 15% (10% before 1 July 2025) Gross receipts from retail sales of taxable cannabis products in Minnesota Retailer is taxpayer; retailer may, but is not required to, collect it from purchaser if separately stated
State general sales tax, Minn. Stat. § 297A.62, subds. 1, 1a 6.875% (6.5% + 0.375% constitutional increase) Gross receipts from retail sales Purchaser, collected by retailer
Local general sales taxes Varies by location — no statewide rate Same retail sale, sourced where customer receives product Purchaser
Local cannabis-only tax Prohibited — —
Qualifying medical cannabis (gross receipts tax) 0% Registry-patient medical items —
Qualifying medical cannabis (sales tax) 0% per Department of Revenue guidance; statutory citation [VERIFY] See § 2.4 —

Sources: Minn. Stat. § 295.81, https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28; Minn. Stat. § 297A.62, https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/297A.62 — Accessed 2026-10-28; Minnesota Department of Revenue, “Cannabis Tax,” https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/cannabis-tax — Accessed 2026-10-28; Minnesota Department of Revenue, Sales Guide (updated 11 June 2026), https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/guide/sales-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.2 Cannabis gross receipts tax — Minn. Stat. § 295.81

2.2.1 Rate and operative text

“A tax equal to 15 percent of gross receipts from retail sales in Minnesota of taxable cannabis products is imposed on any taxable cannabis product retailer that sells these products to customers. A taxable cannabis product retailer may but is not required to collect the tax imposed by this section from the purchaser as long as the tax is separately stated on the receipt, invoice, bill of sale, or similar document given to the purchaser.” — Minn. Stat. § 295.81, subd. 2(a) “If a product subject to the tax imposed under this section is included in a bundled transaction, the entire sales price of the bundled transaction is subject to the tax imposed under this section.” — § 295.81, subd. 2(b) “The tax imposed under this section is in addition to any other tax imposed on the sale or use of taxable cannabis products.” — § 295.81, subd. 2(c)

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Rate history: 10% on enactment; 15% for sales and purchases made after 30 June 2025, by 2025 Minn. Laws, 1st Spec. Sess., ch. 13, art. 3, § 3. Department of Revenue 2025 Cannabis Legislative Bulletin (18 Aug. 2025, final) states this expressly. 10% figure still appearing in some secondary summaries is therefore stale and must not be used for current sales. Source: Minnesota Department of Revenue, 2025 Cannabis Legislative Bulletin, https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/2025-08/2025-cannabis-legislative-bulletin.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.2.2 What “gross receipts” and “taxable cannabis product” cover

  • “Gross receipts” means “the total amount received in money or by barter or exchange for all taxable cannabis product sales at retail as measured by the sales price. Gross receipts include but are not limited to delivery charges and packaging costs.” Excluded are (1) taxes imposed directly on customer that are separately stated, and (2) unreimbursed discounts allowed by seller and taken by purchaser. — § 295.81, subd. 1(j). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • “Taxable cannabis product” means “cannabis flower, cannabis product, cannabis solution product, hemp-derived consumer product, lower-potency hemp edible, and any substantially similar item.” — § 295.81, subd. 1(r). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Retailers covered include cannabis retailer, cannabis microbusiness, cannabis mezzobusiness, medical cannabis combination business, and lower-potency hemp edible retailer, plus in-state and out-of-state retailers and marketplace providers. — § 295.81, subd. 1(s). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Department of Revenue product list subject to Cannabis Tax: cannabis-derived flower, concentrate and cannabinoid-infused products; hemp-derived items for human or animal consumption containing hemp plant parts, hemp concentrate, or artificially derived cannabinoids with other ingredients; lower-potency hemp edibles (THC products eaten or drunk by humans, containing hemp concentrate or artificially derived cannabinoids); vaping solution products containing cannabis or hemp-derived products; and substantially similar products. Delivery charges for cannabis products are also subject to Cannabis Tax. Source: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/guide/sales-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • What is NOT subject to gross receipts tax (but is subject to sales tax): cannabis accessories including vape-related equipment and pipes; growing equipment and supplies including seeds; hemp-derived topical products; cannabis plants. Source: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/guide/sales-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.2.3 Use tax, credits, sourcing and administration

  • Person who receives taxable cannabis products for use or storage in Minnesota, other than from retailer that paid tax under subd. 2, owes use tax at same rate; liability arises on possession in Minnesota. Credit given for tax legally due and paid to another state, up to lesser of amount actually paid or Minnesota tax on that transaction. — § 295.81, subds. 3, 6. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Use tax does not apply to possession/use/storage where (1) aggregate cost in any calendar month to customer is $100 or less, and (2) products were carried into Minnesota by customer. — § 295.81, subd. 4(a). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Sourcing follows Minn. Stat. § 297A.668. — § 295.81, subd. 7. Administration, audit, assessment, refund, penalty, interest, enforcement, collection and appeal follow chapters 270C and 289A as applicable to chapter 297A taxes, except electronic filing/remittance requirement if authorised under § 289A.33. Returns/payment follow filing cycle and due dates in § 289A.20, subd. 4, and chapter 297A. — § 295.81, subds. 8–9. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Tax, interest and penalties are personal debt of person required to file return from time liability arises. — § 295.81, subd. 11 (current numbering; formerly subd. 10 in 2024 text). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.2.4 Lower-potency hemp — no separate tax, and coming federal change

  • LPHE retailers expressly listed as taxable cannabis product retailers, and LPHE expressly listed as taxable cannabis product. No separate LPHE tax rate, return, or fund in § 295.81; LPHE pays same 15% plus sales tax as adult-use cannabis. Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28; https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/guide/sales-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • No separate LPHE collections figure located — see § 2.7: LPHE tax not separately broken out in any official collections table found. [UNAVAILABLE]
  • Forward-looking flag, not current Minnesota law: under federal baseline, after 11 Dec. 2026 federal hemp definition becomes full total-THC definition with 0.4 mg total-THC-per-container cap. Secondary summary reports Office of Cannabis Management has said Minnesota’s LPHE definition is unchanged. No Minnesota statute, rule, or Department of Revenue guidance located for this Part that changes Minnesota 15% rate, LPHE definition, or tax treatment of product that ceases to qualify as hemp federally after that date. Because § 295.81 taxes both cannabis products and hemp-derived consumer products/LPHE at same rate, Minnesota gross receipts rate would not on its face change for such product; its income-tax status under IRC § 280E could change, different question — see § 2.6. [VERIFY — no Minnesota post-11 Dec. 2026 tax guidance located]

2.3 State and local sales taxes

2.3.1 State rate — 6.875%

“a sales tax of 6.5 percent is imposed on the gross receipts from retail sales…” — Minn. Stat. § 297A.62, subd. 1 “an additional sales tax of 0.375 percent, as required under the Minnesota Constitution, article XI, section 15, is imposed on the gross receipts from retail sales… This additional tax expires July 1, 2034.” — § 297A.62, subd. 1a Combined: 6.875%. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/297A.62 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Department of Revenue: “Sales of taxable cannabis products are subject to a gross receipts tax of 15%. In addition to the Cannabis Tax, taxable cannabis products are subject to both: 6.875% state general rate sales tax [and] any applicable local sales taxes based on where the transaction takes place.” And in Sales Guide: “All sales subject to the Cannabis Tax are also subject to the state general rate sales tax and all applicable local sales taxes.” Sources: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/cannabis-tax — Accessed 2026-10-28; https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/guide/sales-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Worked example (state taxes only, before local tax): $100.00 price + $15.00 cannabis tax + $6.88 state sales tax (rounded) = $121.88. Two taxes each applied to $100 price, not stacked on each other. Source for pattern: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/guide/sales-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.3.2 Local sales taxes — general taxes apply; cannabis-only taxes do not

  • Cannabis-only local tax prohibited:

    “A political subdivision of this state is prohibited from imposing a tax solely on the sale of taxable cannabis products as defined under section 295.81, subdivision 1, paragraph (r).” — Minn. Stat. § 295.82 (history: 2023 c. 63, art. 2, § 10) Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.82 — Accessed 2026-10-28 (via search result; section text confirmed in Revisor search extract).

  • General local sales taxes do apply. Department of Revenue: “Some cities and counties have local sales and use taxes. If you are located in or make sales into an area with a local tax, you may owe local sales and use tax,” determined by “location where product is received by customer, which is typically your business address or customer’s delivery address.” No statewide local rate exists, so no combined “state + local” total can be stated for Minnesota as whole; any combined figure above ~22% (e.g. “close to 30% in some cities” in secondary summaries) is location-specific and must be calculated with Department’s Sales Tax Rate Calculator/Map for specific address. Source: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/guide/sales-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • 2024 bill (HF 4325) that would have authorised city cannabis-only tax up to 2% was not enacted as current law and is not counted here; § 295.82 remains prohibition. Source: Minnesota Legislature, HF 4325 (93rd Leg., 2023–2024), https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/93/2024/0/HF/4325/versions/0/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Do not present HF 4325 2% proposal as law.

2.3.3 Tribal-land sales

  • Gross receipts tax does not apply to (1) sales made on Tribally regulated land (as defined in § 3.9228, subd. 1) by cannabis business licensed by Minnesota Tribal government, or (2) use tax on products so purchased. — § 295.81, subd. 4(d). Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Sales tax: “The sale of a taxable cannabis product… that is made on Tribally regulated land… by a cannabis business licensed by a Minnesota Tribal government… is exempt.” — Minn. Stat. § 297A.67, subd. 39, opened in full. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/297A.67 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Off-reservation tribal retail: Minn. Stat. § 270C (tax agreements) authorises Commissioner of Revenue to enter tax agreement with federally recognised Tribe providing for state and Tribe to share state and local sales tax and gross receipts tax on retail sales by Tribally owned business at location off reservation, limited to approximation of Tribe’s regulatory expenses and taxes paid by Tribal members at that location, and only for Tribes with compact under § 3.9228. Specific sharing percentage in any individual compact not located and varies by compact. [VERIFY — compact-specific terms] Source (search extract from Revisor, ch. 270C): https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/270C/full — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.4 Medical cannabis tax treatment

2.4.1 Gross receipts tax — exempt by statute (certain)

“The tax imposed under this section does not apply to sales of medical items purchased by or for a patient enrolled in the registry program, including medical cannabis flower, medical cannabinoid products, or medical cannabis paraphernalia.” — Minn. Stat. § 295.81, subd. 4(b) Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Note limit in same subdivision: “Unless otherwise specified in this section, the exemptions applicable to taxes imposed under chapter 297A are not applicable to the taxes imposed under this section.” — § 295.81, subd. 4(c). Medical exemption therefore comes from § 295.81 itself, not by importing chapter 297A exemption. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.4.2 Sales tax — exempt per Department of Revenue guidance; statutory citation [VERIFY]

Multiple secondary summaries state Department of Revenue Sales Guide provides medical cannabis sold to or for patient enrolled in state medical cannabis registry, by business with medical cannabis retail endorsement, is exempt from both cannabis tax and sales tax, and sales to patients in tribal medical programme and to visiting patients are not exempt. Office of Cannabis Management 2026 legislative-changes summary likewise reported as retaining medical exemption.

What this Part actually verified: full current text of Minn. Stat. § 297A.67 opened (538 lines) and contains no medical-cannabis exemption subdivision; only cannabis exemption is subd. 39 (Tribally regulated land, § 2.3.3). Opened Department of Revenue Sales Guide page states all sales subject to Cannabis Tax are also subject to sales tax — which, for medical sale not subject to Cannabis Tax, does not by itself establish sales-tax exemption.

Treatment: qualifying registry-patient medical sales reported as exempt from state (and, by same guidance, local) sales tax, following Department of Revenue guidance as summarised in secondary sources — but precise statutory authority for sales-tax exemption flagged [VERIFY] and must be confirmed against Department’s Cannabis Publication or written Department ruling before row published as settled law. One secondary source (Cova Software) states opposite — registered medical purchases remain subject to 6.875% sales tax. Conflict unresolved on sources opened and recorded here rather than silently resolved.

Sources for guidance position (secondary, 2026): Minnesota Cannabis Hub, “Minnesota Cannabis Tax Calculator” (updated 1 day before search), https://mncannabishub.com/blog/cannabis-tax-calculator-minnesota — Accessed 2026-10-28; CannBus, “Minnesota Cannabis Market Intelligence Report — Q3 2026,” https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/mn_cannmir.html — Accessed 2026-10-28. Conflicting secondary: Cova Software, “Minnesota Cannabis Dispensary Laws & Licensing,” https://www.covasoftware.com/us-dispensary-laws/minnesota — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Practical consequence if guidance position correct: qualifying medical purchase at same shelf price costs $100.00 with $0 state taxes, versus $121.88 before local tax for adult-use. Patient-registration fee itself is $0 (separate from any provider evaluation fee); fee point outside Part 2 except as context for exemption’s value and not relied on for any tax figure.

2.5 Revenue distribution — current law vs. repealed 80/20 split

2.5.1 Current law (from 1 July 2025 revenues): 100% to General Fund

“The commissioner must deposit the revenues, including penalties and interest, derived from the tax imposed by this section in the general fund.” — Minn. Stat. § 295.81, subd. 10 (current text) Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

No current statutory dedication in § 295.81 to local-government account, youth programme, or any other fund. Any statement that 20% of cannabis tax revenue currently goes to local governments is stale.

2.5.2 Repealed 80/20 regime (historical — do not present as current)

Under original 2023 law, as preserved in 2024 text of § 295.81, subd. 10:

“(a) The commissioner must deposit the revenues, including penalties and interest, derived from the tax imposed by this section as follows: (1) 80 percent to the general fund; and (2) 20 percent to the local government cannabis aid account in the special revenue fund. (b) The local government cannabis aid account is established in the special revenue fund.” Source: Minn. Stat. § 295.81 (2024 text), https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Distribution of that account under former Minn. Stat. § 477A.32: on 30 June each year, 50% of account balance available to counties and 50% to cities; aid certified by 1 Sept. and paid on 26 Dec. of same year. 2.6 Income tax — IRC § 280E and Minnesota decoupling

2.6.1 Minnesota DOES decouple — contrary secondary claim is wrong

Secondary summary (CannBus, “Minnesota Legal Summary — Q3 2026”) states: “Minnesota has not enacted its own state-level 280E decoupling statute.” That statement is contradicted by statute text and Department of Revenue’s own forms, both cited below, and must not be relied on. Minnesota decouples by subtraction from federal taxable income / federal adjusted gross income — it does not ignore federal taxable income altogether, and subtraction available only to extent expense actually disallowed federally.

2.6.2 Operative statute — individuals, estates and trusts

“The amount of expenses of a license holder, as defined under section 342.01, subdivision 48, related to the business of cannabis or hemp and not allowed for federal income tax purposes under section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code is a subtraction.” — Minn. Stat. § 290.0132, subd. 29, “Disallowed section 280E expenses; cannabis licensees” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0132 — Accessed 2026-10-28 (opened directly; subd. 29 text confirmed).

2.6.3 Corporate / business counterpart [VERIFY current numbering]

HF 100 (2023) amended corporate/business counterpart in parallel — Minn. Stat. § 290.0134, subd. 19 in HF 100 first-engrossment text — with same operative language (“expenses of a license holder… related to the business of cannabis or hemp and not allowed for federal income tax purposes under section 280E… is a subtraction”), effective for taxable years beginning after 31 Dec. 2022. Revisor search extract for § 290.0134 confirms same sentence in current text, but direct open of § 290.0134 returned 429 error and was not re-attempted, so current subdivision number flagged [VERIFY]. Department of Revenue 2025 business form confirms mechanism in practice: “Line 16 — Disallowed Section 280E Expenses for Licensed Cannabis or Hemp Businesses: If you are a licensed cannabis or hemp business in the state of Minnesota, you may subtract expenses that were not allowed for federal tax purposes under section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code.”

Sources: HF 100, 1st Engrossment, §§ 4–5 (Revisor BD H0100-1), via https://billcam.com/bill-texts/wjnFG6IWYn — Accessed 2026-10-28; Minnesota Department of Revenue, 2025 Form M1MB instructions, https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/2026-07/m1mb-25.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28; Revisor search extract for § 290.0134, https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0134/version/2024-11-01%2018:32:26+00:00 — Accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY current numbering].

Department of Revenue also lists “Cannabis Income Tax Subtraction” resource stating “licensed cannabis or hemp businesses and medical cannabis manufacturers may qualify to subtract expenses from their income taxes.” Source: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/cannabis-tax — Accessed 2026-10-28.

  1. Medical-only stage: secondary tax-adviser summaries (GreenGrowth CPAs, reviewed Sept. 2026) state medical cannabis manufacturers could first subtract § 280E expenses for tax years beginning after 31 Dec. 2018. 2017 and 2019 bills proposing that subtraction (HF 486, 2017; SF 1070, 2019) located as bills, but enacting session-law chapter for 2019 medical-only subtraction not confirmed from official session-law page. [VERIFY enacting chapter for pre-2023 medical-only subtraction]
  2. All-licensee stage (certain in current law): HF 100 (2023 c. 63) extended subtraction from “medical cannabis manufacturers” to all chapter 342 license holders for business of cannabis or hemp, effective for taxable years beginning after 31 Dec. 2022 — i.e. from tax year 2023. Sources: HF 100 engrossment text above; current § 290.0132, subd. 29, https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0132 — Accessed 2026-10-28; GreenGrowth CPAs summary (secondary, Sept. 2026), https://greengrowthcpas.com/industries/cannabis/minnesota-cannabis-accounting/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.6.5 Interaction with federal Schedule III baseline — medical vs. adult-use vs. combination businesses

Apply commission’s fixed baseline (state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products to Schedule III effective 28 Apr. 2026, 91 FR 22714; adult-use remains Schedule I; § 280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to § 280E):

Business Federal § 280E after 28 Apr. 2026 (baseline, not re-researched) Minnesota state income tax
Pure state-licensed medical Lifted for qualifying medical activity — ordinary business expenses federally deductible Minnesota subtraction becomes moot for expenses now federally allowed, because subtraction by its terms covers only expenses “not allowed for federal income tax purposes.” No double deduction: expense deducted federally cannot also be subtracted in Minnesota. Any expense still federally disallowed for another reason would need separate analysis. [VERIFY — no Minnesota Department of Revenue post-rescheduling guidance on subtraction located]
Pure adult-use Fully applies — expenses (other than cost of goods sold) disallowed federally Minnesota subtraction still applies in full to federally disallowed expenses: business pays federal tax on § 280E-inflated base but Minnesota tax on base from which those expenses subtracted. Subtraction does not reduce federal tax, 15% gross receipts tax, or sales tax.
Medical cannabis combination business / macrobusiness (from 1 Jan. 2027) — combination business Two federal regimes in one entity: medical portion outside § 280E; adult-use portion inside § 280E Minnesota subtraction applies only to adult-use (and any other federally disallowed) portion. Shared costs must be allocated between medical and adult-use activities; no allocation method located in Minnesota statute or Department guidance. [VERIFY — allocation method and any forthcoming IRS/Minnesota guidance]
Pure hemp (industrial hemp; hemp-derived products that remain hemp federally) Hemp excluded from CSA definition of marihuana is not itself subject to § 280E on that basis alone Minnesota subtraction conditional (“not allowed for federal income tax purposes under section 280E”). For pure hemp business with no federally disallowed § 280E expenses, subtraction is zero in practice, despite words “cannabis or hemp” in § 290.0132, subd. 29. If, after 11 Dec. 2026, former hemp product ceases to qualify as hemp federally and becomes Schedule I marijuana, its § 280E status — and therefore availability of Minnesota subtraction — could change. No Minnesota guidance on that transition located. [VERIFY]

What decoupling does not do: does not exempt cannabis business from Minnesota corporate franchise tax, individual income tax on remaining income, sales tax, gross receipts tax, licence fees, or local registration fees; does not create credit (it is subtraction from income, so cash value depends on taxpayer’s marginal Minnesota rate and entity type); does not apply to unlicensed business — statute requires “license holder” as defined in § 342.01, subd. 48. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/290.0132 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

2.8.2 Local retail registration fees — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, subd. 2

“A local unit of government may impose an initial retail registration fee of $500 or up to half the amount of the applicable initial license fee under section 342.11, whichever is less. The local unit of government may also impose a renewal retail registration fee of $1,000 or up to half the amount of the applicable renewal license fee under section 342.11, whichever is less. The initial registration fee shall include the fee for initial registration and the first annual renewal. Any renewal fee imposed… shall be charged at the time of the second renewal and each subsequent annual renewal thereafter.” — § 342.22, subd. 2(a)

No application fee may be charged (subd. 2(b)); registration fees nonrefundable; business holding both cannabis retailer licence and medical cannabis retailer licence for same location may be charged only single registration fee. Worked caps (derived, lesser-of test): retailer initial $500, renewal $1,000; LPHE retailer initial $125, renewal $125; microbusiness initial $0 (half of $0), renewal $1,000; medical combination business initial $500, renewal $1,000. PART 3: LOCAL RULES

Scope/dating: All sources Accessed 2026-10-28. Where a fact rests only on search extract, council document, or secondary source, flagged. No personal phone numbers/emails reproduced. All places in Minnesota; county given for townships/ambiguous cities.

Method limit: Revisor pages opened directly were 2023/2024 cites for §§ 342.13, 342.22, 342.32; 2025 supplement PDFs returned by search show same operative wording for § 342.13(h)–(k) quoted below. OCM Local Government Guide v5.0 (updated 1 August 2026) opened directly for first 342 lines; second attempt returned 429 and was not retried, so later Guide pages cited only from search extracts and flagged [VERIFY] where beyond directly opened text. Paragraph lettering for § 342.13 differs between editions — Revisor text opened letters retailer-limit paragraph (h), while OCM Guide v5.0 cites § 342.13(g) for same rule — lettering flagged [VERIFY]; rely on words, not letter.

3.1 State framework

3.1.1 No bans on possession/use, and no bans on licensed businesses

Minn. Stat. § 342.13, “LOCAL CONTROL,” verbatim:

“(a) A local unit of government may not prohibit the possession, transportation, or use of cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products authorized under this chapter.” “(b) Except as provided in section 342.22, a local unit of government may not prohibit the establishment or operation of a cannabis business or hemp business licensed under this chapter.” — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28

“Except as provided in section 342.22” is registration system, not general opt-out: business lacking required local registration/state licence may not sell, and locality that set and filled lawful retailer cap need not register more. Not authority for permanent jurisdiction-wide ban. OCM summary in search extract to same effect: local governments “cannot prohibit the establishment of a business unless they have set and filled their limit” — OCM Local Government Guide v5.0, 1 Aug 2026, Accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — Guide text beyond line 342 not re-opened after 429].

3.1.2 Reasonable time, place and manner; zoning; buffers

§ 342.13(c) verbatim:

“(c) A local unit of government may adopt reasonable restrictions on the time, place, and manner of the operation of a cannabis business provided that such restrictions do not prohibit the establishment or operation of cannabis businesses. A local unit of government may prohibit the operation of a cannabis business within 1,000 feet of a school, or 500 feet of a day care, residential treatment facility, or an attraction within a public park that is regularly used by minors, including a playground or athletic field.” — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28

These are maximum buffers: locality may prohibit operation within those distances; statute as opened does not authorise additional buffer categories (e.g. churches, residences) as § 342.13(c) power. Contested in practice — secondary reporting notes about 20 localities tracked as conflicting with state law, including extra buffers for churches/residences and county reading school buffer to include colleges — MPR News report, via search extract, Accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary, undated in extract; do not treat as official list of violators].

§ 342.13(d) requires OCM to work with local units to “(1) develop model ordinances for reasonable restrictions on the time, place, and manner of the operation of a cannabis business; (2) develop standardized forms and procedures for the issuance of a retail registration pursuant to section 342.22; and (3) develop model policies and procedures for the performance of compliance checks required under section 342.22” — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28.

§ 342.13(f): within 30 days of receiving copy of application from office, local unit shall certify on form provided by office whether proposed cannabis business complies with local zoning ordinances and, if applicable, state fire code and building code. Office may not issue licence if local unit informs office business does not meet local zoning/land use laws. If local unit does not provide certification within 30 days, office may issue licence. — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28. OCM confirms same 30-day rule — OCM, Local Governments, Accessed 2026-10-28.

Townships: Statute uses “local unit of government” and § 342.22 speaks of “city, town, or county”. Town therefore registers/zones on same basis as city where it has that authority, and may consent to county issuing registrations for its jurisdiction. County-issued registration is expressly consent-based.

3.1.3 Retailer limits: 1-per-12,500 rule

§ 342.13(h)–(j) verbatim:

“(h) A local government unit that issues a cannabis retailer registration under section 342.22 may, by ordinance, limit the number of licensed cannabis retailers, cannabis mezzobusinesses with a retail operations endorsement, and cannabis microbusinesses with a retail operations endorsement to no fewer than one registration for every 12,500 residents.” “(i) If a county has one active registration for every 12,500 residents, a city or town within the county is not obligated to register a cannabis business.” “(j) Nothing in this section shall prohibit a local government unit from allowing licensed cannabis retailers in excess of the minimums set in paragraph (h).” — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28

Consequences: cap is optional (“may, by ordinance”); without ordinance no statutory numeric cap from § 342.13 alone. Cap is floor, not ceiling: may not go below one per 12,500; locality may allow more. OCM Guide v5.0 explains rounding in search extract: “After each increment of 12,500 residents, the number must be rounded up to the next whole number of registrations,” table 1–12,500 = at least 1; 12,501–25,000 = at least 2; 25,001–37,500 = at least 3 — OCM Local Government Guide v5.0, Accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — rounding/Guide table from search extract]. Guide also states in search extract that from 1 January 2027 local governments may also include macrobusinesses with retail endorsement (currently medical cannabis combination businesses) in limitation, and non-retail licence types do not require retail registration and may not be limited — same Guide [VERIFY]. § 342.13(k) bars state licensing in Indian country without Tribal consent: “the state shall not issue a license to any cannabis business to operate in Indian country, as defined in United States Code, title 18, section 1151, of a Minnesota Tribal government without the consent of the Tribal government” — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28. Population source: OCM guidance in July 2025 Q&A states population determined via state demographer’s estimates, and county-wide count for § 342.13(i) includes all local units issuing registrations in county against total county population — OCM Locals Webinar Q&A, 18 July 2025, Accessed 2026-10-28.

3.1.4 Interim ordinances / moratoriums — expired by statute

§ 342.13(e) verbatim:

“If a local unit of government is conducting studies or has authorized a study to be conducted or has held or has scheduled a hearing for the purpose of considering adoption or amendment of reasonable restrictions on the time, place, and manner of the operation of a cannabis business, the governing body of the local unit of government may adopt an interim ordinance applicable to all or part of its jurisdiction for the purpose of protecting the planning process and the health, safety, and welfare of its citizens. Before adopting the interim ordinance, the governing body must hold a public hearing. The interim ordinance may regulate, restrict, or prohibit the operation of a cannabis business within the jurisdiction or a portion thereof until January 1, 2025.” — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28

Therefore: any § 342.13(e) interim ordinance could run only until 1 January 2025. Moratorium still in force after that date cannot rest on § 342.13(e). 2026 bills that would amend § 342.13 (e.g. SF 3740, SF 2142, HF 4202) found only as introduced/proposal texts in search results and are not stated here as law [VERIFY — enactment status not confirmed].

3.1.5 State retail hours, and narrow local power to shorten them

Minn. Stat. § 342.27, subd. 7, in search extract from 2025 Revisor PDF:

“(a) Except as provided by paragraph (b), a cannabis business with a license or endorsement authorizing the retail sale of cannabis flower or cannabis products may not sell cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products between 2:00 a.m. and 8:00 a.m. on the days of Monday through Saturday nor between 2:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m. on Sunday.” “(b) A city or county may adopt an ordinance to prohibit sales for any period between 9:00 p.m. and 2:00 a.m. the following day or between 8:00 a.m. and 10:00 a.m. on the days of Monday through Saturday.” — Minn. Stat. § 342.27, Revisor 2025 PDF, Accessed 2026-10-28

State default effectively sales allowed 8 a.m.–2 a.m. Mon–Sat and 10 a.m.–2 a.m. Sunday; city/county may only shorten within (b) windows (e.g. 9 p.m. close). May not extend past 2 a.m. Local hours stricter than that (e.g. Eden Prairie 10 a.m.–9 p.m., St. Paul proposed 8 a.m.–10 p.m.) rest on § 342.13(c) time-place-manner power plus § 342.27(b) [VERIFY for any single city’s hours authority].

3.1.6 Local public-use ordinances

State baseline — adult use not authorised in public places. Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(a)(7) permits use only in: “(i) a private residence, including the individual’s curtilage or yard; (ii) on private property, not generally accessible by the public, unless the individual is explicitly prohibited from consuming … on the property by the owner of the property; or (iii) on the premises of an establishment or event licensed to permit on-site consumption” — Minn. Stat. § 342.09, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28; Justia extract, Accessed 2026-10-28.

Local enforcement power in Minn. Stat. § 152.0263, subd. 5, in search extract from 2025 Revisor PDF:

“A local unit of government may adopt an ordinance establishing a petty misdemeanor offense for a person who unlawfully uses cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products in a public place provided that the definition of public place does not include the following: (1) a private residence, including the person’s curtilage or yard; (2) private property not generally accessible by the public, unless the person is explicitly prohibited from consuming … on the property by the owner of the property; or (3) the premises of an establishment or event licensed to permit on-site consumption.” — Minn. Stat. § 152.0263, Revisor 2025 PDF, Accessed 2026-10-28

Typical local penalty in model ordinances found is petty misdemeanor up to $300 (e.g. Lyon County, Otter Tail County drafts) — Lyon County public-use ordinance, Accessed 2026-10-28 — but penalty set by each local ordinance, not by § 152.0263 itself in extract opened, so do not generalise $300 statewide [VERIFY]. Separate from § 152.0263, Minn. Stat. § 342.40, subd. 8(e) (2024, cited in Minnesota planners’ fact sheet) allows statutory/home-rule charter city or county to enact measures protecting people from secondhand smoke/aerosol — Minnesota planners fact sheet, Accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary summary; statute text not opened directly — VERIFY before quoting]. For required jurisdictions, public-use rules found: Rochester (city ordinance, § 3.3); St. Cloud (city-parks smoking ban, secondary); Minneapolis (Clean Indoor Air Act indoor-smoking ban, city page). For all other required cities/counties, no public-use ordinance text located — marked [UNAVAILABLE] rather than “no ordinance exists.”

3.1.7 Municipal cannabis retailer — city/county-owned store

Minn. Stat. § 342.32, subd. 5 verbatim, in 2025 Revisor PDF extract:

“Subd. 5. Municipal or county cannabis store. A city or county may establish, own, and operate a municipal cannabis store subject to the restrictions in this chapter. Notwithstanding any law to the contrary, a city or county that establishes, owns, or operates a municipal cannabis store may also hold a lower-potency hemp edible retailer license.” — Minn. Stat. § 342.32, Revisor 2025 PDF, Accessed 2026-10-28

OCM Guide (older v1.4 extract, consistent with statute) adds: “A municipal cannabis store will not be included in the total count of retail licenses issued by the state under Chapter 342.” / “A municipal cannabis store cannot be counted as retail registration for purposes of determining whether a municipality’s cap on retail registrations imposed by ordinance [is met].” — OCM Guide for Local Governments, v1.4 extract, Accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — older Guide version; confirm against Guide v5.0]. In plain terms: city may run own store in addition to private retailers its cap requires it to allow; may not use own store to satisfy 1-per-12,500 minimum.

3.2 Local registration: who must register, fees, issuance, enforcement

Who must register

Minn. Stat. § 342.22, subd. 1 (current Revisor cite opened directly) verbatim:

“Before making retail sales to customers or patients, a cannabis microbusiness, cannabis mezzobusiness, cannabis retailer, cannabis macrobusiness, or lower-potency hemp edible retailer must register with the city, town, or county in which the retail establishment is located. A county may issue a registration in cases where a city or town has provided consent for the county to issue the registration for the jurisdiction.” — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28

Note current text says “cannabis macrobusiness” where older extracts say “medical cannabis combination business” / “medical cannabis retailer” — licence-type names changed for 1 January 2027. Registration is per retail location, not transferable (§ 342.22, subd. 3(d)), and must be renewed when OCM renews licence (§ 342.22, subd. 3(c)) — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28. Non-retail businesses (cultivator, manufacturer, wholesaler, transporter, testing) do not need § 342.22 retail registration; still subject to local zoning certification under § 342.13(f).

Fees — statutory maxima, not statewide fee schedule

§ 342.22, subd. 2 verbatim:

“(a) A local unit of government may impose an initial retail registration fee of $500 or up to half the amount of the applicable initial license fee under section 342.11, whichever is less. The local unit of government may also impose a renewal retail registration fee of $1,000 or up to half the amount of the applicable renewal license fee under section 342.11, whichever is less. The initial registration fee shall include the fee for initial registration and the first annual renewal. Any renewal fee imposed by the local unit of government shall be charged at the time of the second renewal and each subsequent annual renewal thereafter.” “(b) The local unit of government may not charge an application fee.” “(c) Registration fees are nonrefundable.” — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28

Consequences: locality may charge less than maxima, and for licence types whose state initial fee is $0 (microbusiness) “half the state fee” limb can make local initial fee $0. LPHE retailer state fees produce $125 local figure in several local tables (half of $250). Initial fee covers first annual renewal; $1,000 (or half-fee) renewal charged only from second renewal onward. Business holding both cannabis retailer licence and medical cannabis retailer licence for same location may be charged only single registration fee in version of § 342.22, subd. 2(c) shown in 2025 extract — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, 2025 extract, Accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — paragraph not in current Revisor cite opened directly, which lists (c) as “Registration fees are nonrefundable”; do not quote single-fee rule without re-checking current supplement].

Issuance — locality must issue if statutory conditions met

§ 342.22, subd. 3(a): local unit “shall issue” registration to business that: (1) has valid licence or preliminary licence approval from OCM; (2) has paid fee; (3) is found in compliance at any preliminary compliance check locality performs; and (4) if applicable, is current on all property taxes and assessments at location — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28. Locality may conduct preliminary compliance check before issuance (§ 342.22, subd. 3(b)). May not invent additional denial grounds beyond Chapter 342 and lawful § 342.13 ordinances; OCM Guide states locality must issue after verifying licence/preliminary approval, fee, compliance, tax currency — OCM, Local Governments, Accessed 2026-10-28.

Compliance checks, suspension, penalty

  • § 342.22, subd. 4: locality shall conduct compliance checks of every registered retail business; at least once per calendar year, unannounced age-verification checks using persons at least 17 but under 21 (with parental consent if under 18) under direct supervision of law enforcement or local employee; must annually submit compliance-check data to OCM — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • § 342.22, subd. 5: locality may suspend registration up to 30 days if business violates § 342.13 local ordinance or poses immediate threat to public health/safety, must immediately notify OCM with grounds, and must reinstate if OCM orders reinstatement; no sale may be made without valid local registration and valid state licence/endorsement, with local civil penalty up to $2,000 per violation — Minn. Stat. § 342.22, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • § 342.13(g) (2024 lettering) expedited complaint process: OCM must give initial response within 7 days and perform necessary inspections within 30 days; if non-retail business poses immediate threat, OCM must respond within 1 business day — Minn. Stat. § 342.13, Revisor, Accessed 2026-10-28. Local enforcement of local ordinance expressly preserved.

Local process infrastructure (OCM)

OCM requires each local unit to (1) submit Contact and Delegation Form stating zoning/registration jurisdiction and point of contact, and (2) create Accela account for zoning-compliance certification — OCM, Contact and Delegation Form, Accessed 2026-10-28. OCM does not publish that delegation list as public roster in sources opened — see § 3.3, “Official lists.”

PART 4: LICENCE TYPES

Scope: Licence types only. Federal baseline taken as fixed: state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; 280E lifted for Schedule III medical, remains fully applicable to adult-use; hemp PL 119-37 §781 effective 12 November 2026, limited by PL 119-103 §2019 until 11 December 2026, then full total-THC definition plus 0.4 mg per container cap.

Direct-open limitation — read first. Revisor pages opened and read directly: §§342.10, 342.11, 342.14, 342.17, 342.28, 342.29, 342.30, 342.31. Parallel attempt to open §§342.32–342.35 and 342.40 returned browser-service 429 rate limit and was not retried. Facts for retailer, wholesaler, transporter, testing facility, delivery service, event organiser, LPHE and macrobusiness scope therefore rest on Revisor/OCM text returned via search index or OCM releases opened directly, flagged [VERIFY — direct Revisor open not completed] where they depend on that text. No fact presented as directly opened where it was not.

Current list — controlling point. Minn. Stat. §342.10, as now published by Revisor, lists 14 licence types: “(1) cannabis microbusiness; (2) cannabis mezzobusiness; (3) cannabis cultivator; (4) cannabis manufacturer; (5) cannabis retailer; (6) cannabis wholesaler; (7) cannabis transporter; (8) cannabis testing facility; (9) cannabis event organizer; (10) cannabis delivery service; (11) lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer; (12) lower-potency hemp edible wholesaler; (13) lower-potency hemp edible retailer; and (14) cannabis macrobusiness.” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.10 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Transition warning. Pre-2027 name was “medical cannabis combination business.” Revisor’s current §342.10 and §342.11 already list “cannabis macrobusiness” in its place, and 2026 omnibus law (Laws 2026, ch. 123) creates macrobusiness effective 1 January 2027, replacing combination business — Mondaq summary — Accessed 2026-10-28; House Research summary, Laws 2026 ch. 123 — Accessed 2026-10-28. In October 2026 combination business is still operating form; macrobusiness is enacted but not yet in effect. Any source describing macrobusiness as already operating in 2026 is wrong on timing.

1. Master table — fees, caps, canopy and retail footprint

Fees set in statute, not by rule. Minn. Stat. §342.11(a) provides, verbatim in substance: “The initial license fee shall include the fee for initial issuance of the license and the first annual renewal. The renewal fee shall be charged at the time of the second renewal and each subsequent annual renewal thereafter” and “Application fees, initial licensing fees, and renewal licensing fees are nonrefundable.” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.11 — Accessed 2026-10-28. No social-equity fee discount in §342.11 — secondary claim of “reduced” social-equity fees is not in statute and should not be repeated; social equity’s statutory benefit is lottery reservation and grant/loan priority (see §6).

Licence type Application fee Initial licence fee Renewal fee Statewide cap / lottery? Canopy / retail footprint

Cannabis wholesaler $5,000 $5,000 $10,000 Uncapped No canopy; business-to-business only

Event-organiser fee conflict — flagged, not smoothed over. Older summaries list event organiser as $750 application / $750 initial with no renewal fee. Revisor text opened lists $750 application, $0 initial, $750 renewal, plus $750 temporary cannabis event application fee. Current Revisor text followed; change consistent with 2026 move from temporary to annual event-organiser licence effective 1 January 2027 (see §2.10). Do not quote old $750/$750 pairing as current law.

Cap expiry — follow opened text, not secondary summaries. §342.14, subd. 1b(a), as opened: “Before July 1, 2027, the office may issue up to the maximum total number of licenses in each license category listed in paragraphs (b) and (c)” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.14 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Secondary sources stating “before July 1, 2026” appear to reflect pre-2026-amendment version. From 1 July 2027, §342.14, subd. 1b(d) requires OCM to determine numbers itself under market-stability goals, and “the number of licenses available to social equity applicants must be equal to or greater than the number of licenses available to all applicants” — same source. OCM is also “not required to issue licenses to meet the maximum number” (§342.14, subd. 1b(f)) — same source.

Canopy counting rule (all cultivation types). Plant canopy counts each tier of multi-tier setup; space used only for immature plants/seedlings does not count. Stated in secondary summaries of Chapter 342 and consistent with “mature, flowering plants” wording of §§342.28–342.30, but definitional section itself not directly opened — [VERIFY].

2. Detail by licence type

2.1 Cannabis microbusiness — §342.28 (direct open)

What it allows (verbatim scope). “A cannabis microbusiness license, consistent with the specific license endorsement or endorsements, entitles the license holder to perform any or all of the following within the limits established by this section: (1) grow cannabis plants from seed or immature plant to mature plant and harvest cannabis flower…; (2) make cannabis concentrate; (3) make hemp concentrate, including hemp concentrate with a delta-9 [THC] concentration of more than 0.3 percent…; (4) manufacture artificially derived cannabinoids; (5) manufacture adult-use cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, and hemp-derived consumer products…; (6) purchase [plants, flower, products, LPHE and hemp products] from another cannabis microbusiness, a cannabis mezzobusiness, a cannabis cultivator, a cannabis manufacturer, a cannabis wholesaler, a cannabis macrobusiness, a lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer, or a lower-potency hemp edible wholesaler; … (10) package and label… for sale to customers; (11) sell [plants, flower, products, LPHE and hemp products] to other cannabis businesses and to customers; (12) operate an establishment that permits on-site consumption of edible cannabis products and lower-potency hemp edibles; and (13) perform other actions approved by the office.” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.28 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Limits. “A cannabis microbusiness that cultivates cannabis at an indoor facility may cultivate up to 5,000 square feet of plant canopy” and outdoors “up to one-half acre of mature, flowering plants”; OCM may adjust upward for market demand, but “must not impose a limit of less than 5,000 square feet” / “less than one-half acre” in licensing period; manufacturing limit “must be equivalent to the amount of cannabis flower that can be harvested from a facility with a plant canopy of 5,000 square feet in a year”; “A cannabis microbusiness with the appropriate endorsement may operate one retail location” — same source.

Other-licence rule. Microbusiness holder “may also hold a cannabis event organizer license” and, except for that, “may [not] own or operate any other cannabis business or hemp business or hold more than one cannabis microbusiness license” — same source. Note: 2026 change removing general bar on holding both cannabis and hemp licence reported in secondary coverage; §342.28, subd. 5 text opened still states bar, so interaction [VERIFY against Laws 2026, ch. 123 as applied by OCM] before advising holder to add LPHE licence.

Labour-peace exception (unique to microbusiness). Labour-peace-agreement attestation “is not required as part of an application for a cannabis microbusiness license,” but on renewal microbusiness “with ten or more full-time equivalent employees must submit” one — same source.

On-site consumption. Only microbusiness (via endorsement) may permit on-site consumption, and only of edibles and LPHE — not smoked/vaped flower or products — in “definite and distinct” area with distinct entrance, not visible from outside, no alcohol/tobacco on site, no removal from area, no free samples, no sales to under-21s or visibly intoxicated persons — same source. No standalone “consumption lounge” licence in §342.10; any source listing one as Minnesota licence type is wrong.

Research variant. Regionally/nationally accredited higher-education institution (or partner) may hold microbusiness licence for cannabis crop research; research plants/flower “must not be offered for sale or otherwise enter the stream of commerce” — same source.

2.2 Cannabis mezzobusiness — §342.29 (direct open)

Same grow/make/buy/package/sell scope as microbusiness, plus expressly growing “for use as medical cannabis flower or for use in medical cannabinoid products” and “process[ing] medical cannabinoid products” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.29 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Limits. “A cannabis mezzobusiness that cultivates cannabis at an indoor facility may cultivate up to 15,000 square feet of plant canopy”; outdoors “up to one acre of mature, flowering plants unless the office increases that limit… to no more than three acres”; manufacturing limit equivalent to 15,000 sq ft harvest per year; “A cannabis mezzobusiness with the appropriate endorsement may operate up to three retail locations” — same source.

Two-endorsement rule. “Within 18 months of receiving a cannabis mezzobusiness license, a cannabis mezzobusiness must apply for and obtain at least two” of: cultivation, cannabis extraction/concentration, hemp extraction/concentration, artificially derived cannabinoids, edible handler, production of consumer products, or retail operations endorsements; failure may lead to suspension, revocation or non-renewal — same source.

Other-licence rule. Same as microbusiness: may also hold only event-organiser licence — same source.

2.3 Cannabis cultivator — §342.30 (direct open)

With cultivation endorsement, cultivator may “(1) grow cannabis plants within the approved amount of space from seed or immature plant to mature plant; (2) harvest cannabis flower…; (3) package and label immature cannabis plants and seedlings and cannabis flower for sale to other cannabis businesses; (4) sell [them] to other cannabis businesses; (5) transport cannabis flower to a cannabis manufacturer located on the same premises; and (6) perform other actions approved by the office” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.30 — Accessed 2026-10-28. No direct retail sales.

Limits. “A cannabis cultivator that cultivates cannabis at an indoor facility may cultivate up to 30,000 square feet of plant canopy”; outdoors “up to two acres… unless the office increases that limit… to no more than four acres” — same source.

Other-licence rule. Cultivator “may also hold a cannabis manufacturing license, license to grow industrial hemp, and cannabis event organizer license” and otherwise may not own/operate another cannabis or hemp business (same-premises transport to own manufacturer excepted); OCM may by rule limit how many cultivator licences one person/business may hold — same source.

2.4 Cannabis manufacturer — §342.31 (direct open)

Manufacturer licence, consistent with endorsements, entitles holder to purchase flower/products/hemp parts/concentrate/artificially derived cannabinoids from microbusinesses, mezzobusinesses, cultivators, other manufacturers and wholesalers; to “accept cannabis flower from unlicensed persons who are at least 21 years of age provided that the cannabis manufacturer does not accept more than two ounces from an individual on a single occasion”; to make cannabis and hemp concentrate (including hemp concentrate over 0.3% delta-9 by weight), manufacture artificially derived cannabinoids, manufacture adult-use products, LPHE and hemp-derived consumer products, package/label them, and “sell cannabis concentrate, hemp concentrate, artificially derived cannabinoids, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, and hemp-derived consumer products to other cannabis businesses” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.31 — Accessed 2026-10-28. No direct retail sales.

Limits. “The office shall establish a limit on the manufacturing of cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products a cannabis manufacturer may perform” — statute sets no numeric manufacturing cap itself; OCM rule figure not located — [UNAVAILABLE in sources opened; do not quote pounds figure as statute] — same source.

Other-licence rule. Manufacturer “may also hold a cannabis cultivator license and a cannabis event organizer license” and otherwise no other cannabis/hemp business (same-premises exception as cultivator); OCM may by rule limit number held — same source.

2.5 Cannabis retailer — §342.32 [VERIFY — direct open not completed]

Retailers sell immature plants/seedlings, cannabis flower, cannabis products, LPHE and hemp-derived consumer products and other lawfully authorised products to customers 21+ and to registered medical patients (where medically endorsed) — OCM Local Government Guide summary and §342.32 via search index — https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/OCM_Local_Government_Guide_5.0_2026_tcm1202-627967.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.32 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Limits. “A cannabis retailer may operate up to five retail locations”; “No person, cooperative, or business may hold a license to own or operate more than one cannabis retail business in one city and three retail businesses in one county” — §342.32 via search index, [VERIFY — direct open not completed].

Other-licence rule. Retailer “may also hold a cannabis delivery service license and a cannabis event organizer license” and otherwise no other cannabis/hemp business, except municipal store — §342.32 via search index, [VERIFY].

2.6 Cannabis wholesaler — §342.33 [VERIFY — direct open not completed]

Wholesalers buy and sell immature plants/seedlings, cannabis flower, cannabis products, LPHE and hemp-derived consumer products between licensed cannabis businesses, and “may also import hemp-derived consumer products and lower-potency hemp edibles” — OCM Local Government Guide — https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/OCM_Local_Government_Guide_5.0_2026_tcm1202-627967.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. No direct-to-consumer sales. Full §342.33 multiple-licence rule not opened — [VERIFY].

2.7 Cannabis transporter — §342.35 [VERIFY — direct open not completed]
