4. How licence is actually obtained — general requirements

All types share §342.14 pipeline (direct open — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.14 — Accessed 2026-10-28):

  1. Announcement. OCM “must announce the commencement of a licensing period in advance,” stating licence types available, any capped numbers, and open/close dates — §342.14, subd. 2.
  2. Application contents. Name/address/date of birth; ownership-and-control disclosure identifying every “true party of interest” (§342.185); bankruptcy disclosure; general location description and square footage (physical premises not required at application); security plan; trade-name registration; business plan (size, growth, record-keeping, knowledge/experience, environmental plan, finances/operations); standard operating procedures for quality assurance, inventory control/storage/diversion prevention, and accounting/tax compliance; labour-peace-agreement attestation (microbusiness initial application excepted — see §2.1); employee training description; violation disclosure; compliance certification; controlling-person/agent identification; agreement to respond to supplemental requests; background-check release (§342.15); social-equity proof where claimed; attestation that business policies comply with Chapter 342 — §342.14, subd. 1.
  3. Deficiency cure. 14 calendar days from deficiency notice or information request, or application may be denied/rejected — §342.14, subds. 2–3.
  4. Qualified applicant. Applicant not denied under subd. 3 “is a qualified applicant”; qualified status “expires after six months,” except “For an applicant who achieved qualified applicant status before June 1, 2026, qualified applicant status expires on January 1, 2027” — §342.14, subd. 3(f). Practical consequence for October 2026: pre-June 2026 qualified status about to lapse; re-application required after expiry.
  5. Lottery (capped types only). See §6.3.
  6. Background check → preliminary approval. OCM may conduct §342.15 background check before preliminary approval and must notify applicant of result and reasons for any refusal — §342.14, subd. 5. Selected lottery applicants must also provide “a signed labor peace agreement with a bona fide labor organization, securing a site location and approvals from local units of government, and submitting final business plans to OCM” — https://mn.gov/ocm/media/news-releases/?id=1202-690573 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  7. Final authorisation — 18-month clock. “Within 18 months of receiving notice of preliminary license approval, an applicant must provide” address/legal description, local unit of government, and any updated location/security information; OCM then forwards application to local unit for zoning (and fire/building code) certification, schedules site inspection, and requires payment of licence fee; OCM must grant final authorisation or send rejection “Within 90 days of receiving the information required under paragraph (a) and the results of any required background check” — §342.14, subd. 6. Preliminary approval “expires after 18 months unless” revoked or extended; OCM “must grant an initial extension of up to six months upon request” and “may grant an additional extension of up to six months if an applicant has made good faith efforts” — §342.14, subd. 10. Denial of application or final authorisation subject to OCM reconsideration, whose decision “is final” — §342.14, subd. 8.
  8. Retention of unselected applications. If lottery held, OCM “must retain the applications of any applicant not selected in the lottery for one year” and treat retained application as submitted in licensing period beginning within that year, with no additional application fee — §342.14, subd. 9.

Ownership/control limits not fully verified. Per-type multiple-licence rules in §2 above. Broader true-party-of-interest, passive-investment and percentage-ownership rules in §342.185 (including reported 33%-in-up-to-four-social-equity-businesses figure in secondary coverage) were not opened — [VERIFY before advising on investment structure]. Likewise, licence transferability and any three-year social-equity transfer restriction reported in secondary coverage were not verified against current §342.18/§342.21 — [VERIFY].

Local layer (not licence, but gate). Final authorisation requires local zoning certification, and retail locations require local retail registration under §342.22; local governments may cap retail registrations only at or above one per 12,500 residents per secondary summaries — [VERIFY against current §342.13/§342.22]. Licence without local registration does not authorise retail sales.

5. Medical cannabis combination business → macrobusiness, and how combination businesses serve both markets

5.1 What combination business was

Combination business was vertically integrated licence created for Minnesota’s two legacy medical operators to add adult-use sales. Secondary sources consistently describe footprint as up to 60,000 sq ft medical canopy plus up to 30,000 sq ft adult-use canopy (90,000 sq ft total) and one retail location per congressional district (i.e. up to 8 stores) — https://catalyst-bc.com/minnesota-cannabis-consulting/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Both figures secondary and governing §342.515 text not directly opened — [VERIFY against current §342.515 before quoting 60,000 + 30,000 split or per-district store rule as statute]. Two legacy medical operators identified in secondary coverage as Green Goods (Vireo) and RISE (Green Thumb Industries) — https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/mn_cannmir.html — Accessed 2026-10-28 — [VERIFY against OCM licence list; operator names secondary, not OCM-direct].

5.2 Conversion — mandatory, by 1 January 2027

  • 2026 omnibus law “requires OCM to convert all existing medical cannabis combination business licenses or applications to macrobusiness licenses or applications by January 1, 2027” — Mondaq — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • House Research summary of Laws 2026, ch. 123 likewise states section “convert[s] existing medical cannabis combination business licenses to cannabis macrobusiness licenses” effective 1 January 2027, and macrobusinesses must “obtain a medical cannabis manufacturing endorsement and at least one other medical cannabis endorsement” — House Research — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Canopy consequence — contested cut. Macrobusiness indoor canopy “up to 38,000 square feet” (AUDIT NOTE: the 90,000 figure in pre-ch. 123 material was a 60,000 sq ft medical + 30,000 sq ft adult-use combined footprint for combination businesses, and 90,000 lb is separately the interim macrobusiness manufacturing input cap in §342.295, subd. 3(a) until OCM sets a rule limit — it is not a canopy figure; do not compare 38,000 sq ft canopy directly with 90,000 lb input) with “an additional 2,000 square feet” after first renewal, “another 2,000” after second, and “an additional 3,000” after third, “provided the business remains in good standing” (38,000 → 45,000 sq ft) — same Mondaq source. One legislator reported as warning mid-stream cut “could invite litigation” — same source. No such macrobusiness-canopy litigation located — [UNAVAILABLE / no case found; do not assert challenge has or has not been filed].
  • Retail consequence. Up to 8 retail locations; macrobusiness “operating more than five retail locations must ensure that at least three are located in areas identified by OCM as high medical need areas,” and total number of macrobusiness licences capped at 8 before 1 January 2030 — same Mondaq source. Macrobusiness described as “the only license type that would be required to serve the medical market” — same source — [VERIFY: other licence types may serve medical patients via medical endorsements (see §5.3), so “only” should be read as “only type required to,” not “only type permitted to”].

5.3 How any licensee serves both markets — endorsements, not second licence

From 1 January 2027 separate medical/adult-use supply chains merge: 2026 law “eliminate[s], effective January 1, 2027, the requirement for cannabis businesses participating in both the medical and adult-use markets to maintain separate cultivation, manufacturing, and inventory tracking systems,” so “businesses holding a medical cannabis endorsement will be able to serve patients and adult-use customers from a single unified operation” — https://www.cann.dev/minnesota-cannabis-omnibus-bill-2026-3/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Most other 2026 provisions took effect 1 August 2026 — same source.

Endorsement mechanism already in directly opened text: - Microbusiness with cultivation endorsement “may apply for and obtain a medical cannabis cultivation endorsement” and may then cultivate up to 1,000 sq ft indoor / ¼ acre outdoor in addition to ordinary limits — §342.28, subd. 12 — Accessed 2026-10-28. - Mezzobusiness with cultivation endorsement may obtain medical cultivation endorsement adding up to 3,000 sq ft indoor / ½ acre outdoor; with medical manufacturer endorsement may manufacture up to 25% above ordinary manufacturing limit; with medical retail endorsement may operate up to two additional retail locations beyond 3-store limit “if at least two retail locations are located in an area identified by the office as a high medical need area” — §342.29, subds. 11–13 — Accessed 2026-10-28. - Cultivator with cultivation endorsement may obtain medical cultivation endorsement adding up to 6,000 sq ft indoor / 1 acre outdoor — §342.30, subd. 6 — Accessed 2026-10-28. - Manufacturers, microbusinesses and mezzobusinesses may obtain medical manufacturer endorsement (§§342.28, 342.29, 342.31) — Accessed 2026-10-28. - Retail/patient duties. Before distributing medical flower/products, business must confirm registry enrolment, verify recipient is patient, registered designated caregiver, parent, legal guardian or spouse, confirm consultation with certified medical cannabis consultant or licensed pharmacist (chapter 151) where required, apply patient-specific label with dosage, and provide other OCM-required information — §342.51 via bill/search text, [VERIFY — §342.51 not directly opened] — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/342.51/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. Business with medical retail endorsement may not deliver medical products unless it also holds delivery-service licence — same source. 2026 patient-protection additions — pharmacist-or-consultant staffing, priority service (dedicated lines, curbside pickup, advance ordering), mandatory stocking of OCM-identified high-medical-need products, and 24-hour fulfilment expectation for patient requests — reported in secondary coverage of Laws 2026, ch. 123 — [VERIFY against chapter 123 text] — https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/minnesota-governor-walz-signs-landmark-6632817/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

5.4 Schedule III / 280E split for combination/macrobusinesses — analysis, not Minnesota guidance

This paragraph applies commission’s fixed federal baseline; not statement of Minnesota law, and no Minnesota 280E guidance located.

  • Combination/macrobusiness sells two federally different products from one state licence: medical marijuana Schedule III after 28 April 2026, and adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I.
  • Under baseline, 280E lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use activity. Business therefore cannot treat whole operation as either “280E-free” or “280E-bound”: deductions must be allocated between medical and adult-use activity, and allocation method matters more after 1 January 2027 supply-chain unification, because cultivation, manufacturing and inventory will no longer be physically segregated by market.
  • What was not found — do not fill gaps by inference: (a) whether Minnesota conforms to federal 280E for Minnesota income tax, or decouples from it, for either market — [UNAVAILABLE in sources opened] (Note: Part 2, from statute text, concludes Minnesota DOES decouple via §290.0132 subd. 29 subtraction — coordinator reconciliation: Part 2’s statute-based conclusion supersedes Part 4’s “unavailable” on this point; see Part 2 §2.6); (b) any OCM or Minnesota Department of Revenue guidance on allocating shared costs between medical and adult-use sales in unified operation — [UNAVAILABLE]; (c) whether Minnesota treats sale to registered patient at retail location with medical endorsement differently for state cannabis-tax purposes than adult-use sale of same product — tax question, [UNAVAILABLE in Part 4 sources] (see Part 2 §2.4: gross receipts exempt for registry patients; sales-tax authority [VERIFY]). Any claim that macrobusiness “escapes 280E” is wrong as stated: at most, its medical activity escapes 280E under baseline, and only to extent allocation survives IRS scrutiny.

6. Social equity programme

6.1 Who qualifies — §342.17 (direct open)

“An applicant qualifies as a social equity applicant if the applicant:” — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.17 — Accessed 2026-10-28 (direct open):

“(1) was found delinquent for, received a stay of adjudication for, or was convicted of an offense involving the possession or sale of cannabis or marijuana prior to May 1, 2023; (2) had a parent, guardian, child, spouse, or dependent who was convicted of [such an offense] prior to May 1, 2023; (3) was a dependent of an individual who was convicted [of such an offense] prior to May 1, 2023; (4) is a military veteran, including a service-disabled veteran, current or former member of the national guard; (5) is a military veteran or current or former member of the national guard who lost honorable status due to an offense involving the possession or sale of cannabis or marijuana; (6) has been a resident for the last five years of one or more subareas, such as census tracts or neighborhoods: (i) that experienced a disproportionately large amount of cannabis enforcement…; (ii) where the poverty rate was 20 percent or more; (iii) where the median family income did not exceed 80 percent of the statewide median family income or, if in a metropolitan area, did not exceed the greater of 80 percent of the statewide median family income or 80 percent of the median family income for that metropolitan area; (iv) where at least 20 percent of the households receive assistance through [SNAP]; or (v) where the population has a high level of vulnerability according to the [CDC/ATSDR] Social Vulnerability Index; or (7) has participated in the business operation of a farm for at least three years and currently provides the majority of the day-to-day physical labor and management of a farm that had gross farm sales of at least $5,000 but not more than $100,000 in the previous year.”

For business entity, qualifications “apply to at least 65 percent of the controlling ownership of the business entity” — same source. Note what is absent: current §342.17 contains no income-threshold (e.g. “400% of federal poverty”) route and no “registered medical patient/caregiver” route; secondary sources listing those routes appear to describe proposals or other states — do not add them to Minnesota’s list.

6.2 Verification

OCM “must establish a procedure to verify” social-equity status for individual applicant or true party of interest, “may announce social equity applicant verification periods and may require verification… before the office accepts an application,” and “must issue a notice… stating that the office has verified the individual’s status… or that the office has been unable to verify” it — §342.14, subd. 1c — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.14 — Accessed 2026-10-28 (direct open). OCM verification page is operative source for documents accepted — specific document list not opened — [VERIFY on mn.gov/ocm before advising applicant what proof to file]. Secondary coverage notes “expungement paradox” (automatic sealing of pre-May 2023 cannabis records complicating proof of qualifying conviction) — [VERIFY — verification practice, not statute].

6.3 Lottery mechanics — §342.14, subd. 4 (direct open)

“If the number of qualified applicants who are verified social equity applicants seeking a type of license exceeds the number of licenses of that type that are made available for social equity applicants, the office must first conduct a lottery consisting of verified social equity applicants to select qualified applicants for preliminary license approval. If a social equity applicant is not selected in a lottery conducted under this paragraph, the office must include the social equity applicant in the pool of applicants for licenses of that type that are made available to all applicants.” Second lottery required if qualified applicants exceed general-pool licences. Every lottery “must be impartial, random, and in a format determined by the office,” and OCM must notify each entrant whether selected or not — https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.14 — Accessed 2026-10-28. In short: verified social-equity applicant gets two bites — reserved pool, then general pool.

6.4 Grants and loans — OCM Division of Social Equity + DEED

OCM grants page: “Minnesota’s cannabis law established several grant programs that provide funding for technical assistance, financial capital, and workforce training,” run through “OCM’s Division of Social Equity” — https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/grants/ — Accessed 2026-10-28:

  • CanGrow (OCM) — “grants to eligible organizations to help farmers navigate the regulatory structure… and to nonprofits to fund loans to farmers for expansion.” First-round training awards reported as $10,000–$50,000 per project and loan-fund awards $200,000–$500,000 per organisation (individual farmer loans $2,500–$50,000, up to $150,000 with matching funds) — OCM press release via GovDelivery, [VERIFY amounts against current CanGrow RFP — press-release figures, not current award notice] — https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MNOCM/bulletins/3dcfd71 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Secondary coverage reports first CanGrow round announced April 2026 of four $50,000 training grants plus one $382,910 loan grant — [VERIFY].
  • CanRenew (OCM) — “grants to eligible organizations for investments in communities where long-term residents are eligible to be social equity applicants.” First-year funding announced August 2025 reported as $1 million to 11 organisations (AUDIT CORRECTION — not 12) from 145 proposals seeking over $55.9 million; grants page notes request for proposals open through 4:30 p.m. CT on 15 December (year not stated on snippet) — OCM grants page + secondary coverage, [VERIFY current RFP year/deadline on mn.gov/ocm] — same OCM grants link, Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • CanStartup (DEED) — “a loan program available to new cannabis microbusinesses. DEED will award funds to nonprofit corporations…; selected nonprofit will use funds to provide loans to eligible cannabis microbusinesses, with priority given to social equity applicants” — same OCM grants link. DEED announcement lists CanStartup grantee lenders including Propagate Community Development Corporation ($500,000), Seward Redesign ($100,000) and WomenVenture ($500,000) — https://mn.gov/deed/newscenter/press-releases/?id=1045-702706 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • CanNavigate (DEED) — grants to organisations “to help people navigate the regulatory structure… and develop technical assistance resources or navigation services” — same OCM grants link.
  • CanTrain (DEED) — grants to organisations “to develop and implement a workforce development program” for cannabis careers — same OCM grants link; DEED grantees reported include Minneapolis Community and Technical College ($403,530), Minnesota Training Partnerships ($126,116), Minnesota Cannabis College ($250,000), Urban League Twin Cities ($320,000) and White Earth Tribal and Community College ($500,000) — same DEED link.

What social equity does not do: does not reduce §342.11 fees, does not waive background checks, labour-peace agreements (except microbusiness initial-application exception), local zoning certification or site inspection, and does not exempt holder from capped numbers — it reserves half capped licences and gives two lottery entries plus grant/loan priority.

7. How licences were actually awarded — pre-approval, litigation, settlement, lotteries

7.1 Pre-approval design and collapse (2024)

Legislature created one-time pre-approval lottery to give operationally ready, verified social-equity applicants head start. OCM scheduled it for 26 November 2024. Denied applicants sued in Ramsey County District Court, and on 25 November 2024 court stayed lottery — HinshawLaw — Accessed 2026-10-28. OCM then cancelled pre-approval process in December 2024 and pivoted to standard licensing cycle open to both social-equity and general applicants — Cannabis Law Report — Accessed 2026-10-28.

7.2 Court of Appeals — Calm Waters

In In re Calm Waters Cannabis Co. v. Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Minnesota Court of Appeals No. A24-1936 (2025), seven applicants approved for pre-approval lottery sought writ of prohibition to stop district court from enforcing injunction against OCM. Court “dissolve[d] the stay and den[ied] the petition because petitioners have not demonstrated that the district court exceeded its authority in enjoining OCM from conducting the lottery or that they lacked any other adequate remedy” — https://law.justia.com/cases/minnesota/court-of-appeals/2025/a24-1936.html — Accessed 2026-10-28. Outcome: Court of Appeals did not restore pre-approval lottery; left district court’s injunction in place and left approved applicants to other remedies — which mandamus/settlement track in §7.3 then supplied. Opinion’s exact filing date and any subsequent review not captured in snippet — [VERIFY docket/date on Minnesota Judicial Branch site before citing pinpoint date].

7.3 Mandamus and QAPL settlement (April–May 2025)

On 4 April 2025, Ramsey County District Court Judge Stephen L. Smith granted writ of mandamus in favour of pre-approved applicants’ group, holding Minnesota law requires OCM to conduct lottery when qualified applicants exceed available licences, that 648 pre-approved social-equity applicants had no adequate legal remedy, and delay harmed fair market entry; OCM ordered to conduct lottery in “impartial, random” format — JD Supra — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note tension: April 2025 mandamus ordered lottery, while earlier stay blocked pre-approval lottery — two orders address different lotteries (pre-approval vs. standard-cycle), and summary collapsing them into “court ordered, then cancelled, lottery” is misleading.

On 30 May 2025, OCM and Qualified Applicants for a Preapproval Lottery (QAPL) settled. Under settlement: (a) applicants approved for pre-approval lottery as of 25 November 2024 “will now receive prioritization at every stage of the licensing process, including background checks, labor peace agreement reviews, plan of record approvals, and site inspections”; (b) OCM “has agreed to carry forward applications that are not selected in the upcoming lottery into the next round”; and (c) State “has agreed to partially reimburse QAPL for legal costs” — QAPL settlement press release PDF — Accessed 2026-10-28; Blunt Strategies — Accessed 2026-10-28. Settlement is prioritisation agreement, not licence grant — did not itself award any capped licence, and dollar amount for legal-cost reimbursement not stated in sources opened — [UNAVAILABLE].

7.4 Standard cycle — window, vetting and lotteries (2025)

OCM announced it would accept applications “beginning February 18 and ending March 14” 2025, from verified social-equity applicants and general applicants, for microbusiness, mezzobusiness, cultivator, manufacturer, retailer, wholesaler, transporter, testing facility, delivery service and medical cannabis combination business; event-organiser applications would follow later in summer 2025 and LPHE manufacturer/retailer applications in fall 2025; “cities or counties wishing to operate a single municipal cannabis store may apply for a retailer license during the application window” and municipal licences are “not subject to a lottery” — OCM release — Accessed 2026-10-28; OCM release — Accessed 2026-10-28 (both direct OCM releases). Window-date conflict flagged: some secondary sources give 16 March 2025 as close; OCM announcement itself says 14 March, and OCM date followed here.

5 June 2025 — first lotteries (OCM direct release). OCM held lotteries for social-equity and general applicants in capped types — cultivator, manufacturer, mezzobusiness — plus social-equity retailer lottery. Pools and licences available, as published by OCM — https://mn.gov/ocm/media/news-releases/?id=1202-690573 — Accessed 2026-10-28 (direct open):

Type Awaiting lottery — social-equity Awaiting lottery — general Available — social-equity Available — general
Cultivator 51 42 25 25
Manufacturer 41 38 12 12
Mezzobusiness 207 41 50 50
Retailer 356 N/A (second lottery) 75 75 (second lottery)

Lotteries livestreamed, run with Smartplay International drawing systems and Baker Tilly oversight; selected applicants still had to pass background checks, sign labour-peace agreement, secure site and local approvals, and submit final business plans — same OCM release. “Nearly a thousand applicants have reached qualified status and just under 400 more are preliminarily approved” for uncapped types (testing, wholesaler, microbusiness, transporter, delivery, medical combination) at that date — same OCM release. Arithmetic check: 25+25+12+12+50+50+75 = 249 capped licences selected on 5 June.

22 July 2025 — second (retailer general) lottery. OCM held “a lottery for general applicants for the cannabis retailer license, including a second chance for social equity applicants not selected in the first lottery” — https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/licensing/lottery/lottery-results.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28. Secondary reporting puts pool at 569 eligible applicants and 75 selected — Weedworthy — Accessed 2026-10-28 — [VERIFY 569 pool figure against OCM lottery-results page; 75 licences and 22 July date OCM-confirmed]. Total capped licences selected across both lotteries: 249 + 75 = 324 (selections, not issued licences — selection ≠ licence until background, labour-peace, site, local approval and inspection complete).

Subsequent windows (OCM). Testing-facility applications opened 1 August 2025 on ongoing basis and event-organiser applications opened later in summer 2025 on rolling basis; LPHE retailer, manufacturer and wholesaler applications opened 1 October–31 October 2025 — https://mn.gov/ocm/media/news-releases/?id=1202-690573 — Accessed 2026-10-28; https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MNOCM/bulletins/3e7f33e — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Issued-licence counts — secondary, conflicting, use with care. Secondary sources report 135 licences issued at 30 December 2025 (from 3,540 applicants, 1,390 preliminarily approved), 184 licences in April 2026, and 369 licensed businesses in September 2026, plus 153 adult-use retailers / 23 medical dispensaries / 62 cultivation / 30 manufacturing / 7 transport / 6 testing sites in May 2026 — CannBus — Accessed 2026-10-28; CannBus legal summary — Accessed 2026-10-28. Figures come from different snapshots/definitions (issued vs. operating vs. preliminarily approved) and were not confirmed against OCM Summary Application Data page in this session — [VERIFY against OCM current dashboard before quoting any single “licences issued” total]. (Coordinator note: Part 5’s directly opened OCM table at 19 Oct 2026 — 405 cannabis issued — supersedes these secondary snapshots as latest OCM baseline.) OCM June 2025 release directs readers to Summary Application Data page for up-to-date numbers — https://mn.gov/ocm/media/news-releases/?id=1202-690573 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

5.6 OCM — Social equity verification and social-equity licence statistics

  • Qualifications page: https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/equity/qualifications.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28
  • Holder/applicant type: Social equity applicants (individuals meeting at least one statutory criterion).
  • Format: Informational web page + Social Equity Verification Map (ArcGIS, linked from page). No verification-count dashboard described on qualifications page itself.
  • Criteria (as listed by OCM): Prior cannabis possession/sale conviction/delinquency/stay before 1 May 2023 (self or parent/guardian/child/spouse/dependent); military veteran / service-disabled veteran / current-former National Guard member, including loss of honourable status due to cannabis offence; five-year residency in qualifying areas (high enforcement, ≥20% poverty, median family income ≤80% of statewide/metro median as specified, ≥20% SNAP households, high CDC Social Vulnerability Index); or ≥3 years farm operations with majority day-to-day labour/management and $5,000–$100,000 gross sales in previous year — https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/equity/qualifications.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Verification statistics — what exists and what does not: What exists: Social-equity vs general breakdowns inside Summary Application Data tables (§5.2). Examples at 19 Oct 2026 — licences issued, social-equity vs general: testing 0 vs 5; cultivator 22 vs 2; mezzobusiness 24 vs 2; microbusiness 107 vs 189; medical combination 0 vs 3; manufacturer 2 vs 1; transporter 4 vs 8; wholesaler 2 vs 8; retailer social-equity 13 vs general 5 (plus municipal 2, not split by equity in table) — https://mn.gov/ocm/data-reports/application-data/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. What exists (historical): At close of 2025, more than half (55%) of 118 licences issued were to social-equity-qualifying businesses, and four licence types were 100% social-equity at that point (cultivators, manufacturers, mezzobusinesses, retailers) — https://mn.gov/ocm/media/news-releases/?id=1202-719775 — Accessed 2026-10-28. What does NOT exist as standalone source: published count of verified social equity individuals (as distinct from applicants/businesses counted as social-equity in licence table) was not located on opened OCM page — [UNAVAILABLE] as standalone verification-statistics release. OCM also notes it was unable to conduct § 342.04(b) study identifying high-enforcement areas due to lack of relevant data, and invites applicant-submitted studies — https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/equity/qualifications.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Limitations: Verification is pre-licensing status, not licence. Secondary guides describe verification as rolling/ongoing and free [VERIFY] — not confirmed on qualifications page text opened here.

  • Status: [UNAVAILABLE] as standalone register. No OCM page opened presents searchable list of enforcement actions, suspensions, revocations, fines by licensee, or disciplinary-action download. Do not present local or tax-posting lists below as substitute for OCM disciplinary register.

Direct file: https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/OCM_Local_Government_Guide_5.0_2026_tcm1202-627967.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. File name as in URL: OCM_Local_Government_Guide_5.0_2026_tcm1202-627967.pdf. Guide states local governments can submit complaints via OCM enforcement complaint reporting form; OCM expedited complaint process requires initial response within 7 days and inspections within 30 days, and within 1 business day if local government reports immediate threat to public health/safety; local governments can refuse/suspend retail registration for specified reasons (no valid licence, unpaid fee, noncompliance with preliminary/renewal compliance check, local-ordinance noncompliance, immediate threat) and must immediately notify OCM of suspension, after which OCM may reinstate or take enforcement action — same PDF, Accessed 2026-10-28. PART 6: MARKET DATA

6.1 Headline: adult-use sales HAVE begun

  • State-licensed adult-use retail sales in Minnesota began 16 September 2025. OCM: “State-licensed businesses across the state began retail sales of adult-use cannabis one year ago this week, on Sept. 16, 2025, following the beginning of cannabis retail sales on Tribally regulated lands shortly after the passage of the original cannabis bill in August 2023.” Source: OCM press release, 15 Sept 2026, via GovDelivery — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Conflict on launch date, resolved in favour of OCM: some secondary summaries give 17 September 2025. The 16 September date is used throughout; 17 September retained only as noted alternative. Source for alternative: CannBus Minnesota Q3 2026 report — Accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — live dashboard / OCM launch notice to confirm day-count convention].
  • Medical: Minnesota’s first medical dispensary sales began 1 July 2015, registration from 1 June 2015 (background only). Source: Marijuana Policy Project implementation timeline — Accessed 2026-10-28.

6.3 Tribal dispensary sales

  • No officially reported tribal sales total was located — [UNAVAILABLE]. OCM’s $250 million+ figure is for state-licensed businesses; OCM states lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) sales are not in seed-to-sale tracking — a fortiori, no OCM tribal-sales series is published in sources opened.
  • Tribal retail sales on tribally regulated land began shortly after the original cannabis bill passed in August 2023, before state-licensed sales. Source: OCM press release, 15 Sept 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Between May 2025 and March 2026, Minnesota entered intergovernmental agreements — compacts and a cooperative agreement — with nine of the 11 federally recognized Tribal Nations sharing territory with Minnesota. Source: OCM press release, 15 Sept 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Same release’s infographic repeats “9 cooperative agreements and cannabis compacts signed with Tribal Nations.” Source: OCM, “One Year In” infographic, Sept 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Named tribal operators in secondary reporting include Red Lake Nation’s NativeCare, White Earth’s Waabigwan Mashkiki (Moorhead, St. Cloud, Mahnomen, plus East Grand Forks in 2026, under a compact authorising up to eight off-reservation sites), Mille Lacs Band’s Lake Leaf, and Prairie Island’s Island Peži — secondary only, not sales figures. Sources: GovDelivery, Red Lake cooperative agreement release and MN Cannabis Hub, Waabigwan Mashkiki East Grand Forks article, May 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Secondary claim of “13 tribal cannabis dispensaries operated by eight sovereign nations, as of early 2026” located but not adopted as official; conflicts in count basis with nine-agreements figure (agreements ≠ stores) — [VERIFY]. Source: MN Cannabis Hub, Red Lake agreement article — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Tax note: sales on tribally regulated land by a tribally licensed business are carved out of Minnesota’s cannabis gross receipts tax and use tax in statute; off-reservation tribal stores do not automatically carry that carve-out. Source: Minn. Stat. ch. 295, via Revisor — Accessed 2026-10-28.

6.4 Tax collections — cannabis + LPHE combined only

  • $45.6 million in tax revenue for the 10-month period September 2025 to July 2026, combining cannabis and LPHE sales, described by OCM as “the latest figures available from the Minnesota Department of Revenue (DOR).” Source: OCM press release, 15 Sept 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Rate (official statute): 15% gross receipts tax on retail sales of taxable cannabis products, in addition to any other tax on the sale. Source: Minn. Stat. §295.81, via Revisor — Accessed 2026-10-28. Secondary sources consistently report the rate rose from 10% to 15% on 1 July 2025 and that the 6.875% state sales tax sits on top, with medical purchases exempt from gross receipts tax (§295.81, subd. 4(b)) — but the medical sales-tax exemption remains [VERIFY] (see audit) — but the DOR cannabis-tax guidance page itself was not opened directly in this pass, so the sales-tax layer and medical exemption are flagged [VERIFY against revenue.state.mn.us]. Source for secondary rate history: Fox 9, 15 Sept 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Split unavailable: OCM states LPHE sales “are not required to be tracked in the state’s seed-to-sale monitoring system, so sales figures for those products are not available.” No cannabis-only vs. LPHE-only split of the $45.6 million located — [UNAVAILABLE]. Source: OCM press release, 15 Sept 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Dashboard caveat (official): OCM states the Market Monitor “is not used to calculate approximate tax revenue generated from the cannabis taxes” — DOR tracks cannabis tax, sales and use tax, and other state taxes. Do not derive tax revenue by applying 15% to Market Monitor sales. Source: OCM, 15 Jan 2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
