Minnesota Cannabis & Hemp Research — Run 2, Part 7: Hemp Licences

Scope of this part: Every Minnesota hemp licence type — Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA) industrial hemp licences, Office of Cannabis Management (OCM) lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) licences, hemp-derived topical products, research, and tribal hemp licences/plans — plus the state-plan question, registries/holder data, licence counts by year, and the effect of the 12 November / 11 December 2026 federal hemp dates on each licence type.

Run 1 baseline carried forward (not re-litigated here; contradictions flagged, not silently overwritten): State-licensed adult-use sales began 16 September 2025; first-year combined sales >$250 million; tax $45.6 million September 2025–July 2026 (combined cannabis + LPHE, scope unstated). Latest licence baseline OCM 19 October 2026: 405 cannabis + 2,031 LPHE licences issued; no single open-store count adopted. Tax 15% gross receipts + 6.875% state sales tax; medical gross-receipts exempt; Minnesota DOES decouple from federal §280E via Minn. Stat. §290.0132, subd. 29. 2026 omnibus SF 4401 / Laws 2026, ch. 123, signed 26 May 2026, mostly effective 1 August 2026; macrobusiness effective 1 January 2027, capped at 8 through 2030. OCM position: the federal 11 December 2026 0.4 mg THC/container hemp cap does not change Minnesota LPHE law, but LPHE packages over 0.4 mg will become federally noncompliant; no Minnesota legislative fix found as of 28 October 2026.

Federal baseline applied here (fixed, not re-researched): State-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; §280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical only; hemp PL 119-37 §781 effective 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-lab enforcement delayed to 31 December 2026; federal medical appropriations rider through 11 December 2026; no federal cannabis banking law.

Sourcing and dating convention: Every fact below carries a source link and “Accessed 2026-10-28” (live reads were made on the evening of 28 October 2026 U.S. Central time). Official pages were opened and read directly; search snippets were not relied on for law. Where a page could not be opened, or a fact could not be verified on an official source, it is marked [VERIFY] or [UNAVAILABLE]. No personal telephone numbers or personal email addresses of individuals are reproduced in this part. Minnesota townships are given with county where a county is stated in the source; no same-name out-of-state place is used for any Minnesota fact below.

Headline finding: Minnesota does not have one hemp licence. It has two separate licensing regimes that must not be conflated: (1) the MDA industrial hemp licence under Minn. Stat. ch. 18K, which since the USDA-approved 17 November 2025 plan revision is a single comprehensive licence with grower and/or processor categories and registered locations — it covers growing and raw-hemp processing for grain, fiber and (historically) cannabinoid biomass, but since 2026 it does not cover extraction/manufacture/marketing/sale of hemp-derived cannabinoid products, which moved to OCM; and (2) the OCM LPHE licences under Minn. Stat. ch. 342 (manufacturer, wholesaler, retailer), which cover only lower-potency hemp edibles. Hemp-derived topical products need no licence at all under §342.66. Tribal hemp production is a third, separate track: three Minnesota tribes hold USDA-approved tribal plans and two hold USDA hemp producer licences, and none of those is a state licence.

7.1 The two regimes at a glance

Regime Issuer Governing law What it licenses What it does NOT license
Industrial hemp MDA, Plant Protection Division, Industrial Hemp Program Minn. Stat. ch. 18K; Minn. R. ch. 1565; USDA-approved Minnesota State Hemp Plan Growing industrial hemp for commercial or research purposes; processing industrial hemp for commercial purposes (raw hemp into a product); selling hemp fiber products and hemp grain; manufacturing hemp-derived topical products (see §342.65) Growth or sale of adult-use or medical cannabis; extraction, manufacture, marketing or sale of hemp-derived cannabinoid products (OCM since 2026)
Lower-potency hemp edibles OCM Minn. Stat. ch. 342, §§342.43–342.46, §342.11 (fees), §342.44 (application/transfer); Minn. R. ch. 9810 Manufacture, wholesale and retail sale of lower-potency hemp edibles (including beverages and tinctures meeting the LPHE definition) Growing or raw processing of industrial hemp (MDA); hemp-derived consumer products other than LPHEs, which are limited to cannabis-business licensees (see §7.4); hemp-derived topicals (no licence required)

Sources: MDA 2026-season notice — MDA, “Minnesota Hemp Growers and Processors Must Apply by April 30 for 2026 Season” (Accessed 2026-10-28); Minn. Stat. §342.65 — Revisor, §342.65 (Accessed 2026-10-28); Minn. Stat. §342.43 — Revisor, §342.43 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Boundary rule to keep in every later part: An MDA hemp licensee is not thereby an OCM LPHE licensee, and an OCM LPHE licensee is not thereby an MDA hemp licensee. The two licences can be held together (see §7.3.5), but each authorises only its own activities. The MDA’s own 2026 notice states the point in terms: the MDA licence “is not for the growth or sale of adult-use or medical cannabis” and “is not intended for the sale of hemp-derived cannabinoid products”; “[t]he extraction of cannabinoids derived from hemp is now regulated by the OCM.” Source: MDA 2026-season notice (Accessed 2026-10-28).

7.2 MDA industrial hemp licence (Chapter 18K)

7.2.1 One comprehensive licence since 17 November 2025 — Run 1 note VERIFIED

Run 1 noted a revised State Plan consolidating grower + processor into one licence, USDA-approved 17 November 2025. Verified against both MDA and USDA-linked sources.

  • The MDA’s 2025 Hemp Program Annual Report (prepared January 2026) states: “The Minnesota State Hemp Plan was revised in late 2025 to consolidate two license types into one comprehensive hemp license. The revised plan was approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) on November 17, 2025.” Source: MDA, 2025 Hemp Program Annual Report (PDF, Feb 2026 posting) (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • The same report’s history section adds: “On November 17, 2025, another revision of the Minnesota State Plan was approved by the USDA. This revision consolidated grower and processor license types into one hemp license. The current Minnesota plan is available on the USDA Domestic Hemp Program website.” Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Consequence for how counts are read: the 2025 annual report still tabulates “Licensed Growers” and “Licensed Processors” separately for 2025 and warns “Some licensees hold both grower and processor license categories; and therefore, are double counted” (see §7.7). From the 2026 licence year the fee schedule likewise has no separate processor licence fee (see §7.2.3). The licence is therefore best described as one MDA hemp licence, with grower and/or processor categories and one or more registered grow or processing locations, not as two freestanding licences.
  • The USDA plan document itself is titled “Minnesota Industrial Hemp Plan,” revision dated 16 September 2025, Minnesota Department of Agriculture, 625 Robert Street North, St. Paul, MN 55155. Source: USDA AMS, Minnesota Industrial Hemp Plan (PDF) (Accessed 2026-10-28). The file name as posted by USDA AMS is MinnesotaIndustrialHempPlan.pdf. Whether the USDA-posted PDF is the 16 September 2025 revision as approved 17 November 2025, or an earlier revision of the same file name, could not be confirmed from the document’s face in this read [VERIFY — plan PDF version/date against the USDA approval letter; do not cite the PDF’s internal revision date as the approval date].

7.2.2 What the MDA licence allows — verbatim statute

Licence requirement. Minn. Stat. §18K.04, subd. 1(a) (current text, Revisor):

“A person must obtain a license from the commissioner before (1) growing industrial hemp, (2) processing industrial hemp, or (3) researching industrial hemp.”

Source: Revisor, §18K.04 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Chapter 342 savings clause. Minn. Stat. §342.65 (current text, Revisor):

“Nothing in this chapter shall limit the ability of a person licensed under chapter 18K to grow industrial hemp for commercial or research purposes, process industrial hemp for commercial purposes, sell hemp fiber products and hemp grain, manufacture hemp-derived topical products, or perform any other actions authorized by the commissioner of agriculture. For purposes of this section, ‘processing’ has the meaning given in section 18K.02, subdivision 5, and does not include the process of creating artificially derived cannabinoids.”

Source: Revisor, §342.65 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Definitions that set the boundary. Minn. Stat. §18K.02 (current text, Revisor):

  • Subd. 3, “Industrial hemp”: “the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of the plant, whether growing or not, including the plant’s seeds, and all the plant’s derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of not more than 0.3 percent on a dry weight basis. Industrial hemp is not marijuana as defined in section 152.01, subdivision 9.” Source: Revisor, §18K.02 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 5, “Processing”: “rendering by refinement hemp plants or hemp plant parts from their natural or original state after harvest. Processing includes but is not limited to decortication, devitalization, chopping, crushing, extraction, and packaging. Processing does not include typical farm operations such as sorting, grading, baling, and harvesting. Processing does not include the production of artificially derived cannabinoids as defined in section 342.01, subdivision 6.” Source: Revisor, §18K.02 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 7, “Processor”: “a person or business that converts raw hemp into a product.” Source: Revisor, §18K.02 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 6, “Processing location”: “any area, building, plant, or facility registered with and approved by the commissioner in which a licensee converts raw hemp into a marketable product.” Source: Revisor, §18K.02 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Practical reading of “allows” (and its limits):

  • Growing: yes, for commercial or research purposes, at registered locations (§18K.04, subd. 1(c) requires the grow application to include name/address and “the legal description of the land area or areas where industrial hemp will be grown” plus any other information required under 7 CFR part 990). A person licensed to grow “is presumed to be growing industrial hemp for commercial or research purposes” (§18K.04, subd. 1(g)). Sources: Revisor, §18K.04 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Processing: yes — converting raw hemp into a product (fiber, grain, and other raw-hemp products) at a registered processing location. The 2025 annual report’s processor definition is identical in substance: “A processor is defined as any person or business that converts raw hemp into a product.” Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Research: yes — §18K.04, subd. 1(a)(3) requires a licence before “researching industrial hemp,” and §342.65 preserves growing “for commercial or research purposes.” There is no separate MDA “research licence” type in the statute or in MDA’s 2026 application materials located for this part; research is an authorised purpose of the single licence, not a distinct licence class [VERIFY — confirm against Minn. R. ch. 1565 research provisions; the rule text was located only in summary/search form for this part and was not opened in full].
  • Sale of plant parts / propagules / concentrate, and sale to Chapter 342 businesses: this is where the two regimes meet, and it must be stated as a chain, not as a single MDA permission:
  • An MDA licensee may sell hemp fiber products and hemp grain (§342.65, quoted above).
  • An MDA licensee may not sell a hemp crop, or transfer ownership of it, until it has passed MDA testing and received a Fit for Commerce certificate: MDA’s FAQ states, “all hemp crops must be tested by the Minnesota Department of Agriculture, pass the THC Test, and have an issued Fit for Commerce certificate prior to transferring ownership of the crop. Selling or transferring ownership of hemp crop without a Fit for Commerce certificate is a violation.” Source: MDA, FAQs Regarding Minnesota’s Hemp Program (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Downstream, a Chapter 342 LPHE manufacturer may “purchase hemp plant parts and propagules from industrial hemp growers licensed under chapter 18K” and “purchase hemp concentrate from an industrial hemp processor licensed under chapter 18K” (Minn. Stat. §342.45, subd. 1(2)–(3); see §7.3.2). Likewise a cannabis macrobusiness may purchase hemp plant parts/propagules from an 18K grower and hemp concentrate from an 18K processor under the current Chapter 342 text. That is the statutory bridge by which MDA-licensed material enters the Chapter 342 system; it does not make the MDA licence itself a cannabinoid-product licence.
  • Cannabinoid extraction sits on the OCM side of the line from 2026: MDA’s 2026 notice says extraction of cannabinoids derived from hemp “is now regulated by the OCM” and “Those interested in cannabinoid processing will need a license from the OCM,” and that the MDA “does not license or oversee the manufacture or sale of hemp-derived cannabinoid extracts and products.” Source: MDA 2026-season notice (Accessed 2026-10-28). Note the tension with §18K.02, subd. 5, which still lists “extraction” among processing activities: the reconciliation in the current framework is that §18K.02 processing “does not include the production of artificially derived cannabinoids,” and §342.65 likewise excludes artificially derived cannabinoids from its savings clause, while cannabinoid products for human consumption are OCM-regulated. Whether ordinary (non-artificially-derived) hemp-concentrate extraction by an MDA processor remains lawful without an OCM licence, or requires an OCM LPHE manufacturer licence plus an extraction-and-concentration endorsement, is not stated unambiguously on the MDA pages read and is flagged [VERIFY — coordinator to reconcile §18K.02 subd. 5 “extraction” against OCM’s 2026 position and §342.45, subd. 3 endorsement requirements before publishing a one-line rule].

7.2.3 MDA fees — Run 1 figures VERIFIED for 2026, with one correction

Run 1 figures are confirmed for the 2026 licence year on MDA’s own returning-applicant page, with the clarification that the old separate $250 processor licence fee is gone (which is exactly what the single-licence consolidation implies).

MDA 2026 fees (all non-refundable, non-transferable), as posted for returning applicants:

Item 2026 fee
Hemp licence $150
Each location (grow or processing) $250
Minimum cost (licence + one location) $400
Each sample for THC testing $100
Each inspection beyond the first $250
Licence change fee (after the initial application period — e.g. changing the licence holder’s name, adding a grower or processor category, adding/changing grow or processing locations, via Change Request Form) $50

Source: MDA, Application Instructions for Returning Applicants (Accessed 2026-10-28), which states: “The MDA is required to collect annual fees for registration of sites and certification of hemp crops through THC testing. All fees are non-refundable non-transferrable. There is a $50 fee for all license changes made after the initial application period.” and “PLEASE NOTE: THE MINIMUM COST OF A GROWER LICENSE IS $400 ($150 + $250 FOR ONE LOCATION). EACH LICENSE MUST HAVE A MINIMUM OF ONE REGISTERED LOCATION.”

  • Processor fee correction: MDA’s 2026-season notice states: “There is no longer a $250 license fee for processors.” Source: MDA 2026-season notice (Accessed 2026-10-28). Any pre-2026 table showing a $500 minimum processor licence ($250 licence + $250 location) is therefore stale for 2026 and must not be carried forward.
  • THC testing fee detail: “Every hemp variety planted is considered a separate lot and must be reported and tested separately. The licensee will be invoiced for each sample taken. The fee of one THC test is $100. If more than one variety is grown, each one will be sampled separately and invoiced after the inspection at $100 per variety. If more than one inspection at a location during the year is required, then the licensee will be invoiced $250 for the additional inspection, plus $100 per THC test beyond the first one.” Source: MDA returning-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • 5% surcharge — VERIFIED, with statutory citation: “As part of our ongoing efforts to improve our services, the Minnesota Department of Agriculture is introducing a license and permit surcharge (MINN. STAT. 17.033). This surcharge is an application processing charge that will be added to all licensing and permitting applications and renewals beginning Jan. 1, 2025. The surcharge will be calculated as 5% of the license or permit fee, with a minimum charge of $5.” Source: MDA returning-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28). The 2026-season notice confirms the surcharge continues in 2026: “A 5% license surcharge is added to support modernization of the MDA’s technology systems.” Source: MDA 2026-season notice (Accessed 2026-10-28). Worked minimum: $400 × 5% = $20 surcharge, so a one-location 2026 licence costs $420 before any sampling/inspection/change fees. (Arithmetic is this part’s, from the two posted figures.)
  • Statutory fee authority: §18K.04, subd. 1(b) requires the applicant to “pay the annual registration and inspection fee established by the commissioner in accordance with section 16A.1285, subdivision 2.” Source: Revisor, §18K.04 (Accessed 2026-10-28). The dollar figures above are therefore MDA-posted fees under that authority, not figures written into Chapter 18K itself.

7.2.4 MDA requirements: window, expiry, background check, sampling/testing, reporting

Application window and expiry.

  • 2026: applications were due 30 April 2026; the 2027 application period opens in November 2026. Sources: MDA 2026-season notice (Accessed 2026-10-28); MDA returning-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28) (“The application period for a 2026 hemp license has closed. The application period for a 2027 hemp license opens in November.”).
  • Expiry: “A hemp license is valid for one calendar year and expires on December 31st. A license needs to be renewed annually.” Source: MDA returning-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28). Statute to the same effect: “the commissioner must issue a license which is valid until December 31 of the year of application” (§18K.04, subd. 1(f)). Source: Revisor, §18K.04 (Accessed 2026-10-28). Run 1’s “expiry 31 Dec of year issued” is therefore verified.
  • Early-renewal note for indoor growers (from the 2026 application coverage, secondary summary of the MDA notice): those growing hemp indoors beyond 31 December 2025 had to renew before expiration. This is a timing note for the 2025→2026 turn, not a separate rule, and is not relied on for any 2027 statement [VERIFY — 2027 window opening/closing dates had not been posted on the MDA pages read; “opens in November” is the only 2027 date verified].

Background check — yes, and a 10-year felony bar.

  • Statute: “The commissioner must require each first-time applicant for a license to submit to a background investigation conducted by the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension as a condition of licensure. Any first-time authorized representatives designated by the applicant must also submit to a background investigation.” Fingerprints may be exchanged with the FBI for a national check; the applicant pays the investigation cost. Source: Revisor, §18K.04, subd. 2 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MDA application pages: “First-time applicants and authorized representatives need to submit fingerprints and pass a criminal background check. A license will not be issued until the applicant and all authorized representatives pass a criminal history background check.” Sources: MDA returning-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28); MDA first-time-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Felony bar (MDA first-time-applicant page): “Any applicant with a controlled substance-related felony conviction in the previous 10-year period will not be eligible for licensure.” Source: MDA first-time-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28). The corresponding rule-level detail (7 CFR / Minn. R. ch. 1565 felony provisions) was located only in search summary for this part and is not quoted here [VERIFY — confirm the 10-year bar’s exact statutory/rule citation before quoting it as a rule rather than an MDA application-page statement].
  • Returning applicants do not re-fingerprint on the pages read; the background-check requirement is stated for first-time applicants and first-time authorised representatives. Whether a returning applicant with a new authorised representative triggers a fresh check for that representative follows from §18K.04, subd. 2 (“any first-time authorized representatives”) — stated here as a reading of that text, not as a separately verified MDA FAQ answer.

Sampling and testing.

  • Pre-harvest, within 30 days of harvest: “All hemp produced in Minnesota must be sampled and tested within 30 days prior to harvest. Each variety grown is considered a separate lot and must be sampled separately. A grower may not harvest a hemp lot until a sample has been collected. Growers must harvest each lot within 30 days of the sample collection date.” Source: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Sampling method: 30 cuttings (top 5 inches of female flower) from 30 randomly selected plants per lot; at least 75% of female plants must be flowering and there must be at least 5 inches of flower vertically along the stem; lots under 30 plants sampled proportionally. Source: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28). The 2025 annual report describes the same method and adds that the plant material is dried and homogenised before laboratory analysis for total THC. Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Test standard: total THC post-decarboxylation, delta-9 THC + (THCA × 0.877) by HPLC; compliance judged against 0.30% dry weight within the measurement of uncertainty (2025 MU approximately 24% of the test value). Source: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28); MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Risk-based sampling: the pilot/Interim Rule requirement to sample every lot has been replaced under the Final Rule and current plan by random, risk-based sampling giving 95% confidence that hemp entering the marketplace meets the threshold; in 2025 one lot was deemed low-risk and grower-sampled under an MDA protocol. Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28). The MDA FAQ’s “all hemp produced must be sampled” wording and the annual report’s risk-based sampling description therefore describe different layers (the duty vs. the selection method) — do not collapse them into “every lot is MDA-sampled.”
  • Failure, remediation, destruction: lots 0.3%–1% total THC may be remediated (remove/destroy floral material retaining stalk/stem/leaf/seed, or shred whole plant to biomass), retested, and released only with a Fit for Commerce Certificate; lots above 1% must be destroyed; a negligent violation requires a corrective action plan; three negligent violations in five years bars participation for five years; in 2025, 68 samples were collected, 6 failed (initial failure rate 6%, lowest since 2020), 4 growers had failing lots, about one acre destroyed, one negligent violation issued. Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Harvest before results: “The grower may harvest any time after the sample is collected, even before they have received the official lab results/Fit for Commerce certificate from the MDA. However, they cannot combine lots or sell the material until they receive the Fit for Commerce certificate.” Source: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Reporting.

  • FSA first, then MDA: “Licensed growers must first report all planted hemp lots to the Farm Service Agency (FSA) within 10 days after planting, and then to the MDA by filing a Planting Report within 10 days after filing the FSA report.” Source: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28). The FSA form is the FSA-578 (rule summary located in search; form number [VERIFY] against Minn. R. 1565.0400 full text before citing the form number as verified).
  • Harvest Report: “The grower must also submit a Harvest Report to the MDA no more than 30 days and no less than 5 days prior to harvest.” Source: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Records: record-retention period (3 years in older MDA/rule summaries) was not verified on an MDA page opened for this part [VERIFY — do not carry a 3-year figure into the final dossier without a Minn. R. ch. 1565 citation].
  • Location changes mid-year: via Change Request Form, $50 (see §7.2.3). Source: MDA returning-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Info links (MDA).

  • MDA hemp programme hub (as printed in the 2025 annual report): www.mda.state.mn.us/plants/hemp — cited here as printed in the report, not as a link verified by opening that exact hub page in this read [VERIFY — hub page itself was reached via its sub-pages, not opened as a landing page].
  • MDA 2026-season notice: MDA 2026-season notice (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MDA returning applicants: MDA returning-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MDA first-time applicants: MDA first-time-applicant instructions (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MDA FAQs: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MDA 2025 annual report: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28).

7.3 OCM lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) licences (Chapter 342)

7.3.1 The three licence types — verbatim statute

Minn. Stat. §342.43, subd. 1 (current text, Revisor):

“The office shall issue the following types of hemp business licenses: (1) lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer; (2) lower-potency hemp edible wholesaler; and (3) lower-potency hemp edible retailer.”

Source: Revisor, §342.43 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

There is no fourth OCM “hemp” licence type. In particular, there is no freestanding OCM “hemp-derived consumer product” licence: under Chapter 342, manufacturing and retailing hemp-derived consumer products (other than LPHEs and topicals) is limited to cannabis-business licensees, not LPHE licensees — a point OCM’s conversion guide states expressly (see §7.4). No OCM “hemp cultivator” licence exists; cultivation is MDA (§7.2) or, for cannabis, a Chapter 342 cannabis licence.

LPHE product definition (for licence scope). Minn. Stat. §342.01, subd. 50, as amended by Laws 2026, ch. 123, §4 (session law text): an LPHE is a product intended to be eaten or consumed as a beverage by humans, containing hemp concentrate or an artificially derived cannabinoid in combination with food ingredients, not a drug, containing no cannabinoid derived from cannabis plants or flower, of a type approved by the office or substantially similar, meeting either (b)(1) — non-beverage servings ≤5 mg delta-9 THC, beverages ≤10 mg delta-9 THC in a single container, plus the CBD/CBG/CBN/CBC tiers (up to 100 mg each, 400 mg combined) and the ≤0.5 mg combined other-cannabinoids-per-serving limit and the 20:1 artificially-derived-cannabinoid ratio rule — or (b)(2), the hemp-concentrate path (servings ≤5 mg total THC, concentrate processed/refined without increasing targeted-cannabinoid percentage or altering ratios beyond recognised variability or the amount needed to reduce total THC). Source: Laws 2026, ch. 123 (SF 4401), §4 (Accessed 2026-10-28). The pre-2026 shorthand “5 mg/serving, 50 mg/package; beverages 10 mg/container” is therefore superseded in detail by the ch. 123 text (notably the 50 mg/package cap does not appear in the ch. 123 §4 definition text because it lives in the packaging statute, §342.62, subd. 2(f)(1), which ch. 123 did not repeal (AUDIT CORRECTION 30 Oct 2026)); the coordinator should not carry the old 50 mg/package shorthand into Run 2 without a current §342.01, subd. 50 check. Note also that OCM’s own September 2026 federal-changes summary describes the state definition more briefly (5 mg delta-9/serving non-beverage; 10 mg delta-9/container beverage; 5 mg total THC/serving concentrate path) — consistent in outline, not a substitute for the statute. Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28).

7.3.2 What each LPHE licence allows — verbatim operative text

Manufacturer — Minn. Stat. §342.45, subd. 1 (current text, Revisor). A lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer licence, consistent with its endorsements, entitles the holder to:

“(1) purchase hemp plant parts, hemp concentrate, and artificially derived cannabinoids from cannabis microbusinesses, cannabis mezzobusinesses, cannabis manufacturers, cannabis wholesalers, and lower-potency hemp edible manufacturers; (2) purchase hemp plant parts and propagules from industrial hemp growers licensed under chapter 18K; (3) purchase hemp concentrate from an industrial hemp processor licensed under chapter 18K; (4) make hemp concentrate; (5) manufacture artificially derived cannabinoids; (6) manufacture lower-potency hemp edibles for public consumption; (7) package and label lower-potency hemp edibles for sale to customers; (8) sell hemp concentrate, artificially derived cannabinoids, and lower-potency hemp edibles to other cannabis businesses and hemp businesses; (9) manufacture, package, and label products containing cannabinoids that are intended for sale outside of the state; (10) store products containing cannabinoids that are intended for sale outside of the state; (11) sell products containing cannabinoids that do not qualify as lower-potency hemp edibles but are compliant with the importing state’s requirements to customers outside of the state; and (12) perform other actions approved by the office.”

Source: Revisor, §342.45, subd. 1 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Endorsements that gate the most sensitive manufacturer activities (§342.45, subd. 3): a manufacturer seeking to create hemp concentrate must obtain a lower-potency hemp extraction and concentration endorsement; a manufacturer seeking to create artificially derived cannabinoids must obtain a lower-potency hemp creation of artificially derived cannabinoid endorsement; each requires disclosure of methods (and volatile chemicals / catalysts / molecular nomenclature) and office approval before use, plus third-party industrial-hygienist/professional-engineer certification of electrical, gas, fire-suppression and exhaust systems and hazardous-substance storage/disposal plans. Source: Revisor, §342.45, subd. 3 (Accessed 2026-10-28). Laws 2026, ch. 123, §93 amended §342.45, subd. 3 (wording conforming changes; endorsement structure retained). Source: Laws 2026, ch. 123, §93 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Further manufacturer rules: all manufacturing in a facility/equipment meeting OCM health and safety requirements; packaging, labelling and testing compliance (§342.45, subd. 2); edible-handler endorsement for LPHE production (§342.45, subd. 4(a)); no adding cannabis flower/concentrate or cannabis-derived cannabinoid to a product (§342.45, subd. 4(f)); out-of-state products require a hemp product exporter endorsement, physical separation, testing under §342.61, and “not for sale in Minnesota” packaging (§342.45, subd. 4a). Source: Revisor, §342.45 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Wholesaler — Minn. Stat. §342.455, subd. 1 (current text, Revisor). A lower-potency hemp edible wholesaler licence, consistent with its endorsements, entitles the holder to:

“(1) purchase lower-potency hemp edibles from cannabis microbusinesses, cannabis mezzobusinesses, cannabis cultivators, cannabis manufacturers, cannabis wholesalers, other lower-potency hemp edible wholesalers, and lower-potency hemp edible manufacturers; (2) sell lower-potency hemp edibles to lower-potency hemp edible retailers with a retail endorsement, cannabis microbusinesses with a retail endorsement, cannabis mezzobusinesses with a retail endorsement, cannabis retailers, cannabis wholesalers, medical cannabis combination businesses, and other lower-potency hemp edible wholesalers; (3) import lower-potency hemp edibles that contain hemp concentrate or artificially derived cannabinoids that are derived from hemp plants or hemp plant parts; (4) purchase and store products containing cannabinoids that are intended for sale outside of the state; (5) sell products containing cannabinoids that do not qualify as lower-potency hemp edibles to customers outside of the state; and (6) perform other actions approved by the office.”

Source: Revisor, §342.455 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Wholesaler gates: must own or lease warehouse or office space within the state (§342.455, subd. 2(d)); importing out-of-state-manufactured LPHEs for sale to Minnesota businesses requires a lower-potency hemp edible importer endorsement, and the out-of-state manufacturer must be licensed under substantially similar health/safety regulation or shown to engage in substantially similar practices (§342.455, subd. 3); transporting LPHEs to other businesses requires a lower-potency hemp edible transporter endorsement, with $300,000 cargo and $1,000,000/$100,000 liability surety/insurance minima (§342.455, subd. 5). Source: Revisor, §342.455 (Accessed 2026-10-28). Note: the “medical cannabis combination business” buyer category in §342.455, subd. 1(2) is the pre-1-January-2027 name; from 1 January 2027 that licence becomes the cannabis macrobusiness under Laws 2026, ch. 123 (see Run 1 baseline). The Revisor text as read still prints the old name in this subdivision — a conforming-renumbering point for the coordinator, not a substantive change found in this part.

Retailer — Minn. Stat. §342.46, subd. 1(a) (current text, Revisor). A lower-potency hemp edible retailer licence, consistent with its endorsements, entitles the holder to:

“(1) purchase lower-potency hemp edibles from a licensed Minnesota cannabis microbusiness, cannabis mezzobusiness, cannabis manufacturer, cannabis wholesaler, medical cannabis combination business, lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer, or lower-potency hemp edible wholesaler; (2) sell lower-potency hemp edibles that meet all packaging and labeling requirements to customers who are at least 21 years of age; (3) transport and deliver lower-potency hemp edibles to customers; and (4) perform other actions approved by the office.”

Source: Revisor, §342.46 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Retailer gates and prohibitions: retail-establishment operation requires a retailer operations endorsement indication (§342.46, subd. 1a); delivery requires a delivery endorsement ($1,000,000 per-occurrence vehicle/general-liability proof, under-21-avoidance business plan, compliance evidence) (§342.46, subd. 1b); age verification before sale/delivery, 21+ (§342.46, subd. 3); non-beverage display behind a checkout counter or in a locked case, other stock in a secure area (§342.46, subd. 4); a retailer must NOT sell/deliver to under-21s or visibly intoxicated persons, sell/deliver cannabis flower, cannabis products or hemp-derived consumer products, use vending machines, or distribute free samples except on-site-consumption samples consumed on premises (§342.46, subd. 7); on-site consumption requires an on-site consumption endorsement (§342.46, subd. 8; amended by Laws 2026, ch. 123, §94, effective day following final enactment). Source: Revisor, §342.46 (Accessed 2026-10-28); Laws 2026, ch. 123, §94 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Local retail registration (retailers only, separate from the state licence): OCM’s hemp overview page lists “Guidance for Lower-Potency Hemp Edible Retailers: Local Retail Registration Requirement” (updated 16 June 2026) and states: “LPHE retailers must obtain local retail registration before beginning retail operations.” Source: OCM, Hemp Business Overview (Accessed 2026-10-28). The state licence fee does not include the local registration fee (see §342.11(a) and §342.22; local fee details are Part 5 / local-control territory and are not restated here beyond this flag).

No cap. OCM’s LPHE application guidance (v2.0, 1 April 2026): “All lower-potency hemp edible licenses will be issued without a cap on the maximum number of licenses available. Applications for lower-potency hemp edible licenses will be reviewed on a rolling basis in the order received and will be issued to an applicant meeting the criteria described in this document and in Minnesota Statutes, chapter 342.” Source: OCM, LPHE License Application Review and Eligibility Guidance v2.0 (PDF) (Accessed 2026-10-28). This contrasts with capped cannabis licences and must not be confused with the cannabis caps in Part 5.

7.3.3 LPHE fees — Run 1 figures VERIFIED against §342.11

Minn. Stat. §342.11(a) (current text, Revisor):

“The office shall require the payment of application fees, initial licensing fees, and renewal licensing fees as provided in this section. The initial license fee shall include the fee for initial issuance of the license and the first annual renewal. The renewal fee shall be charged at the time of the second renewal and each subsequent annual renewal thereafter. … Application fees, initial licensing fees, and renewal licensing fees are nonrefundable.”

Source: Revisor, §342.11 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

§342.11(b) LPHE rows (current text, Revisor) — Run 1 figures confirmed exactly:

Licence Application Initial licence Renewal
LPHE manufacturer §342.11(b)(11) $250 $1,000 $1,000
LPHE wholesaler §342.11(b)(12) $250 $10,000 $10,000
LPHE retailer §342.11(b)(13) $250 per retail location (or $250 if one location) $250 per retail location $250 per retail location

Verbatim retailer row: “(i) an application fee of $250 or, if the lower-potency hemp retailer operates more than one retail location, $250 per retail location; (ii) an initial license fee of $250 or, if the lower-potency hemp retailer operates more than one retail location, $250 per retail location; and (iii) a renewal license fee of $250 or, if the lower-potency hemp retailer operates more than one retail location, $250 per retail location.” Source: Revisor, §342.11 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Fee-timing trap (applies to all Chapter 342 licences, stated here because it changes what “renewal” means): because the initial fee “shall include the fee for initial issuance of the license and the first annual renewal,” the renewal fee first falls due at the second renewal, not the first. Any table that presents “$1,000 renewal” as due one year after issuance is therefore wrong by one year. The same §342.11 structure was restated in Laws 2026, ch. 123, §13 (cited in secondary fee summaries as effective 1 January 2027 for the macrobusiness/event-organiser rows); the LPHE dollar figures themselves are unchanged between the 2025 Supplement text and the current text as read. [VERIFY — confirm ch. 123, §13’s effective-date treatment of the §342.11 LPHE rows specifically; the session-law effective-date section (§119) makes sections effective 1 August 2026 unless otherwise stated, which would make any §342.11 amendment effective 1 August 2026, not 1 January 2027, unless §13 states otherwise.]

7.3.4 LPHE requirements, transferability, and application windows

Application contents — Minn. Stat. §342.44, subd. 1 (current text, Revisor). Chapter 342’s general application/selection/ownership/operational provisions do not apply to hemp businesses except as provided in §342.44, subd. 1. OCM sets forms/procedures; at minimum an application to obtain or renew must include, if applicable: (1) name, address and date of birth of applicant; (2) address and legal property description of the business; (3) proof of trade name registration; (4) certification of compliance with Chapter 342 hemp-business ownership/operation requirements; (5) identification of one or more controlling persons or managerial employees as agents for dealing with OCM; (6) agreement to respond to OCM supplemental information requests. Source: Revisor, §342.44 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Manufacturer-only extra: “An applicant for a lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer license must submit an attestation signed by a bona fide labor organization stating that the applicant has entered into a labor peace agreement. A labor peace agreement entered into on or after August 15, 2025, must address the duration of the election.” (§342.44, subd. 1(c), current text.) Source: Revisor, §342.44 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Eligibility and renewal — §342.44, subd. 2 (current text, Revisor):

“(a) The office may issue a hemp license to an applicant who: (1) is at least 21 years of age; (2) has completed an application for licensure or application for renewal and has fully and truthfully complied with all information requests relating to license application and renewal; (3) has paid the applicable application and license fees pursuant to section 342.11; and (4) is not employed by the office or any state agency with regulatory authority over this chapter. (b) Licenses must be renewed annually. (c) Licenses may not be transferred.”

Source: Revisor, §342.44 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Transferability — NON-TRANSFERABLE, with a conditional-surrender workaround (not a transfer). OCM’s federal-changes page states the rule and the workaround together:

“Per Minnesota Statues, section 342.44, a hemp business license cannot be transferred, and once a business surrenders a license, they are not able to sell or buy LPHE products. The conditional surrender process is available if a business plans to transition their hemp operations and products to a different business entity by conditioning the surrender of the existing hemp business’s license to the issuance of a new license to the new entity upon successful application while minimizing business interruptions. Minnesota Statutes, section 342.44, subdivision 2, does not allow businesses to transfer a hemp license. As such, businesses need to surrender their current license, and the new business would need to apply for a new LPHE license under the new business entity.”

Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28). (OCM’s “Statues” spelling is in the original.) Practical consequence: a sale of an LPHE business is a surrender + fresh application by the buyer entity, not an assignment; any dossier language about “transferring an LPHE licence” must be corrected to this.

Licence term and renewal notices: “Hemp business licenses must be renewed on an annual basis under Minnesota law” and “Business licenses are issued for one year”; OCM notifies a holder 90 days before expiry, with automated reminders at 60 and 30 days if no renewal application has been submitted. Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28). Note the interplay with §342.11(a): the licence is annual, but the renewal fee first falls due at the second renewal because the initial fee covers the first annual renewal (see §7.3.3).

No fingerprint/background-check requirement in §342.44 as read. Unlike the MDA licence (§7.2.4), §342.44, subd. 2 lists no fingerprint or criminal-history condition; instead §342.44, subd. 1(d) gives OCM discretion: “The office may determine whether any civil or regulatory violation as determined by the office, another state agency, a local government, or any other jurisdiction disqualifies an individual or business from receiving a hemp business license issued under this chapter. The office may determine the length of the disqualification.” Source: Revisor, §342.44 (Accessed 2026-10-28). Do not import the MDA fingerprint rule into the LPHE licence. OCM’s application guidance adds practical requirements (photo ID, trade-name proof, site/security/operations final plans of record per site — one combined plan for retailers covering all sites — workers’ compensation information, and for manufacturers the labour-peace attestation). Source: OCM LPHE Guidance v2.0 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Application windows — both Run 1 statements VERIFIED on OCM sources.

  • First window: opened 1 October 2025, closed noon CDT Friday 31 October 2025. OCM Guidance Memo GM-2025-03 (updated 30 September 2026): “The office opened the window for applications to LPHE manufacturers, LPHE wholesalers, and LPHE retailers on Oct. 1, 2025, and closed the LPHE application window at noon (12 p.m. CDT), Friday, Oct. 31, 2025.” Source: OCM, Guidance Memo GM-2025-03 (via OCM guidance-memo index) (Accessed 2026-10-28). Registration under the old §151.72 system closed 31 August 2025, and registered businesses wishing to continue had to apply in this window — see §7.6.
  • Manufacturer/wholesaler issuance hold in the first window: OCM “will not issue final approvals to hemp manufacturers and wholesalers before March 31, 2026,” with invoicing on or immediately after 31 March 2026, while retailers were issued on a rolling basis. Source: OCM GM-2025-03 summary (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Second (rolling) window — VERIFIED, 1 April 2026: OCM news release: “on April 1, it will begin accepting business license applications for the three lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) license types: LPHE retailers, LPHE manufacturers, and LPHE wholesalers. Applications will then be accepted and reviewed on an ongoing, rolling basis.” And: “By March 31, all applicants for LPHE licenses from 2025 will receive an approval or denial from OCM. Those who wish to reapply — or apply for the first time — may do so, beginning April 1.” Source: OCM news release, “Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management will resume accepting applications … on April 1” (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Still open at access date: OCM’s hemp overview page states at the top: “OCM is accepting applications for lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer, wholesaler, and retailer licenses on an ongoing basis.” Source: OCM, Hemp Business Overview (Accessed 2026-10-28). OCM’s LPHE guidance v2.0 (1 April 2026) states applications “will be available for submission in Accela beginning April 1, 2026, and will be reviewed on an ongoing, rolling basis.” Source: OCM LPHE Guidance v2.0 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • First-window volume (context, not a licence rule): “Last October, OCM received more than 2,200 applications from hemp businesses — including more than 2,000 from retailers.” Source: OCM April 1 news release (Accessed 2026-10-28). OCM’s 1 April 2026 press release adds: “We now have more than 1,500 licensed hemp-derived THC businesses in Minnesota” (secondary bulletin copy of the OCM release; treat the 1,500 figure as an OCM press-release figure at 1 April 2026, not as a registry count — see §7.6 for the later 2,031 Run 1 baseline and the conflicting third-party directory count).

7.3.5 Dual holding with a cannabis licence after Laws 2026, ch. 123 — VERIFIED as current law, with a source conflict the coordinator must see

Current consolidated law (Revisor, as read 28 October 2026) permits dual holding. Minn. Stat. §342.43, subd. 2(d) (current text, Revisor):

“A person, cooperative, or business holding a lower-potency hemp edible manufacturer license, a lower-potency hemp edible wholesaler license, a lower-potency hemp edible retailer license, or any combination of those licenses, may hold a cannabis business license.”

Source: Revisor, §342.43 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

OCM confirms the change in the same direction. OCM’s federal-changes page: “This past session, the Legislature removed the prohibition on holding a cannabis business and hemp business license simultaneously. While there is not currently an open window for applications for cannabis businesses licenses, a large number of prospective cannabis businesses continue to advance through the licensing process that may be available for business partnership or investment.” Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28). OCM’s Cannabis Insider newsletter states the same: “Removal of the prohibition on a business holding both a hemp and cannabis license, creating flexibility across market segments.” Source: OCM, Cannabis Insider (GovDelivery bulletin) (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Other dual holdings (unchanged): §342.43, subd. 2(a) permits any combination of the three LPHE licences; subd. 2(b) permits holding LPHE licences together with a Chapter 18K industrial hemp licence; subd. 2(c) permits holding LPHE licences together with any other licence including food, tobacco/electronic-delivery/nicotine-lobelia, and alcohol licences; subd. 3 permits a city or county operating a municipal cannabis store also to hold an LPHE retailer licence. Source: Revisor, §342.43 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

[CONFLICT — must be reconciled before publication]: The session-law PDF text layer for Laws 2026, ch. 123, §§90 and 92 as fetched for this part was read as the opposite way — AUDIT RESOLUTION 30 Oct 2026: superseded; enacted law is “may hold” — §90 was read as “may not hold a cannabis business license,” and §92 prints §342.44, subd. 2(a) with an added clause (5) “does not hold any cannabis business license.” Source: Laws 2026, ch. 123, §§90, 92 (Accessed 2026-10-28). The current consolidated Revisor text for both sections contains neither prohibition (§342.43, subd. 2(d) reads “may hold”; §342.44, subd. 2(a) ends at clause (4)). One secondary analysis also flags this exact tension (noting OCM’s removal statement against “the statute as printed today” for a related microbusiness cross-holding rule). Possible explanations — strikethrough/underline rendering lost in the session-law PDF text extraction, a later conforming amendment, or a Revisor correction — were not established in this part. Treatment adopted here: the current consolidated Revisor text plus OCM’s own statements are treated as the operative position (dual holding permitted), and the ch. 123 PDF text-layer reading is flagged as a conflict for the coordinator to resolve with the Revisor before the dossier states an effective date for the dual-holding change. Do not state a ch. 123 section number or an effective date (1 August 2026 vs. another date) for the dual-holding change on the basis of this part alone. Note also the practical limit OCM itself states: there is “not currently an open window for applications for cannabis businesses licenses,” so dual holding in practice presently means holding an existing cannabis licence (or acquiring an interest through OCM’s business-change process, §342.14, subd. 1(a)) alongside an LPHE licence — not applying fresh for a cannabis licence on demand.

Related cross-holding caution: the microbusiness rule (§342.28, subd. 5, as summarised in secondary analysis) still restricts a microbusiness holder from holding a second microbusiness or owning/operating another cannabis or hemp business (event-organiser exception). That licence-specific restriction is distinct from the general §342.43 dual-holding permission and must not be generalised in either direction [VERIFY — §342.28, subd. 5 current text was not opened for this part].

7.4 Any other hemp licences and hemp-adjacent permissions

7.4.1 Hemp-derived topical products — NO licence required (§342.66) — scope VERIFIED, with 2026 amendments

Operative text. Minn. Stat. §342.66, subd. 2 (current text, Revisor):

“No license is required to manufacture, market, distribute, or sell hemp-derived topical products.”

Source: Revisor, §342.66 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Scope and limits (all §342.66, current text):

  • Subd. 1 (scope): “This section applies to the manufacture, marketing, distribution, and sale of hemp-derived topical products.” Source: Revisor, §342.66 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 3 (approved cannabinoids): products may contain cannabidiol (CBD) or cannabigerol (CBG); no other cannabinoid unless approved by the office; the office may approve any non-THC cannabinoid it determines is nonintoxicating; other naturally occurring hemp cannabinoids are permitted only up to a total of 1 mg per package. Source: Revisor, §342.66 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 4 (approved products): products sold to consumers “may only be manufactured, marketed, distributed, intended, or generally expected to be used by applying the product externally to a part of the body of a human or animal.” Source: Revisor, §342.66 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 5 (labelling): “Hemp-derived topical products must meet the labeling requirements in section 342.63, subdivision 5.” Source: Revisor, §342.66 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 6 (prohibitions): no disease diagnosis/cure/mitigation/treatment/prevention claims or structure/function claims; no combustion/vaporisation, chewing, injection or application to non-intact skin/mucous membrane (except sublingual application as stated); no filthy/putrid/decomposed substance, unsanitary production, poisonous container, FDA-unsafe additive, mislabelled cannabinoid content, over-limit unapproved cannabinoid, or over-limit contaminant; no sale to anyone under 21 of any product containing any cannabinoid (subd. 6(c)). Source: Revisor, §342.66 (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Subd. 7 (enforcement): OCM may enforce under §342.19, including administrative orders, embargo and civil penalties. Source: Revisor, §342.66 (Accessed 2026-10-28).

2026 changes to §342.66 (flag, do not overstate): Laws 2026, ch. 123 amended §342.66, subd. 3 (THC in topicals). House Research’s ch. 123 summary describes §114 as: “Allows OCM to approve THC in hemp-derived topical products. Prohibits hemp-derived topical products from containing more than 0.3 percent total THC” (effective 1 January 2027 per that summary’s §114 line; the related topical-labelling section §111 establishes additional labelling for THC-containing topicals). The current Revisor §342.66, subd. 3 text as read still frames approval around non-THC cannabinoids, so the 0.3%-total-THC topical cap and any THC-approval mechanism must be treated as a 1 January 2027 change whose consolidated text was not fully verified in this part [VERIFY — current §342.66, subd. 3 as amended, and the §342.63, subd. 5 labelling text, before stating a topical THC rule]. Secondary summaries also assert a “THC-containing topical” two-tier label system under ch. 123, §111 — likewise [VERIFY] as secondary-only.

No-licence ≠ unregulated, and the 0%-THC retail nuance: OCM’s conversion guide states: “Hemp-derived topical products do not require a license or endorsement to be sold,” and its retail product table treats a 0%-THC hemp-derived topical as “Allowed — No license needed” for retail sale, while a >0–0.3% THC topical is listed as “Not allowed — None” in that (pre-2026-amendment) table. The table is an OCM guide, not statute, and its >0% row is overtaken in part by the 2026 THC-topical amendments above. Do not reproduce the guide table as current law without the §342.66 amendment check. Source for the guide’s no-licence statement: OCM, Hemp Registrant to Licensee Conversion Guide (PDF) (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Interaction with the MDA licence: §342.65 expressly preserves an 18K licensee’s ability to “manufacture hemp-derived topical products” (see §7.2.2). That is a savings clause for MDA licensees; it does not convert topical manufacture into an MDA-licenced activity for non-licensees, because §342.66 requires no licence from anyone.

7.4.2 Hemp-derived consumer products (non-LPHE, non-topical) — no LPHE licence suffices

OCM’s conversion guide: “manufacturing and retailing of hemp-derived consumer products is limited to only cannabis business license holders, not LPHE license holders” and “Hemp-derived topical products do not require a license or endorsement to be sold.” Source: OCM Conversion Guide (Accessed 2026-10-28). The same guide’s retail table treats hemp flower (<0.3% THC) and hemp concentrate (<0.3% THC) as hemp-derived consumer products sellable by microbusiness/mezzobusiness/cannabis retailer/medical-combination (now macrobusiness) licensees, and infused hemp flower as “Not allowed — None.” Those product-classification rows are guide-level and pre-date the 2026 amendments in part; they are reported here only to establish the LPHE boundary, not as a verified current product catalogue [VERIFY — current Minn. R. ch. 9810 product-type rules before republishing the flower/concentrate rows].

7.4.3 Research licences — no separate type found

  • MDA: research is a licensed purpose under §18K.04, subd. 1(a)(3) (“researching industrial hemp”), not a separate licence class in the statute or 2026 application materials read (see §7.2.2).
  • OCM/Chapter 342: no “hemp research licence” type exists in §342.43, subd. 1’s exhaustive three-type list.
  • University/research carve-outs, seed-certification (Minnesota Crop Improvement Association) requirements for seed growers, and any MDA research-specific reporting in Minn. R. ch. 1565 were not verified in this part [UNAVAILABLE in this read — do not assert that no research condition exists; assert only that no separate research licence type was located].

7.4.4 Endorsements that function like sub-licences (LPHE system)

For completeness, the following OCM endorsements — not licences — gate activities inside an LPHE licence and are often mistaken for licence types: LPHE manufacturer extraction-and-concentration endorsement; LPHE manufacturer creation-of-artificially-derived-cannabinoid endorsement; LPHE manufacturer edible cannabinoid product handler endorsement; LPHE manufacturer/wholesaler hemp product exporter endorsement; LPHE wholesaler importer endorsement; LPHE wholesaler transporter endorsement; LPHE retailer retail-operations endorsement indication; LPHE retailer delivery endorsement; LPHE retailer on-site consumption endorsement. Sources: Revisor, §342.45 (Accessed 2026-10-28); Revisor, §342.455 (Accessed 2026-10-28); Revisor, §342.46 (Accessed 2026-10-28). Endorsements carry no separate §342.11 fee in the fee table as read; OCM guidance states endorsements are not separately fee-charged in the 2026 framework in secondary summaries only [VERIFY — endorsement fee treatment against §342.11 and OCM guidance before stating “free”].

7.4.5 The former §151.72 registration system — closed, not a licence

Before Chapter 342 licensure, hemp-derived cannabinoid products were sold under OCM registration pursuant to Minn. Stat. §151.72. That system is closed: the registration window closed 31 August 2025; registered businesses wishing to continue had to apply for a Chapter 342 licence by noon CDT 31 October 2025; and Laws 2026, ch. 123, §118 repealed §151.72 (subdivisions 1, 2, 4, 5, 5b, 5c, 6, 7 effective day following final enactment; subdivisions 3 and 5a likewise repealed). Sources: OCM, Registered Hemp Businesses Directory page (Accessed 2026-10-28); Laws 2026, ch. 123, §118 (Accessed 2026-10-28). A §151.72 registration must never be described in Run 2 as a current licence. Historical registration volume (5,380 businesses registered at closure, per secondary summary) is not adopted here as a verified OCM figure [VERIFY if Part 5 needs it].

7.5 Tribal hemp licences and plans — distinct from state licences

Rule that governs the whole section: Anyone growing on tribal lands within a reservation’s boundaries or other lands under tribal jurisdiction (e.g. trust lands off-reservation) must obtain a licence from the tribe or from USDA if the tribe does not have an approved hemp production plan. (MDA application guidance, as summarised in MDA’s 2023-season notice coverage; the underlying jurisdictional rule is federal — 7 CFR part 990 — and is stated here as the MDA-stated rule, with the federal citation [VERIFY] against 7 CFR 990 before quoting it as a federal rule.) The MDA state licence does not authorise growing on tribal land under tribal jurisdiction, and a tribal-plan licence does not authorise growing off tribal land under the state plan. Do not merge tribal and state counts.

USDA status table (USDA AMS, updated 17 February 2026, as read 28 October 2026). Source for every row in this section: USDA AMS, List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans (Accessed 2026-10-28). USDA descriptors: “Approved” = formally approved; “Approved *” = approved under the Final Rule effective 22 March 2021; “USDA Hemp Producer License” = USDA itself issues the producer licence (i.e. no tribal plan; producers licence directly with USDA).

Minnesota tribe (USDA listing name) USDA status What it means
Fond du Lac Chippewa Approved Plan (pdf)* Tribe regulates hemp production under its own USDA-approved plan (Final Rule).
Lower Sioux Indian Community Approved Plan (pdf)* Tribe regulates under its own USDA-approved plan (Final Rule).
Red Lake Band of Chippewa Approved Plan (pdf) Tribe regulates under its own USDA-approved plan (not marked Final Rule “*”).
Bois Forte Band of Chippewa USDA Hemp Producer License No tribal plan; producers on Bois Forte jurisdiction licence directly with USDA.
White Earth Band of the Minnesota Chippewa USDA Hemp Producer License No tribal plan; producers licence directly with USDA.

The correction is only that “USDA producer licence” is not a tribal licence at all — it is a federal licence issued by USDA because the tribe has no approved plan. The five tribes above are the only Minnesota tribes on the USDA list as read; the other Minnesota federally recognised tribes (Grand Portage, Leech Lake, Mille Lacs, Prairie Island, Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux, Upper Sioux — see Minn. Stat. §3.9228’s list of Minnesota Tribal governments) do not appear on the USDA hemp-plan list as read, which means producers in those jurisdictions would fall under the USDA producer-licence route if they grow hemp, or hold no hemp authorisation — the USDA page alone does not prove which, so no per-tribe production claim is made for the non-listed tribes [UNAVAILABLE — tribal hemp activity levels, licence counts per tribe, and tribal cannabis-compact interaction with hemp are not on the USDA status page and were not verified].

Hemp plans for Tribal entities in Minnesota are available on the USDA website.” Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28). Tribal production is therefore excluded from every MDA count in §7.7.

7.6 State plan status: Minnesota runs its own USDA-approved plan (not the USDA programme)

Answer: Minnesota runs its own USDA-approved state plan; producers licence with MDA, not USDA.

  • USDA status page: “Minnesota — MN Approved Plan (pdf) *” (Approved under the Final Rule). Source: USDA AMS, List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • History (MDA 2025 annual report): pilot programme 2016–2020 under the 2014 Farm Bill / Minnesota Industrial Hemp Development Act (Minn. Stat. ch. 18K, enacted 2015); 2018 Farm Bill legalised commercial hemp and required state/tribal plans; Minnesota State Hemp Plan approved July 2020, effective 1 January 2021; revised plan incorporating the federal Final Rule (7 CFR part 990, released 15 January 2021) approved and effective 6 May 2021; MDA published Minn. R. ch. 1565 in fall 2021 mirroring the plan; plan revised again late 2023 (codification of administrative rules + minor statutory changes), approved and effective 12 December 2023; 2024 amendment to Minn. Stat. §18.06 allowing exempt rulemaking to implement federal changes efficiently; latest revision consolidating grower/processor licences approved 17 November 2025. Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MDA’s 2026-season notice confirms the same arc in one line: “Minnesota operated under a hemp pilot program from 2016 to 2020. In 2021, the program began operating under a new, federally approved state plan that governs production and regulation.” Source: MDA 2026-season notice (Accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MDA FAQ gives the 6 May 2021 date the same way: “The Minnesota State Plan was approved on May 6, 2021. Visit the USDA website to view the entirety of the Minnesota plan.” Source: MDA FAQs (Accessed 2026-10-28). (The FAQ’s “approved on May 6, 2021” refers to the revised Final-Rule plan; the original July 2020 approval / 1 January 2021 effectiveness is the annual report’s fuller account. Both dates are correct for different versions — do not present either alone as “the” approval date.)
  • Plan PDF / file name: USDA AMS posts the plan as MinnesotaIndustrialHempPlan.pdf at USDA AMS, Minnesota Industrial Hemp Plan (PDF) (Accessed 2026-10-28); the document face shows a revision date of 16 September 2025. The MDA annual report likewise points readers to “the USDA Domestic Hemp Program website” for the current plan, and its “For More Information” page repeats the same USDA URL. Source: MDA 2025 Annual Report (Accessed 2026-10-28). Caveat [VERIFY]: the USDA-posted PDF’s revision date (16 September 2025) precedes the 17 November 2025 approval; whether the posted file is the approved 17 November 2025 revision under the same file name, or the submitted revision awaiting approval, could not be confirmed from the file face. Cite the approval date from the MDA annual report, and the PDF only as “USDA-posted Minnesota plan (file name as above),” until the coordinator confirms the posted version.
  • What state-plan status means for producers (practical):
  • Off tribal jurisdiction in Minnesota, a producer licences with MDA under Chapter 18K and the state plan (fees, locations, FSA/MDA reporting, MDA sampling, Fit for Commerce — §7.2). They do not hold a USDA producer licence.
  • On tribal jurisdiction, §7.5 applies instead (tribal plan or USDA producer licence).
  • If Minnesota’s plan were withdrawn or revoked, producers would fall to USDA licensing — that contingency has not occurred and is stated here only to explain why the distinction matters; no withdrawal/revocation is reported on the USDA page as read.
  • The state plan covers production and raw processing; it does not itself authorise LPHE manufacture/wholesale/retail, which is Chapter 342/OCM territory (§7.1). The 2025 plan revision’s consolidation is a production-licensing change, not a cannabinoid-product change.
  • Rule layer: Minn. R. ch. 1565 (MDA hemp rules, published fall 2021, mirroring the plan) gives MDA enforcement authority for hemp production and raw processing. The full rule text was not opened for this part; rule citations beyond this summary are [VERIFY] (see gaps list).

7.8 How the 12 November / 11 December 2026 federal hemp dates affect each licence type

Fixed federal frame (from the task baseline, not re-researched): PL 119-37 §781 effective 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. OCM’s page reflects the same two-step history: the November 2025 spending bill “changed the definition of hemp under Title 7, Section 1639o,” the change “will now take effect on Dec. 11, 2026, unless other federal action occurs” after the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act of 2027 (Senate 8 August, House 1 September, signed 3 September) moved the date from 12 November to 11 December. Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28).

OCM’s Minnesota-law position (the Run 1 baseline, VERIFIED on OCM’s current page):

“This federal definition change does not change how Minnesota law defines lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) products and LPHE retailers, manufacturers and wholesalers or the legality of those products in the state. LPHEs are defined in Minnesota Statutes, section 342.01, subdivision 50, and are allowed to be manufactured and sold under state law. Minnesota’s definitions of LPHE licenses and product types will not change after the federal definition changes on Dec. 11, 2026.”

“However, under the new federal definition, many products compliant under Minnesota law (e.g., packages containing more than 0.4 mg of THC) will become federally noncompliant.”

Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28).

What becomes federally excluded (OCM’s list, same page):

  • “The hemp plant and plant parts (including seeds) with more than 0.3% total THC concentration, including THCA (the previous definition included only delta-9 THC).”
  • “Intermediate hemp-derived cannabinoid products with more than 0.3% total THC.”
  • “Final hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing more than 0.4 mg total THC per container.”

Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28).

Effect by licence type (each row states state-law effect vs. federal effect separately — conflating them is the error to avoid):

Licence type Minnesota law after 11 Dec 2026 Federal position after 11 Dec 2026 Practical consequence stated by OCM or following directly from the cap
MDA industrial hemp licence (grower/processor) Unchanged by the federal definition change as a matter of Minnesota licensing law; the state definition in §18K.02, subd. 3 is still delta-9 ≤0.3% dry weight as printed (see §7.2.2). No Minnesota legislative fix was found as of 28 Oct 2026 (Run 1 baseline, still true on the sources read — no MDA/OCM fix notice was located). Plant/plant parts (including seeds) >0.3% total THC (including THCA) are excluded from the federal hemp definition. MDA already tests on a total-THC (post-decarboxylation) basis (delta-9 + THCA×0.877), so MDA-compliant lots (≤0.3% total THC within measurement uncertainty) remain within the federal plant definition; lots that would have passed a delta-9-only test but exceed 0.3% total THC do not. Intermediate products >0.3% total THC are likewise federally excluded. Grain/fiber production — the bulk of 2025 Minnesota acreage (74% grain, 24% fiber) — is the least exposed, because compliant grain/fiber lots are already total-THC compliant. Cannabinoid-biomass growers are the exposed subset: any lot or intermediate over 0.3% total THC loses federal hemp status even if Minnesota-licensed. MDA has published no separate 11 December grower guidance on the pages read [VERIFY — MDA federal-response notice, if any, was not located; OCM’s page is the only Minnesota-agency federal-changes page verified here].
OCM LPHE manufacturer Licence type, definition (§342.01, subd. 50) and authorised actions (§342.45) unchanged under Minnesota law. Final products >0.4 mg total THC per container are federally excluded. A Minnesota LPHE at 5 mg delta-9/serving (non-beverage) or 10 mg/container (beverage) exceeds 0.4 mg/container by an order of magnitude. Most current LPHE SKUs become federally noncompliant while remaining Minnesota-lawful — OCM’s exact warning. Manufacturer exposure is concentrated in: (a) interstate manufacture for out-of-state sale (§342.45, subd. 4a exporter endorsement) — the product must meet the importing state’s requirements, and federal noncompliance now overlays that; (b) hemp-concentrate and artificially-derived-cannabinoid inputs >0.3% total THC (intermediate exclusion); (c) banking/tax/interstate-commerce friction OCM lists as “similar to complexities currently faced in the cannabis industry” (banking, tax and interstate commerce are named as operator considerations in OCM-related social-equity guidance summaries — stated here as OCM-flagged risk areas, not as verified post-11-December outcomes).
OCM LPHE wholesaler Licence type and authorised actions (§342.455) unchanged under Minnesota law, including import (importer endorsement) and export (exporter endorsement) authorities as written. Same 0.4 mg/container final-product exclusion; import/export endorsements were “enacted under the existing federal definition of hemp” (OCM’s words). OCM’s specific warning to endorsement holders: “operators that hold these endorsements should be especially aware of the impact of the federal definition on the interstate hemp market and should consult with legal counsel”; importers must review Guidance Memo 2025-02 (out-of-state hemp product importing) and ensure any imported product is compliant with Minnesota and federal law. Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28). In practice, an LPHE wholesaler can still lawfully distribute Minnesota-compliant LPHEs inside Minnesota under state law, but moving the same product across state lines after 11 December 2026 carries the federal exclusion — the dossier must not describe wholesaler import/export as “unaffected.”
OCM LPHE retailer Licence type and authorised actions (§342.46) unchanged under Minnesota law; 21+ retail sale inside Minnesota remains state-lawful. Same 0.4 mg/container exclusion for the products on the shelf. Retailer exposure is downstream (product supply, banking, and the renewal decision), not a licence-validity event: OCM frames the retailer choice as renew / surrender (including conditional surrender to a new entity) / let expire / consider entering adult-use cannabis (see §7.3.4–7.3.5). No OCM statement was located requiring retailers to pull Minnesota-compliant LPHEs from shelves on 11 December 2026 as a matter of state law [VERIFY — any OCM shelf-pull or enforcement notice after 11 December 2026 would post-date this part’s access date and must be checked before publication].
Hemp-derived topical products (no licence) §342.66 unchanged as a no-licence regime (subject to the 1 January 2027 THC-topical amendments flagged in §7.4.1). Topicals are final hemp-derived cannabinoid products for federal purposes only to the extent they contain THC; CBD/CBG topicals with ≤1 mg/package of other naturally occurring cannabinoids (§342.66, subd. 3(c)) and no THC sit outside the 0.4 mg THC cap by definition (cap is THC-specific). THC-containing topicals above 0.4 mg THC per container would fall under the federal exclusion. The no-licence status does not insulate a THC-containing topical from the federal cap. The 2026 Minnesota 0.3%-total-THC topical cap (effective 1 January 2027, per House Research summary — [VERIFY] per §7.4.1) is a concentration cap, not a per-container milligram cap, and does not by itself bring a topical under 0.4 mg THC/container. Do not equate the two caps.
Tribal plan / USDA producer licence Tribal plans and USDA producer licences are federal-plan instruments; Minnesota law does not amend them. Same federal definition change applies to tribal-plan and USDA-licensed production (the definition is in 7 U.S.C. §1639o itself). Tribal growers face the same total-THC plant/seed/intermediate exclusion as MDA growers. Whether any Minnesota tribe has issued its own 11 December guidance was not located [UNAVAILABLE]. USDA DEA-lab enforcement delay to 31 December 2026 (federal baseline) is the only federal timing relief noted for testing; it does not delay the 11 December definition/cap.

MDA response — gap, stated plainly: No MDA notice responding to the 12 November / 11 December 2026 federal dates was located on the MDA pages opened for this part (2026-season notice, returning/first-time applicant pages, FAQs, 2025 annual report — the last predates the federal change’s enactment timeline in part). OCM’s federal-changes page is therefore the only verified Minnesota-agency response in this part. Do not attribute OCM’s LPHE position to MDA, and do not state that MDA has or has not issued guidance — state only that none was located in this read [UNAVAILABLE in this read].

No Minnesota legislative fix found (Run 1 baseline re-confirmed as of access date): No Minnesota statute, session law, or OCM/MDA notice located in this part enacts a Minnesota fix (e.g. a state-law 0.4 mg conforming cap, a delayed state effective date, or a state-law shield) for the 11 December 2026 federal change. Federal bills OCM lists as “to watch” (Lawful Hemp Protection Act; Beverage Regulatory Parity Act — neither voted in either chamber as of OCM’s page) are federal proposals, not Minnesota law, and their introduction “does not mean that they will pass.” Source: OCM, Federal Hemp Changes (Accessed 2026-10-28). Any post-access-date Minnesota or federal action must be checked before publication, because 11 December 2026 falls after this part’s access date.

12 November vs. 11 December — why both dates appear: 12 November 2026 was the original PL 119-37 §781 effective date; PL 119-103 §2019 (Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act of 2027, signed 3 September 2026) moved the operative date to 11 December 2026. OCM’s page was updated from its 31 August message to reflect the new date, with the rest of the message unchanged. Older OCM releases (e.g. the April 2026 reopening release, which warns of “a federal ban … in November”) therefore read “November” — that is the pre-extension date, not a different ban. The dossier should use 11 December 2026 as the operative date and footnote the 12 November original date, not present them as two separate bans.
