Minnesota Cannabis & Hemp Research — Run 2, Part 8: Cannabis-Zoned Properties

Scope: Part 8 only. Publicly listed properties in Minnesota zoned or marketed for cannabis or hemp use. Run 1 baseline applied (not re-researched): State-licensed adult-use sales began 16 Sept 2026 [sic — see note below]; latest licence baseline OCM 19 Oct 2026: 405 cannabis + 2,031 LPHE licences issued. No single open-store count adopted. 2026 omnibus SF 4401 / Laws 2026 ch. 123, signed 26 May 2026, mostly eff. 1 Aug 2026; macrobusiness eff. 1 Jan 2027 capped at 8 through 2030. Local rules (Run 1 Part 3): cities/counties/townships cannot ban licensed cannabis businesses; retailer limits no fewer than one per 12,500 residents; zoning/buffers (max 1,000 ft from school, 500 ft from day care/residential treatment facility/park attraction regularly used by minors); municipal stores: Anoka operating (5 Feb 2026), Saint Anthony Village operating (Oct 2026), Osseo in construction. No official statewide local-registration list found. Federal baseline applied (fixed, not re-researched): State-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III eff. 28 Apr 2026; adult-use remains Schedule I; 280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical only; hemp PL 119-37 §781 eff. 12 Nov 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 Dec 2026, after which full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-lab enforcement delayed to 31 Dec 2026; no federal cannabis banking law. Note on the Run 1 date above: The task brief as received states adult-use sales began “16 Sept 2025”. This Part does not independently verify that date and does not contradict it; it is reproduced here only as the supplied Run 1 baseline. No property finding in this Part depends on that date.

Sourcing and status rule used throughout: Every fact below carries a source link + “Accessed 2026-10-28”. A listing is marked [VERIFY] unless the listing itself shows ACTIVE status AND a recent date on/near 28 Oct 2026. In practice almost every listing below is therefore [VERIFY] in whole or in part, for a stated reason (undated, stale, price conflict, duplicate, or a broker claim not checked against the city code). “Listing claim” means the words are the broker’s/listing’s, not a code verification by this research. “Code verification” is used only where a city document was actually read (Arden Hills, §8.2; Luverne ordinance, §8.6). Counties are given for every address; where the listing itself does not state the county, the county is the city-county mapping and is labelled as such — it is not presented as a listing-stated fact. No personal phones/emails of individuals are reproduced; only business/listing public contact details that appeared in the listing itself (broker firm names) are named, without phone numbers or personal emails. How to read the prices — the single most important pattern in this market: Most of the headline “prices” on 420Property/BizTrader for Minnesota retail sites are NOT the price of the building. They are the price of the state + municipal cannabis retail approvals (a licence/approvals bundle), PLUS assignment of a long-term lease at a stated monthly NNN rent. The building itself is leased, not sold, in those offers. This Part labels every price as (i) fee-simple sale, (ii) lease rate, (iii) approvals/licence price + lease assignment, or (iv) investment sale of a leased building, and does not add those different things together. Any reader who treats a $495,000 “sale price” as the price of the Roseville building, or a $275,000 Moorhead “price” as a building price, will misread this market.

8.1 Headline count — read this before the table

The Minnesota market is thin, and it is dominated by one broker pattern.

  • Distinct Minnesota addresses counted as cannabis/hemp-marketed properties: 19.
  • By category (each address counted once, in its primary category):
  • (a) Fee-simple / investment sale: 8 — New Hope, Waseca centre, North Mankato, Sandstone, Ely, Lyn-Lake Minneapolis (off-market), St. Cloud RISE (investment, fully leased), Rochester Hwy 52 (investment, fully leased).
  • (a)+(c) Hybrid sale + approvals bundle: 1 — Winona (real property + approvals, with a separate-approvals alternative).
  • (b) Lease + approvals bundle (price = approvals price; building leased): 5 — Roseville, Saint Paul, Moorhead, Alexandria, Belle Plaine.
  • (b) Pure lease / sublease, cannabis-marketed: 3 — Minneapolis Lagoon (Lumen on Lagoon), Arden Hills Portal Warehousing, Hector outdoor grow site.
  • (d) Generic / zoning-contingent only (cannabis named as an ideal or permitted use, not as a licensed cannabis offer): 2 — Savage, Cannon Falls.
  • Total: 8 + 1 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 19.
  • NOT counted in the 19, listed separately so the count is not inflated:
  • (c) Licence-only / business-only offers: at least 7 distinct offers (§8.5). None carries real estate.
  • Duplicates merged, not double-counted: the “Amazing Minneapolis Minnesota Uptown Site” (1201 Lagoon Ave) is the same site as “Lumen on Lagoon” (1201–1203 Lagoon Ave); the Waseca 1270 N State St suite lease and the 1230 N State St centre sale are the same shopping centre; the Roseville site appears under multiple LoopNet IDs.
  • Excluded as out-of-state or unconfirmed-Minnesota, despite appearing in Minnesota searches: §8.6.
  • Hemp-specific properties found: 1 — Sandstone (former CBD growing facility). No standalone hemp-processing facility for sale/lease in Minnesota was found in the routes searched; the Hector listing is cannabis (mezzobusiness fit) and the Arden Hills warehouse is cannabis wholesale, not hemp-specific.
  • Geography: The counted properties cluster in the Twin Cities metro (Roseville, Saint Paul, Minneapolis ×2, Arden Hills, New Hope, Savage, Cannon Falls) plus regional centres (Moorhead, Alexandria, Belle Plaine, Winona, Waseca, North Mankato, Ely, Hector, Sandstone, St. Cloud, Rochester). No counted property was found in Anoka, Saint Anthony Village, or Osseo as a current public listing (§8.4).
  • Zoning pattern: Only three counted listings state a zoning district in the retrieved text and can be tied to a code concept: Lumen on Lagoon C3A (listing claim only, not code-verified), New Hope “Community Business” with cannabis retail expressly listed among permitted uses (listing claim), and Arden Hills GB Gateway Business District with a city-approved Conditional Use Permit for cannabis wholesale (code/document-verified, §8.2). Roseville’s LoopNet facts give C-1 Commercial (listing/LoopNet facts, not a city-code check). Every other counted listing either states no zoning or states only “Industrial”/”Commercial” in general terms. No counted listing was verified against the Run 1 buffer rules (1,000 ft school / 500 ft day care, treatment facility, park) — buffers are not stated in any retrieved listing copy, and this Part does not re-do Run 1 Part 3.

8.3 What the pattern means (property-specific zoning notes only; no re-do of Part 3)

  1. The market is a licence-plus-lease market, not a real-estate market. Five of the 19 (plus Winona’s hybrid) are sold principally on approvals + lease assignment. A buyer in Roseville, Saint Paul, Moorhead, Alexandria, or Belle Plaine is buying the right to occupy a leased unit as a licensed retailer, not a building. Any valuation or “property count” that treats those five as building sales is wrong.
  2. Scarcity claims are broker claims and they conflict. Roseville “one of only three”, Alexandria “four” vs “six” in the same listing, Winona’s price split vs BizTrader total, Belle Plaine $295,000 vs $395,000, Moorhead $695,000 → $475,000 → $275,000, Sandstone $380,000 / $400,000 / $500,000 and 2.5 vs 40 acres — every one of these needs broker/OCM/city confirmation before publication. The conflicts are preserved above rather than resolved by picking the most convenient figure.
  3. Only Arden Hills is code-verified in this Part, and only for wholesale. Its GB zoning + CUP for cannabis wholesale (Resolution 2026-005, 12 Jan 2026) is a document, not a listing claim. It does not prove retail permissibility, suite vacancy, or buffer compliance, and it must not be generalised to other Arden Hills addresses.
  4. School adjacency is a live flag at Waseca. The centre’s own lease copy places it across the street from a high school and a middle school. Under the Run 1 buffer summary that adjacency requires a check; the listing’s “Cannabis Approved Location” headline does not answer it.
  5. No counted listing states a buffer measurement. The 1,000 ft / 500 ft Run 1 buffers appear in no retrieved listing copy. This Part therefore makes no buffer-compliance finding for any counted property.
  6. Retail caps are asserted, never sourced, in listings. Roseville (three), Alexandria (four/six) — no city ordinance or registration list was read to confirm either number. The Run 1 baseline (no official statewide local-registration list found) is consistent with that gap.

A note on the two “Division” names. OCM’s own materials use two names for the same equity/community work, and this Part preserves both rather than choosing one. OCM’s current local-government guide describes a Division of Community and Economic Development (DCED) which “invests in the development, stability, and safety of social equity eligible communities,” and OCM’s grants page says the grants “are available through OCM’s Division of Social Equity, part of the office’s Division of Community and Economic Development.” The cleanest reading is that the social-equity function now sits inside DCED, but OCM has not, in the pages opened for this Part, published a single dated renaming order. 9.1.2 Office of Cannabis Management (OCM)

Creation and mandate. OCM was created by the 2023 adult-use law, 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 63 (HF 100). The Governor’s office describes OCM as “Established in August 2023” and “responsible for developing operational and regulatory systems to launch and oversee Minnesota’s regulated cannabis and intoxicating hemp markets,” with the mission “to foster an equitable cannabis industry that prioritizes public health and safety, consumer confidence, and market integrity.” Source: Governor’s press release, “Governor Walz Appoints Eric Taubel as Executive Director of the Office of Cannabis Management,” https://mn.gov/governor/newsroom/press-releases/?id=1055-701817 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

OCM’s current local-government guide states the mandate in ch. 342 terms:

“Through Minnesota Statutes, chapter 342, OCM is mandated to: (1) Promote public health, safety, and welfare. (2) Eliminate the illicit market for cannabis flower and cannabis products. (3) Meet the market demand for cannabis flower and cannabis products. (4) Promote a craft industry for cannabis flower and cannabis products. (5) Prioritize growth and recovery in communities that have experienced a disproportionate, negative impact from cannabis prohibition.”

Source: OCM, A Guide for Local Minnesota Governments on Adult-Use Cannabis v5.0 (2026), https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/OCM_Local_Government_Guide_5.0_2026_tcm1202-627967.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

What OCM regulates. Adult-use cannabis licensing, compliance and enforcement; the medical cannabis programme (since 1 July 2024, §9.1.4); and hemp-derived cannabinoid / LPHE licensing under ch. 342 (the § 151.72 registration regime transitioned to ch. 342 licensing in the October 2025 LPHE window, §9.2). OCM’s rules are Minnesota Rules chapter 9810, approved by an administrative law judge 2 April 2025 and published in the State Register 14 April 2025 (Run 1 baseline, confirmed in this run — see §9.2 and OCM rulemaking page, http://mn.gov/ocm/laws/rulemaking.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28).

Divisions shown on OCM’s site (as found in this run).

  • Division of Medical Cannabis. OCM’s older local-government guide: “Housed within OCM are the Division of Medical Cannabis (effective July 1, 2024), which operates the medical cannabis program.” The Legislative Reference Library agency record confirms: “Active dates: July 1, 2024 – … The Office of Cannabis Management must administer the medical cannabis registry program and may oversee the licensing and regulation of medical cannabis businesses. Additional duties are outlined in Minn. Stat. 342.54.” Source: https://www.lrl.mn.gov/agencies/detail?AgencyID=2564 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note the LRL nuance, preserved here because it matters: the 2024 Legislature “removed most references to the ‘Division of Medical Cannabis’ in Minn. Stat. chap. 342 and instead gave the Office of Cannabis Management broad oversight over the medical cannabis program. The Office established the Division of Medical Cannabis” as an operating division. The division therefore exists as an OCM operating unit even though ch. 342 no longer names it in the way the 2023 act did.
  • Division of Social Equity / Division of Community and Economic Development. See the naming note at the top of this Part. The current local-government guide (v5.0, 2026) says OCM “houses … the Division of Community and Economic Development, which invests in the development, stability, and safety of social equity eligible communities.” An OCM grants flyer (October 2026) describes DCED as the division that “translates Minnesota’s cannabis legalization into meaningful community and economic opportunity” by “building community capacity via grants, expanding access to capital, supporting entrepreneurs and workers, and implementing social equity policy.” Source: https://content.govdelivery.com/attachments/MNOCM/2026/10/06/file_attachments/3806744/2410002_OCM_DCED_Grants_Overview_Flyer_092926.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. The grants page still attributes CanGrow/CanRenew to “OCM’s Division of Social Equity, part of the office’s Division of Community and Economic Development.” Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/grants/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. No other OCM operating divisions (e.g. a separately named licensing, enforcement or testing division) are presented as “divisions” on the OCM pages opened for this Part; licensing, enforcement/complaints, rulemaking and the ombudsperson function appear as OCM programmes/functions, not named divisions. 9.1.3 Cannabis Advisory Council (§ 342.03)

Statutory basis and verbatim duties. Minn. Stat. § 342.03, subd. 4(a) provides the duties “shall include”:

“(1) reviewing national cannabis policy; (2) examining the effectiveness of state cannabis policy; (3) reviewing developments in the cannabis industry and hemp consumer industry; (4) reviewing developments in the study of cannabis flower, cannabis products, artificially derived cannabinoids, lower-potency hemp edibles, and hemp-derived consumer products; (5) taking public testimony; (6) considering the impact of legalized adult-use cannabis on the rate of cannabis use by minors; and (7) making recommendations to the Office of Cannabis Management.”

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.03 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note: the OCM overview page’s shorter paraphrase omits duty (6) (minors’ use rate); the statute controls.

Membership (§ 342.03, subd. 1). The Council is large by design. It comprises: (1) the OCM director or designee (who chairs, subd. 3(a)); (2)–(13) the commissioners (or designees) of employment and economic development, revenue, health, human services, public safety, human rights, labor, and agriculture; the Pollution Control Agency commissioner; the BCA superintendent; the State Patrol colonel; and the DPS Office of Traffic Safety director; (14) a League of Minnesota Cities representative; (15) an Association of Minnesota Counties representative; (16)–(34) governor-appointed experts (minority business development; economic development for under-resourced communities; farming; cannabis workers; employers; municipal law enforcement with advanced impairment-detection training; social welfare/social justice; criminal-justice reform; substance-use prevention/treatment/recovery; minority business ownership; women-owned businesses; cannabis retailing; cannabis manufacturing; laboratory sciences/toxicology; legal services to cannabis businesses; cannabis cultivation; pediatric medicine; adult medicine; clinical pharmacy); (35) three patient advocates (one enrolled patient, one parent/caregiver of a patient, one patient with mental-health or substance-use-disorder treatment experience); (36) two licensed mental-health professionals; (37) a veteran; (38) one member designated by each of the 11 federally recognised Tribal Nations (Fond du Lac, Grand Portage, Mille Lacs, White Earth, Bois Forte, Leech Lake, Red Lake, Upper Sioux, Lower Sioux, Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux, Prairie Island); (39) a Local Public Health Association of Minnesota representative; and (40) two youth members aged 18–24 (one inside, one outside the seven-county metropolitan area) who have been disproportionately affected by cannabis or cannabis use or have an immediate family member negatively affected by cannabis use. Terms, compensation, removal and vacancies are under Minn. Stat. § 15.059, except that, notwithstanding § 15.059, subd. 6, “the advisory council shall not expire” (§ 342.03, subd. 2). Meetings: quarterly or on the chair’s call, subject to the Open Meeting Law, ch. 13D (§ 342.03, subd. 3).

Robert St., St. Paul, MN 55101, 10:00 a.m.–12:00 p.m. The past-meetings page adds 21 May 2026 and 22 May 2025 meetings. Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/about-us/cannabis-advisory-council/overview.jsp and https://mn.gov/ocm/about-us/cannabis-advisory-council/past-meetings.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28. At the 5 February 2026 meeting the minutes record “29 named members, 24 is quorum”; at 4 September 2025, “30 named members, 24 is quorum” — i.e. the seated membership at those dates was below the full statutory complement, consistent with the overview page showing open seats (two youth seats and a veteran seat) at the time of access. Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/CAC_Q1_2.5.2026_Meeting_Minutes_tcm1202-750922.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. No full current roster with names is asserted here: the overview page opened for this Part does not publish a roster, and reproducing a roster pieced together from meeting-minutes attendance lists would risk naming people who have since left. [VERIFY — current roster if the coordinator needs names]

Role limit. The Council is advisory. It does not issue licences, adopt rules, or enforce. Its recommendations go to OCM.

9.1.4 Department of Health (MDH) — historic medical programme, and what remains

Historic role. The Minnesota Medical Marijuana Act (SF 2470, 2014) created the medical cannabis programme under MDH’s Office of Medical Cannabis, originally codified at Minn. Stat. §§ 152.22–152.37. MDH ran the patient registry, practitioner certification and manufacturer regulation from first sales in 2015 until transfer. MDH also added qualifying conditions over time (intractable pain 2016; PTSD 1 August 2017; chronic pain and age-related macular degeneration decided December 2019, effective August 2020 — secondary summary, see §9.4).

Transfer. 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 63 originally scheduled the MDH → OCM transfer for 1 March 2025. The 2024 Legislature accelerated it. 2024 Minn. Laws ch. 121, § 52, subd. 3(a) provides: “The powers and duties of the Department of Health with respect to the medical cannabis program under Minnesota Statutes 2022, sections 152.22 to 152.37, are transferred to the Office of Cannabis Management under section 15.039,” with subd. 3(c): “This subdivision is effective July 1, 2024.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2024/0/121/laws.2.87.0 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Run 1’s transfer date (1 July 2024) is therefore confirmed against the session law. A secondary source found in this run (IndicaOnline) stating OCM “formally took over the medical cannabis program … on March 1, 2025” is wrong on this point — it repeats the superseded 2023 date — and must not be used. See §9.4, item C-2.

What MDH retains. After transfer, MDH does not run the registry or license medical businesses. The 2023 act established a youth-prevention and education programme run by MDH (with the Departments of Human Services and Education, in coordination with local public health) addressing cannabis use by people under 25 — that prevention/education function is the principal residual MDH cannabis role identified in this run, described in a Minnesota Academy of Family Physicians summary of the law. It is flagged as secondary-sourced; the current statutory home of that programme after the 2024–2026 amendments was not re-verified against current revisor text in this Part. [VERIFY — current MDH prevention-programme statute] MDH’s commissioner (or designee) also sits on the Cannabis Advisory Council (§ 342.03, subd. 1(4)). Old MDH programme URLs forward to OCM.

Contact. MDH generally: https://www.health.state.mn.us/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Medical cannabis questions are now directed to OCM (medical.cannabis@state.mn.us, §9.1.2), not MDH.

9.1.5 Department of Agriculture (MDA) — hemp production

Statutory basis. Minn. Stat. ch. 18K, the Minnesota Industrial Hemp Development Act (IHDA), enacted 2015. MDA’s hemp rules are Minn. Rules ch. 1565 (published fall 2021). The USDA-approved State Hemp Plan governs production licensing, inspection, sampling/testing and enforcement for hemp grown/processed in Minnesota.

What MDA regulates — and the boundary with OCM. MDA regulates hemp production: grower and processor licensing under the USDA plan, including the pilot programme (2016–2020) and the commercial programme from the 2021 growing season. OCM regulates hemp-derived consumer products (LPHE edibles/beverages and other hemp-derived cannabinoid products sold to consumers) under ch. 342. The two regimes meet at processing: MDA’s own plan documents describe MDA enforcement authority for “hemp production and raw hemp processing,” while consumer-product licensing sits with OCM. A 2024 session summary describing the hemp-derived cannabinoid market as “transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the Office of Cannabis Management” refers to the consumer-product market, not to MDA’s production programme, which continued to publish a 2025 Hemp Program Annual Report. Source: https://www.mda.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/docs/2026-02/2025_Hemp_Annual_Report_web.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. The precise statutory line for a processor that both processes raw hemp and manufactures a consumer product was not resolved from primary text in this Part. [VERIFY — processor boundary, ch. 18K vs. ch. 342]

Hemp plan dates (MDA/USDA documents). Plan submitted to USDA 31 March 2020; USDA comments 1 May 2020; USDA approved the Minnesota State Hemp Plan 14 July 2020, effective for the 2021 growing season (1 January 2021); USDA Final Rule 15 January 2021 (86 FR 5596); revised plan resubmitted 18 March / 29 April 2021; revised plan approved 6 May 2021 — described by MDA as the first plan approved under the Final Rule. Sources: https://www.mda.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/inline-files/hemprulesummaryforalj2020_0.pdf and https://mn.gov/oah/assets/9024-37136-agriculture-industrial-hemp-rules-order_tcm19-492317.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Contact. MDA generally: https://www.mda.state.mn.us/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. No hemp-programme-specific public phone/email is asserted here; the MDA hemp pages opened for this Part route enquiries through the Department’s general contacts. [VERIFY — MDA hemp programme direct contact if required]

9.1.6 Department of Revenue (DOR) — cannabis tax

Statutory basis and verbatim rate. Minn. Stat. § 295.81, subd. 2(a) (current text, Revisor):

“A tax equal to 15 percent of gross receipts from retail sales in Minnesota of taxable cannabis products is imposed on any taxable cannabis product retailer that sells these products to customers.”

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/295.81 — Accessed 2026-10-28. The tax is in addition to other taxes on the sale (§ 295.81, subd. 2(c)); in practice that means the 6.875% state general sales tax (ch. 297A) plus any applicable local sales tax. Medical cannabis sold under the medical programme is exempt from the gross receipts tax (DOR guidance, secondary summary — see Part 10/11 for tax detail; the exemption itself is not re-litigated here).

Distribution — Run 1 confirmed. DOR’s 2025 Cannabis Legislative Bulletin (18 August 2025, final) states: § 295.81, subd. 2 was amended “to increase the cannabis gross receipts tax rate from 10 percent to 15 percent. Effective for sales and purchases made after June 30, 2025. 2025 Minn. Laws, 1st Spec. Sess., Ch. 13, Art. 3, § 3”; § 295.81, subd. 10 was amended “to require the commissioner to deposit all revenues from the cannabis gross receipts tax in the general fund and remove the local cannabis aid account in the special revenue fund. The amendment to deposit all revenues in the general fund is effective for revenues received after June 30, 2025. The amendment to remove the local cannabis aid account in the special revenue fund is effective January 2, 2026. 2025 Minn. Laws, 1st Spec. Sess., Ch. 13, Art. 8, § 18”; § 477A.32 (local government cannabis aid) was repealed and “the commissioner will make the last aid payment from this account on December 26, 2025.” Source: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/2025-08/2025-cannabis-legislative-bulletin.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. Run 1’s tax history (10% → 15%; former 80/20 split repealed; 100% General Fund under § 295.81, subd. 10; account removed 2 January 2026; last aid payment 26 December 2025) is therefore confirmed against DOR’s own bulletin.

Tribal tax agreements. Each Tribal Nation may enter a cannabis tax agreement with DOR “providing for payments related to expenses for producing and supplying cannabis to off-reservation locations and taxes paid by Tribal members at that location”; sales off Tribal lands are subject to all state and local taxes. Source: OCM compacts page, http://mn.gov/ocm/tribal-nation/compacts.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Contact. DOR generally: https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. The bulletin itself is addressed from Appeals, Legal Services, and Disclosure Division, 600 N. Robert St., St. Paul, MN 55146-2220. No individual DOR contact is given.

9.1.7 Cannabis Expungement Board (CEB) — remit (full numbers in Part 12)

Creation and composition. Minn. Stat. § 609A.06, subd. 1(a)–(b): “The Cannabis Expungement Board is created with the powers and duties established by law,” composed of five members: (1) the chief justice of the supreme court or a designee; (2) the attorney general or a designee; (3) one public defender, appointed by the governor upon recommendation of the state public defender; (4) the commissioner of corrections or a designee; and (5) one public member with relevant experience, appointed by the governor (the governor “shall prioritize appointment of an individual with experience as an advocate for victim’s rights,” § 609A.06, subd. 1(c)). Three affirmative votes are required for action (§ 609A.06, subd. 1(h), via the SOS commissions record). Source: https://mn.gov/ceb/board-information-minnesota-cannabis-expungement-board/ and https://commissionsandappointments.sos.mn.gov/Agency/Details/325 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Remit — and what it is not. The Board reviews felony cannabis records case by case to determine whether the person committed an act involving sale or possession of cannabis flower or cannabinoid products that would now be a lesser offence or no longer a crime after 1 August 2023, and whether expungement and/or resentencing (including release or sentence reduction) is warranted, weighing the factors in § 609A.06, subd. 1(f) (nature/severity, weapon/bodily-harm facts, risk, release consequences, aggravating/mitigating factors, victim and law-enforcement statements, firearms-rights restoration, and specified background-check openings). It operates “until all records have been reviewed and the Board has determined it has completed its work” (CEB budget/legislative-report language). It meets monthly (CEB board-information page: “The five-person CEB Board meets monthly to review and make determinations about individual cases” — approximately 110,000 cases for review on that page, a figure whose reconciliation with Part 12’s counts is left to Part 12; see §9.4, G-5).

Boundary with the BCA. Automatic expungement of qualifying non-felony cannabis offences is not the Board’s work: under § 609A.055 the BCA identifies eligible individuals, notifies the Judicial Branch, and seals BCA records (within 60 days after notice to the Judicial Branch, unless a court order prohibits sealing). The Board is the route for felonies that are not automatically expunged. Conflating the two is the commonest error in secondary coverage; this Part keeps them separate.

Contact. CEB board-information page: https://mn.gov/ceb/board-information-minnesota-cannabis-expungement-board/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. No CEB public phone/email is asserted here. [VERIFY — CEB public contact channel]

9.1.8 Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) and Department of Public Safety (DPS)

Position. The BCA is a division of DPS. Its superintendent (or designee) sits on the Cannabis Advisory Council (§ 342.03, subd. 1(11)); the DPS commissioner (or designee), the State Patrol colonel, and the DPS Office of Traffic Safety director also sit on the Council (§ 342.03, subd. 1(6), (12), (13)).

Three cannabis roles.

  1. Automatic expungement (§ 609A.055). The BCA “shall identify bureau records that qualify for expungement,” notify the Judicial Branch of each eligible person’s name, date of birth and court file number, grant expungement relief and seal BCA records without requiring an application, petition or motion, and inform arresting/citing agencies. See §9.1.7 for the 60-day sealing rule. Source: Minn. Stat. § 609A.055 (via Revisor/secondary text) — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  2. Licence-applicant criminal-history checks (§ 342.15, subd. 1). On OCM’s request, an applicant (and, for entities, each individual responsible for the entity’s affairs) submits a consent form, classifiable fingerprints and fees to OCM; OCM submits them to the BCA; the BCA conducts the state check, may exchange fingerprints with the FBI for the national check, and returns results to OCM for disqualification determinations. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/cite/342.15/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  3. Cannabis-worker checks (§ 342.151, subd. 2). Before hiring a cannabis worker, the licence holder “must submit to the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension the individual’s full set of fingerprints and written consent for the bureau to conduct a state and national criminal history check”; the BCA determines qualification and notifies the licence holder. Transition note (OCM background-checks page): while DPS/BCA awaited FBI approval, 2024 Minn. Laws ch. 121, art. 2, § 149 authorised interim third-party screening; with FBI approval secured, effective 1 March 2026 businesses and prospective employees who have not yet completed a check must use the BCA process (third-party checks completed before 1 March 2026 remain compliant). Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/resources/background-checks.jsp and https://dps.mn.gov/divisions/bca/bca-divisions/criminal-justice-information-services/background-checks/employers/cannabis-workers — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Public contact (agency). BCA Criminal History / CHA Unit, 1430 Maryland Avenue East, St. Paul, MN 55106 (address as published on the DPS cannabis-workers page for mailing fingerprint cards; the “Reason Fingerprinted” block must reference Minn. Stat. § 342.151 and the ORI field MNBCA0000). Source: DPS page above — Accessed 2026-10-28. No individual BCA/DPS contact is given.

9.1.9 Department of Employment and Economic Development (DEED) — grants, not licensing

DEED administers three cannabis grant programmes created by the 2023 act; OCM administers the other two (§9.1.2). DEED does not license cannabis businesses.

  • CanStartup — Minn. Stat. § 116J.659, subd. 1: “The commissioner of employment and economic development shall establish CanStartup, a program to award grants to nonprofit corporations to fund loans to new cannabis microbusinesses and to support job creation in communities where long-term residents are eligible to be social equity applicants.” Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/cite/116J.659/subd/116J.659.5 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • CanNavigate — Minn. Stat. § 116J.6595: grants to eligible organisations to develop technical-assistance resources and navigation services for the legal cannabis industry, with emphasis on people who have faced barriers to employment or education and on communities where long-term residents are eligible social-equity applicants. Source: DEED CanNavigate annual report, https://mn.gov/deed/assets/cannavigate-2024-annual-report_tcm1045-670609.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • CanTrain — Minn. Stat. § 116L.90: grants to eligible organisations to develop/provide cannabis-industry workforce training, and grants of up to $20,000 to eligible individuals to pursue such training (individual grants awarded by lottery). Source: DEED CanTrain annual report, http://minnesota.gov/deed/assets/2024-can-train-annual-report_tcm1045-668001.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

OCM’s companion programmes: CanRenew (Minn. Stat. § 342.70 — community investments in disproportionately affected communities; FY2027–28 appropriation $10.9 million, awards $50,000–$2,000,000, RFP opened 22 October 2026, applications due 4:30 p.m. CT 15 December 2026) and CanGrow (section number not confirmed in this Part — see §9.4, G-2; farmer navigation grants and nonprofit loans for farmer expansion, in consultation with the Commissioner of Agriculture). Sources: https://mn.gov/ocm/development/grants/canrenew.jsp and https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/grants/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. A further grant mentioned on OCM’s grants page as provided by the Office of Higher Education in collaboration with the Department of Labor and Industry was truncated in the page text opened for this Part and is not described here. [VERIFY — OHE/DLI grant name and statute]

Contact. DEED generally: https://mn.gov/deed/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. No individual DEED contact is given (a named DEED programme director’s phone/email appears in a DEED report; it is deliberately omitted under the contact rule).

9.1.10 Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) — rulemaking review

OAH does not regulate cannabis day to day. Its role in this history is as the independent reviewer of OCM’s expedited rulemaking under Minn. Stat. ch. 14: OCM submitted final draft rules to an OAH administrative law judge on 25 March 2025; the ALJ approved the rules without changes on 2 April 2025; publication in the State Register on 14 April 2025 put Minnesota Rules chapter 9810 into effect. Source: http://mn.gov/ocm/laws/rulemaking.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28. OAH also heard MDA’s hemp rulemaking (ALJ order in the 9024-37136 industrial-hemp rules matter, cited §9.1.5). Contact: https://mn.gov/oah/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

9.1.11 Other agencies with a statutory cannabis/hemp role

  • Department of Human Services / Department of Children, Youth, and Families; Department of Education; Department of Labor and Industry; Department of Human Rights; Pollution Control Agency; Department of Commerce (limited). These appear principally as Cannabis Advisory Council members (§ 342.03, subd. 1) or as partners in the youth-prevention programme (§9.1.4), not as cannabis licensors. No freestanding cannabis licensing statute for any of them was located in this Part, and none is asserted. The Department of Human Services also receives lists of expunged cases under the HF 100 expungement scheme (secondary summary) — a notification role, not a regulatory one. [VERIFY — whether any of these agencies holds a current freestanding cannabis rule or fee authority outside ch. 342]
  • Minnesota Judicial Branch. Issues expungement orders on BCA notice (§ 609A.055) and hears the cannabis licensing litigation (§9.2). Not a regulator.
  • Attorney General / Commissioner of Corrections / State Public Defender. CEB members (§9.1.7), not cannabis regulators as such.
  • Local governments and Tribal regulators. See the summary table (§9.1.1) — these are the two non-state regulators that actually license or register retail activity on the ground (local registration for state licensees; tribal licensing for tribal enterprises).

9.3 Ballot history and public opinion polling

9.3.1 No statewide citizen initiative or referendum — confirmed

Minnesota has no citizen initiative and no referendum for cannabis — or for anything else. The Secretary of State states it in one sentence:

“Minnesota does not have Initiative and Referendum so other than constitutional amendments no other statewide ballot questions are authorized.”

Source: Minnesota Secretary of State, “Ballot questions,” https://sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/how-elections-work/ballot-questions/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Constitutional mechanism. Under Minn. Const. art. IX, § 1, a constitutional amendment must be proposed by a majority of the members of each house, published with the laws of that session, and submitted to the people at a general election; it is ratified only if a majority of all people voting at the election vote for it (so a blank on the amendment counts, in effect, as a “no”). That is the only route to a statewide ballot question in Minnesota. The Secretary of State’s page points to the Legislative Reference Library’s list of proposed constitutional amendments (with ballot language and ratification outcome) as the authoritative inventory. Source: SOS page (above).

Consequence for cannabis. No citizen-initiated cannabis legalisation, cannabis referendum or cannabis veto referendum has ever been, or can currently be, placed on a Minnesota statewide ballot by petition. Cannabis legalisation in Minnesota was achieved entirely by legislation (HF 100, 2023), not by ballot measure — which is why §9.3.2 is short.

9.3.2 Legislative ballot questions touching cannabis

None found. After checking (a) the Secretary of State’s ballot-questions explanation and its pointer to the LRL proposed-amendments list, (b) Ballotpedia’s inventory summary (218 Minnesota ballot measures decided 1857–2025, of which 217 were legislatively referred constitutional amendments and one was the constitution-ratification measure; “citizens do not have the power to initiate constitutional amendments, veto referendums, or state statutes”), and (c) the topics of referred amendments as summarised by Ballotpedia (legislative authority, education funding, highways, suffrage, same-sex marriage, initiative/referendum process itself, redistricting, alcohol prohibition, supermajority rules — no cannabis topic listed), no legislatively referred constitutional amendment touching cannabis was located. Source (secondary inventory): https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/03/25/minnesota-voters-have-decided-218-ballot-measures-since-1857-beginning-with-the-ratification-of-the-state-constitution/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Two adjacent facts are recorded so the coordinator does not mistake them for cannabis ballot questions:

  • Attempts to create initiative/referendum (not cannabis questions): the Legislature placed amendments to establish an initiative and referendum process on the ballot in 1914, 1916 and 1980. Each won more “yes” than “no” votes but none won a majority of all voters at the election, so none was ratified (Ballotpedia summary, above). Minnesota therefore remains one of 24 states without initiative/referendum.
  • A proposal for a constitutional amendment “to let voters decide” cannabis is mentioned in secondary historical narrative about pre-2023 debate (a task-force / constitutional-amendment idea floated when legalisation bills stalled). No such amendment was shown to have been referred to voters, and no ballot language or result was located. Do not list it as a ballot question. [VERIFY — whether any cannabis constitutional amendment was ever formally introduced as a referred-amendment bill; LRL list check by bill topic]

The 2026 ballot amendment is not cannabis. The Secretary of State’s constitutional-amendments page notes one proposed amendment on the 3 November 2026 ballot: “Increasing funding to school districts” from the permanent school fund. It has nothing to do with cannabis and is recorded here only to prevent a future reader from assuming the 2026 question was cannabis-related. Source: https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/whats-on-my-ballot/constitutional-amendments/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

9.3.3 Local ballot questions / advisory votes on cannabis in Minnesota

None found with official results — and the legal structure explains why there are unlikely to be many. The Secretary of State’s rule is: “Unless a question is authorized by law to be voted on it cannot be placed on the ballot” (SOS ballot-questions page, above). For cities and townships, a special-election question requires authorisation by law or charter (Minn. Stat. § 205.10, subd. 1), on council/board motion or on a petition of 20% of votes cast at the last city/town general election, subject to the 84-day county-auditor notice rule (§ 205.10, subd. 5; § 205.16). Separately, ch. 342 prohibits local governments from banning cannabis businesses outright (they may cap retailer registrations only at or above one per 12,500 residents, and regulate time, place and manner) — so a local binding vote to ban cannabis businesses would conflict with ch. 342 as it stands, and a local advisory vote would have no binding effect and no ch. 342 authorisation to point to.

What was checked. (1) SOS ballot-questions page (statewide + city/township/school-district rules); (2) Ballotpedia Minnesota ballot-measure inventory (statewide only — it does not compile local questions, so it cannot prove a negative locally); (3) web searches for Minnesota city/county cannabis ballot/advisory votes 2023–2026 (returns were dominated by other states’ local votes — e.g. West Richland, Washington; Redmond, Oregon — and by Minnesota council actions, not ballot questions); (4) Minnesota House State Fair polls (§9.3.4), which are polls, not ballots. No Minnesota city or county cannabis ballot question with a county/city canvass result was located in this run. Municipal cannabis actions found instead are council/ordinance actions (e.g. Marshall, Lyon County, Ordinance No. 23-019 on public use; Anoka’s municipally owned dispensary, opened February 2026 per secondary reporting; Grand Rapids’ planned municipal dispensary) — none of which is a ballot question.

Limit of this negative finding. There is no single Secretary of State database of local ballot questions to search exhaustively; local questions live in 87 county canvasses and hundreds of city records. This Part therefore reports “none found after the checks listed,” not “none ever existed.” If the coordinator requires an exhaustive local negative, the next step is a targeted search of the SOS election-results database and of city-council minutes for the largest cities (Minneapolis, St. Paul, Duluth, Rochester, Bloomington, Brooklyn Park, Plymouth, Woodbury, Maple Grove, Blaine) for 2023–2026. [UNAVAILABLE — exhaustive local canvass search]

Related, non-ballot democratic channel (for context, not as a ballot). The Legal Marijuana Now Party’s electoral history (candidates on Minnesota ballots, including the 2022 District 2 race in which deceased nominee Paula Overby received 10,728 votes, and the 2024 Minnesota Supreme Court ruling that the party no longer qualified for major-party ballot access under a 2023 law) is candidate ballot access, not a cannabis question on the ballot, and is therefore noted here in one sentence only and not counted in §9.3.2/§9.3.3. Source (secondary): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_political_parties_of_the_United_States — Accessed 2026-10-28.

9.3.4 Public opinion polling on cannabis in Minnesota — most recent first

All items below are secondary sources, labelled as such. No national poll is presented as a Minnesota poll. State Fair polls are informal, unscientific, self-selected fairgoer polls — not probability samples — and are labelled as such wherever they appear. Question wording is quoted verbatim where the source gives it.

Date / field period Pollster / sponsor; sample & method Question (verbatim where available) Result
25 Sept – 6 Nov 2025 (published 14 Jan 2026; updated 20 Oct 2026) Lumaris / Minnesota Community Survey — 1,172 Minnesota adults; online in English or Spanish; margin of error ±3.85 points; statewide probability survey (per publisher) Legalisation support and “has legalisation made things better/worse/no difference” (exact question wording and topline support % are in a chart image in the article, not in the article text opened for this Part) Publisher’s summary: “Minnesotans broadly support legal cannabis, but most say it hasn’t changed their daily lives”; “Democrats support legalization at nearly twice the rate of Republicans”; majorities of both Republicans and Democrats say legalisation has made “no difference” in daily life; Republicans more likely to say it made things worse. Companion article from the same survey: 23% of Minnesota adults reported consuming cannabis in the past month, with the sharpest divides by income, politics and place of birth. Exact topline support % NOT asserted — it must be read from the chart. See §9.4, G-7.
Aug–Sept 2025 (State Fair; results published Sept 2025) Minnesota House Public Information Services Office, 2025 State Fair Poll — 9,945 fairgoers; informal, unscientific, self-selected (House Session Daily) “Should cities and counties be allowed to prohibit cannabis businesses in their community?” Yes 47.8% (4,661); No 41.8% (4,076); Undecided/No Opinion 10.4% (1,011). A plurality for local bans — notable because ch. 342 currently bars outright local bans.
16–18 Sept 2024 Mason-Dixon Polling & Strategy for MPR News / KARE 11 / Minnesota Star Tribune — 800 likely voters; margin of error ±3.5 points Two distinct items reported by MPR: (a) recent use; (b) support for national legalisation (not Minnesota legalisation) (a) Only 14% reported consuming marijuana or THC-infused hemp products in the last month. (b) 61% supported legalisation at the national level. Item (b) must not be quoted as “61% of Minnesotans support Minnesota legalisation” — the question was national.
Aug 2022 (State Fair; results published Sept 2022) Minnesota House Public Information Services Office, 2022 State Fair Poll — 7,110 fairgoers; informal, unscientific, self-selected “Should Minnesota allow the recreational use of marijuana by persons age 21 and over?” Yes 61.4% (4,312); No 30.2% (2,116); Undecided/No Opinion 8.4% (590).
Aug 2021 (State Fair) House State Fair Poll (same series) — 5,231 fairgoers Same recreational-use question (as reported in 2022 coverage) Yes 58%; No 34% (remainder undecided/no opinion).
Aug 2019 (State Fair) House State Fair Poll — 11,239 fairgoers; informal, unscientific “Should Minnesota allow the recreational use of marijuana for those age 21 and over?” Yes 56.3% (6,272); No 33.8% (3,761); Undecided/No Opinion 9.9% (1,102).
Aug 2018 (State Fair) House State Fair Poll (same series) Same recreational-use question Yes 56.2% (per 2019 comparison: “up very slightly from 56.2% the year before”); No 33.9%.
2014 (State Fair) House State Fair Poll (same series) Same recreational-use question (as reported in 2019 coverage) Yes 43%; No 47% — i.e. plurality opposition in 2014, the earliest State Fair data point in this series.
Pre-2014 (PPP / MN NORML, dates not pinned in sources opened) Public Policy Polling, commissioned by MN NORML — statewide survey; sample size and field dates not stated in the secondary summaries opened Medical-marijuana support; full-legalisation support Secondary summaries report ~74–75% support for medical marijuana (Democrats 86%, Independents 69%, Republicans 64% in one summary) and ~50% for full legalisation at the time. These figures are weakly sourced (advocacy-commissioned, undated in the summaries, no methods given) and are included only to show the pre-2014 baseline; they should not be quoted alongside the probability polls without that caveat.

Sources for the table (all Accessed 2026-10-28): Lumaris support article https://www.lumaris.com/blog/2026/01/14/most-minnesotans-support-legal-cannabis-but-few-say-it-has-made-things-better/ ; Lumaris use article https://www.lumaris.com/blog/2026/01/14/who-uses-cannabis-in-minnesota/ ; 2025 State Fair poll https://www.house.mn.gov/SessionDaily/Story/18849 ; MPR/Mason-Dixon Sept 2024 poll via https://www.ivoox.com/minnesota-poll-only-small-fraction-of-minnesotans-say-audios-mp3_rf_134219109_amp_1.html (MPR audio page summarising the poll; the underlying MPR article text was not opened — see §9.4, G-8); 2022 State Fair poll https://www.house.leg.state.mn.us/SessionDaily/Story/17478 ; 2019 State Fair poll https://www.house.mn.gov/sessiondaily/Story/14008 ; PPP/MN NORML summaries https://theweedblog.com/ending-marijuana-prohibition/poll-minnesota-medical-marijuana-legalization and https://theweedblog.com/?p=34950 .

Reading the trend (with methods kept separate). On the same State Fair question, fairgoer support rose from plurality opposition in 2014 (43% yes) through 56–58% in 2018–2021 to 61.4% in 2022, the last year that question was asked in the series found. The series then changes question: in 2025 fairgoers were asked about local bans, not about legalisation itself, and a plurality (47.8%) favoured allowing local bans. That is not a reversal of legalisation support — it is a different question, asked of a self-selected fair crowd after retail rollout began, and it measures local-control sentiment, not legalisation sentiment. The only recent probability-sample evidence in this Part is Lumaris (Sept–Nov 2025), which finds broad support but does not, in text form, give a topline percentage (G-7), and Mason-Dixon (Sept 2024), which asked about national legalisation. There is no recent Minnesota probability poll in this Part that cleanly asks “do you support Minnesota’s adult-use legalisation as it stands” with a published topline. That gap should be stated plainly in any synthesis, not filled with the State Fair or national-question figures.

No 2026 Minnesota cannabis poll was located in this Part. Searches for 2026 Minnesota cannabis polling returned the Lumaris January 2026 publication of the autumn-2025 fieldwork, the 2025 State Fair poll, and national polls. Minnesota Cannabis & Hemp Research — Run 2, Part 10: Tribal and Interstate

Scope: Part 10 only. Tribal Nations, tribal–state compacts/cooperative agreements, tribal medical programmes, tribal hemp, and interstate issues. Date / access stamp: All sources cited as Accessed 2026-10-28, unless a source itself is dated later in the search index (noted where that occurs). Where a search result is dated after 28 October 2026 in the index, it is used only for a non-legal location fact and is labelled secondary; no legal conclusion in this Part rests on a post-28-October source. Method note — read this first: The task required opening official pages directly. In this research window, direct page-open calls for the OCM compacts page, the OCM Tribal Nations page, and the USDA state-and-tribal-plan page failed at the tool layer (transient-grant errors, not a finding that the pages do not exist or are login-blocked). Those three opens were not retried, per instruction. The facts below therefore rest on (a) verbatim text returned by the search index for official pages (Minnesota Revisor of Statutes, OCM pages as indexed, Legislative Reference Library compact PDFs as indexed, USDA plan list as indexed), and (b) secondary sources, labelled as such, for store openings and locations only. Anything that would require reading a full signed compact PDF line-by-line is marked [VERIFY] at the point where the full text was not returned, even where a summary is consistent across sources. Do not cite this Part as a substitute for reading the signed compact PDFs before publication or outreach.

0. Headline answers

  1. Eleven federally recognised Tribal Nations share territory with Minnesota. Nine have an executed cannabis compact or cooperative agreement with the state. Two do not: Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa and Upper Sioux Community. That matches Run 1; it is confirmed, not merely carried forward, by the OCM compacts listing and by Minn. Stat. § 3.9228, subd. 1(g), which names all eleven.
  2. Run 1 compact dates — RESOLVED. Every Run 1 date marked [VERIFY] is confirmed by the OCM “Compacts and Cooperative Agreements” listing as indexed: White Earth 20 May 2025; Mille Lacs 10 September 2025; Prairie Island and Fond du Lac 20 October 2025; Leech Lake 30 October 2025; Red Lake cooperative agreement 12 December 2025; Bois Forte 18 December 2025; Lower Sioux 9 March 2026; Shakopee Mdewakanton 10 March 2026. See §2.
  3. A compact is not what makes tribal cannabis lawful on tribal land. Minnesota law expressly acknowledges that a Tribal government may regulate cannabis within its jurisdiction whether or not it has compacted. A compact proactively addresses jurisdictional, testing, tracking, tax-sharing, and off-reservation issues. See §1.1.
  4. Off-reservation retail cap (common compact pattern, OCM local-government guidance): up to eight off-reservation retail locations per compacting Nation, one per municipality, three per county, following non-cannabis-specific local ordinances (zoning, land use, setbacks, hours). Product moving off tribal lands must be entered into the state’s seed-to-sale system and meet state testing, packaging, and labelling standards. Off-reservation sales are subject to state and local taxes; on-tribal-land sales by tribally licensed businesses are exempt from the cannabis gross receipts tax and from sales tax (see §5).
  5. No officially reported tribal dispensary sales total exists. The “more than $250 million” first-year figure and the $45.6 million tax figure are state-licensed figures. OCM’s own announcement describes them as purchases “from Minnesota businesses since the launch of legal sales at state-licensed businesses,” with adult-use sales at state-licensed businesses beginning 16 September 2025, and it separately notes that retail sales on tribally regulated lands began shortly after the August 2023 bill. Tribal sales are NOT included in the $250 million / $45.6 million figures. Do not add a tribal total, and do not present the state-licensed total as a whole-market total. [UNAVAILABLE: tribal total — see §6.]
  6. Interstate bottom line: a non-resident adult 21+ may buy in Minnesota and use/possess within Minnesota within Minnesota limits; that purchase gives no right to carry cannabis across any state line, including into a state where cannabis is legal, because federal law still treats adult-use cannabis as Schedule I and interstate transport as a federal offence. Compliant hemp is different: 2018 Farm Act § 10114 bars a state or Tribe from prohibiting the transportation/shipment through its territory of hemp produced in accordance with federal hemp law — but that protection does not compel a destination state to allow sale of the product, and after 11 December 2026 (see federal baseline) a product that no longer meets the federal hemp definition loses the premise of that protection. See §7.
  7. No Minnesota agreement with another state on cannabis or hemp was located. See §7.6 — stated as a search result, not as proof that no memorandum of any kind exists in an unindexed file.

1. Legal framework

1.1 The two compacting statutes — verified authorising provisions

Run 1 cited § 3.9228. That citation is confirmed, and completed: there are two parallel provisions, and signed compacts cite both.

  • Minn. Stat. § 3.9224 — Medical Cannabis; Compacts to Be Negotiated. Its subdivision 2(a) acknowledges the sovereign right of Minnesota Tribal governments to regulate the medical cannabis industry and related matters within their jurisdiction “without regard to whether such Tribal government has entered a compact authorized by this section,” and authorises the governor or designee to negotiate in good faith and execute a medical compact with any Minnesota Tribal government wishing to enter one.
  • Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/3.9224 (via indexed text) — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Minn. Stat. § 3.9228 — Adult-Use Cannabis; Compacts to Be Negotiated. Subdivision 1(g) defines “Minnesota Tribal governments” as exactly the eleven Nations listed in §3 below. Subdivision 2 contains the parallel acknowledgment for adult-use cannabis. Subdivision 5 requires publication: “The governor shall post any compact entered into under this section on a publicly accessible website” — the OCM compacts page is that publication route.
  • Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/3.9228 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Signed-compact authority clause (verbatim from the Shakopee Mdewakanton compact as indexed, and identically from the Bois Forte compact as indexed):

    “This Cannabis Compact between the [Tribe] and the State of Minnesota (“Compact”) is entered into pursuant to Minnesota Statutes, sections 3.9224 and 3.9228 (the “Compacting Legislation”).”

  • Sources: Shakopee Mdewakanton compact PDF via Legislative Reference Library, https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2026/other/260550/ShakopeeMdewakantonSiouxCommunity_CannabisCompact.pdf ; Bois Forte compact PDF, https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/Cannabis_Compact_Between_The_Bois_Forte_Band_Of_The_Minnesota_Chippewa_Tribe_And_The_State_Of_Minnesota_tcm1202-717533.pdf — both Accessed 2026-10-28 (indexed text only; full PDFs not opened in this window — see Method note).
  • The Shakopee compact’s purpose clause, also verbatim as indexed, states the sovereignty point in the compact’s own words:

    “The Tribe has a sovereign right to regulate the Cannabis industry on Tribally Regulated Land and address other matters of Cannabis regulation, without regard to whether the Tribe has entered into a compact.”

  • The compact’s stated intent is “to facilitate and promote a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship between the State and the Tribe regarding the legalization of Cannabis, and to enhance public health and safety, ensure a lawful and well-regulated Cannabis market, encourage economic growth, and provide fiscal benefits to the Tribe.”
  • Consequence — do not conflate the two legal orders: tribal cannabis law (tribal ordinance / tribal regulator licence) governs on tribally regulated land; Minnesota Chapter 342 governs state-licensed businesses; a compact is the bridge instrument that (a) lets a tribally licensed business operate off tribal land under tribal regulation with state secondary oversight, and (b) lets tribal and state licensees trade with each other. A tribal licence is not a state licence, and a state licence is not a tribal licence. Minn. Stat. § 342.13(k) reinforces the boundary from the state side (verbatim):

    “Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions, the state shall not issue a license to any cannabis business to operate in Indian country, as defined in United States Code, title 18, section 1151, of a Minnesota Tribal government without the consent of the Tribal government.”

  • Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/342.13 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

1.2 Public Law 280 in Minnesota — what it does and does not do

  • Minnesota is a mandatory Public Law 280 state. Pub. L. 83-280 (1953), codified in relevant part at 18 U.S.C. § 1162 (criminal) and 28 U.S.C. § 1360 (civil), transferred federal criminal jurisdiction over Indian Country to six mandatory states, including Minnesota, and gave those states only limited civil jurisdiction — civil causes of action between private parties — not general civil/regulatory authority over Tribes.
  • The classic statement, quoted in the Minnesota Court of Appeals decision below, is from State v. Stone, 572 N.W.2d 725, 728–729 (Minn. 1997): “In Public Law 280, Congress granted Minnesota broad criminal and limited civil jurisdiction over all Indian country within the state, with the exception of Red Lake Reservation” and § 4 of PL 280 “does not grant the state general civil/regulatory authority.”
  • The Red Lake exception matters and is real. Red Lake Reservation is expressly excepted from Minnesota’s PL 280 criminal jurisdiction; there, tribal and federal authorities share criminal jurisdiction. Every other Minnesota reservation is within PL 280’s criminal grant — but that grant only reaches criminal/prohibitory law.
  • The criminal/prohibitory vs. civil/regulatory test (California v. Cabazon Band of Mission Indians, 480 U.S. 202, 207–208 (1987)). If a state law generally prohibits conduct, PL 280 lets the state enforce it in Indian Country; if the state law generally permits the conduct subject to regulation, PL 280 does not give the state regulatory enforcement authority there, even if violation carries a criminal penalty. Tribes retain attributes of sovereignty over members and territory, “dependent on, and subordinate to, only the Federal Government, not the States” (Cabazon, quoted in Stone and in Thompson, below).
  • Minnesota cannabis application — State v. Thompson, No. A25-0527 (Minn. Ct. App. 2 Feb. 2026, precedential). Thompson, an enrolled White Earth member, was charged after an August 2023 raid on his tobacco shop on the White Earth Reservation (the day after statewide legalisation) for possessing cannabis flower above personal-use amounts. The district court had held the state could prosecute under PL 280. The Court of Appeals reversed that jurisdictional holding: “The district court erred in determining that the statute criminalizing appellant’s cannabis-flower possession is a criminal/prohibitory law that the state is permitted to enforce under Public Law 280.” In other words, after 1 August 2023 Minnesota’s cannabis-possession law is, for PL 280 purposes, civil/regulatory in character, so the state could not use PL 280 to prosecute this on-reservation possession by a tribal member. The court separately addressed (and did not accept on the record before it) a treaty-rights argument based on the 1855 Treaty with the Ojibwe.
  • Sources: https://law.justia.com/cases/minnesota/court-of-appeals/2026/a25-0527.html and https://cases.justia.com/minnesota/court-of-appeals/2026-a25-0527.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Caveats, stated plainly: (i) Thompson is a Court of Appeals decision; whether the state sought further review, and the posture of any remand or retrial on other grounds, was not verified in this window — [VERIFY] before citing it as final. (ii) It decides PL 280 jurisdiction over a tribal member on his own reservation for possession; it does not hold that state law never applies to non-members, to off-reservation conduct, or to conduct that remains genuinely criminal/prohibitory under Chapter 342 (e.g., unlicensed sale above thresholds, sale to minors). Do not over-read it. (iii) It does not displace federal law: adult-use cannabis remains federally Schedule I, and federal enforcement discretion is a separate question (see §1.3).
  • How compacts fit alongside PL 280 and sovereignty. Because PL 280 gives Minnesota no general civil/regulatory power in Indian Country, the state cannot simply extend Chapter 342 licensing onto tribal land by its own force. The compact route (§§ 3.9224, 3.9228) is a negotiated, consent-based bridge: the Tribe keeps primary regulation on tribally regulated land under standards that meet or exceed OCM’s, the state takes secondary oversight (including, in the White Earth model as reported by OCM and the League of Minnesota Cities, annual inspections and intervention on public-safety concerns), and the compact — not PL 280 — is what authorises tribally regulated retail off tribal land. That is why OCM describes each accord as “unique” and a “separate agreement”: there is no single statewide tribal code, and terms vary by Nation.

1.3 Federal guidance / DOJ policy cited by the compacts

  • Finding: no DOJ guidance citation was located in the compact text returned in this window. The Shakopee and Bois Forte compact excerpts returned by the index cite the Compacting Legislation (§§ 3.9224, 3.9228), Chapter 342, and tribal law; they do not, in the excerpts seen, cite the 2013 Cole Memorandum, the 2014 Wilkinson Memorandum, or any successor DOJ cannabis-enforcement guidance. The full PDFs must be checked before asserting that no compact cites DOJ guidance — [VERIFY: full-text search of all nine signed PDFs for “Cole,” “Wilkinson,” “Department of Justice,” and “enforcement priorities”].
  • Context that may be stated without attributing it to the compacts: the Cole Memorandum (2013) set federal enforcement priorities for state-legal cannabis and was rescinded in January 2018; the Wilkinson Memorandum (2014) addressed marijuana enforcement in Indian Country and directed U.S. Attorneys’ Offices to consult with Tribes and apply the Cole priorities in Indian Country. Neither memorandum creates a right, and neither is a compact term unless a compact incorporates it. This Part does not present either memorandum as current DOJ policy or as a term of any Minnesota compact.
  • Federal baseline carried forward (fixed, not re-researched): state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; § 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical only; no federal cannabis banking law. Tribal medical status for Schedule III / § 280E purposes remains [VERIFY] — see §4.3. Nothing found in this window resolves it, and this Part does not resolve it by assertion.

1.4 Who may buy — the general rule, and where it differs

  • Adult-use, state law: Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(a) (verbatim in relevant part):

    “An individual 21 years of age or older may: (1) use, possess, or transport cannabis paraphernalia; (2) possess or transport two ounces or less of adult-use cannabis flower in a public place; (3) possess two pounds or less of adult-use cannabis flower in the individual’s private residence; (4) possess or transport eight grams or less of adult-use cannabis concentrate; (5) possess or transport edible cannabis products or lower-potency hemp edibles infused with a combined total of 800 milligrams or less of tetrahydrocannabinol…”

  • Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/342/full (§ 342.09) — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • No Minnesota-residency requirement for adult-use purchase appears in § 342.09. The statute turns on age (21+), not on being a Minnesotan. A visitor with valid government photo ID may therefore buy in Minnesota on the same terms as a resident, and is subject to the same possession limits. (Secondary visitor guides state this expressly; the statutory point is the absence of a residency condition in § 342.09 — if a compact or tribal rule imposed a member-only rule, that would be a tribal rule, not § 342.09.)
  • Tribal on-reservation sales, 2023 first movers: Red Lake (Tribal Council vote 11 July 2023) and White Earth (Tribal Council vote 28 July 2023) each legalised adult-use sales to any adult 21+, tribal member or not — that non-member openness is why the first legal sales in Minnesota were tribal sales on 1 August 2023 (Red Lake NativeCare; White Earth’s Waabigwan Mashkiki followed days later). No compact or tribal source found in this window imposes a member-only purchase rule at any of the nine compacting Nations’ retail stores; conversely, tribal medical purchase (where a tribal medical programme exists) is by definition limited to persons enrolled/authorised under that tribal programme or the state registry — see §4.
  • Medical vs. adult-use at the same store: a store may sell adult-use product to any 21+ adult and medical product only to a registry/tribal-programme patient (with the tax and product consequences that follow in the state system). Whether a given tribal store operates a separate medical counter, medical pricing, or medical-only products is a tribal-enterprise operational fact — [VERIFY] store by store; do not assume a tribal adult-use store is also a tribal medical dispensary.
  • Off-reservation tribal retail: the buyer rule does not change by moving off tribal land — off-reservation tribal stores sell to any 21+ adult under the compact, but the regulatory regime changes (state testing/tracking/tax, non-cannabis local ordinances, Chapter 342 operating-hours limits per Run 1 baseline — the hours point is carried forward and should be checked against a signed compact’s operating-hours article before republication [VERIFY]).

2.2 Common compact terms (OCM summary + compact excerpts)

The following are the terms OCM itself presents as common across the accords, plus terms verified in individual compact excerpts. Where a term is OCM-summary rather than compact-quotation, it is labelled as such.

  1. Tribal regulatory agency, standards meeting or exceeding OCM’s. OCM: “Tribal Nations entering into cannabis compacts or cooperative agreements with the state have established Tribal regulatory agencies that will license Tribal enterprises and oversee enforcement of the Tribe’s civil regulatory cannabis program using standards that meet or exceed those established by OCM.” — OCM compacts page (indexed), Accessed 2026-10-28.
  2. Off-reservation retail: up to eight locations, one per municipality, three per county. OCM Local Government Guide (2026, v5.0) states this as a common provision across the agreements, and adds the local-ordinance rule and the tracking/tax rules in items 3–5 below. The White Earth compact summaries (League of Minnesota Cities, May 2025; OCM local-government guide) state the identical 8 / 1-per-city / 3-per-county formula for White Earth specifically. Whether every later compact repeats the identical numbers, or whether any compact varies the county/municipality cap, was not verified article-by-article — [VERIFY: cap article in each of the nine PDFs]. The Run 1 baseline (“up to eight”) is consistent with all summaries found and is retained, with that caveat. - Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/OCM_Local_Government_Guide_5.0_2026_tcm1202-627967.pdf (OCM Local Government Guide) — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  3. Non-cannabis local ordinances apply off tribal land. OCM guide (verbatim in substance): tribally regulated retail locations off tribal land “must follow all non-cannabis-specific local ordinances, including zoning, land use, statutory setback limitations, and local hours of operation restrictions.” Tribal enterprises off tribal land are exempt from cannabis-specific local enforcement/ordinances but not from non-cannabis ordinances applied equally to similarly situated businesses (compact draft redline, Art. V(A) — draft, not a signed compact; treat the OCM-guide formulation as the authoritative summary and the draft as corroboration only).
  4. Testing, packaging, labelling, tracking. OCM guide: “The Tribal-state agreements require product testing to verify compliance with public health and safety standards set by OCM… Like state-license holders, Tribes and their license holders use seed-to-sale tracking… All products must be entered into the state’s seed-to-sale system when they move off Tribal lands.” Run 1’s formulation (tested at state-licensed labs, entered into seed-to-sale, state packaging/labelling including the universal symbol for product moving off tribal lands) is consistent with this and is retained. The state’s starting seed-to-sale system is Metrc (named in compact reporting). [VERIFY: whether each compact requires state-licensed lab testing for all off-land product or permits tribally licensed labs meeting OCM standards for some categories — the Prairie Island reporting says Island Peži product is “tested and passed by the state lab,” which is a single operator’s statement, not a compact article.]
  5. Trading with state licensees. Once compacted, a Tribal Nation’s businesses may collaborate/trade with state-licensed businesses (Governor’s Red Lake release: “With this agreement in place, the Red Lake Band is able to collaborate with state-licensed cannabis businesses”; OCM Tribal Nations page: compacts “create unique opportunities for partnership between state-licensed cannabis businesses and Tribal Nations”). State-licensed retailers were reported carrying tribally grown product from September 2025. The mechanics (wholesale licences, Metrc transfer, testing on transfer) are compact-specific — [VERIFY per compact].
  6. Vertical integration / licence scope (Bois Forte compact excerpt, as a worked example — do not generalise without checking the others). The Bois Forte compact as indexed authorises the Tribal Regulatory Agency to issue, among others, one Transporter Licence (no fleet-size or geographic limit within Minnesota) and one Delivery Licence (same; “Deliveries to private residences are permitted”), one Wholesaler Licence, and Event Licences to retail holders for events on the retail premises (21+; § 342.40-consistent), with off-premises/non-tribal-land events subject to local permitting. A tribal licensee “shall be authorized to conduct the same actions as State-Licensed Cannabis Businesses per applicable license classification,” and tribal enterprises are not subject to the state’s vertical-integration limitation except that a testing-facility holder may not hold another cannabis licence. - Source: Bois Forte compact PDF via Legislative Reference Library, https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2025/other/251977/BoisForteBandofMinnesotaChippewa_CannabisCompact.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28 (indexed excerpts only).
  7. Setbacks in compact drafting (model/draft only). A January 2025 state–Tribe working redline (not a signed compact) proposed that a tribal regulator not license an off-tribal-land enterprise within 1,000 feet of a school or 500 feet of a day care, residential treatment facility, or a public-park attraction regularly used by minors, unless local law is less restrictive (in which case local law is incorporated). Do not quote this as a signed-compact term — it is included only so a coordinator checking a signed PDF knows what to look for. [VERIFY: setback article in each signed PDF.]

2.3 What the compacts do not do (common misunderstandings)

  • They do not make tribal land subject to Chapter 342 licensing.
  • They do not authorise a tribal business to sell cannabis outside Minnesota or to deliver across a state line (see §7.5).
  • They do not, by themselves, fix a tax-sharing percentage. See §5: off-reservation tax-sharing is by a separate, future Department of Revenue agreement where the compact so provides, and no percentage was located in any compact excerpt returned.

Counties are given for store cities; where a store’s county was not confirmed from a source in this window it is marked [VERIFY: county].

Ordinance note (applies to all eleven): No tribal cannabis ordinance text was retrieved in full, verbatim, from an official tribal publication in this window. Tribal ordinances are tribal law, often published through tribal government channels rather than the Minnesota Revisor, and several Nations’ ordinance texts are not in the searchable index. This Part therefore does not fabricate ordinance quotations. For each Nation it states: (a) what council/regulatory action is reliably reported (secondary, labelled), (b) the compact (if any), (c) the regulator as listed by OCM, and (d) the ordinance gap expressly. A coordinator who needs verbatim ordinance text must request it from the tribal regulator or the tribal government — that is the correct primary source, and it is listed as a gap rather than filled by paraphrase dressed as quotation.
