4. Tribal medical cannabis programmes

4.1 State-law recognition (verbatim definitions and protections)

  • Minnesota law recognises tribal medical programmes in the state code even though the programmes themselves are tribal law. The operative state definitions (as carried in the pre-Chapter 342 medical code, Minn. Stat. § 152.22, and reflected in Chapter 342’s protections) are:

    “‘Tribal medical cannabis program’ means a program established by a federally recognized Tribal government within the boundaries of Minnesota regarding the commercial production, processing, sale or distribution, and possession of medical cannabis and medical cannabis products.” “‘Tribal medical cannabis program patient’ means a person who possesses a valid registration verification card or equivalent document that is issued under the laws or regulations of a Tribal nation within the boundaries of Minnesota and that verifies that the person is enrolled in or authorized to participate in that Tribal nation’s Tribal medical cannabis program.” “‘Tribal medical cannabis board’ means an agency established by each federally recognized Tribal government and duly authorized by each Tribe’s governing body to perform regulatory oversight and monitor compliance with a Tribal medical cannabis program and applicable regulations.”

  • Sources: Minn. Stat. § 152.22 definitions as indexed (history through 2023 c 63); HF 3162 (2021–2022) engrossment text carrying the same definitions — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note: § 152.22 subdivisions were substantially repealed/restructured effective 1 March 2025 by Laws 2023, ch. 63, art. 6, § 73 — the current location and wording of these definitions in the 2025 code must be re-pulled before republication [VERIFY: current Revisor location].
  • Protections — Minn. Stat. § 342.57 (verbatim excerpts): a patient enrolled in the registry programme or a Tribal medical cannabis programme “must not be subject to any penalty or disciplinary action by an occupational or a professional licensing board” solely because of that enrolment or a positive cannabis test (§ 342.57, subd. 2(h) as indexed); the same parallel protection applies to school enrolment and landlord leasing (§ 342.57, subd. 3). A 2025 bill (SF 2371, 1st engrossment) proposed amending § 342.57, subd. 1 to add an express presumption for “a Tribal medical cannabis program patient” and a rebuttal clause tied to purposes “authorized by the Tribal medical cannabis program” — that is a bill, not enacted law as found, and must not be cited as the statute. Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/cite/342.57 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • What the state recognition does not do: it does not make a tribal medical programme a state programme, does not enrol a tribal patient in the state registry, and does not by itself answer the federal questions in §4.3.

4.2 Which Nations had medical programmes, and the HF 3162 point

  • Run 1’s position is retained with its caveat: Red Lake and White Earth had started medical programmes by the time of a 2023 House committee hearing on HF 3162. The underlying tribal facts corroborate the existence of early medical steps: Red Lake’s May 2020 medical referendum and its early-2023 medical dispensary (NativeCare as a medical provider before adult-use sales); White Earth’s August 2020 medical vote and its Mahnomen medical dispensary opening immediately before adult-use sales in August 2023.
  • HF 3162 enactment: NOT enacted on the evidence found — carried forward as [VERIFY], leaning against enactment. HF 3162 was a 2021–2022 bill (92nd Legislature, 2nd engrossment) that would have added the tribal medical definitions to § 152.22 and related reporting. No session law enacting HF 3162 as a standalone bill was located in this window; the tribal medical definitions that are in Minnesota law arrived through other vehicles (notably 2021 c 30 and the 2023 cannabis act’s restructuring). A coordinator should not cite “HF 3162 (enacted)” — cite the definitions as they appear in the current code and note HF 3162 as the bill that carried them in committee discussion. [VERIFY: HF 3162 final disposition in the Revisor’s bill-status record.]
  • Other Nations’ medical programmes: no verified tribal medical programme (as distinct from adult-use sales that a medical patient may also use) was located for Bois Forte, Fond du Lac, Leech Lake, Mille Lacs, Lower Sioux, Prairie Island, or Shakopee Mdewakanton in this window. That is absence of evidence — several compacting Nations’ regulators (e.g., White Earth’s Medical Cannabis Control Commission) carry “medical” in the regulator’s name, which suggests a medical function, but a name is not a programme description. [VERIFY: programme-by-programme — does each compacting Nation operate a tribal medical programme, a medical endorsement, or adult-use only?]

4.3 Federal Schedule III / § 280E — unresolved, carried forward

  • Carried forward as [VERIFY], explicitly unresolved: whether tribal medical cannabis counts as “state-licensed” medical for purposes of (a) the federal Schedule III rescheduling effective 28 April 2026 (which, per the fixed federal baseline, covers state-licensed medical marijuana) and (b) § 280E relief for Schedule III medical. No primary federal guidance (DEA, IRS, or Treasury) and no compact article addressing tribal medical status for Schedule III/280E was located in this window. Arguments in both directions exist in principle (tribal programmes are government-regulated and state-recognised, but they are not state-licensed in the Chapter 342 sense), and this Part takes neither side. Do not advise any tribal business on 280E on the basis of this Part.

5. Tax — on tribal land vs. off tribal land

5.1 Statute (verbatim)

  • Cannabis gross receipts tax exemption — Minn. Stat. § 295.81, subd. 4(d):

    “The tax imposed under this section does not apply to: (1) sales made on Tribally regulated land as defined in section 3.9228, subdivision 1, by a cannabis business licensed by a Minnesota Tribal government, as defined in section 3.9228, subdivision 1, paragraph (f); or (2) use tax owed on taxable cannabis products purchased on Tribally regulated land as defined in section 3.9228, subdivision 1, from a cannabis business licensed by a Minnesota Tribal government as defined in section 3.9228, subdivision 1, paragraph (f).”

  • Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/minnesota/chapters-289a-295/chapter-295/section-295-81/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note: one indexed version of § 295.81, subd. 4(d)(1) says “sales made in Indian country” rather than “on Tribally regulated land” — the two wordings appear in different vintages/secondary renderings; the operative test in both is a sale by a tribally licensed business on tribal land. [VERIFY: current Revisor wording of § 295.81, subd. 4(d)(1).]
  • Sales tax exemption — Minn. Stat. § 297A.67, subd. 39 (Run 1 citation confirmed):

    “The sale of a taxable cannabis product, as defined in section 295.81, subdivision 1, paragraph (r), that is made in Indian country, as defined in United States Code, title 18, section 1151 on Tribally regulated land as defined in section 3.9228, subdivision 1, by a cannabis business licensed by a Minnesota Tribal government, as defined in section 3.9228, subdivision 1, paragraph (f), is exempt.”

  • Source: https://codes.findlaw.com/mn/excise-and-sales-taxes-ch-296-299/mn-st-sect-297a-67/ (§ 297A.67, subd. 39) — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Numbering flag: a January 2025 compact working redline cited the sales-tax exemption as “§ 297A.67, subd. 40.” The current code as indexed places reservation cannabis sales at subd. 39 and firearm storage units at subd. 40. The redline’s “40” is therefore either a draft-vintage numbering or an error; the current citation to use is subd. 39. Do not copy the redline’s number into a published file.
  • Rate flag (do not publish a rate from this Part alone): secondary 2026 reporting describes Minnesota’s cannabis gross receipts tax as 15% (plus sales tax), while older material (including the 2023–2025 era) describes 10%. A rate increase and its effective date were not verified against the current § 295.81, subd. 2 text in this window. [VERIFY: current § 295.81 rate and effective date before stating any percentage.] The exemption analysis above does not depend on the rate.

5.2 Compact tax-sharing terms

  • On tribal land: no state sales, use, or gross receipts tax is to be collected or remitted by the Tribe for tribally licensed sales on tribally regulated land (compact taxation article, as in the working redline: “Consistent with Minn. Stat. § 295.81, subd. 4(d) and Minn. Stat. § 297A.67, subd. [39], the Tribe shall not be required to collect or remit any State sales, use, or gross receipts tax for Cannabis sales by Tribally licensed businesses on Tribally regulated land”). That is the compact restating the statute, not creating the exemption — the exemption exists by statute with or without a compact.
  • Off tribal land: off-reservation sales by tribally owned businesses are taxed like state sales (OCM guide: “Sales of cannabis products off Tribal lands are subject to all state and local taxes”). A separate tax-sharing agreement with the Department of Revenue is contemplated: the compact formulation (redline and secondary compact analyses agree) is that “a tax agreement, as authorized under [the cannabis act] for sharing of sales and gross receipts tax collected from any Tribally owned cannabis business that operates off-Reservation, may be negotiated between the Tribe and the Minnesota Department of Revenue in the future,” with Prairie Island analyses citing Minn. Stat. § 270C.19, subd. 6 as the Department’s tax-sharing authority.
  • Percentages: [VERIFY] by compact — none located. No revenue-sharing percentage, split, or formula for any of the nine Nations was found in any compact excerpt, OCM summary, or Department of Revenue publication returned in this window. Do not invent a split (e.g., do not assume 50/50, and do not assume the Tribe keeps all off-reservation tax). If a Department of Revenue tax agreement has since been executed for any Nation, it is a separate instrument from the compact and must be sourced separately. The Run 1 baseline (“percentages [VERIFY] by compact”) is therefore carried forward unresolved, with the refinement that the sharing instrument may be a Department of Revenue agreement rather than a compact article.
  • Consumer consequence (stated carefully): a customer buying on tribal land at a tribally licensed store does not pay Minnesota cannabis gross receipts / sales tax on that sale by operation of the exemptions above; the same customer buying at that Nation’s off-reservation store pays state and local taxes like any state-licensed sale, subject to whatever sharing agreement (if any) the Tribe and the Department have since made — the sharing agreement divides revenue between governments; it does not, on the evidence found, change what the customer pays at the till. Tribal tribal taxes or fees, if a Nation imposes any on its own sales, are tribal law and were not verified — [VERIFY] before describing any “no tax at all” claim.

6. Sales figures — what exists and what does not

  • State-licensed first year (OCM, September 2026 announcement): “consumers and patients have purchased more than $250 million in combined adult-use and medical cannabis products from Minnesota businesses since the launch of legal sales at state-licensed businesses across the state one year ago” — approximately $150 million adult-use + $100 million medical, across ~1.2 million combined transactions; state-licensed adult-use sales began 16 September 2025; tribal-land retail sales began shortly after the August 2023 bill. Tax: $45.6 million reported for the first-year period in secondary summaries of the OCM release (ten months of tax data in one secondary analysis, which also notes the figure folds in lower-potency hemp edibles/beverages outside seed-to-sale — treat the $45.6 million composition as [VERIFY] against the OCM release itself).

  • Tribal sales total: [UNAVAILABLE]. No OCM, Department of Revenue, or tribal-government publication reporting an aggregate tribal dispensary sales total was located. Tribal sales are not in the $250 million because that figure is defined by its own announcement as state-licensed-business sales. Individual tribal operators’ revenues, if disclosed in tribal financial reporting, were not located and are not estimated here.
  • Do not do this: do not add tribal and state-licensed figures together, do not describe $250 million as “Minnesota cannabis sales,” and do not back-solve a tribal total from store counts or tax figures.

7. Interstate issues

7.1 Hemp shipments into and out of Minnesota

  • Federal transport protection — 2018 Farm Act (Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018, Pub. L. 115-334), § 10114 (7 U.S.C. § 1639o note / § 10114):

    “No State or Indian Tribe shall prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products produced in accordance with subtitle G of the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 through the State or the territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable.” And the rule of construction: nothing in the Farm Act title prohibits the interstate commerce of hemp or hemp products. USDA’s post-Farm Act guidance reads § 10114(b) as pre-empting state laws that would interfere with interstate shipment of lawfully produced hemp.

  • Sources: 2018 Farm Act § 10114 as reproduced in federal-court briefing and USDA guidance summaries — Accessed 2026-10-28. (Statute text via a court filing is a secondary reproduction; the primary citation is Pub. L. 115-334, § 10114 — [VERIFY against the enrolled Act before quoting in a legal filing].)
  • Through vs. into — the distinction that decides most real cases: § 10114 protects transportation through a state/Tribal territory. It does not require a destination state to permit retail sale of the same product within its borders, and states/Tribes may still regulate (including more stringently) production and sale within their jurisdiction. A shipment lawfully produced in Minnesota and merely transiting Wisconsin is in a different legal position from a Minnesota retailer selling into Wisconsin to a Wisconsin consumer.
  • Minnesota’s hemp framework (for the “lawfully produced” premise): Minnesota operates under a USDA-approved state hemp plan (Minnesota Department of Agriculture), and tribal production operates under an approved tribal plan or a USDA producer licence (see §3.12). Minnesota’s lower-potency hemp edible (LPHE) law — Minn. Stat. § 151.72 and Chapter 342’s LPHE provisions as carried in Run 1 — permits hemp-derived edibles/beverages within Minnesota’s own limits (including the 5 mg THC per serving / 50 mg per package LPHE structure as enacted; exact current LPHE limits are in the state hemp/cannabis code and are not re-verified in this Part — cross-check with the Part covering LPHE before quoting numbers).
  • The post-11 December 2026 problem (fixed federal baseline, applied): PL 119-37 § 781 (effective 12 November 2026) is limited by PL 119-103 § 2019 until 11 December 2026, after which the full federal total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. The consequence for interstate hemp is structural: 1. A Minnesota-lawful LPHE product above 0.4 mg total THC per container (e.g., a standard 5 mg or 10 mg beverage/edible) would, after 11 December 2026, no longer meet the federal definition of hemp — it would be federally marijuana (Schedule I for adult-use purposes; Schedule III only for state-licensed medical, which an LPHE beverage is not). 2. Such a product therefore loses the § 10114 premise (“produced in accordance with subtitle G” / meeting the federal hemp definition) for interstate shipment protection. Minnesota law alone cannot restore federal hemp status to a federally noncompliant product, and Minnesota’s unchanged LPHE law does not change the federal definition. 3. Practically: after 11 December 2026, interstate shipment into or out of Minnesota of a >0.4 mg/container hemp-derived product carries federal exposure that a compliant (≤0.4 mg/container, total-THC-compliant) hemp product does not, and a destination state’s own ban or restriction on such products is no longer answered by § 10114. Intrastate Minnesota sale/possession under Minnesota law is a separate question from interstate shipment — do not conflate “still lawful to sell in Minnesota under state law” with “lawful to ship across a state line.” 4. [VERIFY: whether Minnesota has amended, or announced it will amend, its LPHE law in response to PL 119-37/119-103, and whether USDA/DEA have issued shipment guidance for the transition — neither was located in this window.]
  • Hemp into Minnesota from another state: the same test in reverse. Hemp/hemp products lawfully produced under another state’s approved plan, a tribal plan, or a USDA licence, and meeting the (then-current) federal hemp definition, may be transported through Minnesota and sold in Minnesota only if they also comply with Minnesota law (LPHE limits, labelling, registration, and any Chapter 342 hemp provisions). A product lawful in its origin state but noncompliant with Minnesota’s sale rules may transit but may not lawfully be sold in Minnesota. No Minnesota import licence or interstate hemp compact was located — [VERIFY: Minnesota Department of Agriculture hemp import/registration rules].

7.2 Residents of neighbouring states buying in Minnesota

General Minnesota rule (see §1.4): no Minnesota-residency requirement for adult-use purchase; 21+ with valid government photo ID may buy, within § 342.09 possession limits (2 oz flower in public / 2 lb at a private residence, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg THC in edibles/LPHE combined). Medical purchase is different: state-registry enrolment (or tribal-programme enrolment at a tribal medical outlet) is required; an out-of-state medical card does not enrol a person in Minnesota’s registry, and Minnesota does not recognise out-of-state medical cards as registry verification on the evidence found — [VERIFY: current § 342.51 / Division of Medical Cannabis reciprocity position, if any].

By home state (adult-use cannabis bought in Minnesota, then the home-state position on possession there — the buyer may lawfully buy and consume in Minnesota, but may not lawfully take it home):

  • Wisconsin — adult-use illegal; medical limited to low-THC/CBD only. Wisconsin has no comprehensive medical programme and no adult-use programme. A Wisconsin resident 21+ may buy in Minnesota and consume in Minnesota, but possession of Minnesota-bought cannabis in Wisconsin is unlawful under Wisconsin law (subject to Wisconsin’s own limited CBD/low-THC provisions, which do not cover Minnesota adult-use flower, concentrates, or standard edibles). Wisconsin is also a mandatory PL 280 state, but that is irrelevant to a Wisconsin resident’s off-reservation possession in Wisconsin — Wisconsin state law applies in full there.
  • Iowa — adult-use illegal; medical limited (low-THC programme, reported 4.5 g THC / 90-day cap in secondary summaries). Same structure as Wisconsin: lawful purchase/consumption in Minnesota, unlawful possession of adult-use cannabis in Iowa, and Iowa’s medical programme does not authorise Minnesota adult-use products. [VERIFY: current Iowa Code ch. 124E caps and product forms before quoting the 4.5 g figure in a published file — it is secondary here.]
  • North Dakota — adult-use illegal; medical legal (comprehensive medical programme). A North Dakota resident who is not a North Dakota medical patient may not lawfully possess adult-use cannabis in North Dakota; a North Dakota medical patient may possess only product obtained through North Dakota’s programme within its limits — Minnesota adult-use purchases are not North Dakota programme product. North Dakota voters have rejected adult-use legalisation at the ballot (secondary summaries).
  • South Dakota — adult-use illegal; medical legal. Same structure as North Dakota. South Dakota additionally restricts hemp-derived cannabinoid products under its 2024 hemp-cannabinoid law (secondary summary) — a Minnesota hemp product lawful in Minnesota may therefore face a separate South Dakota restriction even if it is federally compliant hemp. [VERIFY: current South Dakota hemp-cannabinoid statute before advising on any specific product.]
  • Canada (for completeness — Minnesota’s northern border): cannabis is legal nationally in Canada, but taking Minnesota cannabis across the international border is a federal/international offence regardless of Canadian legality, and Canadian border rules independently prohibit import without authorisation. Included only to prevent a “legal both sides, therefore legal to carry” error.

Practical warning that belongs in any consumer-facing summary: the lawful course for a neighbouring-state visitor is to buy only what will be consumed in Minnesota, within Minnesota limits, and to leave nothing to carry home. Dispensary ID checks verify age, not residency, and do not create a right of export.

7.3 What can legally be taken across state lines

  • Cannabis (adult-use and, outside its own programme, medical): nothing. Federal law (Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. § 812; interstate transport/distribution provisions) prohibits interstate transport of marijuana. That prohibition applies:
  • even if both states have legalised cannabis;
  • even if the amount is within both states’ personal possession limits;
  • even if the traveller holds a medical card (in either state);
  • by car, by mail, by common carrier, and by air (including in checked baggage — federal jurisdiction over air travel and airports is independent of state law). State legality at the origin and destination does not create a federal exception, and no Minnesota statute, compact, or interstate agreement found in this window creates one. Secondary transport guides describe interstate cannabis transport as a federal felony exposure (up to 5 years / $250,000 in the secondary summary — penalty figures are secondary and must be checked against 21 U.S.C. §§ 841, 844 before republication; the existence of federal criminal exposure is not in doubt).
  • Hemp: compliant hemp products only, with the post-11 December 2026 caveat in §7.1. A product that (a) meets the federal hemp definition in force on the date of shipment, (b) was produced under an approved state/tribal plan or USDA licence, and (c) complies with the destination state’s sale rules (if it is to be sold there, as opposed to merely transiting) may lawfully move interstate. A product failing (a) after 11 December 2026 is not saved by Minnesota law, by a tribal plan, or by § 10114.
  • Tribal land is not a workaround for interstate transport. Moving cannabis from tribal land in Minnesota to tribal land in another state, or from Minnesota tribal land to non-tribal land in another state, is still interstate transport of federally controlled cannabis. No compact found authorises interstate tribal-to-tribal cannabis shipment, and § 3.9228’s inter-tribal delivery protection (see §7.5) is expressly about delivery within Minnesota (including transit through the state outside a reservation — i.e., intra-Minnesota transit, not export).

7.4 Border enforcement and transport rules applied to the interstate context

  • Minnesota personal transport (§ 342.09): the § 342.09 limits are possession/transport within Minnesota limits. They do not authorise transport out of Minnesota, and they cease to protect the traveller the moment the traveller crosses into a jurisdiction where possession is unlawful or federally prohibited. The statute’s public-place limit (2 oz flower) is the relevant figure for a traveller’s car in Minnesota; the 2 lb figure is a private-residence limit, not a vehicle limit — do not advise a traveller they may drive with 2 lb.
  • Vehicle rules (§ 342.09, subd. 1(b)): an individual may not use cannabis flower/products/LPHE/hemp-derived consumer products in a motor vehicle (as defined in Minn. Stat. § 169A.03, subd. 15), and may not use/possess/transport them if under 21 (subject to medical exceptions in § 342.09, subd. 1(c)). Secondary guides add the familiar sealed-package / trunk rule for transport; the statutory vehicle-use prohibition is verified, but a general “must be in the trunk” rule for all adult-use transport was not verified as a § 342.09 requirement in this window — [VERIFY: current § 342.09, subd. 1(b) full text and any separate open-package provision before advising on vehicle storage for personal transport].
  • Commercial transport/delivery (§§ 342.36, 342.42; Minn. R. ch. 9810):
  • § 342.42, subd. 1: before completing a delivery, a delivery service must verify the customer is at least 21 or enrolled in the registry programme.
  • § 342.42, subd. 4: receipt and delivery must be recorded in the statewide monitoring system (Metrc) within the time set by rule.
  • § 342.42, subd. 5 (verbatim): “Cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, and hemp-derived consumer products must be transported in a locked, safe, and secure storage compartment that is part of the cannabis delivery service vehicle or in a locked storage container that has a separate key or combination pad. Cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, and hemp-derived consumer products may not be visible from outside the cannabis delivery service vehicle.”
  • § 342.42, subd. 6: no delivery vehicle/trailer may bear an image depicting the items transported (including a cannabis/hemp leaf) or a name suggesting cannabis delivery use. Subd. 7: only a cannabis worker 21+ employed/contracted by the delivery service may transport; all passengers must be such workers. Subd. 8: delivery vehicles are subject to inspection at any time.
  • Minn. R. 9810.1500, subp. 17 adds GPS (location at all times, data retained ≥30 days), climate control, insurance, and secure communications for transport/delivery vehicles.
  • Interstate application: none of these provisions authorises a Minnesota delivery service to deliver outside Minnesota. A delivery route that crossed a state line would violate federal law and the destination state’s law even if every Minnesota vehicle rule were followed. The rules matter at the border because they are how Minnesota distinguishes licensed commercial transport (manifested, tracked, locked, unmarked) from unlicensed personal transport — and a border stop that finds unmanifested commercial quantities will be treated as unlicensed activity, not as a delivery in progress.
  • Border enforcement reality (stated as enforcement context, not as a legal rule): federal authorities may enforce federal cannabis law at borders, on federal lands, and in air travel regardless of state law; neighbouring-state law enforcement enforces its own possession law once the traveller is in that state; tribal law enforcement enforces tribal law on tribal land (subject to PL 280’s criminal grant for non-Red Lake reservations and to federal jurisdiction). No “border checkpoint” regime specific to Minnesota cannabis was located — do not invent one.

7.5 Delivery to tribal land and across state lines (§§ 342.41–342.42 and the compacts) — Run 1 [UNAVAILABLE] partially resolved

Run 1 marked delivery to tribal land / across state lines in §§ 342.41–342.42 as [UNAVAILABLE]. The position after this window is:

  • What §§ 342.41–342.42 themselves say: § 342.41 authorises a state cannabis delivery service licence (purchase from licensed retailers/microbusinesses/mezzobusinesses/medical combination businesses; transport and deliver to customers). § 342.42 sets the operations rules quoted in §7.4. Neither section, in the text returned, expressly addresses delivery to tribal land, delivery by a tribal licensee, or delivery across a state line. That silence is the reason for the Run 1 flag, and it remains true of the statute text.
  • What resolves part of the gap — the compacts and § 3.9228:
  • Minn. Stat. § 3.9228 (as indexed) provides that purchase, sale, receipt, or delivery (including delivery involving transit through the state, outside a reservation) of adult-use cannabis flower/seed/product from or to another Minnesota Tribal government or a tribally licensed cannabis business does not constitute a state criminal or civil offence when performed by a Minnesota Tribal government, a tribally licensed business, or their employees — regardless of whether the licensing Tribe has compacted. That is an inter-tribal, intra-Minnesota delivery protection, and it expressly contemplates transit through Minnesota outside a reservation. It is not an interstate-export protection.
  • § 3.9228 also provides that a state-licensed testing facility may provide testing services to a tribal business, and tribal possession/transport for that purpose is not a state offence.
  • Compact delivery licences (Bois Forte example, §2.2 item 6): a tribal delivery licence permits deliveries to private residences, with no fleet/geographic limit within Minnesota. That is a compact-granted tribal delivery right inside the state.
  • What remains [UNAVAILABLE] / [VERIFY]:
  • Whether a state-licensed delivery service may deliver to a customer on tribal land (as opposed to a tribally licensed delivery service delivering on tribal land) — no § 342.41/342.42 provision or OCM guidance answering this was located. The answer likely turns on the relevant compact and on tribal consent for state-licensed activity in Indian Country (§ 342.13(k)), but that is an inference, not a located rule — [VERIFY: OCM delivery guidance + one compact’s delivery article].
  • Whether any compact permits delivery to an address that is on tribal land of a different Nation, or delivery from a tribal business to a state licensee’s premises — [VERIFY per compact].
  • Delivery across a state line by any licensee (state or tribal): not authorised by any source found; federal prohibition applies (see §7.3). This part of the Run 1 gap is resolved negatively: no authority was found, and the federal rule points the other way.

7.6 Interstate laws, agreements, and compacts — search result

Minnesota’s cannabis/hemp interstate instruments found are all federal (Farm Act § 10114; USDA plan approvals) or tribal–state (the nine accords above), not state–state.
  • What to check before publishing “none exists”: the Minnesota Department of Agriculture’s hemp-programme memoranda (USDA plan administration sometimes involves interstate administrative agreements), and any Midwest governors’ cannabis coordination statements. Those were not searched exhaustively, so the correct published wording is: “No Minnesota–other-state cannabis or hemp agreement was located in the sources searched for this Part” — not an absolute “Minnesota has no such agreement.”
  • No tribal–state compact with a Tribe outside Minnesota (e.g., a Wisconsin or Dakota Tribe) for Minnesota cannabis activity was located either; the nine accords are all with Minnesota-territory Nations, as § 3.9228 contemplates.

Minnesota Cannabis & Hemp Research — Run 2, Part 11: Operations Rules

Scope: PART 11 ONLY. This part covers testing, licence rules, cultivation rules, security, waste, environmental rules, sampling/giveaways/discounts/promotions, drug-testing and background checks, and research/university licences. It does not redo Parts 1–10 or 12.

Run 1 baseline applied: The Run 1 baselines stated in the commission are carried forward and are NOT contradicted except where this part expressly flags a correction with new primary evidence. The two material corrections in this part are: (1) licence transfers are §342.12, not §§342.18/342.21 — §342.21 is suspension/revocation/hearing, and §342.18 is selection criteria in the Revisor index; and (2) the seed-to-sale vendor is no longer [UNAVAILABLE] — OCM’s own inventory page states OCM has contracted with Metrc (see §11.1.9 and §11.2.11).

Sources and dating: Every fact below carries a source link and “Accessed 2026-10-28” as commissioned. In practice the Revisor and OCM pages were re-opened in this research window and the Revisor copies cited are the 25 April 2025 electronic publication of Minnesota Rules Chapter 9810 (49 SR 1143) and the Minnesota Statutes 2024/2025 texts as cited. Where a page could not be opened directly, or a proposition rests only on a search snippet or a secondary source, it is marked [VERIFY] or [UNAVAILABLE] and is NOT presented as settled law. Two page-read attempts in this run failed at the tool-transport layer (not a source denial); the sections those attempts would have covered are therefore sourced from search-index text of the same Revisor pages and are flagged where that matters. No personal phones or emails of individuals are reproduced.

Federal baseline (fixed, not re-researched): State-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III eff. 28 Apr 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; 280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical only; hemp PL 119-37 §781 eff. 12 Nov 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 Dec 2026, after which the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-lab enforcement delayed to 31 Dec 2026; federal medical appropriations rider through 11 Dec 2026; no federal cannabis banking law. Any contradiction with that baseline found in Minnesota sources is flagged; none was found in the sources checked for this part.

How to read the flags: [VERIFY] = proposition located but not confirmed against a directly opened official text in this run, or two sources conflict; the coordinator should re-pull it before publication. [UNAVAILABLE] = no source located in this run; do not fill it by inference. “No rule located” means no such rule was found in Chapter 342 or Rule 9810 text checked — it is not a claim that no agency guidance exists anywhere.

11.1 Testing

11.1.1 The gate: no sale or transfer before a passing test

Minnesota Statutes §342.61, subdivision 1(a) provides, verbatim in operative part:

“Cannabis businesses and hemp businesses shall not sell or offer for sale cannabis flower, cannabis products, artificially derived cannabinoids, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products to another cannabis business or hemp business, or to a customer or patient, or otherwise transfer [such products] to another cannabis business or hemp business, unless: (1) a representative sample of the batch … has been tested according to this section and rules adopted under this chapter; (2) the testing was completed by a cannabis testing facility licensed under this chapter or meeting the requirements of paragraph (b); and (3) the tested sample … was found to meet testing standards established by the office.”

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/342.61 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Rule 9810.3100, subpart 2 repeats the prohibition in final-packaging form: a person must not offer any regulated product in final packaging for wholesale distribution or retail sale if it has not undergone required testing or does not meet OCM acceptance criteria. The office may at any time require immediate testing of a regulated product suspected to be a potential human-health hazard or threat to public safety (9810.3100, subp. 1).

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

ISO/IEC 17025 window — correction/confirmation of the Run 1 baseline. §342.61, subd. 1(b) as published in the 2024 Statutes text opened for this part reads:

“Testing of lower-potency hemp edibles and hemp-derived consumer products that do not contain intoxicating cannabinoids may be performed by any laboratory that has been accredited pursuant to standard ISO/IEC 17025 … with specific accreditation for cannabis testing until January 1, 2026.”

Run 1 stated the window as “until 31 May 2027”. A 2026 bill (HF 3615 / SF 3520-line bills in the 2025–2026 session) proposes to extend that date to 31 May 2027, and OCM guidance and secondary reporting in 2026 describe the extension as the operative position. This part does NOT treat the extension as enacted law on the basis of a bill text alone. The 31 May 2027 date is carried as [VERIFY — confirm against the 2026 Supplement / session law as enacted before publication; the 2024 text still prints 1 Jan 2026]. The substantive point is unchanged either way: the ISO window covers only LPHE/hemp-derived products that do not contain intoxicating cannabinoids; intoxicating products must go to an OCM-licensed testing facility.

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/342.61; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/94/2025/0/SF/3520/versions/latest/ (bill text, not enacted law) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.1.2 Required tests, by category — potency, homogeneity, stability, contaminants

Statute. §342.61, subd. 2(a) requires OCM by rule to establish procedures for sampling, handling, testing, storage and transportation; the contaminants to be tested; standards for potency and homogeneity testing; and procedures for batches that fail contaminant limits, potency limits, or label cannabinoid-profile conformity. Subd. 3 requires OCM by rule to set allowable contaminant levels, including at minimum residual solvents, foreign material, microbiological contaminants, heavy metals, pesticide residue, and mycotoxins. Subd. 4(c) requires the testing facility to select one or more representative samples from each batch, test for contaminants, and test for potency and homogeneity so the product can be accurately labelled with its cannabinoid profile.

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/342.61 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Rule — mandatory testing (9810.3100, subp. 5). A testing facility must test a batch of regulated products to verify:

  • (A)(1) “the potency and stability of the cannabinoids in the products for accurate labeling”; and
  • (A)(2) “the homogeneity of the cannabinoids in each serving in the batch to meet the acceptance criteria established by the office and for accurate labeling.”
  • (B) If the facility finds any of the following contaminants, the batch does not meet acceptance criteria: (1) foreign material; (2) heavy metals; (3) microbiological contaminants; (4) mycotoxins; (5) pesticide residue; or (6) residual solvents.

Two qualifications in the same subpart matter for operators:

  • (C) A cannabis-derived or hemp-derived ingredient testing report meets the subpart 5 requirement if (1) the production process does not introduce a contaminant or increase the potential for introducing one, or (2) handling has not altered the stability, potency, or homogeneity of the product. [VERIFY — the ingredient-report route is stated in the rule text; its practical scope (which ingredient reports OCM accepts in a given product line) was not confirmed against OCM guidance in this run.]
  • (D) A product offered for sale is not required to be tested for a contaminant “when the contaminant is not hazardous and the cannabis business provides supporting written documentation to the office that the contaminant is not hazardous.” This is a documentation-based carve-out, not a general exemption from contaminant testing.

Timing of tests within the production flow (9810.3100, subp. 5(E)–(F)):

  • Stability and homogeneity testing must occur after the batch has been packaged as a regulated product.
  • Contaminant and potency testing may occur before packaging.
  • Stability testing is required for every batch, “except that the first batch of a regulated product may have a six-month expiration date.” The rule text checked does not state a longer default shelf-life or a retest interval for later batches; any longer expiry or stability protocol beyond that sentence is [VERIFY — it lives, if anywhere, in the Technical Authority standards document, not in 9810.3100].

Product-type variation. 9810.3100, subp. 6 requires OCM to publish, no later than 1 July each year, an annual report for testing thresholds identifying: (1) approved analytical methods for each contaminant category in subp. 5(B); (2) the specific contaminants required to be tested for each product type in part 9810.2100; (3) acceptance criteria by product category and contaminant type; (4) analytical methods and acceptance criteria for homogeneity; and (5) reporting requirements for labs for each analyte and product category. Licensed testing facilities must update their protocols/SOPs to reflect annual-report changes no later than 1 August each year, and OCM may amend the report off-schedule only if necessary to protect public health and safety (9810.3100, subp. 6(B)–(C)).

Practical consequence: there is no single flat test panel in the rule itself. The contaminant-by-product-type matrix is in the annual report / Technical Authority, not in 9810.3100. Approved product categories for that matrix are in 9810.2100: dried flower (dried raw flower, fresh flower, shake); ingestibles (edibles, beverages, cannabis-derived tinctures); concentrates (hash, hash oils, cured/live resin, cured/live rosin, kief, full extract cannabis oil, distillate); combination products (infused pre-rolls, infused dried raw flower); transdermal/topical; LPHE (edibles, beverages, hemp-derived tinctures); and hemp-derived consumer products (dried raw hemp flower; hemp-derived oils for combustion/vaporization and inhalation).

Source for the rule text: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Technical Authority standards document (Version 2.0, updated 1 July 2026). OCM’s Testing Standards page links a PDF titled “Cannabis Technical Authority: Standards for Sampling and Testing Cannabis and Hemp Products (Version 2.0, updated July 1, 2026)” and states that the testing requirements in that document apply to all cannabis and hemp products produced or sold by OCM-licensed operators, that cultivators/manufacturers must comply with the sampling requirements in Chapter 9810 and that document, and that OCM-licensed testing facilities must test to the levels in that document and communicate results through Metrc or compliant certificates of analysis. The PDF itself was not opened line-by-line in this run, so numeric thresholds (action levels, limits of detection/quantitation, analyte lists) are NOT reproduced here and are [VERIFY — pull the Technical Authority v2.0 PDF directly before publishing any numeric limit]. Secondary reporting of that document states a lab must start microbial testing within five days of receiving a sample and complete all testing within ten business days, notifying OCM if it cannot meet the timeline; that day-count is secondary-reported and is likewise [VERIFY] against the PDF, not asserted here as rule text. Note the tension: 9810.3100 itself states no 5-day/10-day turnaround; if the Technical Authority imposes one, it is guidance/standards-document law, not 9810.3100 text.

Sources: https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/resources/product-testing/technical-authority.jsp; https://www.cannapath.org/post/minnesota-cannabis-testing-labs-2026 (secondary, for the 5/10-day summary only) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

What “stability” does and does not mean here. In 9810.3100, stability is a batch attribute verified for accurate labelling and expiry (subp. 5(A)(1), (E)–(F)), and unanalysed sample portions may be held for stability testing instead of being disposed of under 9810.1200 (9810.3000, subp. 11). No separate Minnesota “stability study” protocol (e.g. accelerated-ageing conditions, time points) was located in Chapter 342 or Rule 9810 text checked; that detail, if it exists, is in the Technical Authority [VERIFY].

11.1.3 Sampling rules

Who samples, and from what. §342.61, subd. 4(a): on a schedule determined by OCM, every microbusiness, mezzobusiness, cultivator, manufacturer, wholesaler with an import endorsement, LPHE manufacturer, or medical cannabis combination business must make each batch grown, manufactured, or imported available to a testing facility. Subd. 4(b) requires full disclosure to the testing facility of all known pesticides, fertilizers, solvents, or other foreign materials — including catalysts used for artificially derived cannabinoids — applied or added to the batch, including accidental applications by any person. Subd. 4(c): the testing facility selects one or more representative samples from each batch. A testing facility must destroy or return any part of the sample that remains after testing (§342.61, subd. 4(c), last sentence).

Rule sampling mechanics (9810.3100, subps. 3, 4, 7, 8).

  • Testing facilities must maintain written SOPs for collecting representative samples for each regulated product handled, addressing sample/data collection and laboratory analysis, with enough detail for accurate and consistent action, and supervisor verification; staff doing sampling/testing must be knowledgeable in the SOPs, and training records must be kept three years (subp. 3).
  • Composite preparation (subp. 4): a facility must grind a representative sample to create a homogeneous composite batch sample, except it need not do so when performing gross foreign matter, microbiological, or homogeneity testing; for those tests it must take a representative sample before creating the composite for other mandatory testing. It must grind a raw cannabis sample and may also use a paddle blender on all or part of a representative sample. Required testing is performed on the homogeneous composite batch sample.
  • Collection methods (subp. 7): methods must ensure accurate representation of the batch, based on random sampling and considering (1) statistical criteria for component variability, confidence levels, and precision desired; (2) inherent product characteristics affecting batch consistency; and (3) quantity needed for analysis. Methods must maintain sample integrity: containers/tools/supplies must not alter accuracy; must be cleaned and handled to prevent introduced contaminants; collection must be performed in a manner visible to mandatory recording devices; containers must be opened, filled, and resealed to prevent contamination of contents and other samples; sterile equipment/utensils and aseptic techniques must be used; each sample must be identified with product name, batch number, date taken, and identity of the collector; and containers must be sealed immediately in a tamper-evident manner.
  • Licensee responsibility (subp. 8): the license holder must ensure sampling workers are properly trained; all mandatory testing is completed by an OCM-licensed testing facility; sample identity and integrity are maintained from collection until the testing facility or licensed transporter receives the sample; and complete, accurate disclosure of cultivation/production methods required by §342.61, subd. 4 (or other information necessary for accurate analysis/reporting) is made to the testing facility.

Batch definition note. Neither §342.61 nor 9810.3100 text checked defines “batch” by weight, unit count, or harvest lot in a single sentence; cultivators must describe their batch numbering in the cultivation plan (9810.2000, subp. 3(A)(9)), and the statewide monitoring system carries the batch number assigned in the system (9810.1302, subp. 2(C)). A batch-size ceiling for testing purposes was not located [UNAVAILABLE — do not import another state’s batch-size limit].

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.1.4 Failed tests, remediation, retesting, and recalls

Statutory disposition. §342.61, subd. 5(a): if a sample meets standards, the testing facility issues a certification and the business may then sell or transfer the batch or offer it for sale. “If a sample does not meet the applicable testing standards or if the testing facility is unable to test for a substance identified pursuant to subdivision 4, paragraph (b), the batch from which the sample was taken shall be subject to procedures established by the office for such batches, including destruction, remediation, or retesting.”

Rule disposition (9810.3100, subp. 9 — remediation).

  • A license holder must ensure batches failing OCM acceptance criteria for contaminant categories or homogeneity are either (1) disposed of under part 9810.1200, or (2) remediated under an OCM-approved plan.
  • The holder must submit a written remediation plan on OCM-prescribed forms and must not conduct any remediation activities until OCM approves the plan.
  • Product awaiting remediation or disposal must be identified and quarantined to prevent use; no remediation method outside the approved plan may be used.
  • All remediated material must meet OCM acceptance criteria, standards, and specifications as part of the approved plan.
  • OCM must approve a plan that renders a product compliant; OCM must not approve a plan that relies on increasing the batch size to achieve compliance (i.e. dilution by batch enlargement is prohibited as a remediation strategy).

Note the scope limit in the rule text: subp. 9 by its terms covers contaminant-category and homogeneity failures. A batch that fails potency limits or label-profile conformity is within §342.61, subd. 2(a)’s rulemaking mandate (“procedures applicable to … batches that fail to meet the potency limits … or that do not conform with the content of the cannabinoid profile listed on the label”), but 9810.3100, subp. 9 as checked does not spell out a separate potency-failure remediation pathway; whether potency failures are remediable at all (versus destruction or relabelling, which the rule does not authorise in the text checked) is [VERIFY — do not assume a potency failure can be “remediated” like a contaminant failure].

Mandatory notification of failures (9810.3100, subp. 10). A license holder whose product fails mandatory testing criteria must notify OCM of all noncompliant testing reports, including (1) the criteria not met, (2) the production status of the batch, and (3) the holder’s decision to dispose of or remediate under subp. 9. Separately, a holder must notify OCM of all testing results, including batches that have and have not completed production processes. In the statewide monitoring system, a testing facility reports results in the record of the batch tested, and in a failed-test case the cannabis business must record remediation steps taken and results of subsequent testing (9810.1302, subp. 6(C)).

Retesting. Retesting after remediation is the mechanism by which remediated material is shown to meet acceptance criteria (9810.3100, subp. 9(E)); the rule text checked does not state a numeric limit on the number of retests, a “retest the same sample vs. new sample” rule, or a distinct retest procedure for a batch that fails a second time. Secondary guidance (Metrc bulletin MN_IB_0065, 24 June 2026) describes the same sequence — OCM-approved remediation plan first, then recording in Metrc — but a retest-count rule is [UNAVAILABLE] on the sources checked. Do not state “one retest only” or any similar limit.

Source for the Metrc bulletin (secondary, vendor guidance, not OCM law): https://www.metrc.com/bulletin/mn-bulletin-65-remediation/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Recalls — who orders, and public notice (9810.1101). This is the operative recall rule; it is distinct from the failed-batch remediation rule above, although a failed test can trigger it.

  • Factors — OCM must require a recall if OCM has evidence the regulated product: (A) contains a contaminant level exceeding OCM acceptance criteria for foreign material, heavy metals, microbiological contaminants, mycotoxins, pesticide residues, or residual solvents; (B) contains an undeclared allergen as defined in Minnesota Food Law, ch. 31; (C) is otherwise unfit for human use, consumption, or application; (D) was not cultivated or manufactured by a licensed cannabis or hemp business as required by ch. 342; (E) has packaging that fails to disclose a known allergen; (F) has packaging that does not comply with labelling requirements in §342.63; or (G) otherwise poses a risk to public health or safety.
  • Mandatory recall process (subp. 2). On OCM’s request, the license holder must perform a traceback and trace-forward investigation to identify all affected businesses, markets, and consumers and must respond to all OCM information requests within 24 hours of OCM’s request. OCM may take control of a recall process at any time.
  • OCM notice and public posting. If OCM determines a recall is necessary, OCM must (1) issue the license holder a notice of recall with the specific product and the basis under subp. 1, and (2) post the notice of recall on OCM’s website. That website posting is the public-notice mechanism in the rule text checked; no separate newspaper, press-release, or point-of-sale posting duty is stated in 9810.1101 text checked [VERIFY if a separate OCM recall-notice template imposes more].
  • Licensee duties within one day of receiving OCM’s notice: (1) notify any other business impacted; (2) notify all individuals who may have purchased the recalled product and reimburse individuals for any returned product; and (3) ensure all recalled products are destroyed in accordance with Chapter 9810 and record the destruction in the business’s seed-to-sale tracking system.
  • Compliance notice within three days: the holder must notify OCM of compliance with those three duties within three days of receiving the recall notice.
  • Voluntary recall (subp. 3). A holder may initiate a recall when it has information a product is mislabeled, defective, or unsafe for consumption. It must (A) give OCM notice including a description of the product and the basis; on receipt OCM must post the notice on OCM’s website noting the holder initiated it; and (B) comply with subp. 2, item B (the one-day notify/reimburse/destroy duties).

Record retention — three clocks, do not conflate:

  • Business test results under §342.61, subd. 5(b): at least five years after the date of testing; and under subd. 5(c) the business must make those results available for review by any member of the public on request, in plain language.
  • Testing-facility data packages under 9810.3000, subp. 9(A): recorded in the statewide monitoring system, retained at least three years.
  • Testing-facility testing reports under 9810.3100, subp. 5(G): retained at least three years from the report date, available to OCM on request.

Testing-facility sample-result reports must be recorded in the statewide monitoring system, state whether the complete sample was homogenised and tested as received or a portion was sampled, report measurement uncertainty and limits of detection/quantitation, and be accompanied by a certificate of analysis to the submitting entity containing facility/submitter names and licence numbers, product category/type/name, batch number, analytical summary (identifier, methods, target compounds, result, reporting limit, qualifier, units, preparation and analysis dates), and, for homogeneity and contaminant analysis, a determination whether results meet OCM acceptance criteria (9810.3000, subp. 10).

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.1.5 Licensed testing facilities — count confirmed, roster NOT reproduced as official

What is verified: Run 1 recorded 5 licensed testing facilities issued at 19 Oct 2026 from an OCM table. Secondary reporting in September–October 2026 independently reports the same count (5) and the same market-monitor figure (five testing facility licences; five testing sites). OCM’s own September 2025 press release confirms the roster mechanism: “For details about licensed testing facilities — including contact information and, if applicable, the tests they are currently authorized to conduct — visit our Licensed Testing Facilities webpage.”

What is NOT verified in this run, as the commission requires: the current OCM Licensed Testing Facilities webpage itself was not opened line-by-line in this run, so no roster is reproduced here as an official OCM roster. Secondary sources name five facilities — Adams Independent Testing (Moorhead), ChRi Laboratories (St. Paul), FINA Analytics (Waseca), PhytoLab MN (Chisago City), and True North Analytical (Roseville) — and report differing scopes (Adams and True North authorised across every listed field; ChRi authorised for most fields but not residual solvents or terpenes, operating under an OCM variance; FINA authorised for potency and microbial testing; PhytoLab for potency and microbial testing on finished products only), and report that Legend Technical Services, licensed in September 2025, is no longer authorised after its variances expired and security/testing requirements went unaddressed. Treat every name, location, and scope in this paragraph as secondary-reported only [VERIFY against the live OCM Licensed Testing Facilities page before any publication]. In particular, do not publish the five names as “the OCM roster” on the basis of this part.

Structural rules that ARE verified and explain why scopes differ:

  • A testing facility need not seek approval for all fields to maintain licensure; it must have OCM approval for at least one field of testing (9810.3000, subp. 6, as checked). Approval requires peer-reviewed, independently third-party-validated, internally verified methods (AOAC Official Methods of Analysis Appendices J/K, incorporated by reference), with specificity/sensitivity meeting reporting limits for each analyte sought.
  • A testing facility licence may be held with no other licence: 9810.1000, subp. 6 caps a person at three testing facility licences, and secondary OCM guidance states a testing facility licensee may not hold another cannabis/hemp licence or be employed by another cannabis/hemp business, with a conflict-of-interest policy required [VERIFY the employment/conflict sentence against 9810.3000 text or OCM guidance; the “no other licence” proposition is the Run 1 baseline and is consistent with the rule structure, but the full employment sentence was not opened in this run].
  • OCM must revoke a testing facility’s approval for any and all analytical methods if the facility fails to submit accurate application materials, comply with application requirements or applicable law, allow OCM physical inspection, or submit ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation-body or proficiency-testing inspection/corrective reports on request (9810.3000, subp. 7).
  • A testing facility must operate under at least one technical manager responsible for quality and analytical standards (9810.3000, subp. 8), and may seek a variance from Chapter 9810 under the six-part test in 9810.3000, subp. 12 (complete request, no adverse public-health/safety/environmental effect, equivalent-or-better alternative measures, undue burden, no deviation from a statutory standard or federal law, future effect only).

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00; https://www.cannapath.org/post/minnesota-cannabis-testing-labs-2026 (secondary, roster/scopes only); https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MNOCM/bulletins/3f2eafc (OCM press release, roster mechanism) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.1.6 Research-and-development testing exemption

9810.3100, subp. 11: cannabis flower and cannabis product batches are exempt from Part 9810.3100 if (A) a cannabis microbusiness licensed under §342.28, subd. 1a produces them solely for research and development, and (B) they are not consumed by humans. This is the testing-side companion to the §342.28, subd. 1a research microbusiness licence in §11.9 below. It does not exempt research batches from the “must not enter commerce” rule in §342.28, subd. 1a.

11.2 Licence rules

11.2.1 Transfers and sales — §342.12 (correction of the Run 1 citation)

Correction: Run 1 cited “§§342.18/342.21” for transfers. The transfer provision is §342.12, “Licenses; transfers; adjustments.” §342.21 is suspension/revocation/hearing (§11.2.7 below). §342.18 appears in the Revisor index as selection criteria, not transfers. The coordinator should correct the Run 1 cross-reference.

§342.12, subdivision 1 (transfer of licences), as amended and as confirmed in 2026 bill text restating the section:

  • (a) Licences “available to all applicants pursuant to section 342.14, subdivision 1b, paragraph (c), may be freely transferred subject to the prior written approval of the office unless the license holder has not received a final site inspection or the license holder is a social equity applicant.” “Freely transferred” therefore still requires prior written OCM approval, and is unavailable pre-final-inspection.
  • (b) Licences issued as social equity licences (under §342.14, subd. 1b(b) or §342.175(b)) “may only be transferred to another social equity applicant for three years after the date on which the office issues the license. Three years after the date of issuance, a license holder may transfer a license to any entity.” Transfer of a social-equity licence must be reviewed by the Division of Social Equity and is subject to prior written OCM approval.
  • (c) Preliminary license approval issued under §342.14, subd. 5 may not be transferred. This is distinct from a licence transfer: pre-approval itself is non-transferable.
  • (d) A new licence must be obtained when (1) the holder’s legal business structure converts or changes to a different type, or (2) the holder dissolves, consolidates, reorganises, undergoes bankruptcy/insolvency/receivership, merges with another legal organisation, or assigns all or substantially all assets for creditors’ benefit.

Secondary OCM-applicant guidance (Qualified Applicant Guide, via a mirrored copy) is consistent on the pre-licensure side: applicants cannot transfer ownership of an application before receiving a licence; a preliminarily approved applicant cannot sell a majority ownership interest to a third party; pre-licensure ownership changes are reviewed only at site registration. That guidance is secondary [VERIFY against the current OCM guide], but it aligns with §342.12(c).

Retail registrations are separately non-transferable at the local level. Local ordinances implementing §342.22 state retail registrations “shall not be transferred” (e.g. Red Wing City Code §6.28). That is a local-registration rule, not a §342.12 licence-transfer rule; do not conflate the two.

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/94/2026/0/HF/4199/versions/0/ (restating §342.12); https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2026/0/Session+Law/Chapter/123/pdf/ (§342.12 relocation paragraph, §11.2.6); https://www.redwingmn.gov/DocumentCenter/View/8903/Red-Wing-City-Code-Chapter-6-Section-628-PDF (local non-transferability, secondary/local) — Accessed 2026-10-28. The direct Revisor text of current §342.12 was not opened as a standalone page in this run; the subdivision language above is confirmed across two independent 2026 bill restatements, but the coordinator should still pull https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.12 directly before publication [VERIFY — formality, high confidence].

11.2.2 Ownership changes and true party of interest — §342.185

The 2025 text (directly opened via Revisor PDF in search-index form). §342.185, subd. 2 (application number limitations): “An individual may not be a true party of interest for more than one application for (1) any single type of license, or (2) multiple types of licenses if the individual would be prohibited from holding the licenses under section 342.18, subdivision 2.” The limitation does not apply to an individual who holds no more than ten percent ownership of the business entity. Subd. 3 (licence number limitations): “An individual may not be a true party of interest for more than one license unless explicitly allowed by this chapter,” with the same ten-percent-or-less controlling-ownership exception (plus, in later text, ESOP-trustee and ESOP-owned-business employee exceptions).

Who is NOT a true party of interest (subd. 1 exclusions, 2025 text): among others, (2) an employee receiving salary/hourly compensation who holds no ownership interest and no right to exercise control; (3) an individual receiving a sales bonus/commission not exceeding ten percent of sales in a bonus/commission period under a written agreement; (4) a passive investor as described in 31 CFR §800.243; (5) a person contracting for a commission on sale of the business or real property; (6) a flat/hourly consultant under a written agreement; (7) a service contractor (e.g. branding or staffing company) obtaining no ownership or control; and (8) a financial institution. Options agreements count: OCM correspondence in litigation (Aranguiz/Connolly v. OCM, Minn. Ct. App. 2025) treated an undisclosed options agreement as a true-party-of-interest disclosure failure under §342.185, subd. 2, and applicants were expected to withdraw and reapply on a separate track.

The 33% question [VERIFY — unresolved in this run]. The commission asks whether 2026 ch. 123 contains “any 33% investor rule.” A current secondary compilation (ArkLegal, citing §342.185) prints subd. 2/3 exceptions including “an individual who holds up to 33 percent controlling ownership of up to four business entities that are social equity applicants” (applications) / “up to four business entities that hold a social equity license” (licences), and a municipal-contractor exception for up to ten municipal stores under §342.32, subd. 5. Separately, a 2026 bill (HF 3681) proposed raising the ten-percent threshold to 35 percent. Those two figures (33% in a compilation vs. 35% in a bill) are not the same proposition, and neither was confirmed against the Revisor’s current §342.185 text or the enrolled text of 2026 ch. 123 in this run. Do not publish a 33% (or 35%) threshold as law on the basis of this part. What can be stated: the 2025 text is ten percent; a social-equity multi-entity exception at a higher percentage is claimed in secondary compilations and requires direct verification against the 2026 Supplement.

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/2025-10-21%2016:21:44+00:00/cite/342.185/pdf (2025 text); https://arklegal.ai/state_statute/3546226/download.pdf?tagged=1 (secondary compilation, 33% claim only); https://law.justia.com/cases/minnesota/court-of-appeals/2025/a24-1873.html (options-agreement disclosure) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Disclosure duty in practice. Applicants must maintain compliance with §§342.14, 342.15, 342.16, 342.17, and 342.185, and failure to do so will result in an application not proceeding (OCM pre-approval correspondence, via Shorewood publication). Pre-licensure ownership changes that (i) change the majority holder, (ii) require a new Secretary of State business registration, (iii) cause a social-equity application to lose social-equity qualification, (iv) add an owner ineligible on criminal/civil history, or (v) violate §342.185 are prohibited in that OCM guidance. That list is OCM guidance, not statute text [VERIFY against the current OCM guide if quoted verbatim].

Source: https://www.shorewoodmn.gov/DocumentCenter/View/2241/State-of-Minnesota-Office-of-Cannabis-Management-License-Pre-Approval-Confirmation — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.2.3 Renewal, preliminary approval, and tier adjustment

  • Annual renewal. §342.12(e): “Licenses must be renewed annually.”
  • Initial fee includes first renewal; renewal fee due at second renewal. Per §342.11(a) as summarised in OCM’s Qualified Applicant Guide: “the initial license fee shall include the fee for the initial issuance of the license and the first annual renewal. License holders must pay the renewal fee at the time of the second renewal and each subsequent annual renewal thereafter. All license fees are nonrefundable.” The same structure is mirrored in local retail-registration ordinances (initial registration fee includes first-year operation and the second-year renewal fee; no fee due at first annual renewal; renewal fee charged at second and subsequent renewals). The Run 1 fee table in the commission is therefore consistent with this timing rule and is carried forward; the testing-facility fee conflict in Run 1 ($5,000/$5,000/$10,000 vs. $10,000/$10,000/$20,000 secondary) was not resolved in this run [VERIFY].
  • Preliminary approval clock (as amended by 2026 ch. 123, §19, amending §342.14, subd. 10). (a) “A preliminary license approval expires after 18 months unless the office revokes the preliminary license approval or grants an extension. The office must grant an initial extension of up to six months upon request by the applicant. The office may grant an additional extension of up to six months if an applicant has made good faith efforts to convert a preliminary license approval into a license. The office must not issue a license to an applicant whose preliminary license approval has expired.” (b) OCM may revoke preliminary approval if the applicant is not eligible for a licence. (c) OCM must notify the applicant of revocation or expiry. Maximum ordinary runway is therefore 18 + 6 + 6 = 30 months, with the first six months mandatory on request and the second six discretionary on good-faith efforts.
  • Site-registration / final authorisation timing. OCM guidance summarised in local-government materials states OCM must respond to a site registration within 90 days (issue the licence or a denial), and preliminarily approved applicants should not complete site registration until they have all local zoning approvals, are compliant with state fire/building codes, and are fewer than 90 days from opening. That 90-day figure is guidance summary [VERIFY against §342.14, subd. 6 current text].
  • Tier adjustment / reclassification. §342.12(f): “License holders may petition the office to adjust the tier of a license issued within a license category if the license holder meets all applicable requirements.” 2026 ch. 123 materials describe a broader reclassification petition process (micro → mezzo → macro) effective 1 Jan 2027, with social-equity and medical-endorsement prioritisation in secondary summaries. The broader process beyond §342.12(f)’s within-category tier adjustment is [VERIFY against ch. 123 text] and is not stated here as a standalone right.
  • Renewal application content. 9810.1102, subp. 2(E) requires an applicant/licensee to include a description of its employee training and education programme in its licence or licence-renewal application. A cultivator must submit a cultivation plan on initial application, annual renewal, endorsement application, or notified change in business activity (9810.2000, subp. 2(A)).

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2026/0/Session+Law/Chapter/123/pdf/ (§342.14, subd. 10); https://ramyaliving.com/?_= %2Focm%2Fassets%2FOCM_Qualified_Applicant_Guide_3.0_tcm1202-669481.pdf (OCM guide via mirror, secondary); https://content.govdelivery.com/attachments/MNOCM/2025/08/11/file_attachments/3352910/Locals%20Webinar%20July%2018th%20Q&A%20Responses%20%20-%20PDF.pdf (90-day site-registration summary, secondary) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.2.4 Ownership caps, vertical-integration limits, and retail-location limits

Per-licence-type licence-count caps (9810.1000, as checked). The rule states, in the portions confirmed: no person holding a cannabis manufacturer licence may hold more than one manufacturer licence; no person holding a retailer licence may hold more than one retailer licence; likewise one wholesaler licence, one transporter licence, and one delivery service licence per person; and no person holding a testing facility licence may hold more than three testing facility licences. The microbusiness/mezzobusiness/cultivator subparts of 9810.1000 were not fully reproduced in the sources checked for this part [VERIFY — pull 9810.1000, subps. 1–2 directly; do not assume they mirror the one-licence pattern].

Vertical-integration / cross-holding limits (statute, by licence type). The pattern is type-specific, not a single “no vertical integration” rule:

  • Retailer (§342.32, subd. 4) — directly confirmed, resolving the Run 1 [VERIFY]. (a) A retailer licensee may also hold a delivery service licence and an event organiser licence. (b) Except as provided in (a) (and, in the 2025 text, subd. 5 municipal stores), no retailer licensee may own or operate any other cannabis or hemp business. (c) “No person, cooperative, or business may hold a license to own or operate more than one cannabis retail business in one city and three retail businesses in one county.” (d) OCM by rule may further limit retailer licences a person may hold. (e) The restriction applies to every cooperative member and every director, manager, and general partner.
  • Retailer locations (§342.32, subd. 2). “A cannabis retailer may operate up to five retail locations.” Combined with subd. 4(c), the operative retail cap is therefore: up to 5 locations per retailer licence, max 1 retail business per city, max 3 per county. The Run 1 baseline on this point is confirmed, not merely carried.
  • Testing facility. May hold no other licence (Run 1 baseline; see §11.1.5 for the rule basis and its verification limit).
  • Microbusiness / mezzobusiness / cultivator / manufacturer / wholesaler / transporter / delivery / event organiser cross-holding. Each licence section (§§342.28–342.31, 342.33, 342.35, 342.39, 342.41) states its own “multiple licences” or “limitations” subdivision. Those subdivisions were not all opened in this run. Do not generalise the retailer rule to other types. The coordinator should pull §§342.28–342.41 “multiple licenses; limits” subdivisions as a set before publishing a cross-holding table [VERIFY — open item, not a gap in the law].
  • True-party-of-interest licence-count rule (§342.185, subd. 3) overlays all of the above: an individual may not be a true party of interest for more than one licence unless explicitly allowed by Chapter 342, subject to the percentage exceptions in §11.2.2.
  • Municipal stores (§342.32, subd. 5). A city or county may establish, own, and operate a municipal cannabis store; in the 2025 text it may also hold an LPHE retailer licence. Run 1’s “single store, not counted against state maximums or local caps” proposition was not re-verified against current §342.32, subd. 5 text in this run [VERIFY — the 2025 text opened confirms municipal-store authority and the LPHE add-on, but not the counting sentence].

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/342.32; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/2025-10-19%2013:12:45+00:00/cite/342.32/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.
