If a ch. 123 investor cap exists, it was not located in the ch. 123 excerpts checked [UNAVAILABLE — do not state an investor percentage cap as law].

11.2.6 Relocation

Two distinct relocation mechanisms must not be conflated:

  1. Local zoning certification (the Run 1 “30-day gate”). §342.13(f): within 30 days of receiving a copy of a state licence application from OCM, a local unit of government shall certify on an OCM-provided form whether a proposed cannabis retail business complies with local zoning ordinances and, if applicable, whether it complies with the state fire code and building code. Local materials summarise the consequence: OCM may issue a licence if the local unit does not certify within 30 days, and may not issue a licence if the local unit informs OCM the business does not comply with local zoning/land-use law. This gate is stated for retail businesses in the §342.13(f) summaries; whether the same 30-day certification applies to a relocation of a non-retail premises is [VERIFY — the §342.12(g) relocation paragraph below does not restate a 30-day local clock].
  2. Licence relocation by rule (§342.12(g), as restated in 2026 materials). “The office by rule may permit the relocation of a licensed cannabis business; permit the relocation of an approved operational location, including a cultivation, manufacturing, processing, or retail location; adopt requirements for the submission of a license relocation application; establish standards for the approval of a relocation application; and charge a fee not to exceed $250 for reviewing and processing applications. Relocation of a licensed premises pursuant to this paragraph does not extend or otherwise modify the license term of the license subject to relocation.” Separately, OCM guidance on indoor/outdoor switching states a licensee may switch between indoor and outdoor cultivation (or vice versa) only by submitting a new site registration and final plans of record, and may not switch until that new site registration is approved — that is a site-registration change, not a §342.12(g) relocation, and is secondary guidance [VERIFY].

Multiple locations generally. 9810.1100, subp. 5: a licensee endorsed for multiple activities may perform each activity at a separate location if it provides location information to OCM and receives any required local-government permission; multiple license holders must not occupy or conduct OCM-authorised activities on the same premises.

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2026/0/Session+Law/Chapter/123/pdf/ (§342.12(g) paragraph); https://www.co.aitkin.mn.us/board/2024/11-12-2024/pdf/3A%20-%20Second%20Reading%20-%20Aitkin%20County%20Cannabis%20Ordinance.pdf and https://content.govdelivery.com/attachments/MNOCM/2025/08/11/file_attachments/3352910/Locals%20Webinar%20July%2018th%20Q&A%20Responses%20%20-%20PDF.pdf (§342.13(f) summaries); https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MNOCM/bulletins/40cd5f5 (indoor/outdoor switching guidance, secondary) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.2.7 Surrender, revocation, nonrenewal, and temporary suspension — §342.21

Grounds. §342.21, subd. 1: “The office may revoke or not renew a license when the office has cause to believe that a cannabis business or hemp business has violated an ownership or operational requirement in this chapter or rules adopted pursuant to this chapter.” No exhaustive list of revocation grounds is stated in §342.21 itself; grounds are therefore any ownership/operational violation of Chapter 342 or its rules, plus the specific disqualification and non-issuance rules in §342.15/9810.1001 (see §11.8).

Procedure — revocation/nonrenewal (subd. 2). Before revoking or not renewing, OCM must provide the holder a statement of the complaints and hold a hearing to determine whether to revoke or deny renewal. The holder must receive notice at least 20 days before the hearing, served by certified mail to the address on the licence application or as provided by law for service of a summons. At the hearing OCM (or its authorised employee/agent) receives evidence, administers oaths, and examines witnesses. After the hearing (or on the holder’s failure to appear), OCM must take action as deemed advisable and issue written findings mailed to the holder. An action under this paragraph is subject to judicial review under Chapter 14. Contested hearings under Chapter 342 are conducted by the Office of Administrative Hearings as OCM’s agent under §342.21, subd. 2, under Minn. R. pts. 1400.5010–1400.8401 and §§14.48–14.62 (9810.1002).

Temporary suspension without hearing (subd. 3). OCM may temporarily, without hearing, suspend the licence and operating privilege of a licensed business for up to 90 days if continuing operation would threaten the health or safety of any person (text truncated in the source excerpt at that phrase; the balance of subd. 3 — including any post-suspension hearing right — was not fully reproduced in the sources checked [VERIFY the tail of subd. 3]).

Surrender — voluntary surrender procedure [UNAVAILABLE]. No voluntary-surrender procedure, surrender form, or surrender-specific inventory disposition rule was located in §342.21 text checked or in Rule 9810 text checked for this part. In particular, §342.21 does not in the text checked state what happens to inventory or employees on revocation, nonrenewal, or surrender (transfer to another licensee, destruction, wind-down period, employee notification). Do not import another state’s wind-down rule. Related but distinct rules that do exist: recalled product must be destroyed and the destruction recorded (9810.1101, §11.1.4); failed-test product must be disposed of under 9810.1200 or remediated under an approved plan (9810.3100, subp. 9); and a designated caregiver must dispose of unused medical cannabis within ten days of a patient’s disenrollment/death or a recall (9810.4001, subp. 3(C)). None of those is a general surrender/inventory rule.

Enforcement overlay. Non-compliance with an environmental requirement in 9810.1200, subp. 1(A), as found by the enforcing agency, may lead OCM to deny an application, revoke a licence, deny renewal, or take any other enforcement action under Chapter 342 (9810.1200, subp. 1(B)). That is an example of §342.21’s “operational requirement” ground, not a separate revocation standard.

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/342.21/pdf; https://law.justia.com/codes/minnesota/chapters-324-342/chapter-342/section-342-21/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.2.9 Track-and-trace (needed to read the licence rules above)

§342.05 requires OCM to contract with an outside vendor for a statewide monitoring system; the statute does not name the vendor. The vendor question is now resolved by OCM itself: OCM’s Inventory Management (Metrc) page states: “The Office of Cannabis Management (OCM) has contracted with Metrc to develop and administer a digital tracking infrastructure, which traces cannabis products starting from cultivation through processing, testing, distribution and sale,” and that licensed businesses must create a Metrc account, attach serialized tags to every plant and product, use the system (software, tagging, labelling tools), and bear all costs of purchase and use, with a high-speed internet connection required. Rule 9810.1301 confirms the operational duties: use OCM’s statewide monitoring system; designate system administrators (trained) and system users (trained, supervised, unique logins); terminate inactive/departed users’ accounts within 24 hours of notice; comply with administrative holds; maintain a 12-month record of administrators/users; and report in the system regardless of any supplemental software used. 9810.1302 requires daily inventory reconciliation (accurate at end of each business day), tagging of all plants over eight inches in height or width and all units packaged for transfer/sale (other than final sale/delivery), and reporting of sales (actual price and any discount amount), crop-input applications, destruction, sampling removals, theft/loss (to OCM within eight hours of discovery and to local law enforcement immediately), weight/quantity adjustments with justification, testing removals (as laboratory sample packages, transferable only to a licensed testing facility), and approved demonstration removals (employee samples, retailer display samples, promotional samples to a licensed business). On system outage: written reporting to OCM for up to three calendar days, then (except cultivation) written reporting must cease, back-entry within 12 hours of restoration, and no sales while the system is unavailable (9810.1302, subp. 8).

Medical/adult-use system split — in transition [VERIFY]. 9810.1301, subps. 2–3 (2025 rules) still describe separate adult-use and medical statewide monitoring systems (a business without a medical endorsement records only in the adult-use system; a business with a medical endorsement records medical flower/products in the medical system). 2026-law secondary summaries describe a move to a single unified Metrc operation for both markets. Whether, and from what date, the 9810.1301 split is superseded is the same unresolved merger-date question as in §11.3.4; do not cite the 2025 split as current without checking OCM’s Metrc guidance for the transition date.

Sources: https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/resources/metrc/; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 (9810.1300–1302) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.2.10 General operations duties that underpin licence compliance

9810.1100 requires written, up-to-date SOPs covering general operations, worker training/safety, statewide-monitoring data entry, safe/sanitary storage, segregation/disposal of damaged/broken-seal/contaminated/expired/recalled product, authorised-personnel designation and worker ID for restricted areas, private/nonpublic consumer-data access, data-breach response (§§325E.61, 325E.64), testing/research sampling procedures, and disclosure of cultivation/manufacturing/packaging substances to the testing facility. SOPs must be on-site for personnel and OCM on request. Financial records must be kept for the current plus previous three fiscal years (tax records ten years), all records must be producible to OCM within 24 hours of request, and the three-year record set in 9810.1100, subp. 3(B)(1) (training, security plan/testing/maintenance, cultivation plan/records, manufacturing SOP verification, sanitation, equipment maintenance, storage procedures/records) must be available for inspection. No OCM-authorised activity may occur in a dwelling, and any approved area must be accessible without passing through a dwelling — except an activity specifically authorised under §342.09 (9810.1100, subp. 4; 9810.2000, subp. 8(A) to the same effect).

Micro +1,000 sq ft indoor / ¼ acre outdoor; mezz +3,000 sq ft / ½ acre and +25% manufacturing with a medical manufacturer endorsement, +2 retail locations with a medical retail endorsement if at least 2 are in high-medical-need areas; cultivator +6,000 sq ft / 1 acre. These additions were not re-verified against current §342.51 text in this run [VERIFY — they describe the endorsement structure that ch. 123’s unified operation may supersede from 1 Jan 2027; see §11.3.4].

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.28 (microbusiness canopy, via secondary compilation restating §342.28, subd. 2); https://catalyst-bc.com/minnesota-cannabis-consulting/ (secondary table agreeing with Run 1 canopy figures); https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2026/0/Session+Law/Chapter/123/pdf/ (macrobusiness retail paragraph; manufacturing volume); https://www.mondaq.com/unitedstates/government/1798036/minnesotas-new-cannabis-and-hemp-laws and https://harris-sliwoski.com/cannalawblog/minnesotas-new-cannabis-and-hemp-laws/ (secondary, macrobusiness endpoints and cap) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.3.2 Plant counts, indoor/outdoor/greenhouse rules

  • No commercial plant-count cap was located. Commercial cultivation is controlled by canopy (sq ft / acres), not by a plant number, in the licence sections and in 9810.2000. The plant-count limits in Minnesota law are the home-grow limits in §342.09, subd. 2 (§11.3.5) and the caregiver limit in §342.52, subd. 9(d). Do not apply the 8-plant home limit to a licensed cultivator.
  • Indoor vs. outdoor election. A cultivator must indicate in its cultivation plan whether it will cultivate indoors or outdoors (9810.2000, subp. 3(A)). The plan must include: size/layout diagram of cultivation areas including total canopy; ventilation/air-filtration diagram; electricity/water/utility plans; wastewater and solid-waste disposal plans; recycling plans for supplies/environmental inputs including water and packaging; an integrated-pest-management protocol (as defined in §17.114, subd. 2(b)); vendor name/contact/invoices for all propagation products (seeds, clones, fertilisers, nutrients, chemical/biological pest-control products); record-keeping procedures for crop inputs entered in the statewide monitoring system and declared for lab testing/regulatory review/inspection; batch-numbering description; growing schedules (seeding/planting/cutting-propagation dates); harvesting timelines/methods; drying/curing/storage methods; and a security plan under 9810.1500. The cultivator must regularly update the plan, provide it to OCM on request, submit a plan on initial application, annual renewal, endorsement application, or notified change, conduct only plan-approved activities, and notify OCM of plan changes at least ten business days before implementing them (9810.2000, subps. 2–3).
  • Greenhouse / mixed-light. 9810.0200, subp. 43 defines “outdoor mixed-light facility” as “a hoop house, greenhouse, or other structure with nonrigid walls that uses natural light, in whole or in part, for cultivation.” A greenhouse with nonrigid walls using natural light is therefore treated in the definitions as an outdoor mixed-light facility, not as indoor cultivation. A rigid-wall, fully artificially lit greenhouse is not defined as outdoor mixed-light in the text checked; its indoor/outdoor classification for canopy purposes is [VERIFY — the cultivation plan’s indoor/outdoor election and OCM’s site-registration determination govern in practice].
  • Outdoor security (see also §11.4). Outdoor cultivation areas must be enclosed by fencing and locked gates, at least six feet high, obscuring or covered to obscure the area from ready view outside, commercial/security grade (not agricultural/residential grade), designed to prevent unauthorised access (9810.1500, subp. 15).
  • Premises rules. Cultivation, drying, processing, and storage must not occur in dwellings unless specifically authorised under §342.09; all approved activities must occur in an area accessible without passing through a dwelling (9810.2000, subp. 8(A)). Production areas must allow authorised individuals unobstructed access, observation, and inventory of all plant canopy (subp. 8(D)). All electrical equipment including growing lights must be evaluated/approved for applicable use by an OSHA Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory Program organisation (subp. 8(C)). Direct-to-consumer sales on cultivation premises require a wall/barrier with proper security separating customer areas from limited-access areas, including sample collection/packaging/sealing areas (subp. 8(F)).
  • Plant tagging and sourcing. All plants over eight inches in height or width must be physically tagged with a unique identifier recorded in the statewide monitoring system (9810.1302, subp. 4(A)); the system inventory must record growth phase for all living plants and a unique ID for plants over eight inches (subp. 2(D)). After 1 Dec 2025, a cultivator must obtain seeds, immature plants, mother plants, plants, and other propagation sources from a source authorised by OCM to sell those products (9810.2000, subp. 9(A)). Volunteer plants must be destroyed/disposed of under 9810.1200 (subp. 9(B)). A cultivator must not sell propagative material to a buyer it knows or reasonably should know would use it for activities prohibited by ch. 342 or applicable local/state law (subp. 7).
  • Canopy ceiling enforcement. “The total area in square feet in which cannabis plants are cultivated must never exceed the total area for which the cannabis cultivator is approved by the office” (9810.2000, subp. 6(B), as checked).
  • Medical/adult-use separation on the same premises (2025 rules). 9810.2000, subp. 14: a business endorsed/authorised for both may cultivate both only if its cultivation plan addresses both and it holds a valid medical endorsement under §342.51 or is licensed under §342.515; it must cultivate medical in an area separated from adult-use, track and store separately, never cultivate medical and adult-use simultaneously on the same equipment, and keep an equipment log (worker, tracking information, date/time/duration, resulting concentrate/product tracking) available to OCM on request. See §11.3.4 for the merger question.

11.3.3 Manufacturing volume limits (cultivation-adjacent, for completeness)

9810.2101, subp. 1 (annual, raw concentrates dry-weight equivalent): mezzobusiness 30,000 lb; microbusiness 10,000 lb; medical combination business 90,000 lb, of which at least two-thirds must be used for the medical market. Ch. 123 restatement for a macrobusiness: until OCM establishes limits by rule, a macrobusiness must not use more than 90,000 lb (with a medical manufacturer endorsement required and compliance with §342.51, subd. 1c). Potency limits in the same part: vaporised-delivery concentrates for adult-use must not exceed 80% THC; hemp-derived consumer products must not exceed 0.3% THC; combination products must not exceed 50% total THC; transdermal/topical must not exceed 1,000 mg THC per package (9810.2101, subp. 2). These are manufacturing/potency limits, not canopy, and are included here only because the Run 1 canopy baseline is often misread as a production-volume cap.

11.3.4 Medical/adult-use supply-chain merger — date UNRESOLVED [VERIFY]

Run 1 flagged two secondary dates for the merger of medical and adult-use supply chains into a single unified operation: 1 Aug 2026 vs. 1 Jan 2027. This run does not resolve that conflict. What is established:

  • The 2025 rules still require separation (9810.2000, subp. 14; 9810.1301, subps. 2–3; see §§11.2.9, 11.3.2).
  • 2026-law secondary summaries (Mondaq, Harris Sliwoski, OCM proposal materials) describe the new law as eliminating the separate-supply-chain requirement, allowing a single cultivation/manufacturing/inventory system including unified tracking in Metrc, with medical safeguards (pharmacist or medical cannabis consultant employment, priority service, high-medical-need stocking, 24-hour fulfilment expectation) preserved.
  • The macrobusiness licence itself is effective 1 Jan 2027 (secondary summaries agree; ch. 123 materials describe the combination licence sunsetting and the macrobusiness replacing it).

Whether the unified-operation permission itself is effective 1 Aug 2026 (for existing endorsement holders, ahead of the macrobusiness start) or only 1 Jan 2027 is not stated in the ch. 123 excerpts opened in this run. Do not publish either date as the merger effective date until the enrolled ch. 123 effective-date section is pulled. Until then, cite the 2025 separation rules as the rule text and the unified operation as 2026-law direction, with the date flagged.

11.3.5 Home grow and patient/caregiver grow — cross-reference, no contradiction

§342.09, subd. 2 (confirmed against 2025 text):

“Up to eight cannabis plants, with no more than four being mature, flowering plants may be grown at a single residence, including the curtilage or yard, without a license to cultivate cannabis issued under this chapter provided that cultivation takes place at the primary residence of an individual 21 years of age or older and in an enclosed, locked space that is not open to public view.”

  • The limit is per residence, not per adult.
  • Excess plants: civil penalty up to $500 per excess plant (Run 1 baseline; the penalty provision is §342.09, subd. 6, cited in §342.15, subd. 2 as a non-issuance bar for persons fined under it — see §11.8.2).
  • §342.09, subd. 3: volatile-solvent home extraction is prohibited without a microbusiness, mezzobusiness, manufacturer, medical cannabis processor, or LPHE manufacturer licence. (Run 1 lists the licence set as “a listed licence (§342.09 subd. 3)”; the 2025 text opened lists those five licence types — the medical-cannabis-processor reference is pre-ch. 123 terminology and should be conformed to the macrobusiness/endorsement terminology on republication [VERIFY].)
  • Caregiver grow (§342.09, subd. 2(b), incorporating §342.52, subd. 9(d)): a registered designated caregiver may cultivate up to eight plants for not more than one patient household, plus up to eight plants for the caregiver’s own personal adult use; of the 16 or fewer total plants at the caregiver’s residence, no more than eight may be mature/flowering.
  • Commercial cultivation rules (9810.2000) expressly do not apply to personal-use cultivation under §342.09 or caregiver cultivation on behalf of a patient under §342.52 (9810.2000, subp. 1).

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/2025-10-19%2013:12:15+00:00/cite/342.09/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.4 Security requirements

All citations in this section are to Minn. R. pt. 9810.1500 (49 SR 1143, published 25 Apr 2025) unless a statute is named. Source for the part: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.4.1 Required measures, testing, and response

  • Responsibility (subp. 1). A cannabis business must provide security at its premises. A cannabis event organiser must provide security while clones, seedlings, plants, adult-use flower/products, LPHE, and hemp-derived consumer products are on site at a temporary cannabis event.
  • Five required measures (subp. 2(A)). Security measures must include: (1) an alarm system; (2) video surveillance; (3) lighting; (4) locks; and (5) an immediate response protocol initiated within 30 minutes after a security event occurs. Additional features not violating local/state/federal law are permitted (subp. 2(B)). Cannabis delivery and transport licensees are exempt from item (A)(2) (video surveillance as a premises measure) — their vehicle security is governed by subp. 17 and 9810.2300/2600 instead.
  • Testing and maintenance (subp. 3). A protocol for testing/maintaining security measures, including periodic testing/inspection at least once every 90 days (which may be contracted to an outside security business) and prompt repairs. Alarm repairs must be completed within 72 hours of failure; if repair within 72 hours is impossible and the alarm cannot operate as required, the business must cease all operations until repairs are completed, unless it contacts OCM to request an extension. Compliance records must be kept and made available to OCM on request.
  • Protection scope (subps. 4–5). Documented, implemented, maintained measures to protect business assets, facilities, regulated products, workers, visitors, and the community; and to guard against theft and diversion of clones, plants, seedlings, flower, products, artificially derived cannabinoids, hemp plant parts/concentrate, LPHE, hemp-derived consumer products, and currency.

11.4.2 Alarms

Subp. 8: install, operate, and maintain in good working order a security alarm system, active 24 hours/day, 7 days/week, monitored by a contracted security company or a cannabis worker employed by the business. It must provide: (1) immediate alerts to authorised personnel and local law enforcement of unauthorised breach or alarm-system failure; (2) immediate alerts to authorised personnel and local emergency services of hazardous conditions detected; (3) a back-up alarm activating immediately/automatically on loss of electricity and alerting authorised personnel of the loss; (4) an audible alarm hearable within a 100-foot radius from entrances/exits; and (5) remote disable capability by authorised personnel. If an alarm failure is expected to last longer than eight hours, the business must promptly notify local law enforcement and OCM and implement alternative security measures under the security plan required by §342.14, subd. 1(a), cl. (6). If no alternative measure is in place or it fails, the business must not continue operations until the primary or alternative system is operational.

11.4.3 Video surveillance (cameras)

Subp. 9:

  • Surveillance of all premises associated with the licence, active 24/7, and active for the entirety of any temporary cannabis event.
  • Cameras must be placed to clearly record activity within at least a 20-foot radius from all points of entry/exit; affixed exterior and interior to identify individuals entering/exiting the premises, limited-access areas, and restricted-access areas; and at temporary events mounted to record the public-accessible area including designated retail areas and entry/exit points.
  • Cameras must monitor each entry/exit point of the perimeter, limited-access areas, and restricted-access areas, and be permanently placed to allow viewing in its entirety of any areas where cannabis is: (1) cultivated; (2) manufactured; (3) stored; (4) packaged and labelled; (5) prepared for transfer; (6) displayed or sold at a point-of-sale area; (7) collected as samples for mandatory testing and prepared/sealed for transport to a testing facility; and (8) destroyed or made unusable as waste.
  • Technical specs (subp. 9(E)): video files stored in a secure place for a minimum of 90 days; 24-hour recording at minimum 15 frames per second; minimum 720p resolution; date-and-time stamps on all recordings; capability to continue recording for an additional eight hours during a power outage.
  • Handling (subp. 9(F)): recordings must be available to OCM on request; saved in an industry-standard format playable by OCM staff without purchase of particular software/equipment; retained at least 90 calendar days; maintained free of alteration/corruption; and erased/destroyed before disposal.

Sample collection visibility is a linked requirement: mandatory-testing sample collection must be performed in a manner visible to mandatory recording devices (9810.3100, subp. 7(B)(3)).

11.4.4 Lighting, locks, access control, fencing

  • Lighting (subp. 10). Maintain all lighting in good working order inside/outside premises and any temporary event. Lighting must deter nuisance/criminal activity by allowing observers to see and cameras to record activity within at least a 20-foot radius around all entrances/exits. Exterior lighting must not disturb surrounding businesses/neighbours (adjust lumens/radius to only the required areas). Deficient/inoperable lighting must be repaired within 48 hours of detection.
  • Motion sensors (subp. 11, permissive). May be installed to provide lighting in low-light required areas or to protect cultivation light-dark cycles.
  • Locks (subp. 12). All external entrances to indoor facilities and perimeter windows must be in good condition and lockable. All doors, windows, gates, and fences must have commercial-grade locks. All perimeter entry doors must have electronic locks and keypads.
  • Worker badges and signage (subp. 6). All cannabis workers must have an employment identification badge issued by the business, displaying a visual coding system indicating activities the worker may perform and areas they may access; badges must always be visibly displayed when conducting business activities. Signage not less than 12 × 12 inches at all points of access to areas containing cannabis stating “Do Not Enter - Access Limited to Authorized Employees Only” in lettering no smaller than one inch.
  • Restricted areas (subp. 13; §342.24, subd. 3). Entry to a restricted area requires meeting §342.24, subd. 3 (in summary: cannabis worker employed/contracted with the business; OCM or other enforcement-agency employee; contractor whose scope does not involve handling cannabis/hemp products, supervised at all times if in an area with immediate access to products; or a person with explicit OCM authorisation, likewise supervised if in immediate-access areas). The business must record names of individuals entering restricted areas and keep those records at least three years, available to OCM on request. §342.24, subd. 3 also requires recording name, time of entry, time of exit, and authorisation via an electronic or manual entry log.
  • Storage-area access (9810.1104, subp. 3). Storage areas must be kept locked with access restricted to authorised personnel only, with signage “Restricted Access. Authorized Personnel Only” at the entrance. Products must be stored at least six inches above the ground in a clean, well-ventilated area free from condensation, sewage, dust, dirt, pests, chemicals, and other contaminants (subp. 2); storage areas used only for regulated products, with no mixing between batch numbers or product types (subp. 1(A)); and access records (date/time, individual name, products added/removed) maintained for inspection (subp. 1(B)).
  • Fencing generally (subp. 14). Unless required by Chapter 9810 or ch. 342, a business may erect a commercial-grade fence around its premises perimeter; fencing must meet local law. (Outdoor cultivation fencing is mandatory, not permissive — see below.)
  • Outdoor cultivation (subp. 15). The area must be enclosed by fencing and locked gates to prevent unauthorised access; fencing/gates must be secure, at least six feet high, and obscure or covered to obscure the fenced area from ready view outside; fencing must be commercial or security grade, not agricultural or residential grade, and designed to prevent unauthorised access.
  • Security personnel (subp. 16). Except when required under §342.40, a business may employ/contract security guards as defined in §326.32, subd. 13. A security guard for a cannabis business must be at least 21 and meet training requirements in §326.3361.

11.4.5 Transport and delivery security (Rule 9810 specifics)

Vehicle equipment (9810.1500, subp. 17(B)). Each transport and delivery vehicle must: (1) have a storage compartment complying with §342.36, subd. 3 (transporter) or §342.42, subd. 5 (delivery), as applicable; (2) have a GPS device identifying geographic location at all times when in operation (whether or not the engine is running), permanently or temporarily affixed while in operation, with GPS data saved/maintained at least 30 days and available to OCM on request; (3) have functioning heating/air conditioning maintaining appropriate storage temperatures; (4) carry the DOT/Commerce/federal-required insurance amount; and (5) have a secure form of communication (e.g. mobile phone) at all times during transport/delivery.

Worker conduct in vehicles (subp. 17(C)). A cannabis worker must: (1) possess a cannabis business identification card and their own valid nonprobationary driver’s licence appropriate for the vehicle type at all times while transporting/delivering, presenting both to OCM or law enforcement on request; (2) not leave clones, plants, seedlings, flower, products, artificially derived cannabinoids, hemp plant parts/concentrate, LPHE, or hemp-derived consumer products in an unattended vehicle; and (3) not leave cannabis in a vehicle overnight or outside the operating hours of the transporting/delivering business.

Statutory compartment and visibility rules (confirmed, Run 1 baseline). §342.36, subd. 3 (transporter) and §342.42, subd. 5 (delivery) both require a locked, safe, secure storage compartment that is part of the vehicle or a locked storage container with a separate key/combination pad, and that products may not be visible from outside the vehicle. §342.42, subd. 6 (delivery): no delivery vehicle or trailer may contain an image depicting the items transported (including a cannabis/hemp leaf) or a name suggesting the vehicle transports cannabis/hemp products. §342.42, subd. 7: only a cannabis worker employed/contracted with the delivery service and at least 21 may transport; all passengers must be such workers. §342.42, subd. 8: any delivery vehicle is subject to inspection at any time.

Rule transport details (9810.2300, as checked). Before transporting, a transporter must obtain a shipping manifest on an OCM-established form, keep it with the products at all times, and maintain a copy in records; transportation records (manifests, chain-of-custody log including every employee/vehicle, financial records for transport services) must be kept at least three years at the place of business, subject to OCM/law-enforcement inspection (§342.36, subds. 1–2). A non-integral container may be used only if locked, secured against removal, and products not visible from outside. The entire cargo bay/trunk may be used only if protected by a lock/keypad separate from vehicle door locks, inaccessible from driver/passenger areas, and products not visible from outside. Vehicles must not contain images prohibited by §342.36 and must comply with §221.031, subd. 6 and 49 CFR §390.21. Routes/delivery times must be reasonably randomised: at a minimum the same individual must not, on a recurring scheduled basis, deliver to the same business, on the same weekday, and at the same time of day; the transporter must not deviate unnecessarily from a planned route/schedule and must record necessary stops, route changes, and departure/delivery-time changes in the manifest and the statewide monitoring system. Delivery-vehicle staffing (9810.2300, subp. 9, as checked): a delivery vehicle transporting regulated products must be staffed by at least two individuals, at least one remaining with the vehicle at all times; all occupants must be cannabis workers employed/contracted with the transporter, at least 21, carrying a valid driver’s licence with proper endorsements while operating. [VERIFY — subp. 9’s “transporter” wording in the excerpt vs. delivery-vehicle application; the two-person rule is stated for delivery vehicles in the excerpt, but the coordinator should confirm it was not amended for single-driver retail delivery in later OCM guidance.]

Delivery-service rule (9810.2600). A delivery licensee must have an SOP ensuring compliance with 9810.1100 and chs. 221 and 342, and comply with DPS/Commerce/Revenue commercial-vehicle requirements. Delivery limit (subp. 2): a delivery driver may not transport more than $5,000 worth of regulated products on a single delivery route. This resolves the Run 1 [VERIFY] on the Rule 9810 delivery amount (for delivery services; it is a dollar-value route limit, not a weight/possession limit, and it is distinct from any transporter manifest limit). Drivers must hold a valid Minnesota driver’s licence; vehicles must be in working condition with no defects preventing lawful operation, have an anti-theft security system, and carry DOT/Commerce/federal-required insurance. Drivers may deliver only on behalf of a retail-licensed/endorsed business to a customer who has paid before delivery. Each delivery requires a shipping manifest (remainder of subp. 3 not fully reproduced in sources checked [VERIFY]).

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 (9810.1500, 9810.2300 excerpts); https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/9810.2600/; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810.2300/2025-04-25%2010:19:24+00:00 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.5 Waste disposal rules

11.5.1 What counts as cannabis waste

9810.0200, subp. 15: “‘Cannabis waste’ means discarded cannabis materials created from the cultivation, harvesting, processing, manufacturing, packaging, storage, transport, delivery, or sale of products of the cannabis industry or the hemp consumer industry.” Subp. 26/41 split waste into hazardous cannabis waste (meets the hazardous-waste definition in §116.06, subd. 11) and nonhazardous cannabis waste (does not meet that definition). Failed-test product is expressly included in waste storage: 9810.1104, subp. 5 requires cannabis waste, including products that failed testing, to be stored in a secure, separate location from saleable products until disposed of or remediated; a “secure and separate location” includes a container, closet, or room able to be locked or secured.

11.5.2 Classification, rendering unusable/unrecognisable (or nonretrievable), and disposal methods

9810.1200, subps. 2–5:

  • Subp. 2 — classify everything. “A cannabis business must determine the classification of all waste, including cannabis waste, of the business. A cannabis business must ensure that all waste is stored, secured, maintained, and disposed of in accordance with this chapter and all other applicable local, state, and federal laws and regulations.”
  • Subp. 3 — nonhazardous. “A cannabis business must render nonhazardous cannabis waste for disposal unusable and unrecognizable before allowing the nonhazardous cannabis waste to leave the premises of the business. A cannabis business must follow the requirements of part 7035.2836 when composting unusable and unrecognizable nonhazardous cannabis waste.”
  • Subp. 4 — hazardous. “A cannabis business must render hazardous cannabis waste nonretrievable before allowing the hazardous cannabis waste to leave the premises of the business. A cannabis business must follow the requirements of chapter 7045 when handling hazardous cannabis waste.”
  • Subp. 5 — exceptions (materials that are NOT cannabis waste and need no unusable/unrecognisable or nonretrievable treatment), provided the cannabis does not contain any flower or leaves with visible trichomes: (A) root balls, soil, or growing media; (B) stalks of cannabis plants; and (C) leaves and branches removed from immature cannabis plants.

Note the two different verbs: nonhazardous waste is rendered unusable and unrecognizable; hazardous waste is rendered nonretrievable. The rule text checked does not prescribe a specific rendering method (e.g. grinding with a named inert material at a named ratio) — no ratio, mixture, or method list is stated in 9810.1200, subps. 3–4. Any such method detail, if it exists, is in MPCA guidance or OCM guidance, not in the rule text checked [VERIFY before publishing a method]. Do not import another state’s 50%-inert-material rule.

Disposal-adjacent rules: recalled product must be destroyed under Chapter 9810 and the destruction recorded in the seed-to-sale system (9810.1101, subp. 2(B)(3)); failed-test batches must be disposed of under 9810.1200 or remediated under an approved plan (9810.3100, subp. 9(A)(1)); testing facilities must dispose of unanalysed sample portions under 9810.1200 unless held at OCM’s request or for stability testing (9810.3000, subp. 11); volunteer plants must be destroyed/disposed of under 9810.1200 (9810.2000, subp. 9(B)); unused medical cannabis must be rendered nonrecoverable under 9810.1200 in the caregiver-disposal context (9810.4001, subp. 9, as referenced in the rule text).

Packaging waste (distinct from cannabis waste). 9810.1200, subp. 6: a business may reuse a container designed/constructed for reuse only if all previous labels/marketing are removed and the container is cleaned/sanitised to remove all traces of cannabinoid products and harmful substances previously held; it must develop cleaning/sanitising procedures and maintain compliance records available to OCM on request. This is a reuse permission with conditions, not a cannabis-waste disposal method.

11.5.3 Waste record-keeping

9810.1200, subp. 7: “A cannabis business must enter and maintain accurate and comprehensive waste-tracking records in the statewide monitoring system. A cannabis business must ensure that waste-tracking records describe all the operator’s activity related to the disposal of cannabis waste and cannabis plant material.” 9810.1302, subp. 3 repeats: a business must report production and disposal of all cannabis waste as described in 9810.1200 in the statewide monitoring system. Destruction removals from inventory also require a written description with justification for intentional destruction (9810.1302, subp. 5(C)).

11.5.4 Hemp-waste differences

No separate hemp-waste rendering rule was located in 9810.1200 text checked. The 9810.0200 definition of cannabis waste expressly includes materials from “the hemp consumer industry,” and 9810.1200 applies to “a cannabis business.” Whether an MDA-licensed industrial hemp grower/processor under Chapter 18K (which is outside OCM’s Chapter 9810 scope — 9810.0100 applies to businesses subject to ch. 342) is subject to a different MDA waste rule, or to no cannabis-specific waste rule at all, was not located in this run [UNAVAILABLE — do not state that hemp waste follows, or is exempt from, the 9810.1200 unusable/unrecognisable rule]. The safe statement is: for OCM-licensed businesses, hemp-consumer-industry waste falls inside the 9810.0200 definition; for MDA-only hemp licensees, no waste rule was located in this part.

Source for this section: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 (9810.0200, 9810.1104, 9810.1200, 9810.1302) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.6 Environmental rules

11.6.1 The operative rule: incorporation of existing regimes, not a cannabis-specific code

9810.1200, subp. 1(A): “A cannabis business must not cultivate, process, manufacture, sell, handle, or store cannabis unless the business complies with the following business operation requirements”:

  1. Water-standard requirements for disposal systems under chapter 7049, as administered by the Pollution Control Agency (MPCA);
  2. Solid-waste requirements under chapter 7035, as administered by MPCA;
  3. Hazardous-waste requirements under chapter 7045, as administered by MPCA;
  4. Energy-standard requirements established in statute or under applicable rules of the Department of Commerce;
  5. Odor-standard requirements as established in ordinance by a local unit of government or by §116.064 or rules thereunder; and
  6. Pesticide controls and requirements under chapter 18B and rules thereunder.

Subp. 1(B): if the agency authorised to enforce a requirement in item A finds non-compliance, OCM may deny the application, revoke the licence, deny renewal, or take any other enforcement action under ch. 342.

Energy — the Run 1 question answered explicitly. Run 1 flagged whether any energy standards exist in Chapter 342. On the text checked, there is no cannabis-specific energy standard in Chapter 342 or in Rule 9810 — no lighting power density, no PPE (photosynthetic photon efficacy) minimum, no kWh-per-gram cap, no renewable-energy percentage, no energy audit/reporting duty stated in either source. 9810.1200, subp. 1(A)(4) incorporates only “energy standard requirements established in statute or under applicable rules of the Department of Commerce” — i.e. whatever generally applicable Commerce energy standards apply to the premises — and no cannabis-specific Commerce rule was located in this run. Do not import another state’s energy standards (e.g. another state’s lighting or HVAC efficiency rules) into Minnesota. If the coordinator needs a Commerce-rule citation, it must be pulled from Commerce rules directly [VERIFY — general Commerce applicability, not a cannabis rule].

Water, solid/hazardous waste. Beyond the incorporation in 9810.1200, subp. 1(A)(1)–(3), the cultivation plan must address water usage, recycling, and solid-waste disposal (§342.25, subd. 4, as summarised in LawServer restatement; 9810.2000, subp. 3(A)(3)–(5) requires utility/water plans, wastewater and solid-waste disposal plans, and recycling plans for supplies/environmental inputs including water and packaging). No cannabis-specific water-use volume limit, discharge limit, or water-recycling percentage was located in ch. 342/9810 text checked [UNAVAILABLE].

Odor. Odor control is local-ordinance and §116.064 based (9810.1200, subp. 1(A)(5)). Retail areas must have ventilation/filtration for odor control as required by state and local law (9810.2500, subp. 2(A)). Cultivation plans must diagram ventilation/air filtration (9810.2000, subp. 3(A)(2)). No statewide numeric odor threshold was located [UNAVAILABLE].

11.6.2 Pesticides — approved lists vs. prohibited pesticides

There is no Minnesota “approved pesticides for cannabis” list in the sources checked, and the Technical Authority pesticide table is NOT such a list. OCM guidance (GovDelivery compliance bulletin) states this expressly: because EPA has not approved any pesticide for cannabis (cannabis remains federally illegal to grow), “the table of pesticides listed on page 9 of OCM’s Cannabis Technical Authority: Standards for Sampling and Testing Cannabis Products does not constitute a list of compounds approved for application to cannabis or hemp plants. The table lists compounds for which cannabis will be tested. It includes both high risk compounds and compounds that might be suitable for use on cannabis and/or hemp.” Before applying any pesticide, the applicator must read the product label’s Directions for Use, including prohibitions (weather, growth stage, non-target organisms); violating a label statement violates FIFRA, and MDA regulates pesticide use in Minnesota.

What the law does require:

  • §342.25, subd. 5 (cultivation): (a) a cultivator must comply with chapters 18B, 18C, 18D, and any other pesticide/fertiliser/soil-amendment/plant-amendment laws/rules enforced by the commissioner of agriculture; (b) a cultivator must not apply pesticides when pollinators are present or allow pesticides to drift to flowering plants that are attractive to pollinators.
  • 9810.2000, subp. 11 (crop inputs): inputs must be handled/applied to prevent contamination with filth/residues/substances likely to render products injurious to health; must comply with chs. 18B/18C/18D and other applicable laws; must be stored in original containers with original labels intact (or in working containers of diluted/prepared applications labelled as required by chs. 18B/18C/18D); must be documented in the statewide monitoring system (9810.1300–1302); and all crop inputs, rinsate, and containers must be diluted, applied, stored, and disposed of per label instructions and applicable law. Cultivation records must include, for crop inputs, weight/concentration applied, a copy of the input label, and vendor/origin (9810.2000, subp. 13(D)).
  • 9810.2000, subp. 3(A)(6)–(7): the cultivation plan must include an IPM protocol (per §17.114, subd. 2(b)) and vendor/invoice information for all chemical/biological pest-control products.
  • §342.61, subd. 4(b): all pesticides/fertilisers/solvents/foreign materials applied to a batch must be disclosed to the testing facility (see §11.1.3); pesticide residue is a mandatory contaminant test (9810.3100, subp. 5(B)(5)).
  • Medical-cannabis minimum-risk rule (narrow, historical). §18B.091: a person working on behalf of an approved medical cannabis manufacturer may apply minimum risk pesticide for growing medical cannabis (as defined in §152.22, subd. 6) unless the commissioner determines the label prohibits it, or the commissioner (in consultation with Health) determines continued use would cause unreasonable adverse effects on human health, or the commissioner determines it would cause unreasonable adverse effects on the environment. This is a medical-manufacturer provision; it is not a general approved list for adult-use cultivation, and its current applicability after the ch. 123 medical restructuring is [VERIFY].

Prohibited pesticides: No freestanding “prohibited pesticide” list for cannabis was located in ch. 342/9810 text checked. Prohibition operates through (i) label prohibitions (FIFRA), (ii) ch. 18B restrictions, (iii) the pollinator/drift rule above, and (iv) the testing consequence (a batch failing pesticide-residue acceptance criteria must be disposed of or remediated under an approved plan). Do not publish a prohibited-active-ingredient list for Minnesota on the basis of this part [UNAVAILABLE].

11.6.3 OCM environmental reporting

No standalone OCM environmental report (e.g. annual energy/water/pesticide-use report to OCM) was located in ch. 342/9810 text checked, apart from: (i) cultivation-plan contents (water, recycling, waste, IPM) submitted with the licence/renewal/endorsement application and updated on change (9810.2000, subps. 2–3); (ii) crop-input applications recorded in the statewide monitoring system (9810.1302, subp. 5(B)) — OCM guidance summarises this as recording each application by end of the same business day, with one total daily entry for repeated irrigation-system applications [secondary guidance, VERIFY against 9810.1302 text, which requires reporting but does not state the same-day rule in the excerpt checked]; and (iii) waste-tracking records in the system (9810.1200, subp. 7). If an OCM environmental-reporting form exists, it was not located [UNAVAILABLE].

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 (9810.1200, 9810.2000); https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MNOCM/bulletins/3ef697d (pesticide-table disclaimer, OCM guidance); https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/cite/18B/full (§18B.091); https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/minnesota/mn-statutes/minnesota_statutes_342-25 (§342.25 summary) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts, and promotions

This section covers operational sampling/giveaway/discount rules. Advertising content limits in §342.64 are cross-referenced at §11.7.5; Part 1’s advertising treatment is not redone except where a promotion rule depends on it.

11.7.1 The general giveaway prohibition — and its two express carve-outs

§342.24 (general operational requirements and prohibitions) contains, in the Chapter 342 text checked, a prohibition whose carve-outs are the operative giveaway law:

  • Sample jars / free samples to retailers/wholesalers (subd. 5, as excerpted). A sample jar may not contain more than eight grams of usable cannabis flower, more than eight grams of cannabis concentrate, an edible infused with more than 100 mg THC, an LPHE infused with more than 50 mg THC, or a hemp-derived consumer product over eight grams total weight. “This prohibition does not apply to free samples … provided to a retailer or cannabis wholesaler for the purposes of quality control and to allow retailers to determine whether to offer a product for sale,” subject to the same caps (8 g flower, 8 g concentrate, 100 mg edible THC, 50 mg LPHE THC, 8 g hemp product).
  • Event-organiser fees are not giveaways. The prohibition does not apply to any fee charged by a licensed cannabis event organiser to a cannabis/hemp business for participation in an event (§342.24, subd. 5(e), as excerpted).

No general “free product to consumers” permission was located. Secondary summaries state “businesses cannot give away cannabis as promotional samples or freebies” to consumers. That summary is consistent with the structure (free samples are authorised only to retailers/wholesalers for QC/sale-determination, and to workers for QC/education under §11.7.2), but the precise consumer-giveaway prohibition sentence in §342.24 was not opened as a standalone subdivision in this run. State it carefully: the only free-sample permissions located are B2B (retailer/wholesaler) and employee-QC samples below; a consumer promotional giveaway is not among them, and any consumer “free gift with purchase” should be treated as [VERIFY — confirm the §342.24, subd. 5(a)–(c) prohibition text before advising on it].

11.7.2 Business-to-business and employee samples — Rule 9810.1103 (the complete sample rule)

  • Recording and age gate (subp. 1). A cannabis business must record in the statewide monitoring system any sample or regulated product, except LPHE, that it provides to an individual. It must not provide a sample or regulated product to a person under 21.
  • Samples to retailers/wholesalers (subp. 2). When providing a sample to a retailer or wholesaler, the business must: (1) hold a valid OCM licence; (2) provide it solely for business-to-business marketing; (3) ensure it was tested under 9810.3100; and (4) ensure it is in packaging compliant with 9810.1400–1403 and §342.63. (B) A business must not sell a sample to another cannabis business, a customer, a patient, or a designated caregiver. (C) A sample must not be a cannabis seed or cannabis plant.
  • Samples to cannabis workers (subp. 3). Only in accordance with this subpart and §342.24. The business must: (A) provide it solely for quality control and educational purposes; (B) ensure it was tested under 9810.3100; and (C) ensure compliant packaging under 9810.1400–1403 and §342.63.
  • Nonintoxicating showcase samples (subp. 4). If a business produces a sample designed to showcase flavour/texture of an ingestible product but containing no THC, it must indicate on the marketing layer that the product does not contain THC.
  • Employee consumption limits (§342.24, subd. 2). A business may not permit a non-employee to consume cannabis/hemp products on licensed premises unless licensed for on-site consumption. It may not permit an employee to consume on premises or while engaged in course/scope employment, except (c) a patient-employee may use medical products, and (d) “For quality control, employees of a licensed cannabis business may sample cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products. Employees may not interact directly with customers for at least three hours after sampling a product. Employees may not consume more than three samples in a single 24-hour period. All samples must be recorded in the statewide monitoring system.”
  • System recording of demonstration samples. 9810.1302, subp. 5(H) requires reporting of products removed for an approved demonstration purpose, including (1) an employee sample, (2) a retailer display sample, and (3) a promotional sample provided to a licensed cannabis business. “Promotional sample” in that tracking paragraph means a B2B promotional sample to a licensee, not a consumer promotion.

11.7.3 Discounts and loyalty — what was and was not located

  • No loyalty-program rule was located in 9810.2500/2501 text checked or in §342.24 excerpts checked. No rule in the sources checked authorises, prohibits, or conditions a loyalty programme, points programme, or “buy-one-get-one” promotion as such. Do not state that loyalty programmes are banned or permitted in Minnesota on the basis of this part [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Discounts are contemplated and must be recorded. 9810.1302, subp. 5(A): when reporting a sale in the statewide monitoring system, a business must include “the actual price of the product and any discount amount.” A discount is therefore a reportable sale term, not an off-system adjustment.
  • Payment methods at retail (9810.2501, subp. 5(C), as checked). “A retailer may accept payment from a customer using any legal method of payment, gift card prepayments, or prepayment accounts established with the retailer, except that a customer must not make a payment for a regulated product with an electronic benefits transfer services card.” Gift-card prepayments and retailer prepayment accounts are thus expressly contemplated; EBT payment is prohibited.
  • Transaction limits (9810.2501, subp. 6). “In a single transaction, a cannabis retailer must not sell more regulated products to a customer than the customer is able to legally transport.” A discount or promotion cannot lawfully push a single transaction over the customer’s legal transport/possession limit (Run 1 baseline: 2 oz public / 2 lb home flower, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg edibles — possession limits are Part 1 law, cross-referenced here only as the transaction-limit yardstick).
  • Online/telephone sales (9810.2501, subp. 5, as checked). Orders must include customer name, address, phone, email, and date of birth; before in-store handover the retailer must verify the name on the §342.27, subd. 4(b) identification and that the customer is 21+. Retailers must collect only information necessary to complete a transaction, use it only for that purpose, and maintain a data-security/privacy SOP covering any online-sales contractor.

11.7.4 On-site consumption and display samples

On-site consumption by non-employees is permitted only where the business is licensed to permit on-site consumption (§342.24, subd. 2(a); microbusiness on-site consumption endorsement in §342.28, subd. 1(12)). Display samples to retailers are a tracked demonstration removal (9810.1302, subp. 5(H)(2)), distinct from a consumable sample. No rule in the sources checked authorises a retailer to let a customer consume a display sample on premises without an on-site-consumption licence [VERIFY if an on-site-consumption endorsement rule in 9810.2501 states more].

11.7.5 Advertising limits that touch promotions — §342.64 (cross-reference only)

§342.64, subd. 1 (limitations applicable to all advertisements): a cannabis business, hemp business, or other person shall not publish or cause to be published an advertisement for a cannabis/hemp business or product in a manner that: (1) contains false or misleading statements; (2) contains unverified claims about health/therapeutic benefits or effects; (3) promotes overconsumption; (4) depicts a person under 21 consuming the product; (5) includes an image designed or likely to appeal to individuals under 21, including cartoons, toys, animals, or children, or any other likeness/character/phrase designed to appeal to under-21s or encourage consumption by them; and (6) does not contain a warning as specified by OCM regarding impairment and health risks.

Subd. 2 (outdoor advertisements/signs): except as provided, an outdoor advertisement is prohibited; businesses may erect up to two fixed outdoor signs on the exterior of the building/property; the prohibition does not apply to a hemp-business outdoor advertisement unrelated to LPHE manufacture/sale that includes no image/description/reference to LPHE manufacture/sale.

Bill, not law — do not cite as current. A 2025–2026 bill (SF 2326) would replace subd. 2 and impose a 30%-under-21-audience test for print/radio/television/other media (based on reliable, current audience-composition data). That audience test is proposed legislation in the bill text checked, not §342.64 as enacted, and must not be presented as the current advertising rule.

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.24/pdf; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/pdf/9810/2025-04-25%2010%3A19%3A49%2B00%3A00 (9810.1103, 9810.1302); https://www.revisor.mn.gov/rules/9810.2501/; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/342/pdf (§342.64); https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/94/2025/0/SF/2326/versions/latest/?list=open&body=Senate (bill only) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.8 Drug testing and background checks for licence holders and staff

Keep three regimes separate. Do not collapse them:

Regime Who it governs Operative rule
A. General employment (DATWA / lawful consumable products) All Minnesota employers/employees, including cannabis licensees as employers §§181.950–181.957 (DATWA), §181.938 (lawful consumable products), §342.57, subd. 5 (medical-patient employment protection) — §11.8.4
B. Licence-holder / applicant criminal history Applicants, holders, and persons responsible for the entity’s affairs §342.15 + 9810.1001 — §11.8.2
C. Cannabis-worker criminal history Individuals employed/contracted as cannabis workers by a licensee §342.151 + OCM/BCA process — §11.8.3

Regime C is licence-holder-specific; Regime A is general employment law that applies to a licensee as an employer. A licensee must satisfy both: a worker can pass the §342.151 check and still be subject to DATWA limits on workplace testing, and vice versa.

11.8.1 No state-issued worker badge/licence system was located

Unlike some states, Minnesota’s model as checked places the duty on the license holder: §342.151, subd. 2 states a license holder “may employ or contract with as many unlicensed individuals as may be necessary, provided that the license holder is at all times accountable for the good conduct of every individual employed by or contracted with the license holder.” Workers carry a business-issued employment identification badge (9810.1500, subp. 6) and, for transport/delivery, a cannabis business identification card plus driver’s licence (9810.1500, subp. 17(C)(1)) — those are business-issued cards, not OCM worker licences. No OCM worker-licence application, fee, or badge-renewal rule was located [UNAVAILABLE — do not describe a Minnesota “budtender licence”].

11.8.2 Licence holders and applicants — §342.15 and Rule 9810.1001

§342.15, subd. 1 (criminal history check). Upon OCM request, every licence applicant, licence holder, or, for a business entity, every individual responsible for conducting the entity’s affairs — including but not limited to every owner and every cooperative member or director, manager, and general partner — must submit a completed criminal-history records-check consent form, a full set of classifiable fingerprints, and required fees to OCM. OCM submits them to the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA); BCA conducts a Minnesota check and may exchange fingerprints with the FBI for a national check; BCA returns state and federal results to OCM to determine disqualification under rules adopted under §342.15. OCM may by rule except cooperative members holding less than five percent ownership. Fees go to a dedicated cannabis business background-check account in the special revenue fund, appropriated to pay BCA/FBI check costs (subd. 1a).

§342.15, subd. 2 (criminal offences; disqualifications) — this resolves the Run 1 [VERIFY] that §342.15 text had not been opened. (a) OCM may by rule determine whether any felony convictions — including but not limited to noncannabis controlled-substance crimes in the first or second degree, human trafficking, labor trafficking, fraud, or financial crimes — disqualify an individual from holding/receiving a licence or working for a cannabis business, and the length of disqualification. In adopting such rules, OCM shall not disqualify an individual for a violation of §152.025 (controlled-substance crime in the fifth degree — i.e. low-level possession). (b) OCM must not issue a licence to any person/business convicted of illegally selling cannabis after 1 Aug 2023 unless five years have passed since conviction. (c) OCM must not issue a licence to any person/business who violated Chapter 342 after 1 Aug 2023 unless five years have passed since violation; OCM may set aside the violation if it finds it resulted from a good-faith mistake without gross negligence, illegal sale, or public harm. OCM must not issue a licence to any person/business OCM has assessed a fine against under §342.09, subd. 6. (The balance of §342.15 — subds. 3–5, including civil/regulatory-offence disqualification by OCM determination under subd. 5 as described in rulemaking materials — was not fully reproduced in the sources checked [VERIFY the full subd. 3–5 text].)

Rule disqualifications (9810.1001, subp. 1). A license holder, applicant, or, for an entity, every individual responsible for conducting its affairs (including every owner and every cooperative member/director/manager/general partner) convicted of a listed crime is disqualified from holding a licence. Listed Minnesota offences confirmed in the text checked include:

  • Noncannabis controlled-substance crimes: §152.021 (1st degree), §152.022 (2nd degree), §152.0262 (possession with intent to manufacture methamphetamine), §152.0264, subd. 1, cl. (1) (sale of cannabis to a minor), §152.097 (counterfeit drugs), §609.228 (great bodily harm caused by distribution of drugs), §609.235 (use of drugs to injure/facilitate crime);
  • Human/labor trafficking: §609.282 (labor trafficking), §609.322 (solicitation/inducement/promotion of prostitution; sex trafficking), §609.283 (unlawful conduct with documents in furtherance of labor/sex trafficking);
  • Fraud/financial crimes: beginning with §609.41 (false tax statement), §609.42 (bribery), §609.425 (corruptly influencing legislator), §609.445 (failure to pay over state funds), §609.48 (perjury) — the full fraud/financial list continues beyond the excerpt checked and is not fully reproduced here [VERIFY the complete subp. 1(A)(3) list and any subp. 1(B) out-of-state-equivalent provision before publishing a complete disqualification list].

Length and variance (9810.1001, subps. 2–4, as checked). Disqualification for the §342.15-type administrative-order category expires five years from the OCM administrative order; for the conviction category in subp. 1(A)(4) (as numbered in the State Register excerpt), disqualification expires five years from conviction; for disqualifying felony convictions, disqualification is permanent. A permanently disqualified holder/applicant may seek a nonpermanent disqualification by evidencing that permanent disqualification does not serve the public interest, on criteria including: nature/responsibility of the position; nature/seriousness of the crime; age at commission; specific circumstances; at least five years since release from incarceration or conviction (whichever more recent); isolated-incident status; rehabilitation evidence (good conduct, counselling/psychiatric treatment, academic/vocational education, work-release, supervisor/mentor recommendations); and community benefit of granting/renewing the licence. Subp. 2 (other-state bars / civil-regulatory disqualification, referenced in rulemaking materials as §342.15, subd. 5 authority) was not fully reproduced in the sources checked [VERIFY].

Appeal of disqualification-related contested cases. 9810.1002: OCM contested hearings are conducted by the Office of Administrative Hearings under §§14.48–14.62 and Minn. R. pts. 1400.5010–1400.8401.

11.8.3 Cannabis workers — §342.151

Definitions (subd. 1). “License holder” for §342.151 includes a microbusiness, mezzobusiness, cultivator, manufacturer, retailer, wholesaler, transporter, testing facility, event organiser, delivery service, LPHE manufacturer, LPHE retailer, or medical cannabis combination business. (Post-ch. 123 terminology — macrobusiness in place of combination business — should be conformed on republication [VERIFY].)

Check (subd. 2, verbatim in operative part). “Before hiring an individual as a cannabis worker, the license holder must submit to the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension the individual’s full set of fingerprints and written consent for the bureau to conduct a state and national criminal history check. The bureau may exchange an individual’s fingerprints with the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The Bureau of Criminal Apprehension must determine whether the individual is qualified to be employed as a cannabis worker and must notify the license holder of the bureau’s determination. The license holder must not employ an individual who is disqualified from being employed as a cannabis worker.”

Worker disqualification (subd. 3) — a narrower list than the licensee list, do not conflate them. A business must not employ an individual as a cannabis worker if the individual has been convicted of any of the following crimes that would constitute a felony, if committed in Minnesota or any other jurisdiction and a full pardon or similar relief has not been granted: (1) human trafficking; (2) noncannabis controlled-substance crimes in the first or second degree; (3) labor trafficking; (4) fraud; (5) embezzlement; (6) extortion; (7) money laundering; or (8) insider trading. A business must also not employ an individual as a cannabis worker if the individual made any false statement in an application for employment.

Note what is absent from the worker list: cannabis offences themselves are not worker-disqualifying under §342.151, subd. 3 (contrast the licensee rule, where sale of cannabis to a minor, §152.0264, is listed in 9810.1001). A cannabis conviction does not, on the §342.151 text checked, disqualify a worker. Do not state otherwise.

Process transition — BCA now, third-party interim ended 1 Mar 2026. OCM’s Background Checks page states: DPS/BCA awaited FBI approval for fingerprint checks; in the interim the Legislature authorised third-party consumer-reporting/background-screening companies (2024 ch. 121? — OCM cites “Minnesota Session Law chapter 121, article 2, section 149” [VERIFY chapter/year citation — OCM’s page says chapter 121; do not expand it to a year without checking]); with FBI approval secured, “Effective March 1, 2026, cannabis businesses and their prospective employees who have not yet completed a background check must do so through the BCA process. Background checks completed by a third-party before March 1 remain compliant.” License holders should maintain hiring/background documentation (including confirmation each employee passed before employment) for OCM request/inspection. DPS/BCA instructions require a consent form, BCA-payable fee, FBI applicant fingerprint card (ORI MNBCA0000, “Reason Fingerprinted” citing §342.151), and a stamped self-addressed envelope to BCA CHA Unit, 1430 Maryland Avenue East, St. Paul, MN 55106 — the street address is reproduced here because it is a government submission address for the process, not an individual’s personal contact [if the coordinator’s policy is to omit even agency mailing addresses, delete it; no individual phone/email is included].

Worker training and safety (9810.1102). Licensees must comply with worker safety/health provisions under ch. 5205, ch. 182, and DLI standards under ch. 182 (subp. 1). Annual training, tailored to role/authority/responsibilities, must include: (1) SOPs under 9810.1100, subp. 2(A); (2) state and applicable federal cannabis laws; (3) state/federal data-privacy/confidentiality laws; (4) proper use of the business’s security measures/controls under 9810.1500 and ch. 342; (5) emergency response (fire, power loss, robbery, natural disaster, workplace violence); and (6) product recall procedures (subp. 2(B)). An edible cannabinoid product handler’s endorsement must be obtained by any person to whom §342.07, subd. 3 applies (subp. 2(C)). Training records (including who completed required training) must be kept and made available to OCM on request; the training/education programme description must be in the licence/renewal application (subp. 2(D)–(E)). Worker safety duties include a functioning carbon-monoxide detection system, prominently displayed emergency/evacuation/shelter-in-place procedures, Right-to-Know hazardous-material information, and safe equipment/tool handling information (subp. 3). This subpart applies to cannabis workers and volunteers, not to hemp workers who do not meet the §342.01, subd. 23 cannabis-worker definition (subp. 2(A)).

Age note. No general “all cannabis workers must be 21” sentence was located in §342.151 or 9810.1102 text checked. Age-21 rules located are activity-specific: retail sales to under-21s prohibited (§342.24, subd. 1(c) framework; §342.27, subd. 4 ID verification); limited-access areas accessible only to over-21s (9810.0200, subd. 34); delivery/transport workers at least 21 (§342.42, subd. 7; 9810.2300, subp. 9); security guards at least 21 (9810.1500, subp. 16). Do not generalise to “all workers must be 21” without a source [VERIFY if OCM guidance imposes a broader 21+ worker rule].

11.8.4 General employment drug testing — DATWA and lawful consumable products (distinct from §11.8.2–11.8.3)

Lawful consumable products (§181.938, as amended 2023). Cannabis is a “lawful consumable product” for off-duty, off-premises use purposes. An employer generally may not refuse to hire, discipline, or discharge an employee for off-duty cannabis use, and is not required to permit use, possession, impairment, transfer, or sale during work or on premises. Employers may still act on impairment/performance and on use during work. This is general employment law, not a cannabis-licence rule.

DATWA — §181.951, subds. 8–9 (resolving the Run 1 [VERIFY] on exempt positions). The exempt positions are in the statute, in subd. 9, not subd. 8 — Run 1’s note that they were “NOT in that subdivision as extracted” is explained: they are in the next subdivision:

  • Subd. 8 (limitations on cannabis testing). (a) An employer must not request/require a job applicant to undergo cannabis testing solely to determine presence/absence of cannabis as a condition of employment unless otherwise required by state or federal law. (b) Unless otherwise required by state/federal law, an employer must not refuse to hire an applicant solely because the applicant submitted to an authorised cannabis or drug/alcohol test and the result indicates cannabis presence. (c) An employer must not request/require cannabis testing of an employee/applicant on an arbitrary or capricious basis. (d) Cannabis testing authorised under the following paragraph must comply with §§181.953–181.954 safeguards.
  • Subd. 9 (cannabis testing exceptions). For the following positions, cannabis and its metabolites are considered a drug subject to §§181.950–181.957: (1) a safety-sensitive position as defined in §181.950, subd. 13; (2) a peace officer position (§626.84, subd. 1); (3) a firefighter position (§299N.01, subd. 3); (4) a position requiring face-to-face care, training, education, supervision, counselling, consultation, or medical assistance to children, vulnerable adults, or patients receiving health-care services for treatment/examination/emergency care of a medical, psychiatric, or mental condition; (5) a position requiring a commercial driver’s licence or operating a motor vehicle for which state/federal law requires drug/alcohol testing; (6) a position funded by a federal grant; and (7) a position for which federal law requires pre-employment cannabis testing. Secondary summaries add childcare workers as a category; the §181.951, subd. 9 text excerpt checked lists the seven categories above, with category (4) covering face-to-face care of children — the “childcare” shorthand should be read as category (4), not as a separate eighth category [VERIFY the full subd. 9 text if a standalone childcare clause exists in a later amendment].

Other DATWA rules that still apply to cannabis testing where authorised: written policy requirements, confidentiality, prompt notice of results, explanation of rights, confirmatory-test and retest rights (employee notice within three working days, retest request within five working days at employee expense in secondary summaries — [VERIFY against §§181.953–181.954 text before publishing day-counts]); no legal duty to test (§181.951, subd. 7); and the general DATWA bar on discharging for a first confirmed positive without first offering counselling/rehabilitation participation (secondary summary — [VERIFY against §181.951/§181.953 text]). Random, reasonable-suspicion, post-accident, and treatment-programme testing for cannabis remain available in the circumstances DATWA allows, principally for safety-sensitive positions. Nothing in DATWA requires a cannabis licensee to drug-test its workers for cannabis, and nothing in §342.151 requires a licensee to conduct DATWA testing — §342.151 requires a criminal-history check, not a drug test. Conflating the two is the error this section exists to prevent.

Medical-registry-patient employment protection (§342.57, subd. 5). Run 1 baseline: medical-registry-patient protections in §342.57, subd. 5. Secondary summaries state it is unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a registry enrollee unless the employer would lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law/regulations, and that a patient may present registry verification if testing positive. The full subd. 5 text (including any notice period — one secondary summary claims 14 days’ written notice citing the specific regulation necessitating action) was not opened in this run [VERIFY the full §342.57, subd. 5 text, including any 14-day notice sentence, before publishing it].
