11.9 Research and university cannabis and hemp licences

Headline finding: there is no standalone OCM “research licence” type. Research is authorised through (a) a research microbusiness licence, (b) OCM applied-research grants, (c) an R&D testing exemption, and (d) MDA industrial-hemp research licensing — four different instruments, none of which is a generic OCM research licence. Do not list “OCM research licence” as a licence type.

11.9.1 Cannabis crop research — §342.28, subdivision 1a (the research microbusiness)

Verbatim in operative part:

“An institution of higher education, any department or program of an institution of higher education that is regionally or nationally accredited, and any entity working in partnership with an institution of higher education may apply for a cannabis microbusiness license to conduct cannabis crop research. A cannabis researcher with a cannabis microbusiness license may perform activities identified in subdivision 1, clauses (1) to (9) and (13). Cannabis plants and cannabis flower grown for research purposes must not be offered for sale or otherwise enter the stream of commerce. As used in this subdivision, ‘institution of higher education’ has the meaning given in sections 135A.51, subdivision 5, and 136A.28, subdivision 6.”

Clauses (1)–(9) cover growing from seed/immature plant to mature plant and harvesting flower; making cannabis concentrate; making hemp concentrate (including >0.3% delta-9 by weight); manufacturing artificially derived cannabinoids; manufacturing adult-use products, LPHE, and hemp-derived consumer products for public consumption; purchasing immature plants/seedlings and flower from other licensees; purchasing hemp plant parts/propagules from an 18K grower; purchasing hemp concentrate from an 18K processor; and purchasing concentrates/artificially derived cannabinoids from other licensees for manufacturing. Clause (13) is “other actions approved by the office.” Notably, the research researcher may not perform clause (10) (packaging/labelling for sale to customers), (11) (sale to businesses/customers), or (12) (on-site consumption establishment) — the exclusion is structural: research product must not enter commerce.

Testing companion: 9810.3100, subp. 11 exempts §342.28, subd. 1a microbusiness R&D batches from Part 9810.3100 only if produced solely for R&D and not consumed by humans (§11.1.6).

University of Minnesota — what was and was not located. No University of Minnesota-specific cannabis research programme, licence, or registration was located in this run, and no UMN cannabis research licence is claimed here. What can be stated is structural: the University of Minnesota is an institution of higher education within §342.28, subd. 1a’s definition route (via §§135A.51/136A.28), so UMN, a UMN department/programme, or an entity partnering with UMN may apply for a research microbusiness licence on the same terms as any other qualifying institution. Whether UMN holds such a licence, or operates a named cannabis research programme, is [UNAVAILABLE — check the OCM licence list / UMN programme pages directly; do not infer a UMN programme from eligibility]. UMN Extension appears in Chapter 18B school-pest-management consultation lists, which is not a cannabis research programme and is not cited as one.

11.9.2 Medical applied research — §342.60 (grants, not a licence)

“The office may conduct, or award grants to health care providers or research organizations to conduct, applied research on the safety and efficacy of using medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products to treat a specific health condition. A health care provider or research organization receiving a grant under this section must provide the office with access to all data collected in applied research funded under this section. The office may use data from applied research conducted or funded under this section as evidence to approve additional qualifying medical conditions or additional allowable forms of medical cannabis.”

§342.60 creates a grant/research authority, not a licence to cultivate, manufacture, or sell. A grantee that needs to handle cannabis must still hold the applicable licence/endorsement (e.g. a §342.28, subd. 1a research microbusiness licence for crop work) unless its work uses only lawfully obtained product within its existing authority — that linkage is not stated in §342.60 text and is [VERIFY if a grant programme’s terms impose a licence condition].

Source: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.60 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

11.9.3 Industrial hemp research — MDA, Chapter 18K (distinct from OCM)

  • Licence requirement (§18K.04, subd. 1). “A person must obtain a license from the commissioner [of agriculture] before (1) growing industrial hemp, (2) processing industrial hemp, or (3) researching industrial hemp.” Application is on the commissioner’s prescribed form with the annual registration/inspection fee set under §16A.1285, subd. 2. A grow/process licence application must include applicant name/address and legal description of the land/processing location plus any 7 CFR Part 990 information; a research licence’s application contents beyond name/address/fee are as prescribed by the commissioner [VERIFY the current MDA research-licence form — the 2026 bill excerpt checked restates the grow/process contents and strikes/reletters paragraphs, but does not reproduce a research-specific contents list]. A licence is valid until 31 December of the year of application. A person licensed to grow industrial hemp is presumed to be growing for commercial or research purposes.
  • Pilot/other research (§18K.09). Chapter 18K, §18K.09 is headed “Pilot program; other research authorized.” Its current text was not opened in this run [VERIFY — do not summarise its scope beyond its headnote].
  • Definition note for the federal transition. Chapter 18K defines industrial hemp by delta-9 THC ≤0.3% on a dry-weight basis (§18K.02, subd. 3, as published in the 2017 text checked; current text should be re-pulled given the federal total-THC redefinition effective 11 Dec 2026 under PL 119-103 §2019 — Minnesota’s conformity, if any, is a Part 1/Part 12 question, not resolved here [VERIFY]).
  • Hemp vs. cannabis research boundary. MDA hemp research licensing covers industrial hemp (Chapter 18K). It does not authorise research on intoxicating cannabis; that requires the §342.28, subd. 1a route (or a medical grant route with lawful product sourcing). A hemp researcher must not use an 18K research licence as authority to grow intoxicating cannabis.

11.9.4 Other university/college research — and the White Earth distinction

  • Other colleges/universities. Any regionally/nationally accredited institution of higher education, department/programme, or partnering entity may apply under §342.28, subd. 1a on the same terms as UMN (§11.9.1). No other named Minnesota college/university cannabis research licence or programme was located in this run [UNAVAILABLE — do not list a college as a research licensee without an OCM licence-list check].
  • White Earth Tribal and Community College — training, NOT research. White Earth Tribal and Community College received a $500,000 DEED CanTrain grant to “provide professional development opportunities in the cannabis sector in the areas of horticulture, extraction, manufacturing, budtending, retail, and the business of cannabis,” with objectives to prepare training/resources for entry-level cannabis jobs (legislative report: 75 enrol, 45 complete with certificate/credential, 37 placed in unsubsidised jobs). CanTrain “provides grants to eligible organizations to create and implement workforce development programs to provide support, navigation services and training to individuals leading to a relevant career in the legal cannabis industry.” That is a workforce-training grant, not a research licence, not a §342.28, subd. 1a research microbusiness licence, and not evidence of a White Earth cannabis research programme. The same DEED announcement lists CanTrain grantees Minneapolis Community & Technical College ($403,530), Minnesota Training Partnership ($126,116), Minnesota Cannabis College ($250,000), Urban League Twin Cities ($320,000), and White Earth ($500,000). OCM’s complementary programmes are CanRenew (community-needs projects) and CanGrow (farmer navigation/loans) — also not research licences.
  • No OCM research licence type — restated for the coordinator. If a future OCM rule creates a standalone research licence, it is not in Chapter 342 or Rule 9810 text checked for this part. The only OCM research-adjacent provisions located are §342.28, subd. 1a, §342.60, and 9810.3100, subp. 11.

Sources: https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.28; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.60; https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2017/cite/18K/full (Chapter 18K table/definitions); https://mn.gov/deed/newscenter/press-releases/?id=1045-702706; https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2026/mandated/260253.pdf (CanTrain work plans, White Earth) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

The 2026 cannabis omnibus created § 342.245 as a general endorsements framework (endorsement application forms; no fee for an endorsement application; denial grounds including a cancelled endorsement in the last 5 years, outstanding fines, or failure to meet location requirements — Senate committee summary of SF 4401, § 5, and secondary summary of the same bill). The on-site-consumption endorsements themselves live elsewhere: § 342.28, subd. 10 (cannabis microbusiness), § 342.46, subd. 8 (lower-potency hemp edible retailer), and § 342.40, subd. 8 (cannabis events). Headline answers.

  • No per se THC driving limit in Minnesota. This Part resolves the Run 1 [UNAVAILABLE]/[VERIFY] on this point: § 169A.20, subd. 1 has an alcohol per se clause (0.08; 0.04 for commercial vehicles) and an “any amount” clause for Schedule I/II controlled substances, but the “any amount” clause expressly excludes cannabis flower, cannabis products, LPHEs, hemp-derived consumer products, artificially derived cannabinoids and tetrahydrocannabinols, and cannabis impairment is instead charged under a separate “under the influence” clause, § 169A.20, subd. 1(8). See § 12.2.
  • No standalone adult-use “social consumption lounge” licence. On-site consumption exists only through (i) a microbusiness on-site-consumption endorsement (edibles/LPHEs only, no smoking or vaping anywhere on the premises), (ii) an LPHE-retailer on-site-consumption endorsement (LPHEs only), and (iii) a licensed cannabis event’s locally approved consumption area (which may include flower, subject to the Clean Indoor Air Act). See § 12.4.
  • Minnesota law shields lawful cannabis users from a state firearms denial, but it does not override federal law. § 624.7152 and § 624.714, subd. 6(f) bar a state denial solely on the basis of registry enrolment or lawful adult-use use; 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) and ATF Form 4473 remain the operative federal conflict, narrowed but not eliminated by Hemani and the 2026 ATF rule. See § 12.7.
  • Expungement is two different tracks, not one. Nonfelony cannabis records in § 609A.055 are automatic through the BCA; felony cannabis records in § 609A.06 are not automatic and go to the Cannabis Expungement Board for case-by-case review, then to the courts for an order. The published counts for the two tracks must not be added together. See § 12.3.

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke shop rules

12.1.1 What “cannabis paraphernalia” means, and what a 21+ adult may do with it

Minn. Stat. § 342.01, subd. 18 defines “cannabis paraphernalia” as:

“all equipment, products, and materials of any kind that are knowingly or intentionally used primarily in: (1) manufacturing cannabis products; (2) ingesting, inhaling, or otherwise introducing cannabis flower or cannabis products into the human body; and (3) testing the strength, effectiveness, or purity of cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products.”

Source: Minnesota Statutes 2025, § 342.01 (Revisor PDF, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/2025-10-19%2013:12:06+00:00/cite/342.01/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(a)(1) then provides that an individual 21 years of age or older may “use, possess, or transport cannabis paraphernalia.” Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.09 (Revisor, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/342.09/subd/342.09.3 — Accessed 2026-10-28. A separate definition, § 342.01, subd. 54a, defines “medical cannabis paraphernalia” as “a delivery device, related supply, or educational material used by a patient enrolled in the registry program to administer medical cannabis and medical cannabinoid products.” Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.01, subd. 54a. https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/cite/342.01/subd/342.01.54a — Accessed 2026-10-28.

The adult-use permission is age-gated and place-gated, not unlimited: § 342.09, subd. 1(b) prohibits, except as provided in paragraph (c), (1) use, possession or transport by a person under 21; (2) use in a motor vehicle as defined in § 169A.03, subd. 15; (3) inhaled use at any location where smoking is prohibited under § 144.414; (4) use or possession in a public school or charter school (including all facilities and school-controlled vehicles); (5) use or possession in a state correctional facility; (6) operating a motor vehicle while under the influence; (7) giving for no remuneration to a person under 21; (8) giving flower or products as a sample or promotional gift by a person in the business of selling goods or services; and (9) vaporizing or smoking where the smoke, aerosol or vapor would be inhaled by a minor. Paragraph (c) then carves medical use back out of clauses (1)–(4) only, and only for use “other than by smoking or by a vaporized delivery method,” possession, or transportation of medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products by a patient, a registered designated caregiver, or a parent, legal guardian or spouse of a patient. Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.09 (Revisor, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/342/full — Accessed 2026-10-28.

12.1.2 The old “drug paraphernalia” crime — what remains and what does not

This is the point on which a reader relying on pre-2023 compilations will be misled, and it is stated here in full because the old text still circulates in historical Revisor versions.

  • Possession/use of drug paraphernalia is no longer a state crime. Former Minn. Stat. § 152.092 (“It is unlawful for any person knowingly or intentionally to use or to possess drug paraphernalia. Any violation of this section is a petty misdemeanor,” with a 90-day / $1,000 crime on a third or subsequent violation) was repealed, 2023 c. 52, art. 15, § 17, effective 1 Aug 2023. Source: Revisor historical version page for § 152.092 (“Recent History: 2023 152.092 Repealed 2023 c 52 art 15 s 17”). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2000/cite/152.092 — Accessed 2026-10-28; and House Research summary of HF 2041 (2023), “Repealer. Repeals § 152.092 (possession of drug paraphernalia crime).” https://www.house.mn.gov/hrd/bs/93/hf2041i.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. A City of Burnsville council work-session report (14 May 2024) states the practical consequence: “possession of all drug paraphernalia, not just cannabis paraphernalia, is no longer a crime in Minnesota, even if that paraphernalia contains residual amounts of controlled substances.” Source (secondary, municipal): https://burnsville.civicweb.net/document/222851/Drug Use Law Changes.pdf?handle=91F61281E6824CA69B00E8DD451AAAA7 — Accessed 2026-10-28. That Burnsville report cites § 152.025, subd. 2 for this proposition, which appears to be a citation slip for the § 152.092 repeal; the repeal itself is confirmed by the Revisor history above, so the conclusion is retained and the Burnsville citation is not relied on.
  • Definition narrowed. The same 2023 act amended § 152.01, subd. 18 to remove testing equipment from the definition of “drug paraphernalia” and to exclude hypodermic syringes/needles in accordance with § 151.40, subd. 2 and products that detect fentanyl or a fentanyl analog. Source: HF 2041 first engrossment, §§ 5–6. https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/93/2023/0/HF/2041/versions/1/pdf/ — Accessed 2026-10-28; Network for Public Health Law, 50-State Drug Checking Equipment Fact Sheet (2024), Minnesota note 108. https://www.networkforphl.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/2024-50-State-DCE-Fact-Sheet.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • What remains on the books [VERIFY current wording]. The secondary Network summary states that the 2023 act removed the freestanding delivery prohibition from § 152.093, while “intentional manufacture of drug paraphernalia for delivery and delivery of drug paraphernalia to a minor that was intentionally manufactured for delivery remain illegal” under §§ 152.093 and 152.094, and that § 152.095 (advertisement, misdemeanor) remains. Historical Revisor text (pre-2023) reads: § 152.093, delivery or possession/manufacture for delivery, misdemeanor; § 152.094, delivery by a person 18+ to a person under 18 at least three years younger, gross misdemeanor; § 152.095, advertisement in a newspaper, magazine, handbill or other publication, misdemeanor. Because historical and current versions are both circulating in search results, the coordinator should confirm the current § 152.093 text from the live Revisor before publishing any sentence that says “delivery of paraphernalia is / is not a crime” in the present tense. What can be stated without that confirmation: (i) simple possession/use is repealed; (ii) manufacture for delivery and delivery to a minor are described in current secondary summaries as still unlawful; (iii) no paraphernalia-sale licence is created by Chapter 342.
  • Local ordinances are expressly not preempted. Minn. Stat. § 152.205 provides that § 152.01, subd. 18 and §§ 152.093 to 152.095 “do not preempt enforcement or preclude adoption of municipal or county ordinances prohibiting or otherwise regulating the manufacture, delivery, possession, or advertisement of drug paraphernalia.” (The pre-2023 version of the same section also listed § 152.092; that reference was struck when § 152.092 was repealed.) Source: Minn. Stat. § 152.205 (Revisor, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/152/full — Accessed 2026-10-28. Practical consequence: a city or county may still regulate paraphernalia locally even though the state possession crime is gone. Any local rule must be checked jurisdiction by jurisdiction; none is generalised here.

12.1.3 Smoke shops, tobacco shops, general retail, and what licence a shop needs

There is no single “smoke shop licence” in Chapter 342. What a shop needs depends on what it sells, not on what it calls itself:

  • Selling cannabis flower or cannabis products requires a cannabis business licence (retailer, microbusiness with retail endorsement, mezzobusiness, or medical combination business, as applicable) plus local retail registration under § 342.22. Selling LPHEs requires an LPHE retailer licence (or a cannabis business licence that covers LPHEs). Selling hemp-derived consumer products (as distinct from LPHEs) is, under the OCM Hemp Registrant to License Holder Conversion Guide, limited to cannabis business licence holders, not LPHE licence holders; hemp-derived topical products with 0% THC are stated in the same guide to need no licence or endorsement. Source: OCM Conversion Guide v1.3, pp. 9–10. https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/2410008_OCM_Hemp_Registrant_to_Licensee_Conversion_Guide_v1.3_tcm1202-683554.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. A county example of the same rule in practice: Washington County, Minnesota, states that registration is required for any business selling cannabis retail products, LPHEs, THC beverages, or “any consumable product containing THC or CBD,” and that “[t]his includes smoke shops, convenience stores, specialty retailers, and any business adding cannabis/hemp products to existing inventory,” per location, in addition to the state licence. Source (county, secondary for state law but primary for the county’s own process): https://www.washingtoncountymn.gov/3754/Cannabis-and-Hemp-Retail-Sales — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Selling only empty hardware (pipes, vaporizers, rolling papers, with no cannabis, LPHE or hemp-derived consumable in or with them) is not, on any source located in this run, a Chapter 342 licensed activity in itself. No statute or OCM guidance located in this run creates a paraphernalia-retail licence, and no source located states that a tobacco licence is required for empty cannabis hardware. [VERIFY: confirm with OCM that a general retailer selling only non-cannabis hardware needs no Chapter 342 licence; the converse — that adding any consumable triggers licensing — is confirmed by the sources above.] A tobacco licence remains a separate licence for tobacco products; holding one does not authorise cannabis or LPHE sales, and holding a cannabis/LPHE licence does not authorise tobacco sales (see the on-site-consumption bans on tobacco sale/consumption in § 12.4).
  • Shared-entrance / shared-premises rules — St. Paul note NOT verified; do not generalise. The Run 1 note about a St. Paul zoning shared-entrance rule could not be verified in Run 2 searches: no City of Saint Paul ordinance text stating a cannabis/tobacco shared-entrance rule was located. What was located is a different jurisdiction’s rule that illustrates the type of rule that exists locally, and it must not be attributed to St. Paul or to the state: Douglas County, Minnesota, draft/adopted cannabis ordinance, § B.3: “A cannabis retail business is prohibited from sharing a common entrance or a premises with a business licensed for retail tobacco sales. Lower-potency hemp edible sales are exempt from this provision.” Source: https://www.douglascountymn.gov/draft-douglas-county-cannabis-adult-public-use-ord — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY: the St. Paul rule, if any, and whether Douglas County’s provision was adopted as drafted; check the St. Paul Legislative Code and the relevant city zoning text directly before any St. Paul-specific statement is published.]
  • LPHE/hemp in general retail vs. smoke shops. The distinction is the licence, not the shopfront: a convenience store, grocery, liquor store or smoke shop may sell LPHEs if it holds an LPHE retailer licence (and local registration) and complies with § 342.46 (21+, display/storage behind the checkout counter or in a locked case, beverages excepted — Run 1 baseline, carried forward); a smoke shop has no special advantage or exemption. A shop that sells only hemp-derived topical products at 0% THC needs no licence for that product line under the OCM guide above, but the moment it adds an ingestible LPHE or a cannabis product, the corresponding licence is required. Infused hemp flower is stated in the OCM guide to be “Not allowed — None” (no licence authorises retail sale of infused hemp flower). Source: OCM Conversion Guide, p. 9, as above — Accessed 2026-10-28.

12.2 THC driving limits and impairment testing

12.2.1 RESOLVED: there is no per se THC blood or urine limit in Minnesota

Minnesota has no per se (numeric) THC limit for driving — blood or urine. This resolves the Run 1 [UNAVAILABLE]/[VERIFY] item. The proof is in the structure of Minn. Stat. § 169A.20, subd. 1, quoted verbatim in the operative clauses:

“It is a crime for any person to drive, operate, or be in physical control of any motor vehicle, as defined in section 169A.03, subdivision 15, within this state or on any boundary water of this state when: … (5) the person’s alcohol concentration at the time, or as measured within two hours of the time, of driving, operating, or being in physical control of the motor vehicle is 0.08 or more; (6) the vehicle is a commercial motor vehicle and the person’s alcohol concentration … is 0.04 or more; (7) the person’s body contains any amount of a controlled substance listed in Schedule I or II, or its metabolite, other than cannabis flower, a cannabis product, a lower-potency hemp edible, a hemp-derived consumer product, an artificially derived cannabinoid, or tetrahydrocannabinols; or (8) the person is under the influence of cannabis flower, a cannabis product, a lower-potency hemp edible, a hemp-derived consumer product, an artificially derived cannabinoid, or tetrahydrocannabinols.”

Source: Minn. Stat. § 169A.20, subd. 1 (Revisor, search-indexed copy; the same text appears in the 2025 Justia compilation). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/169A/full and https://law.justia.com/codes/minnesota/chapters-160-174a/chapter-169a/section-169a-20/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Clauses (1)–(4) add the general impairment clauses (alcohol; controlled substance; intoxicating substance known to be capable of causing impairment; combinations of (1)–(3) or (8)).

Three consequences follow, and each is stated so the coordinator does not have to infer it:

  1. The only numeric per se thresholds in § 169A.20, subd. 1 are for alcohol (0.08 generally, 0.04 for a commercial motor vehicle). There is no “0.08 equivalent” for THC, no nanogram-per-millilitre blood threshold, and no urine threshold in the statute.
  2. The “any amount” clause does not apply to cannabis. Clause (7) is a presence offence for Schedule I/II substances, but cannabis flower, cannabis products, LPHEs, hemp-derived consumer products, artificially derived cannabinoids and THC themselves are carved out of it. A positive cannabis test, without more, therefore does not satisfy clause (7). It may be evidence toward clause (8), but the State must prove the driver was “under the influence” — i.e., impaired — at the time of driving. Secondary commentary agrees: “Unlike the 0.08% BAC standard for alcohol, Minnesota has no numeric THC threshold. Officers must prove you were actually impaired by cannabis, not just that you consumed it recently” (secondary, but consistent with the statute text above). The same point is made in the standard jury-instruction formulation quoted in secondary literature: “There is no set standard as to the quantity of a controlled substance a person must ingest before [they are] regarded as being ‘under the influence.’”
  3. § 169A.36 was checked and does not supply a THC limit. No THC numeric limit was located in § 169A.36 in this run, and the implied-consent machinery is in § 169A.51 (see § 12.2.3), not § 169A.36. [VERIFY: confirm § 169A.36’s current subject matter from the live Revisor chapter, since the task’s pointer to § 169A.36 did not resolve to a THC provision in search-indexed text; the “no per se limit” conclusion itself rests on the full § 169A.20, subd. 1 text above and does not depend on § 169A.36.]

Related prohibitions that are not driving offences but are often confused with them: § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(2) prohibits using cannabis in a motor vehicle, and § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(6) prohibits operating a motor vehicle while under the influence — both in addition to the § 169A.20 DWI crime. Source: § 342.09 as above — Accessed 2026-10-28.

12.2.2 Impairment-based DWI as it applies to cannabis

  • Standard. The State must prove, under clause (8) (and, where applicable, clauses (2)–(4)), that the driver was under the influence of cannabis/LPHE/hemp-derived product/artificially derived cannabinoid/THC at the time of driving, operating or being in physical control. Mere prior use, tolerance, or a metabolite result that cannot be tied to the driving window is not, without more, the offence. The case illustration in secondary literature makes the evidentiary gap concrete: in a Hennepin County jury trial reported by defence counsel, a urine screen positive for 11-nor-9-carboxy-delta-9-THC (carboxy-THC, described as a nonpsychoactive metabolite) and DRE testimony did not persuade the jury, because the BCA scientist could not say when the driver consumed cannabis, how much, or that he was impaired at the time of driving, and the jury acquitted on DWI and careless driving. Source (secondary, single-case illustration — not precedent, and not a statement of Minnesota law): https://ramsayresults.com/not-guilty-minnesota-jury-rejects-cannabis-dwi-and-careless-driving-charges/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. The lesson for the dossier is evidentiary, not doctrinal: a metabolite screen proves exposure, not impairment.
  • Medical use is no defence to impaired driving. § 342.56, subd. 1(a)(4) expressly preserves penalties for “operating, navigating, or being in actual physical control of a motor vehicle, aircraft, train, or motorboat or working on transportation property, equipment, or facilities while under the influence of medical cannabis flower or a medical cannabinoid product.” Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.56 (Justia 2025 compilation of the Revisor text). https://law.justia.com/codes/minnesota/chapters-324-342/chapter-342/section-342-56/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Registry enrolment therefore does not immunise impaired driving, and there is no prescription-drug affirmative defence in § 169A.20, subd. 1(8) comparable to the Schedule II prescription defence for clause (7) cases under § 169A.46, subd. 2 (secondary summary; [VERIFY § 169A.46 text]).
  • What changed after 2023. The cannabis-specific architecture — clause (7)’s carve-out and clause (8)’s impairment clause, with cannabis flower, cannabis products, LPHEs, hemp-derived consumer products, artificially derived cannabinoids and THC named in both — is the post-legalisation form of the statute. No post-2023 amendment adding a numeric THC threshold was located in this run. [VERIFY: session-law chapter for the clause (7)/(8) wording — the 2023 Adult-Use Cannabis Act (2023 c. 63) is the expected vehicle, but the amending section number was not confirmed in this run.]

12.2.3 Drug recognition experts, testing methods, and the oral-fluid pilot

  • DREs. A Drug Recognition Evaluator is an officer trained to determine whether a motorist is impaired by substances other than (or in addition to) alcohol, through a 30-to-45-minute evaluation, after which the DRE can determine the category of drug(s) impairing the driver. DPS describes the prosecution model as three-pronged: (1) the officer documents driving impairment; (2) the DRE further documents specific controlled-substance use and impairment; (3) the BCA laboratory verifies the presence of controlled substances. DPS states there are “over 125 DRE trained officers throughout Minnesota” and “over 30,000 DWI arrests in Minnesota each year,” a significant number drug- or drug-and-alcohol-related. Source: Minnesota Department of Public Safety, DRE job description page (undated; figures as stated on the page). https://dps.mn.gov/divisions/msp/jobs/state-patrol-training/law-enforcement-training/drugged-driving-and-impairment/drugged-driving-law-enforcement-support-and-training/dre-job-description — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Oral-fluid roadside screening — pilot only, and its limits matter. DPS Office of Traffic Safety and the State Patrol ran a pilot in which DREs were trained on two oral-fluid instruments, the Abbott SoToxa Oral Fluid Mobile Test System and the Dräger DrugTest 5000, which detect THC and five other drug classes (amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cocaine, methamphetamines, opiates). Fifty-seven DREs from 41 agencies across 36 counties participated. Critically, the pilot was voluntary for drivers, results were not admissible in DWI court proceedings, could not be used to establish probable cause for a DWI arrest, and officers could not see the results during the pilot. Sources: DPS, “Roadside testing project will give traffic safety experts new data on drugged driving” and “Roadside screening tools could help law enforcement detect drug-impaired driving.” https://dps.mn.gov/news/ots/roadside-testing-project-will-give-traffic-safety-experts-new-data-drugged-driving and https://dps.mn.gov/news/ots/roadside-screening-tools-could-help-law-enforcement-detect-drug-impaired-driving — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY: whether any post-pilot statute or rule has since authorised oral-fluid screening as an implied-consent or probable-cause tool. 2026 bills introducing oral-fluid language into § 169A.41 / § 169A.51 (e.g., SF 4285, 94th Leg.) were located as introductions; no enacted oral-fluid implied-consent law was confirmed in this run. Do not present roadside oral-fluid testing as an ordinary, admissible DWI test in Minnesota on the current record.]
  • Blood, breath and urine under implied consent. Under § 169A.51, subd. 1(a), a person who drives, operates or is in physical control of a motor vehicle consents to a chemical test of blood, breath or urine to determine the presence of alcohol, a controlled substance or its metabolite, cannabis flower, a cannabis product, an LPHE, a hemp-derived consumer product, artificially derived cannabinoids, or THC, or an intoxicating substance, administered at the direction of a peace officer, when the officer has probable cause and one of the stated conditions exists (lawful arrest for § 169A.20; accident with property damage, personal injury or death; refusal of a preliminary screening test; or a screening test indicating 0.08+ or the presence of a controlled/intoxicating substance). Under § 169A.51, subd. 3, an officer must obtain a search warrant to require a blood or urine sample, executed as provided in § 171.177; refusal to comply with execution of such a warrant triggers licence revocation by the Commissioner of Public Safety under § 171.177, subd. 4. Refusal to submit to a chemical test is itself a crime under § 169A.20, subd. 2. Sources: § 169A.51 as summarised in SF 4285 (2026 introduction, quoting current § 169A.51, subd. 1) and Court of Appeals discussion in Wolters v. Commissioner of Public Safety, A25-2036 (10 Aug 2026, nonprecedential), summarising §§ 169A.51, subd. 1(b)(1), subd. 3, and 171.177. https://www.revisor.mn.gov/bills/94/2026/0/SF/4285/versions/0/ and https://cases.justia.com/minnesota/court-of-appeals/2026-a25-2036.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note the advisory wrinkle: the § 169A.51, subd. 2 implied-consent advisory as indexed in older compilations still speaks in terms of Schedule I/II presence “other than marijuana or tetrahydrocannabinols” — a formulation that predates the current clause (7)/(8) structure. [VERIFY: current advisory wording; do not quote the advisory from an older compilation as current.]

12.2.4 Penalties

Cannabis DWI is sentenced under the same degree structure as alcohol DWI (§§ 169A.24–169A.27), not under a separate cannabis penalty ladder. The degree turns on aggravating factors (prior impaired-driving incidents, test refusal, child passenger, and alcohol concentration where alcohol is involved — the alcohol-concentration aggravator does not translate to a THC number, because there is no THC number). General maxima, from secondary compilations of §§ 169A.24–169A.27, are: fourth-degree (misdemeanour, no aggravating factors), up to 90 days’ jail and $1,000 fine; third- and second-degree (gross misdemeanours), up to one year and $3,000; first-degree (felony — fourth incident or a prior felony DWI / criminal vehicular operation conviction), up to 7 years’ imprisonment and $14,000 fine. Licence consequences are separate and administrative as well as conviction-based: a first fourth-degree conviction with no prior in the look-back period is described as at least 90 days’ suspension (one year at 0.16+ BAC — an alcohol figure, not applicable to a cannabis-only case); second conviction within the look-back, revocation with a multi-year ignition-interlock requirement; third, six-year cancellation; fourth or subsequent, ten-year cancellation, each with interlock before full restoration. Sources (secondary compilations; the degree maxima are consistent across them): https://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/minnesota-dui-dwi-33630.html and https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2018/other/180740.pdf (Legislative Reference Library overview, older look-back) — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY: the current look-back period — secondary sources in this run variously state 10 years and 20 years, and the Nolo summary (2026) uses 20 years for licence purposes; the criminal-degree look-back must be confirmed from current §§ 169A.24–169A.27 before any “within X years” sentence is published. Licence revocation on refusal applies even though there is no per se THC revocation trigger: a cannabis-only driver is not subject to an automatic pre-conviction revocation for a THC number, because there is no number, but refusal carries its own criminal and administrative consequences as above.]

12.3 Automatic expungement and the Cannabis Expungement Board

12.3.1 Automatic expungement: what, who, and how — § 609A.055

Minn. Stat. § 609A.055, “Automatic Expungement of Certain Cannabis Offenses,” covers nonfelony cannabis matters. Subd. 1(a) makes a person eligible for expungement:

  1. upon dismissal and discharge under § 152.18, subd. 1 for violation of § 152.024, § 152.025 or § 152.027;
  2. if convicted of or given a stayed sentence for violation of § 152.027, subd. 3 or 4;
  3. if arrested and all charges were dismissed prior to a determination of probable cause for charges under § 152.021, subd. 2(a), cl. (6); § 152.022, subd. 2(a), cl. (6); § 152.023, subd. 2(a), cl. (5); § 152.024, subd. 2, cl. (2); § 152.025, subd. 2, cl. (1); or § 152.027, subd. 3 or 4; or
  4. if all pending actions or proceedings were resolved in favour of the person for charges under those same provisions (a verdict of not guilty by reason of mental illness is not a resolution in favour of the person; an order under § 590.11 determining exoneration-compensation eligibility is).

Subd. 2 then requires the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension to identify bureau records qualifying under subd. 1 and to notify the Judicial Branch of the name and date of birth of each eligible person and the court file number of the eligible case. Subd. 3 (relief and notification) follows. Source: Minn. Stat. § 609A.055 (Revisor 2025 PDF, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/2025-10-19%2014:30:21+00:00/cite/609A.055/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. History: 2023 c. 52, art. 7 (Adult-Use Cannabis Act expungement article) — the section number and article are confirmed by the 2024 Chapter 609A compilation; the precise section number within the article is [VERIFY] if the coordinator needs it on the cover.

What “expungement” means here. It means sealing from public view, not deletion. DPS/BCA states: “The BCA does not delete expunged criminal history records — they are simply hidden from public view. They are always available to the subject of the data.” Source: DPS, Expungements page. https://dps.mn.gov/divisions/bca/bca-divisions/professional-services/expungements — Accessed 2026-10-28. Two further limits: (i) because Minnesota is part of the National Crime Prevention and Privacy Compact, records remain visible in other states unless a court orders the record sealed from view in other states on petition; (ii) a landlord or employer has no duty to discover or use a record expunged under Chapter 609A or other law for a housing or employment decision (§ 609A.05). Sources: same DPS page; Minn. Stat. § 609A.05 (2024 Chapter 609A compilation). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/609A/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

12.3.2 Numbers for the automatic track — with cut-off dates, not updated by inference

  • Initial eligibility estimate (pre-implementation, DPS). “Based on our initial analysis, more than 66,000 criminal history records are eligible for automatic expungement under the Adult-Use Cannabis Act. An additional 230,000 felony records are eligible for review by the Cannabis Expungement Board.” Source: DPS, “Work moving forward on expungements tied to cannabis and Clean Slate legislation” (2023–2024 implementation period). https://dps.mn.gov/news/bca/work-moving-forward-expungements-tied-cannabis-and-clean-slate-legislation — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note: the 230,000 figure is a felony-review pool, not an automatic-expungement count, and it predates the Board’s case-by-case screening (which eliminates non-cannabis offences — see § 12.3.4).
  • Completed automatic round (May 2024). “The Minnesota Department of Public Safety Bureau of Criminal Apprehension (BCA) has expunged (also referred to as sealing) 57,780 records in CHS almost three months ahead of schedule. The Minnesota Judicial Branch determined that 213 records should not be expunged.” The qualifying records “are no longer visible to the public in the Minnesota Criminal History System (CHS).” Source: DPS, “Adult-Use Cannabis Act: Automatic expungements of BCA records complete” (May 2024). https://dps.mn.gov/news/bca/adult-use-cannabis-act-automatic-expungements-bca-records-complete — Accessed 2026-10-28. 57,780 is records, not persons, and it is the May 2024 round only.
  • Second look. DPS states the BCA “will review records in the system again in 2026 to identify and expunge any additional records that were still in the court process when the 2024 expungements occurred” (same DPS Expungements page). No completed 2026 second-round count was located in this run; do not carry the 57,780 forward as a 2026 total. [VERIFY: 2026 second-round result, if published after the DPS page’s last crawl.]
  • Do not merge with Clean Slate. The Clean Slate Act (Minn. Stat. § 609A.015) is a separate automatic-expungement law, effective 1 Jan 2025, covering qualifying offences beyond cannabis. The BCA’s public CHS site states that work on Clean Slate records requiring individual review “is expected to be complete by the end of 2026” and that all CHS records carry a notice that they may contain information qualifying for automatic expungement. Source: https://chs.state.mn.us/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. A secondary compilation’s claim that BCA had expunged “roughly 1.57 million of about 2.03 million eligible records” by 14 Apr 2026 is not adopted here: it appears to describe the broader Clean Slate pool, it was not confirmed against a BCA/DPS release in this run, and adding it to the cannabis 57,780 would be a category error. [VERIFY before any Clean Slate number is published.]

12.3.3 Board review: what requires it, who is eligible, and how it works — § 609A.06

Felony cannabis convictions are not automatically expunged. They go to the Cannabis Expungement Board (CEB) under Minn. Stat. § 609A.06.

Eligibility (§ 609A.06, subd. 3(a), as summarised from the statute text). A person is eligible for expungement or resentencing to a lesser offense if: (1) convicted of, or adjudication stayed for, a first- through fifth-degree controlled-substance crime involving sale or possession of marijuana or THC under §§ 152.021–152.025 (or a previous version of those or any other statutes criminalising possession, sale, transportation or cultivation of marijuana/THC); (2) the offence did not involve a dangerous weapon, the intentional infliction of bodily harm on another, an attempt to inflict bodily harm, or an act committed with intent to cause fear in another of immediate bodily harm or death; (3) the act would either be a lesser offense or no longer be a crime after 1 Aug 2023; and (4) the person did not appeal, any appeal was denied, or the appeal deadline expired. A person eligible under (a) is also eligible for expungement of any other cannabis-related offence charged along with the underlying crime that was dismissed. “Lesser offense” means a nonfelony offense if the person was charged with a felony. Source: Minn. Stat. § 609A.06 (search-indexed statute text). https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/minnesota/mn-statutes/minnesota_statutes_609a-06 — Accessed 2026-10-28. The CEB’s own FAQ states the same exclusions in plain terms: “Cases involving dangerous weapons or violence, or that are a felony under current law, are not eligible for expungement.” Source: https://mn.gov/ceb/faqs-minnesota-cannabis-expungement-board/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Process. The BCA identifies convictions and stays of adjudication qualifying for review and notifies the Board (name, date of birth, and case information). Board staff complete conviction reviews from case documents, screening out weapon/violence/fear cases, but “[s]taff alone are not authorized to eliminate cases from consideration without Board review.” The Board reviews all available records; expungement is presumed to be in the public interest “unless there is clear and convincing evidence that an expungement or resentencing to a lesser offense would create a risk to public safety.” If expungement is in the public interest, the Board determines whether the conviction should be vacated and charges dismissed, and whether the limitations in § 609A.03, subd. 5a and subd. 7a(b), cl. (5) apply (these concern, respectively, firearm-rights restoration and professional-educator-licensing sealing questions — see the CEB budget presentation’s eight-factor slide). If expungement is not in the public interest, the Board determines resentencing to a lesser offense. The eight factors the Board must consider include: nature and severity (including amount possessed and weapon/violence/fear); risk to others or society; danger from release of sentence; aggravating or mitigating factors; victim or law-enforcement statements; good cause to restore firearm rights; educational background-check sealing; and any other relevant factor. Victims and law enforcement may provide oral or written statements at any meeting where the Board reviews their case. Only three Board members must vote in favour for an expungement or resentencing (unanimity is not required). The person’s identity is protected by an identifier in public meetings and public records. The Board then notifies the Minnesota Judicial Branch of the action to be taken; it is the courts that issue the expungement order or proceed with resentencing. Sources: § 609A.06, subd. 7 (search-indexed text, as above); CEB FAQ (as above); CEB FY 2026–27 Enacted Budget, pp. 1–2 (strategies and subd. 7 steps). https://mn.gov/mmb-stat/documents/budget/2026-27-biennial-budget-books/enacted-budget/cannabis-expungement-board.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. The Board meets monthly, on the second Wednesday, in public session for case consideration. Source: CEB 2025 Annual Report (see § 12.3.4). No individual application form is asserted here: the § 609A.06 track is agency-initiated (BCA identification → Board review → court order), distinct from a Chapter 609A petition a person files themselves. [VERIFY: whether the CEB operates a public intake/request process for a person who believes their felony case has been missed — the budget book mentions community engagement, expungement clinics and “an accessible intake process,” but no intake form or deadline was located in this run.]

Timelines. No statutory deadline for completing all Board reviews was located; the Board “will operate until all records have been reviewed and the Board has determined it has completed its work” (CEB budget book). The annual report to the Legislature is due 15 January each year under § 609A.06, subd. 9 (2023 c. 63, art. 5, § 3, subd. 9). Do not promise an individual a decision date.
