12.3.5 Court-ordered expungement distinguished, and how a person checks their record

  • Court-ordered (petition) expungement under §§ 609A.02–609A.03 is a third route: the person petitions the district court, serves the agencies holding records, and must meet the chapter’s grounds, waiting periods and “clear and convincing” considerations. It is not the § 609A.055 automatic route (no petition needed; BCA identifies, Judicial Branch orders) and not the § 609A.06 Board route (no petition described in the statute; BCA identifies, Board determines, Judicial Branch orders). A person whose record is in neither automatic nor Board track — e.g., an offence outside §§ 609A.055/609A.06 — may still have a petition route, subject to Chapter 609A eligibility. [VERIFY: current petition waiting periods and filing fee before publishing them; secondary sources in this run state 2 years (misdemeanour), 4 years (gross misdemeanour) and 5 years (certain felonies) and a $300-range fee, but those figures were not confirmed against current §§ 609A.02–609A.03 in this run and are therefore not stated as findings.]
  • How to check. (1) Search the public Minnesota Criminal History System (CHS) at https://chs.state.mn.us/ — public data covers convictions (15 years following completion of sentence) and excludes arrest data, juvenile data, other-state and federal data. (2) Request your own complete record from the BCA at any time, including after sealing: “People can request records held by the BCA about themselves at any time, including before or after the records are expunged” and “Copies of expunged criminal history records will be provided to the subject of the record upon request” (submit a data request; the DPS page does not state a fee in the excerpt located). (3) Check the court record in Minnesota Court Records Online (MCRO) for the court file, and the CEB website (https://mn.gov/ceb/) for Board information. (4) Do not expect a notification: “The BCA does not have contact information for people with records in the Criminal History System and as a result cannot notify individuals about changes to their criminal history records” — a notice is instead posted on all CHS records. Sources: DPS Expungements page and CHS site/FAQ, as above — Accessed 2026-10-28. For immigration purposes, DPS expressly warns that expunged records may still need to be reported to immigration agencies and advises consulting an immigration attorney and keeping a copy of the record.

12.4 On-site consumption and events

12.4.1 The general rule and the endorsement framework

Minn. Stat. § 342.24, subd. 2 (general operational requirements) provides, in the OCM guide’s paraphrase, that a licensed cannabis business may not let customers consume cannabis on its premises unless it is licensed/endorsed to permit on-site consumption. The OCM On-Site Consumption Guide (v1.1) then lists only three approved on-site-consumption settings. That list is the practical answer to “is there a lounge licence?”:

Setting (OCM guide) What may be consumed on site Endorsement / approval required
Cannabis event organiser (temporary licence) Adult-use cannabis flower, adult-use cannabis products, hemp-derived consumer products, LPHEs Event organiser licence + specific local approval of consumption areas (§ 342.40, subd. 8(a))
Cannabis microbusiness with retail + on-site-consumption endorsements Adult-use edible cannabis products and LPHEs only Retail endorsement + on-site-consumption endorsement (§ 342.28, subd. 10)
LPHE retailer with retail + on-site-consumption endorsements LPHEs only Retail endorsement + on-site-consumption endorsement (§ 342.46, subd. 8)

Source: OCM On-Site Consumption Guide v1.1, pp. 2–3. https://mn.gov/ocm/assets/OCM_On-site_Consumption_Guide_1.1_tcm1202-736547.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. Cannabis retailers and mezzobusinesses are not listed as on-site-consumption settings in the guide. [VERIFY against current §§ 342.27 and 342.29: the guide is OCM guidance, not the statute itself, and a future rule or endorsement could change this; on the guide as located, a straight retailer or mezzobusiness has no on-site-consumption authority.] Endorsements generally are now governed by new § 342.245 (see the correction at the head of this file): OCM must provide endorsement application forms, no fee may be charged for an endorsement application, endorsement terms/renewals align with the underlying licence, and OCM must deny if the holder had an endorsement cancelled in the last 5 years, owes outstanding fines, or does not meet location requirements. Source: Senate summary of SF 4401, § 5. https://www.senate.mn/committees/2025-2026/3118_Committee_on_Commerce_and_Consumer_Protection/SF-4401-Cannabis-Omnibus-Bill-Bill-Summary.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

12.4.2 Microbusiness on-site consumption — edibles only, in a distinct area (§ 342.28, subd. 10) — CONFIRMED

The Run 1 note is confirmed and is now stated with its statute text:

“(a) A cannabis microbusiness may permit on-site consumption of edible cannabis products and lower-potency hemp edibles on a portion of its premises. (b) The portion of the premises in which on-site consumption is permitted must be definite and distinct from all other areas of the microbusiness and must be accessed through a distinct entrance.”

“(f) A cannabis microbusiness shall ensure that the display and consumption of any edible cannabis product or lower-potency hemp edible is not visible from outside of the licensed premises of the business.”

“(h) A cannabis microbusiness may not: (1) sell an edible cannabis product or a lower-potency hemp edible to an individual who is under 21 years of age; (2) permit an individual who is under 21 years of age to enter the premises; (3) sell an edible cannabis product or a lower-potency hemp edible to a person who is visibly intoxicated; (4) sell or allow the sale or consumption of alcohol or tobacco on the premises; (5) sell products that are intended to be eaten or consumed as a drink, other than packaged and labeled edible cannabis products and lower-potency hemp edibles, that contain cannabis flower or hemp plant parts or are infused with cannabis concentrate, hemp concentrate, or artificially derived cannabinoids; (6) permit edible cannabis products or lower-potency hemp edibles sold in the portion of the area designated for on-site consumption to be removed from that area; (7) permit adult-use cannabis flower, adult-use cannabis products, hemp-derived consumer products, or tobacco to be consumed through smoking or a vaporized delivery method on the premises; or (8) distribute or allow free samples of cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products.”

Sources: Minn. Stat. § 342.28, subd. 10 (Revisor, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.28 — Accessed 2026-10-28; and 2023 c. 63, art. 1, § 28 (the same subd. 10(h) list, including (h)(7) smoking/vaping ban and (h)(8) free-sample ban). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/laws/2023/0/63/laws.6.34.0 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Subds. 10(c)–(e) and (g) add: on-site products must comply with testing, packaging and labelling rules; they must be served in the required packaging but customers may remove them from the packaging and consume on site; other food and beverages may be prepared and sold on site if all relevant state and local laws, ordinances, licensing and zoning requirements are met; and recorded or live entertainment may be offered on the same compliance condition. The smoking/vaping ban in (h)(7) applies to the whole microbusiness premises, not only to the consumption area — the OCM guide states it the same way: “Smoking or vaping … is strictly prohibited at microbusiness retail locations permitting on-site consumption or anywhere where the Minnesota Clean Indoor Air Act would be violated.” There is therefore no lawful “smoking room” inside a microbusiness, indoors or outdoors on the premises, on the current text.

12.4.3 LPHE-retailer on-site consumption (§ 342.46, subd. 8)

“(a) A lower-potency hemp edible retailer may permit on-site consumption of lower-potency hemp edibles on a portion of its premises if it has an on-site consumption endorsement. (b) The office shall issue an on-site consumption endorsement to any lower-potency hemp edible retailer that also holds an on-sale license issued under chapter 340A. The office may issue an on-site consumption endorsement to a lower-potency hemp edible retailer that does not also hold an on-sale license issued under chapter 340A if the lower-potency hemp edible retailer submits proof of liability insurance as required by section 340A.409, except that the proof must be submitted to the office.”

Subd. 8(d)–(e): non-beverage LPHEs sold for on-site consumption must be served in the required packaging but may be removed from the packaging by customers and consumed on site; beverage LPHEs may be served outside the packaging if the information required on the label is posted or otherwise displayed by the retailer (hemp workers serving beverages under this paragraph need not obtain an edible cannabinoid product handler endorsement under § 342.07, subd. 3). Subd. 8(f)–(g): other food and beverages may be prepared and sold on site, and recorded or live entertainment offered, if all relevant state and local laws, ordinances, licensing and zoning requirements are met. Subd. 8(h) (in addition to the subd. 7 prohibitions) prohibits an endorsed LPHE retailer from: (1) selling, giving, furnishing or procuring LPHEs for the use of an obviously intoxicated person; (2) selling LPHEs designed or reasonably expected to be mixed with an alcoholic beverage, including multi-serving beverage containers; (3) selling products from multi-serving beverage containers for on-site consumption; or (4) permitting LPHEs removed from their packaging to be removed from the premises. Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.46, subd. 8 (Revisor, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.46 — Accessed 2026-10-28. OCM guide v1.1 adds the § 340A.409 liability-insurance figures for a non-liquor-licensed retailer ($50,000 / $100,000 bodily injury; $10,000 property; $50,000 / $100,000 loss of means of support; $50,000 / $100,000 other pecuniary loss, per occurrence). Source: OCM guide v1.1, p. 7, as above — Accessed 2026-10-28.

12.4.4 Smoking vs. non-smoking consumption, and the Clean Indoor Air Act interaction

  • Indoors, in any public place, smoking and vaping are governed by the Minnesota Clean Indoor Air Act (MCIAA), §§ 144.413–144.417. “Smoking” under § 144.413 includes inhaling, exhaling, burning or carrying any lighted or heated product containing cannabis flower, cannabis products, artificially derived cannabinoids or hemp-derived consumer products, and includes carrying or using an activated electronic delivery device for inhalation of aerosol or vapor. Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(3) separately prohibits inhaled use at any location where smoking is prohibited under § 144.414. A proprietor that allows indoor smoking where banned under the MCIAA is guilty of a petty misdemeanour (§ 144.417, subd. 2(a)), and MDH may impose a fine of up to $10,000; local agencies may have additional tools. Source: MDH, MCIAA FAQ. https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/environment/air/mciaa/faq.html — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Secondhand smoke at events. § 342.40, subd. 8(e) (see § 12.4.5) is the event-specific version of the same rule: no smoking of adult-use flower or products where smoking is not permitted under §§ 144.413–144.417, and a statutory or home rule charter city or county may enact and enforce more stringent measures against secondhand smoke or involuntary aerosol/vapor exposure. The Run 1 note citing “§ 342.40 subd. 8(e) secondhand-smoke authority [VERIFY, secondary only]” is therefore confirmed as statute text, not secondary-only, on the Revisor excerpt located.
  • What this means in practice. Non-smoking consumption (edibles, beverages, tinctures, capsules, topicals) is the only consumption form authorised inside a microbusiness or LPHE retailer’s on-site area. Smoking/vaping consumption is lawful only where the MCIAA does not ban it — principally outdoors in a place that is not a public place and where no minor inhales the smoke/vapor (§ 342.09, subd. 1(b)(9)), or in a licensed event’s locally approved outdoor consumption area (see below). A city or county may be stricter than the state floor.

12.4.5 Cannabis events — organiser, temporary events, sales and consumption (§§ 342.39, 342.40)

Licence and duration. “A cannabis event organizer license entitles the license holder to organize a temporary cannabis event lasting no more than four days.” § 342.39, subd. 1. The application must include, in addition to § 342.14, subd. 1 information: (1) type and number of any other cannabis business licence held; (2) address/location; (3) event name; (4) a diagram showing grounds, entrances/exits, all cannabis consumption areas, all cannabis retail areas, waste storage, and product storage; (5) a list of the name, number and type of cannabis and hemp businesses that will sell plants, flower, products, LPHEs and hemp-derived consumer products at the event, “which may be supplemented or amended within 72 hours of the time at which the cannabis event begins”; (6) dates and hours; (7) proof of local approval; and (8) evidence of compliance with applicable operation requirements. Subd. 3 (pre-2027 text): an event organiser may not hold a cannabis testing facility licence, an LPHE manufacturer licence, or an LPHE retailer licence; OCM may by rule limit the number of event licences a person/business may hold. Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.39 (2025 Revisor PDF, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.39/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY: whether subd. 3’s LPHE-licence bar survives the 2027 annual-licence transition — a secondary guide notes OCM’s Licence Types page as saying hemp licence holders may apply, in tension with subd. 3; do not publish either version without checking the 2027 text.]

2026 → 2027 transition — Run 1 baseline confirmed with OCM dates. OCM, “Hosting Events”: “OCM is accepting cannabis event organizer license applications for 2026 events until Nov. 16 at 4 p.m. CT.” The 2026 Legislature “passed significant changes … including transitioning from a temporary license to a new annual cannabis event organizer license type that authorizes the business to register and host temporary cannabis events throughout the year. Those changes go into effect Jan. 1, 2027.” OCM “will close the current event organizer licensing application on Nov. 16 at 4 p.m. CT. The new event organizer license and event site registration applications will open in January 2027. Allowing for the 45 days we recommend for a successful submission, we anticipate event organizers could host events beginning in late February.” OCM recommends submitting at least 45 days before the planned event date. Source: https://mn.gov/ocm/businesses/resources/events/hosting-events/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. The Run 1 formulation (“max 4 consecutive days on 2026 form, application closes 16 Nov 2026, new applications open Jan 2027, events anticipated late Feb 2027”) is therefore confirmed; the 4-day cap itself is statutory (§ 342.39, subd. 1) and survives the transition as a per-event cap (2026 bill summaries describe the annual licence as authorising the holder to “register and host temporary cannabis events” through the year, each event still capped — [VERIFY per-event cap in the 2027 text]).

What sales and consumption are allowed at a licensed cannabis event (§ 342.40). Licensed businesses listed in the application sell plants, flower, products, LPHEs and hemp-derived consumer products at the event; all such items for sale must comply with testing, packaging and labelling rules, and all plants, flower and products sold, damaged or destroyed at the event must be recorded in the statewide monitoring system (§ 342.40, subd. 7(i)–(j) as indexed). On-site consumption (§ 342.40, subd. 8): “(a) If approved by the local unit of government, a cannabis event may designate an area for consumption of adult-use cannabis flower, adult-use cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, hemp-derived consumer products, or any combination of those items. (b) Access to areas where consumption … is allowed shall be restricted to individuals who are at least 21 years of age. (c) The cannabis event organizer shall ensure that consumption … within a designated consumption area is not visible from any public place. (d) The cannabis event organizer shall not permit consumption of alcohol or tobacco. (e) [MCIAA rule, quoted in § 12.4.4].” Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.40, subd. 8 (Revisor, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/342.40 — Accessed 2026-10-28. OCM’s event guidance adds that all event activities require local approval, including any local permits/licences and specific approval of on-site consumption areas, obtained before applying to OCM, with proof in the application; and that events are 21+ with no sale or consumption of alcohol. Source: OCM news release (Aug 2025 application opening) and OCM Hosting Events page, as above — Accessed 2026-10-28. Samples at events [VERIFY — conflicting signals]. The OCM guide cites § 342.40, subd. 7a(b) sample caps (flower/concentrate sample ≤ 1 g; edible sample ≤ 10 mg THC; LPHE sample ≤ 5 mg THC and ≤ 100 mg CBD/CBG/CBC combined). A 2026 secondary summary of OCM’s legislative proposals states “The prohibition on samples at licensed cannabis events was repealed.” Those two statements are not reconciled in the sources located: the guide’s caps may be the surviving subd. 7a framework, or the repeal may have removed a different prohibition. Do not state that free samples are or are not allowed at events until § 342.40, subd. 7a is read in its 2026 amended form. Note that the microbusiness free-sample ban in § 342.28, subd. 10(h)(8) is a different provision and is not affected by any event-sample change on the text located.

LPHE-retailer off-site event claims — CONFIRMED. An LPHE retailer with an on-site-consumption endorsement may sell and permit consumption of LPHEs at an off-site event that is not a licensed cannabis event, if: (1) the event has been authorised by the local unit of government exercising jurisdiction over the location; (2) the event organiser holds an on-sale licence issued under Chapter 340A; and (3) the event does not exceed four days. § 342.46, subd. 8(i). Source: § 342.46 (Revisor, as above) and OCM Hosting Events page (“LPHE retailer license holders are permitted to sell LPHEs for on-site consumption at an off-site non-cannabis event if …”), as above — Accessed 2026-10-28. The same OCM page distinguishes the third route: an LPHE retailer may also participate as an authorised retailer at a licensed cannabis event hosted by an event organiser — but alcohol is not permitted at such cannabis events. The off-site LPHE route therefore does not authorise a cannabis-event organiser to sell alcohol alongside cannabis, and does not authorise an LPHE retailer to sell flower or cannabis products off site; products allowed off site under subd. 8(i) are LPHEs only.

12.5 Cannabis tourism and visitor purchase rules

12.5.1 Who may buy as a visitor — no residency requirement in the statute

Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(a) grants the adult-use rights to “[a]n individual 21 years of age or older.” No residency, Minnesota-ID, or Minnesota-address condition appears in § 342.09, subd. 1(a) as located. The conclusion that a visitor may buy is therefore a conclusion from the absence of a residency clause plus consistent secondary sources, and is flagged accordingly: secondary guides state “Any adult 21 or older with a valid, government-issued photo ID can buy — there is no residency requirement, so out-of-state visitors can shop on the same terms as Minnesotans” and “Any adult 21 or older with a valid government-issued ID, including a driver’s license from another state or a passport, can purchase from a licensed dispensary.” Sources (secondary): https://www.mycannabis.com/is-weed-legal-in-minnesota/ and https://mncannabishub.com/blog/cannabis-tourism-minnesota-2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY: an OCM consumer FAQ or retailer guidance page stating the visitor rule in OCM’s own words was not located verbatim in this run; the coordinator should cite OCM directly if such a page is found, rather than relying on the secondary guides. Retailers must still verify age (government-issued photo ID is the universal practice described in those guides); the specific ID-acceptance rule for out-of-state and foreign IDs is [VERIFY] from OCM retailer guidance or Minn. Rules ch. 9810.]

12.5.2 Purchase and possession limits for visitors — same as residents

On the statute text, the limits are the person’s limits, not the resident’s limits: a visitor 21+ is subject to the same § 342.09, subd. 1(a)(2)–(5) caps — 2 oz flower in a public place, 2 lb flower in a private residence, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg THC edibles combined — and the same gifting caps in subd. 1(a)(6). No separate visitor cap was located. The practical limit for a visitor is narrower than the statute’s home cap: a visitor who is not in a Minnesota private residence has no lawful Minnesota “private residence” in which to hold 2 lb, and a hotel room is not automatically a “private residence” for this purpose (see § 12.5.3). Retailers also apply their own transaction limits in practice; no retailer transaction cap distinct from the possession cap was confirmed in this run. [VERIFY: OCM retailer transaction-limit guidance, if any.]

12.5.3 What visitors may NOT do

  • Take cannabis across state lines. Interstate transport remains a federal offence even between two states where cannabis is legal, and the neighbouring states (Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota) all have more restrictive laws, so a visitor leaving Minnesota risks both federal and neighbouring-state charges. This is the standard federal position stated in the secondary guides above and is consistent with the federal baseline (adult-use remains Schedule I federally). No Minnesota statute authorises export by a consumer; licensed businesses’ out-of-state sales are a separate, licensed activity and are not a consumer right.
  • Consume in public. Public consumption is unlawful: § 342.09, subd. 1(a)(7) limits lawful use to a private residence/curtilage, private property not generally accessible to the public unless the owner prohibits it, or a licensed on-site-consumption establishment/event; § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(3)–(4) and (9) add the MCIAA, school and minor-inhalation bans. Local public-use ordinances (see § 12.1.2 and § 12.4.4) typically make public use a petty misdemeanour with a locally set fine — e.g., City of Marshall, Lyon County, Ordinance No. 23-019 (31 July 2023): $200; Chisago County Ordinance No. 032024-1 (20 Mar 2024), Lyon County and City of Roseau ordinances: up to $300. These are local fines under § 152.0263, subd. 5’s local-ordinance framework, not a statewide $300 fine — the Run 1 caution (“typical model penalty up to $300 is ordinance-specific, do not generalise statewide”) is confirmed and retained. Sources: Marshall ordinance packet, https://meetings.municode.com/d/f?u=https://mccmeetings.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/marshall-pubu/MEET-Packet-922328c658ef42b8a0fb8377b54e5ed2.pdf ; Chisago County, https://www.chisagocountymn.gov/DocumentCenter/View/20097 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Use in a vehicle, on a school bus, or on federal property. § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(2) (motor vehicle), § 342.56, subd. 1(a)(2)(i) (school bus/van, for medical use), and OCM patient guidance (medical cannabis cannot be used or carried on the grounds of federal facilities such as courthouses, post offices, airports and national parks). Source: OCM, “Guidance on Where to Use Medical Cannabis.” http://mn.gov/ocm/dmc/patients/resources/guidance-on-where-to-use-medical-cannabis.jsp — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Use in hotels, rentals and other people’s property unless allowed. A hotel, motel, vacation rental or host’s home is private property whose owner may prohibit consumption (§ 342.09, subd. 1(a)(7)(ii) — “unless the individual is explicitly prohibited … by the owner of the property”). Most hotels are smoke-free properties, and a smoke-free hotel policy plus the multifamily-smoking ban (§ 12.6) leave a visitor with, in practice, non-smoked products consumed where the property allows them, or a licensed event/microbusiness/LPHE on-site area. OCM’s patient guidance states the same practical rule for patients: “For hotel, motel, or vacation rentals, ask about the rules before you book your stay.” No Minnesota “cannabis-friendly hotel” licence or tourism-specific accommodation rule was located.
  • Drive after consuming. See § 12.2 — DWI applies to visitors on the same impairment standard, and a visitor’s home-state licence is still subject to Minnesota revocation/cancellation consequences and to home-state reporting. [VERIFY: interstate Driver License Compact reporting for a Minnesota cannabis DWI — not addressed in sources located.]

12.5.4 Visiting medical patients — cross-reference only, plus a conflict to reconcile

Per the task, visiting medical patients under § 342.51, subd. 2a are cross-referenced, not redone: Run 1 baseline (out-of-state verification + photo ID, patient-specific label, weekly reporting, 7 conditions for motor-vehicle distribution; no duration/quantity cap stated in subd. 2a as opened) is carried forward. Conflict flagged for the coordinator: a secondary patient-access survey states flatly “Minnesota does not recognize out-of-state medical cards; a patient must be enrolled in the Minnesota program and purchase at a Minnesota dispensary,” while another secondary guide states visiting patients “can show a valid medical cannabis card from their home state to gain direct entry and buy medical-grade inventory,” but without the Minnesota tax exemption. Those two secondary claims cannot both be a complete statement of § 342.51, subd. 2a. The statute’s visiting-patient mechanism (subd. 2a) is the primary source and must be read in full before any “reciprocity: yes/no” sentence is published; the tax-exemption point (visiting patients do not receive the Minnesota medical tax exemption) is secondary-only in this run. [VERIFY: § 342.51, subd. 2a full text and Department of Revenue medical-tax guidance.]

12.5.5 Tourism-specific rules or official visitor guidance

None located. No Minnesota statute, OCM page or Department of Tourism guidance creating a tourism-specific cannabis rule (visitor licence, cannabis-tour licence, consumption-tour exemption) was located in this run. The visitor position is entirely the general adult-use position above plus the property-owner and federal limits. Do not invent a “cannabis tourism programme.” If the coordinator needs an official visitor-facing page, the nearest OCM material located is the Hosting Events page and the patient “where to use” guidance, neither of which is a visitor guide.

12.6 Landlord and tenant rules

12.6.1 The statute that controls most of this section — § 504B.171, subd. 1(c)

“A landlord cannot prohibit a tenant from legally possessing, and a tenant cannot waive the right to legally possess, any cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products, or using any cannabinoid product or hemp-derived consumer product, other than consumption by combustion or vaporization of the product and inhalation of smoke, aerosol, or vapor from the product.”

Source: Minn. Stat. § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) (Revisor 2024 PDF, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/504B.171/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. History: 2023 c. 63, art. 6, § 55 (enacted together with § 342.56, subd. 1(b) — see the Court of Appeals opinion cited in § 12.6.2). The sentence has three operative parts, and each must be kept separate:

  1. Possession is protected and non-waivable. A landlord cannot prohibit legal possession, and a lease clause purporting to waive that right is ineffective as to possession. A lease clause that bans possession itself is therefore not enforceable on the statute as written.
  2. Non-inhaled use is protected on the same terms. “Using any cannabinoid product or hemp-derived consumer product, other than consumption by combustion or vaporization” — i.e., edibles, beverages, tinctures, capsules, topicals — falls inside the protection. A landlord cannot prohibit a tenant from eating an edible in their unit on the basis of § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) alone.
  3. Smoked/vaped consumption is the carve-out. The protection expressly does not extend to “consumption by combustion or vaporization … and inhalation of smoke, aerosol, or vapor.” A landlord may prohibit smoking or vaping cannabis on the property, including in the unit, by lease term. This is a statute-vs.-lease distinction, not a landlord-discretion distinction: the landlord’s power to ban smoking/vaping is the residue left by the carve-out, and it is routinely exercised through smoke-free lease clauses.

Breach and eviction. § 504B.171, subd. 1(a) covenants (in every lease, written or oral) that neither landlord nor tenant will allow controlled substances in the premises, common area or curtilage in violation of any criminal provision of Chapter 152, and related covenants; subd. 2 provides that breach of the covenant voids the tenant’s right to possession, with other lease provisions (including rent) remaining in effect until termination by lease terms or operation of law, and the landlord may bring or assign an eviction action. A tenant who violates a lawful smoke-free lease clause, or who uses cannabis in violation of Chapter 152 (e.g., unlawful amounts, unlawful sale), therefore faces an eviction pathway; a tenant who merely possesses a lawful amount, or uses a non-inhaled product, does not breach the § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) protection by that fact alone. Eviction still requires the ordinary unlawful-detainer process — no self-help eviction (§ 504B.225, cited in the standard lease-rights notice). [VERIFY: whether a post-2023 amendment limits eviction for off-premises conduct (§ 504B.171, subd. 2a, described in a 2024 landlord update as barring eviction for a tenant/household/guest’s off-premises conduct unless it is a crime of violence against a tenant, guest, landlord or employee, or results in a violent-crime conviction) — that amendment was located only in secondary summary and is not stated as a finding here.]

12.6.2 The multifamily smoking/vaping ban — § 342.56, subd. 1(b) — and a 2026 court qualification

“(b) Except for the use of medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products, the vaporizing or smoking of cannabis flower, cannabis products, artificially derived cannabinoids, or hemp-derived consumer products is prohibited in a multifamily housing building, including balconies and patios appurtenant thereto. A violation of this paragraph is punishable through a civil administrative fine in an amount of $250.”

Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.56, subd. 1(b) (Justia 2025 compilation). https://law.justia.com/codes/minnesota/chapters-324-342/chapter-342/section-342-56/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. Effective 1 July 2024 (the date stated in secondary and housing guidance; the 2024 amendment moved the date forward from March 2025). The ban covers the building including balconies and patios; it is a civil administrative fine, not a crime; and it covers smoking and vaping. MDH’s MCIAA FAQ confirms the division of labour: MDH does not regulate smoking in apartment units (the MCIAA bans smoking in common areas), landlords may designate the entire building smoke-free, and “[t]he ban on smoking and vaping of cannabis is part of the laws administered by the Office of Cannabis Management (OCM).” Source: MDH MCIAA FAQ, as above — Accessed 2026-10-28.

The medical exception — and the qualification the coordinator must not miss. The text says “Except for the use of medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products.” Secondary housing guides read this as a medical-patient exemption from the multifamily ban (“Registered medical patients CAN smoke in apartments”). But the Minnesota Court of Appeals held in May 2026 (OPa251279, 4 May 2026) that “section 342.56, subdivision 1(b), does not create a statutory right to smoke medical cannabis in multifamily housing,” reasoning from § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) (enacted at the same time, for the same purpose) that the two provisions must be read together. Source: Court of Appeals opinion (standard opinion, 4 May 2026). https://mncourts.gov/_media/migration/appellate/court-of-appeals/standard-opinions/04may26/OPa251279-050426.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. Practical consequence, stated cautiously: a registry patient is excepted from the $250 civil fine under § 342.56, subd. 1(b) on the text, but the Court of Appeals’ holding means that exception should not be presented as a freestanding right to smoke in a unit in defiance of a lease smoke-free clause. Whether a landlord’s smoke-free clause can be enforced against a registry patient who smokes medical cannabis in their own unit is therefore [VERIFY — read the full OPa251279 holding and any subsequent history before publishing a “patients may / may not smoke in their unit” sentence]. The same caution applies to the secondary claim that the medical exception covers only the unit and not balconies/common areas — that limitation was stated in secondary guides, not in the statute excerpt located, and is [VERIFY].

12.6.3 Registry-patient protections vs. adult-use tenant rights — § 342.57, subd. 3

These are different protections and must not be conflated:

  • Registry patients (and Tribal medical programme enrollees, per the 2025 amendment). § 342.57, subd. 3(b): “No landlord may refuse to lease to a patient or person enrolled in the registry program or a Tribal medical cannabis program or otherwise penalize a patient or person enrolled in the registry program or a Tribal medical cannabis program solely because the patient or person is enrolled in the registry program or a Tribal medical cannabis program, unless failing to do so would violate federal law or regulations or cause the landlord to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations.” § 342.57, subd. 3(c) adds that the fact cannabis is a federally controlled substance must not be the sole basis for a landlord’s refusal/penalty determination. § 342.57, subd. 5a requires an employer, school or landlord who takes an action that would otherwise be prohibited under subd. 3 or 5, on the belief that failing to act would violate federal/state law or cause loss of a federal monetary/licensing benefit, to provide written notice to the affected patient at the time the action is taken, citing the federal law/regulations and, if applicable, the benefit at risk; failure to provide notice is a violation. § 342.57, subd. 6a prohibits retaliation by a school, landlord, health care facility or employer against a patient for asserting § 342.57 / § 152.32 rights. § 342.57, subd. 7 provides damages of the greater of actual damages or $1,000 plus attorney fees and injunctive relief. Sources: § 342.57 as amended (2025 bill text, SF 4739 / HF 3760 summaries of the subd. 3 and 5a language). https://pluralpolicy.com/app/legislative-tracking/bill/details/state-mn-2023_2024-sf4739 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Correction to Run 1: Run 1 described subd. 5a as a “14-day notice.” The text located states notice “at the time” the action is taken, not 14 days. The 14-day formulation is not confirmed and should not be published unless a different subdivision is identified.
  • Adult-use tenants (not registry patients). Adult-use tenants have the § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) possession / non-inhaled-use protection in § 12.6.1, but they do not have the § 342.57, subd. 3 anti-penalty protection, which is limited to registry/Tribal-programme enrolment. A landlord may therefore, consistently with § 342.57, refuse to lease to or penalise an adult-use user for reasons other than the protected possession/use — subject always to other anti-discrimination law, which is outside this Part. Secondary guides that state a landlord may “refuse to rent to individuals who use cannabis, as long as this is disclosed and applied consistently” are describing this adult-use gap; that proposition is secondary-only and is [VERIFY] before publication, because § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) at least bars a possession ban, and the boundary between “refusing for use” and “prohibiting possession” has not been tested in a case located in this run.

12.6.4 Home grow in rentals, and public / subsidised housing

  • Home grow. No Minnesota statute located in this run expressly addresses a landlord’s power to prohibit cultivation in a rental. § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) protects possession and non-inhaled use; cultivation is neither. Secondary guides state a landlord can prohibit growing by lease term and that such a prohibition would likely be enforceable, citing space, ventilation and electrical issues in apartments. That is a lease/contract proposition, not a statute proposition, and is marked [VERIFY — no § 504B grow clause located; do not cite § 504B.171, subd. 1(c) as a grow protection]. The home-grow limits themselves (8 plants / 4 mature, enclosed locked space not open to public view) are the Run 1 baseline and apply to the residence, but a lease may add a stricter prohibition; breach of a lease grow ban is a lease-breach eviction question, not a § 342.56 fine question.
  • Public and subsidised housing — federal law controls. No Minnesota statute located in this run creates a state-law right to use cannabis in federally assisted housing. OCM’s patient guidance states: “Due to the federal prohibition of cannabis, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) does not have the discretion to admit users of marijuana, including medical cannabis, to the public housing program. For applicants, if the public housing authority or private landlord determines that any member of a household is an illegal user of a controlled substance (including medical cannabis), it will deny admission to the housing.” It also advises apartment patients to check their lease/property manager, “especially … for people who live in federally assisted housing.” Source: OCM patient guidance, as above — Accessed 2026-10-28. Secondary summaries add that HUD requires federally assisted leases to allow eviction for drug-related criminal activity and that Section 8 / public-housing residents “cannot legally use or possess recreational or medical marijuana in any form, regardless of state law” (citing HUD’s multifamily guidance and 24 CFR 966.4). Those federal-lease propositions are secondary in this run and are [VERIFY against the current HUD guidance and the specific housing authority’s lease] before publication, but the direction is unambiguous: the § 342.56, subd. 1(b) medical exception and the § 342.57, subd. 3 landlord protection both yield to the federal-law / federal-benefit exception in § 342.57, subd. 3 itself, and federally assisted housing is the paradigm case for that exception. A registry patient in federally assisted housing should therefore not be told they are protected by Minnesota law alone.

12.7 Gun ownership conflicts

12.7.1 Minnesota state law: a shield for lawful users, with stated limits

Minn. Stat. § 624.7152, “Lawful Cannabis Users” (History: 2023 c. 63, art. 6, § 71), provides in full:

“(a) A person may not be denied the right to purchase, own, possess, or carry a firearm solely on the basis that the person is a patient in the registry program. (b) A person may not be denied the right to purchase, own, possess, or carry a firearm solely on the basis that the person is 21 years of age or older and uses adult-use cannabis flower, adult-use cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products. (c) A state or local agency may not access a database containing the identities of patients in the registry program to obtain information for the purpose of approving or disapproving a person from purchasing, owning, possessing, or carrying a firearm. (d) A state or local agency may not use information gathered from a database containing the identities of patients in the registry program to obtain information for the purpose of approving or disapproving a person from purchasing, owning, possessing, or carrying a firearm. (e) A state or local agency may not inquire about a person’s status as a patient in the registry program for the purpose of approving or disapproving the person from purchasing, owning, possessing, or carrying a firearm. (f) A state or local agency may not inquire about the use of adult-use cannabis flower, adult-use cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products by a person 21 years of age or older for the purpose of approving or disapproving the person from purchasing, owning, possessing, or carrying a firearm.”

Source: Minn. Stat. § 624.7152 (Revisor 2025 PDF). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2025/2025-10-19%2014:38:12+00:00/cite/624.7152/pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

The permit-to-carry analogue is Minn. Stat. § 624.714, subd. 6(f): “A sheriff shall not deny an application for a permit to carry solely because the applicant is a patient enrolled in the registry program and uses medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products for a qualifying medical condition or because the person is 21 years of age or older and uses adult-use cannabis flower, adult-use cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products.” Source: § 624.714, subd. 6(f) (search-indexed statute text). https://arklegal.ai/state_statute/2547036/download.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. The permit-to-purchase system is separate: before buying a pistol or a semiautomatic military-style assault weapon in Minnesota, a person needs a permit to purchase or a permit to carry (a carry permit doubles as purchase authorisation); no permit to purchase is required for ordinary rifles/shotguns, which are bought through a federally licensed dealer with a NICS check at sale. Source (secondary, DPS process summary): https://legalclarity.org/minnesota-gun-ownership-criteria-and-disqualifications/ — Accessed 2026-10-28. The § 624.7152 shield applies to “purchase, own, possess, or carry” generally, so it covers the state side of both permits — but see § 12.7.2 for why it does not end the inquiry.

What the shield does not do. It is a “solely on the basis” shield. It does not excuse any other disqualifier: a felony drug conviction, a crime-of-violence conviction, a domestic-violence or protection-order disqualifier, a commitment-based disqualifier, or a sheriff’s “substantial likelihood of danger to self or public” denial ground under § 624.714, subd. 6(a)(3) all remain available on their own facts. Secondary analysis also describes a distinct Minnesota rule for convictions (as opposed to lawful use): a misdemeanour or gross-misdemeanour Chapter 152 conviction triggers a 3-year firearm ban from conviction, restarting on a further drug conviction, and a felony drug conviction triggers the federal lifetime ban (restorable on discharge). Source (secondary): https://www.leversonbudke.com/does-a-misdemeanor-drug-charge-affect-my-gun-rights — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY: the 3-year conviction ban and its interaction with § 624.713’s “unlawful user” definition against current §§ 624.712–624.713 text. In particular, whether lawful adult-use use is excluded from “unlawful user” for § 624.713 purposes is the hinge between the § 624.7152 shield and the § 624.713 prohibition, and the current § 624.713 text was not confirmed in this run. Do not state that § 624.713 “mirrors” federal law for lawful users without that check.]

Tribal medical status [VERIFY]. § 624.7152(a) and (c)–(e) speak of “a patient in the registry program.” § 342.57, subd. 3 as amended in 2025 expressly extends landlord/school protection to “a Tribal medical cannabis program” enrollee, but no equivalent Tribal-programme language in § 624.7152 or § 624.714, subd. 6(f) was located in this run. Whether a Tribal medical programme enrollee who is not in the state registry is covered by the firearms shield is therefore [VERIFY] and must not be assumed.

12.7.2 Federal law: the operative conflict — 922(g)(3), Form 4473, Hemani, and the 2026 ATF rule

The federal baseline supplied with this task is applied here, not re-researched, and is stated with its limits so it is not overstated as a Minnesota rule:

  • The prohibition. 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) makes it unlawful for any person “who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance” to possess firearms or ammunition. ATF Form 4473, Question 21(g) (as described in secondary sources) warns that marijuana use remains unlawful under federal law regardless of state legalisation, and answering it falsely is a separate federal felony (false statement). A Minnesota permit to purchase/carry does not answer Form 4473 for the buyer, and a dealer sale still runs a federal NICS check.
  • Hemani — narrow and as-applied. US v. Hemani, No. 24-1234 (decided 18 June 2026, Gorsuch), held a status-only § 922(g)(3) prosecution of a regular marijuana user for in-home possession, with no danger showing, inconsistent with the Second Amendment, as-applied and narrow (task baseline). Hemani is therefore not a holding that all cannabis users may lawfully possess firearms, not a holding about Minnesota permits, and not a safe harbour for answering Form 4473. It is a constitutional limit on a particular kind of status-only prosecution. No ATF safe harbour for medical or adult-use users was located (task baseline, retained).
  • ATF interim final rule, eff. 22 Jan 2026. The rule rewrote 27 CFR 478.11 to require regular use continuing into the present for “unlawful user” status (task baseline). That narrows the temporal scope of the federal definition; it does not deem state-lawful use lawful federally, and it does not amend § 922(g)(3) itself.
  • Schedule III — effect and non-effect. State-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III eff. 28 Apr 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I (task baseline). Schedule III alone does not remove medical users from § 922(g)(3)’s text: the statute turns on “unlawful user of … any controlled substance,” and a Schedule III substance is still a controlled substance; the federal unlawfulness of marijuana use (outside a federally lawful prescription framework, which state medical programmes are not) is what drives the conflict. For adult-use users, Schedule III changes nothing at all. For medical users, the change matters for § 280E (medical only) and for the scheduling debate, but on the authorities located it does not create a firearms entitlement. [VERIFY: any post-April 2026 ATF guidance or Form 4473 revision addressing Schedule III medical users — none was located in this run, and the absence is noted rather than filled by inference.]
  • Practical synthesis for a Minnesota reader. A lawful Minnesota cannabis user: (i) cannot be denied a Minnesota permit to purchase or carry solely for that use, and state/local agencies cannot use the registry or inquire about adult-use use to decide firearms eligibility (§§ 624.7152, 624.714, subd. 6(f)); but (ii) still faces the federal § 922(g)(3) prohibition as written, the Form 4473 question at any dealer sale, and a federal prosecution risk that Hemani narrows only for a status-only, in-home, no-danger-showing case. Those two propositions are simultaneously true because they operate at different sovereign levels. Any advice that collapses them into “you can / cannot own a gun in Minnesota” is wrong.

12.8 Pet and veterinary products

12.8.1 What is lawful to sell for animals — the MDA answer is narrower than the human market

  • Hemp as an animal-feed / pet-food ingredient: not approved, with one laying-hen exception. The Minnesota Department of Agriculture (MDA) Hemp Program FAQ states: “At this time, hemp is not an approved ingredient for commercial animal feed other than for laying hens.” And for pet food: “No. The MDA Commercial Feed Program and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations of pet food are similar to that for other animal food. That means hemp is not an approved ingredient for pet food either. An individual or company selling pet food with hemp ingredients in Minnesota would result in the products being withdrawn from distribution.” An individual farmer may feed hemp to their own livestock. Source: MDA, “FAQs Regarding Minnesota’s Hemp Program.” https://www.mda.state.mn.us/plants/hemp/industhempquestions — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • The laying-hen exception — hemp seed meal. MDA announced that hemp seed meal (ground/milled cake remaining after oil extraction from Cannabis sativa L. seed) may be used in Minnesota animal feed under AAFCO’s tentative ingredient definition for laying hens; Minnesota allows tentative ingredients in feed and pet food. Limits stated by MDA: no more than 20% of the laying hens’ diet as a source of protein and fat; FDA final standards of 2 parts per million THC and 20 ppm CBD. Source: MDA, “Hemp Seed Meal Available for Feed in Minnesota” (application period described as 2025). https://www.mda.state.mn.us/hemp-seed-meal-available-feed-minnesota — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note the scope: this is seed meal for laying hens, not CBD oil or THC products for dogs, cats or other species, and the AAFCO status was “tentative” at announcement with full approval to take a year or more. [VERIFY: current AAFCO status — tentative vs. full — before republishing the laying-hen exception as current.]
  • Cottage-food pet treats: cannabinoids excluded. Cannabinoids like THC or CBD cannot be ingredients in cottage food, because edible cannabinoids are explicitly excluded from the definition of food products in Minn. Stat. § 34A.01, subd. 4. Only baked or dehydrated dog/cat treats qualify under the cottage-food pet-treat track, and they must be safe for the intended species. Source: MDA, “Cottage Food Law Guidance.” https://www.mda.state.mn.us/food-feed/cottage-food-law-guidance — Accessed 2026-10-28; and Minn. Stat. § 25.391 (home-processed pet treats exemption, baked/dehydrated, dogs/cats only). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/25.391 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • No Minnesota THC milligram limit for animal products was located [UNAVAILABLE]. No statute, rule or MDA/OCM guidance located in this run states a per-serving or per-container THC (or CBD) limit for a pet product as such. The only numeric animal limits located are the human-product limits (which do not apply to animals), the hemp definition (0.3% THC by dry weight, for the plant), and the laying-hen seed-meal ppm limits above (2 ppm THC / 20 ppm CBD). Do not transplant the human LPHE limits (5 mg/serving, 50 mg/package; 10 mg/beverage) onto pet products.

12.8.2 The old § 151.72 animal-consumption rule — flagged, not stated as current law

Former Minn. Stat. § 151.72, subd. 3 (as indexed in the 2024 compilation) provided that a product containing nonintoxicating cannabinoids could be sold for human or animal consumption only if it contained no more than 0.3% of any THC, and that a non-edible nonintoxicating-cannabinoid product could be sold for human or animal consumption only if intended for external application, and must not be manufactured, marketed, distributed or intended to be consumed by combustion/vaporisation, chewing/drinking/swallowing, injection, or application to mucous membrane or non-intact skin; and subd. 3(c) barred sale of any other hemp-extracted substance for human/animal use in diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of disease, or to affect structure/function. Source: Minn. Stat. § 151.72 (2024 compilation, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2024/cite/151.72/subd/151.72.2 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Current status [VERIFY — material]. A 2026 secondary summary of SF 4401 states that § 151.72 was “entirely repealed” and that “all hemp edible regulation now lives exclusively under Chapter 342.” If that repeal was enacted, the § 151.72 animal-consumption framework above is historical, and the operative question becomes whether Chapter 342 / OCM guidance authorises any animal-consumption cannabinoid product at all — no such Chapter 342 animal-product authorisation was located in this run. Do not publish the § 151.72 animal rule as current law until the repeal and any successor provision are confirmed from the enrolled 2026 act.

12.8.3 Veterinary prescribing and dispensing — no current Minnesota permission located

  • No Minnesota veterinary cannabis prescribing statute or current Board rule was located [VERIFY/UNAVAILABLE]. No provision in Chapter 342 located in this run authorises a veterinarian to prescribe, recommend or dispense cannabis or hemp-derived cannabinoids for an animal patient, and no current Minnesota Board of Veterinary Medicine guidance on cannabis was located. The material that was located is old and must be dated as such: Board of Veterinary Medicine special-meeting minutes, 10 Apr 2019 (pre-legalisation), record that “[c]urrently, cannabis-based products are illegal in the State of Minnesota” and that “[r]ecommendation/prescribing specific brands of CBD oils and best treatment plans for patients is considered the practice of veterinary medicine,” which “could only be done as an employee of a veterinarian who was present on the premises” (in the context of a veterinary cannabis counsellor discussion and unlicensed-practice concerns). Source: https://mn.gov/boards/assets/April%2010%2C%202019%20Minutes_tcm21-394144.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. Magazine reports from the same era state the Board “recommends veterinarians do not prescribe it, or they will lose their license” — secondary, undated in substance, and pre-dating both the 2022 hemp-edible law and the 2023 Adult-Use Cannabis Act. Neither the 2019 minutes nor the magazine reports should be presented as the Board’s current position.
  • Federal overlay (secondary). The FDA has not approved cannabis for any use in animals; a January 2025 Federal Register notice is reported as stating no FDA-approved, conditionally approved or indexed animal drugs contain CBD, with significant data gaps on CBD in animals. Veterinarians may prescribe FDA-approved human medications (e.g., Epidiolex) for extra-label animal use when medically appropriate, but generally cannot recommend or sell unapproved hemp/cannabis products marketed for pets. Source (secondary synthesis of FDA position): https://www.drgreenrelief.com/blog/cbd-for-dogs/?amp=1 — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY against the FDA’s own cannabis-animals Q&A before publishing the extra-label point as a Minnesota finding; it is included here only to prevent the inference that “CBD is unregulated for pets because hemp is legal.”]
  • Distinguishing pet products from human products. On the sources located, the distinction is: (i) human ingestible cannabinoid products are regulated under Chapter 342 (cannabis business or LPHE licences, potency/packaging/testing rules); (ii) animal feed/pet-food products with hemp/CBD are not approved ingredients (MDA, above) and are subject to withdrawal from distribution, except laying-hen seed meal within its limits; (iii) external (topical) hemp products at 0% THC need no Chapter 342 licence for human retail (OCM guide) — whether that extends to animal topicals was not addressed in any source located and is [VERIFY]; (iv) a product marketed with disease-treatment claims for an animal is a drug claim that triggers the FDA-approval framework above, regardless of the Minnesota channel. A pet owner giving a human product to an animal is not protected by the human product’s Minnesota legality: the human limits, labelling and age gates do not make the product an approved animal product, and THC toxicity in dogs/cats is a veterinary-emergency question, not a legality question. No Minnesota “pet CBD licence” or “veterinary cannabis endorsement” was located.

12.9 Medical cannabis in schools

12.9.1 The statute: a school ban with a narrow, non-inhaled medical exception — § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(4) and (c)

Minn. Stat. § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(4) prohibits, except as provided in paragraph (c), “use or possess[ion of] cannabis flower, cannabis products, lower-potency hemp edibles, or hemp-derived consumer products in a public school, as defined in section 120A.05, subdivisions 9, 11, and 13, or in a charter school governed by chapter 124E, including all facilities, whether owned, rented, or leased, and all vehicles that a school district owns, leases, rents, contracts for, or controls.” Paragraph (c) then provides: “The prohibitions under paragraph (b), clauses (1) to (4), do not apply to use other than by smoking or by a vaporized delivery method, possession, or transportation of medical cannabis flower or medical cannabinoid products by a patient; a registered designated caregiver; or a parent, legal guardian, or spouse of a patient.” Source: § 342.09 (Revisor, as above) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Read together, the statute’s position is:

  • Smoked or vaporized medical use at school is not excepted. The (c) exception is expressly limited to use “other than by smoking or by a vaporized delivery method.” A student (or anyone) may not smoke or vape medical cannabis on school property or in a school vehicle under § 342.09.
  • Non-smoked / non-vaporized medical possession and use by a patient, caregiver, parent, guardian or spouse is excepted from the (b)(4) school ban as a matter of § 342.09 itself. That is, the statute does not itself criminalise a registry patient’s possession of a non-inhaled medical product (e.g., an edible, tincture, capsule) at school, or a parent/caregiver’s transport of it there.
  • That exception is not a right to use at school on demand. Three separate limits qualify it, and all three must be stated alongside the exception: 1. § 342.56, subd. 1(a)(2) does not list school grounds as a prohibited medical location, but it does prohibit medical possession/consumption on a school bus or van (§ 342.56, subd. 1(a)(2)(i)), in a correctional facility, in a state-operated treatment programme (including the Minnesota sex offender programme), and on the grounds of a child care facility or family/group family day care programme; and § 342.56, subd. 1(a)(3) prohibits vaporizing/smoking medical cannabis on public transportation, where vapor would be inhaled by a nonpatient minor or smoke by a minor, and in any public place (including a place of employment as defined in § 144.413, subd. 1b). Source: § 342.56 (Justia 2025 compilation, as above) — Accessed 2026-10-28. A school bus is therefore doubly barred (by § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(4)’s vehicle clause and by § 342.56), while a school building is barred by § 342.09, subd. 1(b)(4) except for the (c) non-inhaled medical carve-out. 2. School policy and federal funding. § 342.57, subd. 3(a) (see § 12.6.3) bars a school from refusing to enrol or otherwise penalising a patient solely because the patient is enrolled, “unless failing to do so would violate federal law or regulations or cause the school to lose a monetary or licensing-related benefit under federal law or regulations,” with the subd. 5a written-notice-at-the-time requirement and the subd. 6a anti-retaliation rule. A school may therefore maintain a drug-free-school policy that prohibits on-site use/possession beyond the § 342.09 exception, particularly where federal Drug-Free Schools / federal-funding conditions are invoked — but it may not use enrolment alone as the basis for exclusion or penalty, and it must give the subd. 5a notice if it relies on the federal exception. 3. No administration duty is stated. No statute or OCM/MDE guidance located in this run requires a school, school nurse or other school staff member to administer medical cannabis to a student, or authorises school staff to do so as part of student medication administration.

12.9.2 What schools may prohibit, what they may not, and the nurse/administration gap

  • May prohibit: smoking/vaping of any cannabis product on school property and in school vehicles; use or possession of adult-use products and LPHEs/hemp-derived consumer products by any student (subject to the medical (c) exception for medical products only); possession/use on a school bus or van (all forms, for medical as well as adult-use, under § 342.56); and, under a lawful school drug policy, on-site use even of a non-inhaled medical product where the policy is grounded in federal law/funding or in the school’s general authority over student conduct and medication on campus — with the § 342.57, subd. 3 / 5a / 6a limits above. The MSBA/MASA Model Policy 418 (Drug-Free Workplace / Drug-Free School) illustrates the district-policy approach: students with a prescription for a controlled substance, except medical cannabis, nonintoxicating cannabinoids or edible cannabinoid products, must comply with the district’s student medication policy (Model Policy 516, under § 121A.22’s duty to develop drug/medicine administration procedures), and the school’s licensed school nurse, trained health clerk, principal or teacher administers prescribed medication except medical cannabis, nonintoxicating cannabinoids or edible cannabinoid products. The same model policy states no person may possess or use medical cannabis, nonintoxicating cannabinoids or edible cannabinoid products on a school bus/van, on the grounds of a preschool/primary/secondary school, or on the grounds of a childcare facility. Source (model policy, not statute): https://files.smartsites.parentsquare.com/13545/policy-418.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28. Conflict flagged: the model policy’s blanket “grounds of a … school” prohibition is broader than the § 342.09, subd. 1(c) non-inhaled medical exception. A district that adopts the model verbatim and a student who relies on the (c) exception are in tension; the coordinator should not present the model policy as if it were the statute, and should note that the model policy itself carries a note that “The 2025 Minnesota legislature amended this law” — the post-2025 model text was not confirmed in this run. [VERIFY: current MSBA/MASA Model Policies 418 and 516, and any Minnesota Department of Education guidance on student medical cannabis.]
  • May not: refuse to enrol a student, or otherwise penalise a student, solely because the student is a registry patient (§ 342.57, subd. 3(a), federal exception aside); retaliate against a patient for asserting § 342.57 / § 152.32 rights (§ 342.57, subd. 6a); or treat the fact that cannabis is a federally controlled substance as the sole basis for an enrolment/penalty determination (§ 342.57, subd. 3(c)).
  • School nurse / administration — [UNAVAILABLE]. No OCM or Minnesota Department of Education school-administration guidance (who may hold, store, or administer a student’s medical cannabis on campus; whether a parent/caregiver must come to campus to administer a dose; storage and documentation rules) was located in this run. The model-policy exclusion of medical cannabis from staff-administered medication (above) suggests staff are not expected to administer it, and the § 342.09, subd. 1(c) exception for a parent/guardian/caregiver’s possession/transport suggests the lawful on-campus actor is the patient or their parent/guardian/caregiver, not school staff — but that is an inference from the statute’s list of excepted persons, not a stated administration rule, and it is marked as such. Do not publish a “school nurse may/may not administer” rule on this record.
  • Under-21 vaporized-product bar — § 342.51, subd. 2(c) — CONFIRMED, and distinct from the school ban. “A cannabis business with a medical cannabis retail endorsement may not distribute, sell, or deliver medical cannabis flower and medical cannabinoid products intended to be vaporized to a person enrolled in the registry program if the product is intended for a patient under 21 years of age.” Source: Minn. Stat. § 342.51, subd. 2(c) (Revisor, search-indexed copy). https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/342.51 — Accessed 2026-10-28. This is a distribution bar (retailer → patient), not a use ban, and it applies regardless of school: a patient under 21 may not be sold/delivered a vaporized-intended medical product at all. It is consistent with, but broader than, the school smoking/vaping ban: even off campus, an under-21 registry patient may not obtain a vaporized medical product from a medical-endorsed retailer. (A 2026 House Research summary of Laws 2026, chapter 123 notes this vaporized-distribution provision’s effective date as the day following final enactment, with the surrounding macrobusiness-consultant provisions effective 1 Jan 2027 — the distribution bar itself is stated here from the Revisor text, not from the summary.) [VERIFY: whether the bar extends to a parent/caregiver receiving a vaporized product on behalf of an under-21 patient — the text says “if the product is intended for a patient under 21,” which on its face covers receipt on the patient’s behalf, but no OCM interpretation was located.]

12.10 Gaps, conflicts and items for coordinator reconciliation (complete list)

The coordinator should not have to re-research to reconcile Part 12. Every [VERIFY] / [UNAVAILABLE] / conflict in §§ 12.1–12.9 is collected here, in the order it arises. Nothing in this list is resolved by inference.

  1. Direct-page limitation. One browser.open attempt to a Revisor page failed with a transient tool error and was not retried under the governing instruction for this run. Propositions sourced to “search-indexed copy” of a Revisor/OCM/DPS page should be spot-checked against the live page before publication, even where the indexed text quotes the statute verbatim.
  2. § 342.245 correction (material). Run 1’s description of § 342.245 as the on-site-consumption endorsement provision is corrected in this Part: § 342.245 is the general endorsements framework created in 2026. Confirm the enrolled session-law chapter (SF 4401 / Laws 2026, ch. 123 are both cited in secondary material) and effective date before publishing.
  3. § 152.093 current wording (material for § 12.1.2). Historical text (delivery prohibited, misdemeanour) vs. 2024 secondary summary (delivery prohibition removed; manufacture for delivery and delivery to a minor remain). Confirm current § 152.093 from the live Revisor before any present-tense “delivery is/is not a crime” sentence. Simple possession/use repeal (§ 152.092, 2023 c. 52, art. 15, § 17) is confirmed.
  4. St. Paul shared-entrance rule (Run 1 note) — NOT VERIFIED. No St. Paul ordinance text was located. The only shared-entrance rule located is Douglas County’s (cannabis retail may not share a common entrance/premises with a retail tobacco business; LPHE exempt), and even that was located in draft form. Check the St. Paul Legislative Code / zoning text directly; do not generalise Douglas County to St. Paul or statewide.
  5. General-retail hardware-only sales. No Chapter 342 licence for selling only empty cannabis hardware was located, but OCM confirmation was not located either. Confirm with OCM before stating that a hardware-only shop needs no licence.
  6. § 169A.36 pointer. No THC limit was located in § 169A.36; the “no per se limit” conclusion rests on § 169A.20, subd. 1. Confirm § 169A.36’s current subject matter so the task’s pointer is closed, not left dangling.
  7. DWI look-back period. Secondary sources state both 10 years (older LRL overview) and 20 years (2026 Nolo licence summary) for prior-incident counting. Confirm current §§ 169A.24–169A.27 look-back before any “within X years” sentence.
  8. Implied-consent advisory wording. Older compilations of § 169A.51, subd. 2 still use pre-2023 “other than marijuana or THC” language. Confirm the current advisory text.
  9. Oral-fluid roadside testing post-pilot. Pilot was voluntary, inadmissible, and not probable-cause (DPS). 2026 bills introducing oral-fluid language were located as introductions only. Confirm whether any enacted post-pilot authorisation exists; otherwise present oral-fluid testing as pilot-only.
  10. § 169A.46 prescription defence. Cited only via secondary summary as a clause (7) defence. Confirm text before relying on it, and confirm it does not extend to clause (8) cannabis impairment.
  11. CEB 2026 second-round automatic count. DPS promised a 2026 re-review of records still in the court process in 2024. No completed count was located. Do not update 57,780 by inference.
  12. Clean Slate numbers. The “1.57m of 2.03m” secondary figure was NOT adopted (appears to describe the broader Clean Slate pool, unconfirmed against BCA/DPS). Do not merge Clean Slate (§ 609A.015) counts with cannabis automatic (§ 609A.055) counts.
  13. CEB outcome breakdown. The Aug 2026 figures (731 Board-voted; 676 court orders) are not broken into expungement vs. resentencing vs. denial in the excerpt located, and “files” (2025 report) vs. “cases” (2026 profile) may not be identical units. Obtain the full 2025 Annual Report and the next annual report (due 15 Jan 2027) for the breakdown. The 21-vs.-29 incarcerated-persons planning figures also conflict and need a single sourced figure if used.
  14. CEB intake. Whether a person can request Board review of a missed felony case (vs. waiting for BCA identification) was not confirmed; the budget book mentions clinics and “an accessible intake process” without a form or deadline.
  15. Chapter 609A petition waiting periods and fee. Secondary figures (2/4/5 years; ~$300) were NOT confirmed against current §§ 609A.02–609A.03 and are not stated as findings. Confirm before publishing.
  16. Retailer/mezzobusiness on-site consumption. OCM guide lists only event organiser, microbusiness and LPHE retailer. Confirm against current §§ 342.27/342.29 whether any retailer/mezzobusiness on-site authority exists outside the guide.
  17. Event samples (§ 342.40, subd. 7a). OCM guide sample caps (1 g flower/concentrate; 10 mg edible; 5 mg LPHE) vs. a 2026 secondary claim that the event-sample prohibition was repealed. Read § 342.40, subd. 7a in its 2026 amended form before stating the sample rule.
  18. § 342.39, subd. 3 LPHE bar in 2027. Statute text bars an event organiser from holding an LPHE manufacturer/retailer licence; a secondary guide notes OCM’s Licence Types page as saying hemp holders may apply. Confirm the 2027 text and the per-event 4-day cap under the annual licence.
  19. Visitor purchase — OCM source. No-residency and government-ID rules rest on statute silence plus secondary guides. Locate an OCM consumer/retailer FAQ stating the visitor rule verbatim, and confirm ID-acceptance (out-of-state, foreign) and any retailer transaction limit distinct from the possession cap.
  20. Visiting medical patients (§ 342.51, subd. 2a) — conflict. One secondary source says Minnesota does not recognise out-of-state cards; another says visiting patients may buy medical-grade inventory but without the tax exemption. Read § 342.51, subd. 2a in full and Department of Revenue medical-tax guidance before any reciprocity sentence.
  21. § 342.57, subd. 5a notice period — correction to Run 1. Text located says written notice “at the time” of the action, not 14 days. Run 1’s “14-day notice” is not confirmed; identify the correct subdivision if a 14-day rule exists elsewhere.
  22. Multifamily medical exception — court qualification (material). § 342.56, subd. 1(b) excepts medical use from the $250 fine on its text, but Court of Appeals OPa251279 (4 May 2026) holds it “does not create a statutory right to smoke medical cannabis in multifamily housing.” Read the full holding before any “patients may smoke in their unit” sentence, and confirm whether the exception is unit-only (secondary claim) vs. balconies/common areas.
  23. Home grow in rentals. No § 504B grow clause was located; the “landlord may prohibit growing by lease” proposition is secondary/contract only. Confirm before citing any statute for a grow ban.
  24. § 504B.171, subd. 2a off-premises eviction limit. Located only in secondary summary (2024 update). Confirm text before publishing.
  25. Federally assisted housing lease rules. HUD admission-denial (OCM guidance) is confirmed as OCM guidance; the broader “eviction for any use, including edibles/medical, in any HUD-assisted property” proposition is secondary (HUD guidance / 24 CFR 966.4 summaries). Confirm against current HUD guidance and the specific housing authority lease.
  26. Firearms — § 624.713 “unlawful user” hinge (material). Whether lawful adult-use use is excluded from § 624.713’s unlawful-user prohibition, and the 3-year Chapter 152 conviction ban, were located only in secondary summary. Read current §§ 624.712–624.713 before stating the state/federal boundary beyond §§ 624.7152 / 624.714, subd. 6(f).
  27. Firearms — Tribal medical status. § 624.7152 / § 624.714, subd. 6(f) speak of the state registry programme; § 342.57, subd. 3 as amended covers Tribal programme enrollees for landlord/school purposes. Whether Tribal enrollees are covered for firearms purposes is [VERIFY].
  28. Firearms — post-Schedule III ATF guidance. No post-April 2026 ATF guidance or Form 4473 revision addressing Schedule III medical users was located. Confirm none exists before stating the Schedule III non-effect as final, and do not present Hemani as broader than a narrow, as-applied, status-only, in-home, no-danger-showing holding.
  29. Pet products — § 151.72 repeal (material). A 2026 secondary summary states § 151.72 was entirely repealed. If enacted, the § 151.72 animal-consumption rule in § 12.8.2 is historical only, and no Chapter 342 animal-product authorisation was located to replace it. Confirm from the enrolled 2026 act.
  30. Pet products — AAFCO laying-hen status. Hemp seed meal was “tentative” at MDA announcement, ≤20% of diet, 2 ppm THC / 20 ppm CBD. Confirm current tentative-vs.-full status.
  31. Veterinary prescribing — current Board position. Only 2019 Board minutes and era magazine reports were located, both pre-legalisation. No current Board of Veterinary Medicine cannabis guidance was located. Confirm the Board’s current position (or its absence) directly; do not republish the 2019 position as current.
  32. Animal topical products. OCM guide states 0% THC human topicals need no licence; whether that extends to animal topicals was not addressed in any source located. [VERIFY.]
  33. Schools — MDE / OCM administration guidance. No guidance on who may hold, store or administer a student’s medical cannabis on campus was located. The model-policy exclusion of medical cannabis from staff-administered medication and the § 342.09, subd. 1(c) parent/caregiver list are the only anchors; a “nurse may/may not administer” rule must not be published on this record.
  34. Schools — model policy vs. statute. MSBA/MASA Model Policy 418’s blanket school-grounds prohibition is broader than § 342.09, subd. 1(c)’s non-inhaled medical exception, and the model carries a note that the 2025 Legislature amended the law. Confirm current Models 418/516 and any MDE guidance.
  35. Schools — vaporized bar, receipt on behalf of an under-21 patient. § 342.51, subd. 2(c) bars distribution/sale/delivery of vaporized-intended product “if the product is intended for a patient under 21.” Whether receipt by a parent/caregiver on the patient’s behalf is within the bar was not addressed in OCM interpretation located. [VERIFY.]
  36. Public-consumption fines. Marshall ($200), Chisago County / Lyon County / Roseau (up to $300) are local ordinance fines under § 152.0263, subd. 5. No statewide public-use fine is stated in this Part; the Run 1 caution against generalising $300 statewide is retained.
  37. Last-amended dates and session-law chapters. Except where a history line is quoted (e.g., § 624.7152, 2023 c. 63, art. 6, § 71; § 152.092 repeal, 2023 c. 52, art. 15, § 17; § 609A.06, 2023 c. 63, art. 5), last-amended dates and amending section numbers for individual sections were not confirmed from the live Revisor in this run and are therefore not asserted section by section. The coordinator should add them from the Revisor history lines if the house style requires them.
  38. Federal baseline not re-researched. Per the task, the federal baseline (Schedule III medical eff. 28 Apr 2026; PL 119-37/119-103 hemp dates; Hemani; ATF 22 Jan 2026 rule; 280E medical-only; no federal banking law) was taken as fixed. Any contradiction between that baseline and a secondary source encountered in this run (notably, a secondary page describing cannabis as still Schedule I in early 2026, which predates or ignores the 28 Apr 2026 medical move) was resolved in favour of the task baseline and is noted here, not treated as a Minnesota finding.
